size_dependence: Fixed group size of four; varies by composition (introvert/extravert mix and cue range), not by size.
note: Simulation output, not a fit to people: cue strengths chosen by the author and Antill's numbers not given. Replicated to two decimals by 046's Python re-implementation [simulated]. The table's fourth row (full range, published 0.17 0.21 0.28 0.34) was not replicated.

statement: Time share depends on relative cue strength and intensity on absolute cue strength (derived): a 4:1 cue ratio gives roughly a 3:1 time ratio, and scaling all cues by 4 changes intensity (80 to 320) but not shares
work: Derived in 046 from the CTA dynamics of Revelle 2008 draft and Revelle & Condon 2015 draft, doi:10.1016/j.jrp.2014.12.006
note: [derived] from max-rule on A plus cross-inhibition twenty times self-cost. A clean, falsifiable prediction for a rival-inhibition system, not a test against data.

statement: Exploratory group-size runs (single deterministic run per size): one extravert (cue 4.0) with N-1 introverts (cues 1.0-1.25) gives extravert time share 0.92, 0.83, 0.48, 0.41, 0.33 for N = 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, against fair share 1/N; balanced 2k-person mixes give an extravert multiple of fair share of about 1.5-1.7 at every size
work: Simulated in 046 from Revelle 2008 draft and Revelle & Condon 2015 draft, doi:10.1016/j.jrp.2014.12.006
size_dependence: Extravert multiple of fair share 1.8, 2.5, 1.9, 2.5, 2.6 for N = 2, 3, 4, 6, 8; introverts' multiple 0.17, 0.25, 0.70, 0.70, 0.77. No clear Antill-type size trend in the quick scan.
note: The file says this is not a result: one run per size, no noise, no tie-breaking sweep. A lead for D069 and D070.

statement: Antill (1974), a dissertation abstract cited in Revelle 2008 and Revelle & Condon 2015: an introversion-extraversion effect on conversational patterns, linked to group size in 2008 and to within-group range of introversion-extraversion in 2015; the data are not available
work: Antill 1974, Dissertation Abstracts International 35(1-B) (no DOI; not found, not read)
size_dependence: Revelle 2008 ties the effect to group size and says variations in group size do not reproduce it; Revelle & Condon 2015 ties it to composition (range of introversion-extraversion within the group). Unresolved.
note: Crossref finds nothing, as expected for a dissertation abstract. The reference string is confirmed in both Revelle papers. The content of the effect is unknown.

statement: Revelle 2015: "few researchers were interested in testing the implications of computer simulations with studies of human behavior"; Blankenship (1987) is the important exception
work: Revelle & Condon 2015 draft, doi:10.1016/j.jrp.2014.12.006 (author draft, not the published version)
note: Tagged [read]. The file's own absence claims (no meta-analysis, no direct test of the stream or switching rule) come from a search that was not repeated in validation, so they are sa.

statement: Simulation-as-argument studies, not tests: Birch 1972; Birch, Atkinson & Bongort 1974; Atkinson, Bongort & Price 1977 (low internal consistency of simulated TAT measures is expected even with correct classification); Reuman, Atkinson & Gallop 1986 (90 simulated individuals, three motives, nine behaviours)
work: Named as cited in Blankenship, Tumlinson & Sims 1995, doi:10.3758/BF03204740; not resolved individually (validation log)
note: Read second-hand from Blankenship et al. 1995. They use the model to argue about measurement and do not test it.

statement: Consummatory force: C = c·T (Revelle 2008, Eq. 2) versus C = c·BAR-T, printed 'C = c- BAR-T' (Blankenship, Tumlinson & Sims 1995)
work: Revelle 2008 draft (https://personality-project.org/revelle/publications/cta.pdf; no DOI); Blankenship, Tumlinson & Sims 1995, doi:10.3758/BF03204740; Atkinson & Birch 1970 (book not read)
note: Side A (Revelle): C = c·T, resultant asymptote F/c - I/r. Side B (Blankenship): C = c·(T - N) gives T → F/c + N and resultant → F/c independent of N. Verdict: unresolved without the 1970 book. Decides whether inhibition acts on the sign of the state or on its rate of discharge.

statement: Force of resistance: R = r·N (Revelle 2008, Eq. 5) versus R = r·min(T, N) (Blankenship et al. 1995, citing Atkinson & Birch 1970 p. 239)
work: Revelle 2008 draft (https://personality-project.org/revelle/publications/cta.pdf; no DOI); Blankenship, Tumlinson & Sims 1995, doi:10.3758/BF03204740
note: Verdict per file: the min form is better attested (it carries a page citation to the book); R = r·N is the simplification. Unresolved for the book. Changes the latency bound, not the delay-not-prevent result.

statement: Brown & Revelle (2021) is cited in the psych::cta docs (file 16 §6) versus not listed among the psych::cta 2.5.6 docs references (046 §0, §8)
work: Brown & Revelle 2021, doi:10.1016/B978-0-12-819200-9.00012-0 (content not read); psych::cta docs, https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/psych/versions/2.5.6/topics/cta
note: Verdict: 046 is right, 16 is wrong on the attribution. The DOI is fine in both. Checked against the psych 2.5.6 docs: references are Atkinson & Birch 1970, Revelle 1986, Revelle 2008, Revelle & Condon 2015 only.

statement: Antill and the four-person model: Revelle 2008 says simple variations of group size keeping cue range constant do not reproduce the effect; Revelle & Condon 2015 says extraverts dominate when groups differ in introversion-extraversion range, citing Antill (1974) as supporting data
work: Revelle 2008 draft (https://personality-project.org/revelle/publications/cta.pdf; no DOI); Revelle & Condon 2015 draft, doi:10.1016/j.jrp.2014.12.006
size_dependence: Negative on group size (2008); positive on within-group range of introversion-extraversion (2015).
note: Verdict: both right about their own source. File 16's 'the one test of it failed' is stale and incomplete: the 2008 negative was group size, the 2015 claim is composition. Neither is a test against data.

statement: Selection: CTA's dynamics have no max rule, selection emerging from mutual inhibition (file 16 §6), versus the reported action being which.max(act) in Revelle's appendix code (046 §3.2c)
work: Revelle 2008 draft, appendix code (lines ~773, 787) (https://personality-project.org/revelle/publications/cta.pdf; no DOI)
note: Verdict: a scope difference, not a factual clash. True of the dynamics; the reported behaviour applies the max rule to the output. 046 is right.

statement: Printed CTA asymptotes, Revelle 2008 Eqs 12-13 (T∞ = s·C·i/c, A∞ = e·C/c) versus the corrected forms A∞ = s·C/c and T∞ = i·s·C/(e·c)
work: Revelle 2008 draft, Eqs 12-13 (https://personality-project.org/revelle/publications/cta.pdf; no DOI); Revelle & Condon 2015 draft, doi:10.1016/j.jrp.2014.12.006
note: Verdict: printed forms wrong unless s = e = 1. The corrected forms are derived and simulated (see the corrected CTA asymptotes line). Settled in favour of the correction by both.

statement: Revelle 2008 draft's reference list prints Kuhl & Blankenship (1979) as Psych. Rev. 85, 239-248, versus Crossref vol. 86(2), 141-151, doi:10.1037/0033-295x.86.2.141
work: Kuhl & Blankenship 1979, doi:10.1037/0033-295x.86.2.141; Revelle 2008 draft (https://personality-project.org/revelle/publications/cta.pdf; no DOI)
note: Verdict: Crossref is right and the draft is misprinted. No other file cites Kuhl & Blankenship, so no conflict in the ledger; recorded so later files are not seeded with the misprint.

statement: Persistence: Blankenship 1992 supports differential persistence of low-resultant-motivation subjects, contrary to Atkinson 1957's persistence prediction
work: Blankenship 1992, doi:10.1007/BF00996486 (not read); Atkinson 1957, doi:10.1037/h0043445 (not read)
note: Both sides second-hand. The file gives no verdict and the simulations could not model all of the experimental results. Unresolved.

statement: Homeostatic drive: state is a vector H of N regulated variables with setpoint H*; drive D(H_t) is a norm of the deficit from setpoint; the operand is the internal state, the operator an additive outcome vector K (H_{t+1} = H_t + K_t)
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, doi 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: Their vocabulary: homeostatic space, H*, D(H_t), K_t, SDD and SDR. Also 19 §12 states the same. The file's operand/operator reading is its own translation, not a separate published definition.

statement: Cognitive and social setpoints: the drive is extended to non-physiological goals (financial stability, moral worth, physical health, social status, social capital) with no inter-agent term
work: Juechems & Summerfield 2019, doi 10.1016/j.tics.2019.07.012
note: Asserted, not derived or tested. The social dimensions are one-sentence examples. Opinion piece.

statement: Affective-empathy coupled drive D = D_possessor + w·D_partner, with w = 0.5 in the food-sharing task
work: Yoshida & Man 2024, arXiv 2412.12103
note: Cognitive empathy is only observing the partner's state. Drives in Exp 1 are -ln P*(s); grid and 2-D environments use ||s||^2. No theorem in the paper.

statement: Surprise-form drive D = -ln P*(s), with P*(High)=0.95 and P*(Low)=0.05, giving D(High) ~ 0.051 and D(Low) ~ 3.0 in Yoshida & Man Experiment 1
work: Yoshida & Man 2024, arXiv 2412.12103
note: Drive has no zero in Exp 1 (D(High) is not 0), so any theorem needing D(H*) = 0 does not apply to that setup without terminal correction or infinite-horizon form.

statement: Priors act as drives or goals to enslave action; drive is described verbally as the interoceptive prediction error reporting a discrepancy from the optimal level; no drive function is stated
work: Pezzulo, Rigoli & Friston 2015, doi 10.1016/j.pneurobio.2015.09.001
note: Text only from PMC. Equations did not survive extraction, so no stated drive function is unconfirmed rather than absent. Validation corrected the file: this paper does NOT cite Keramati & Gutkin; its Keramati 2011 reference is Keramati, Dezfouli & Piray 2011 (PLoS Comput Biol 7:e1002055), on habitual vs goal-directed control.

statement: Active-inference drive as negative log prior preference: drive equals surprise, p(H_t) proportional to exp(-D(H_t)), so -ln p = D up to a constant
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, doi 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: K&G's own mapping (Eq 14 and Relationship section). Validation: the paper writes proportionality then equality; -ln p = D holds only up to the normaliser ln Z, so the equality is a derived correction.

statement: D(H_t) = (sum over i=1..N of |h*_i - h_{i,t}|^n)^(1/m), with m and n free parameters; in one dimension D = |h* - h|^(n/m); Euclidean at m = n = 2
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, doi 10.7554/eLife.04811
size_dependence: Number of regulated variables N enters the sum; no size threshold stated.
note: Eq 1, from MathML so exponents are exact (m-th root applies to the sum). The 2011 paper gives the same form. Validation confirmed. Fig 6 simulations use n = 4 (supplement caption); m used there was not extracted.

statement: Reward is drive reduction: r(H_t, K_t) = D(H_t) - D(H_t + K_t)
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, doi 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: Eq 2. Also 062 §1 and §3 and 19 §12 state it.

statement: Anticipatory reward from sensory estimate: r(H_t, K-hat_t) = D(H_t) - D(H_t + K-hat_t), where K-hat is the sensory estimate of the outcome effect, so reward is available before digestion
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, doi 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: Eq 10.

statement: Palatability-augmented reward: r = D(H_t) - D(H_t + K_t) + T, with T > 0 a drive-independent palatability term; for the quadratic case T is equivalent to moving the setpoint to H* + T/(2K_t)
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, doi 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: Eq 11 and S6. The file's own check (x^2 - (x+K)^2 + T = -2K(x - T/(2K)) - K^2) agrees. The paper's label 'm/n = 1' for the quadratic case looks garbled: the quadratic case needs n/m = 2 since D = |x|^(n/m).

statement: First-order form: r = dD(H_t+K_t)/dK_t (eq 12) and r approximately -K_t . grad D(H_t) + O(grad^2 D) (eq 13); the linear form reproduces older deprivation-times-magnitude reward models; the nonlinear form predicts an inverted-U utility in outcome size because overshooting the setpoint makes reward fall and then go negative
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, doi 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: Inverted-U is shown in Fig 11. The linear models named are decision field theory (Singh et al. 2010) and MOTIVATOR.

statement: Eq 14: p(H_t) proportional to exp(-D(H_t)) = exp(-(sum |h*_i - h_{i,t}|^n)^(1/m))
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, doi 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: Drive as surprise. Gaussian only when D is quadratic (m = 1, n = 2). Gaussian prior with precision matrix Pi gives D = 1/2 (o-o*)^T Pi (o-o*).

statement: Printed behavioural properties, condition n > m > 1: d r/d k_j > 0 (eq 6, reward rises with dose); d r/d|h*_j - h_j| > 0 (eq 7, deprivation potentiates reward); d^2 r/d k_j^2 < 0 (eq 9, concavity, hence risk aversion); eq 8 printed as d r/d|h*_i - h_i| > 0 for i != j (inhibition by irrelevant drives)
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, doi 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: Eq 8 as printed has the wrong sign (see contradictions). The n > m > 1 condition is not proved in the paper; it is presented as properties of the form.

statement: Derived: eqs 6, 7 and 9 hold for every tested (n,m) with n/m > 1 or m > 1, provided k is small enough not to overshoot the deficit
work: Derived in 047 from Keramati & Gutkin 2014, doi 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: [derived/numeric] own check in 2-D with deficits x_j = -5, x_i = -3, k = 1, over (n,m) in {(4,2),(3,2),(2,2),(2,1),(4,3),(1.5,1.2),(1,1)}. Not a published result. Validation recomputed the Eq 8 numerics.

statement: Derived: cross-drive inhibition condition: d r/ds = (1/m)[(s+a^n)^(1/m-1) - (s+a'^n)^(1/m-1)] < 0 exactly when m > 1 and a > a', so the condition is m > 1, not n > m > 1; at m = 1 the drive is additively separable and drives do not interact
work: Derived in 047 from Keramati & Gutkin 2014, doi 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: s = sum over i != j of |dev_i|^n; a, a' are deficits in dimension j before and after the outcome. Numerics: -0.909 at (n,m) = (4,2), -0.289 at (4,3), 0 at m = 1. Concavity of one-dimensional reward needs n/m > 1. Validation re-derived analytically and confirmed.

statement: 2011 Eq 8: Q_1(s,a) = [d(H_1)/d(H_0)] . Q_0(s,a), the energising update after a motivational shift
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2011, NeurIPS 24 (no DOI found)
note: Main text read from the proceedings PDF. Page range pp. 82-90 is unconfirmed (see contradictions).

statement: Proposition 2 (2011): the Eq 8 energising update is exact only when H_1 = c . H_0 with c >= 0
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2011, NeurIPS 24 (no DOI found)
note: Stated in the supplement, which the file says was NOT accessed. Validation log marks the condition as confirmed; the original file did not read it. Keep sa unless the supplement is opened.

statement: 2011 Eq 9: V(S_C, k_X) = [d(x*) - d(x*+k_X)] + gamma[d(x*+k_X) - d(x*+k_X-l_X)] + gamma^2[d(x*+k_X-l_X) - d(x*)], the anticipatory-shivering example
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2011, NeurIPS 24 (no DOI found)
note: Main text read. Eq 9 is the example; the optimum claim is Proposition 3 below.

statement: Proposition 3 (2011): the optimum is k_X = l_X/2 when gamma is not 1 but sufficiently close to 1
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2011, NeurIPS 24 (no DOI found)
note: Supplement not accessed. Validation confirmed the statement as printed.

statement: Derived: for a quadratic drive, d V/dk = 0 gives k = gamma . l/(1 + gamma), which tends to l/2 only as gamma tends to 1; for an L1 drive (n = m = 1) V is piecewise linear and the interior optimum disappears
work: Derived in 047 from Keramati & Gutkin 2011, NeurIPS 24 (no DOI found)
note: So the l/2 result needs both a convex drive and gamma near 1. Validation re-derived k = gamma l/(1+gamma).

statement: Discounted telescoping theorem (S3): for any H_0, if gamma < 1, argmin over p in P(H_0) of SD_D equals argmax over p in P(H_0) of SD_R, where SD_D = sum_t gamma^t D(H_{t+1}) and SD_R = sum_t gamma^t [D(H_t) - D(H_{t+1})]
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, doi 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: eLife Methods, 'Rationality of the theory' (S1-S3). The continuous Eqs 3-5 in the main text are loosely typeset; the discrete Methods version is the one to cite (validation corrected an earlier reading).

statement: Telescoping identity: along a trajectory with D_w = 0, SD_R = D_0 + (gamma - 1) . SD_D
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, doi 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: The file's check: the telescoping in S5 is correct. It is Abel summation, an identity and not an optimality result about behaviour. The theorem uses no property of D except D(H*) = 0. It says nothing about which D is used.

statement: Derived: terminal state free: SD_R = D_0 + (gamma - 1) . SD_D - gamma^w . D_w for any trajectory of length w ending in H_w
work: Derived in 047 from Keramati & Gutkin 2014, doi 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: Checked at w = 1. With D_w = 0 the arg-orderings coincide exactly when trajectories differ in length.

statement: Derived: infinite horizon, bounded D, gamma < 1: SD_R^inf = D_0 + (gamma - 1) . SD_D^inf, so policy orderings by discounted reward and by discounted drive coincide for every start state, with no requirement that the setpoint be reachable
work: Derived in 047 from Keramati & Gutkin 2014, doi 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: The paper's finite-trajectory restriction P(H_0) is stronger than needed. Also for gamma = 1, SD_R = D_0 - D_w depends only on endpoints; gamma > 1 reverses the ordering.

statement: Derived: the identity is linear in D, so it holds in expectation for stochastic transitions, E[SD_R] = D_0 + (gamma - 1) . E[SD_D]; shifting D by a constant (D' = D + c) leaves the trajectory ranking unchanged
work: Derived in 047 from Keramati & Gutkin 2014, doi 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: Items (c) and (e) of the file's generalisations list.

statement: Yoshida & Man reward per agent: r_{t+1} = beta (D_t - D_{t+1})
work: Yoshida & Man 2024, arXiv 2412.12103
note: Appendix B.2 calls beta 'a learning rate', but in the reward equation it is a scaling constant. Validation recorded this wording fix.

statement: Derived: coupled drive D_c = D_s + w . D_p with fixed w gives reward r_c = r_s + w . r_p exactly, and the telescoping identity extends verbatim: SD_R^c = D_c(x_0) + (gamma - 1) . SD_D^c - gamma^w D_c(x_w)
work: Derived in 047 from Yoshida & Man 2024, arXiv 2412.12103
note: Conditions: w is a constant parameter; the same D_c is used at both ends of every step. The file's own check, not a published theorem. No theorem exists for coupled drives as far as read.

statement: Derived: if the weight w_t varies in time, the identity acquires the correction sum over t >= 1 of gamma^(t-1) (w_t - w_{t-1}) D_{p,t}; a state-dependent weight (relationship strength, trust) therefore breaks the theorem unless the correction is carried
work: Derived in 047 from Yoshida & Man 2024, arXiv 2412.12103
note: File's recommendation: w should be a parameter of an operator, not a state variable, unless the correction term is carried.

statement: Derived: for w >= 0 the setpoint form has a joint minimum of 0 at the joint setpoint; for w < 0 (rivalry, schadenfreude) D_c is minimised at the spiteful corner of the state space, so the finite-trajectory form is not meaningful while the infinite-horizon form still is
work: Derived in 047 from Yoshida & Man 2024, arXiv 2412.12103
note: Resource-conserving settings (single food item) can make the joint setpoint unreachable, so the finite proposition is vacuous there.

statement: Derived: two agents with D^1 = D_a + w_1 D_b and D^2 = D_b + w_2 D_a have the same ordering over joint trajectories iff w_1 . w_2 = 1 and w_2 > 0; w_1 = w_2 = 1 is the team case; w_1 = w_2 = -1 gives exactly opposite orderings (zero-sum)
work: Derived in 047 from Yoshida & Man 2024, arXiv 2412.12103
note: Validation fixed the sign condition: 'iff w_1 . w_2 = 1' alone was incomplete. For w_1 . w_2 < 1 the agents agree only partly and the problem is a game, so the single-agent argmin/argmax equivalence says nothing about equilibria.

statement: Derived: N agents with weight matrix W (W_ii = 1): D^i = sum_j W_ij D_j and r^i = sum_j W_ij rho_j, where rho_j = D_j(t) - D_j(t+1); the identity becomes SD_R^i = sum_j W_ij [D_{j,0} + (gamma - 1) SD_{D_j}] (terminal terms aside)
work: Derived in 047 from Yoshida & Man 2024, arXiv 2412.12103
size_dependence: Grows with the number of agents through the N x N matrix W; no threshold is stated.
note: The file calls this the nearest published-compatible object to an operator on drives. Derived, not published.

statement: Derived design suggestion: if each agent internalises partners' coupled drives (contagion), the effective matrix is the Neumann series (I - Omega)^(-1), convergent when the spectral radius of Omega is below 1
work: Derived in 047 from Yoshida & Man 2024, arXiv 2412.12103
note: File says explicitly: a design suggestion, not a published result. Omega holds the off-diagonal weights.

statement: Derived: additive coupling D_s + w . D_p is a sum of norms, so d r_self / d(partner deficit) = 0 exactly: own-need relief is equally rewarding when the partner is starving
work: Derived in 047 from Yoshida & Man 2024, arXiv 2412.12103
note: [derived/numeric]. Limitation of the additive form, not a finding about behaviour.

statement: Derived: a joint Minkowski aggregation (sum |.|^n)^(1/m) with m > 1 over own and partner deficits makes partner deficit lower the reward value of own relief, giving 'you do not enjoy your meal while your child starves' as a consequence
work: Derived in 047 from Keramati & Gutkin 2014, doi 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: Candidate alternative model with one new exponent. Not a published model; the file says it is a candidate to test against.

statement: Derived: Yoshida-Man's surprise form turns the coupling into a tempered product of preferences: exp(-D_c) = P*(s_s) . P*(s_p)^w, with w an exponent on the partner's preference density
work: Derived in 047 from Yoshida & Man 2024, arXiv 2412.12103
note: Links the coupling to the active-inference reading in §6.

statement: Juechems & Summerfield Eq 1: theta_t = X_t x U + theta_{t-1} x A_theta, the internal state driven by chosen option features X through a learned map U, plus intrinsic dynamics A_theta (decay without input)
work: Juechems & Summerfield 2019, doi 10.1016/j.tics.2019.07.012
note: Box 2 Eq 1. Read from the author-accepted ORA manuscript.

statement: Juechems & Summerfield Eq 2: delta_{t+1} = ||theta_{t+1} - theta*||_k, printed as the p-th root of sum |theta_{t+1} - theta*|^q with p = q (one exponent k)
work: Juechems & Summerfield 2019, doi 10.1016/j.tics.2019.07.012
size_dependence: Exponent k controls bundle preference: k < 1 favours single-asset bundles, k = 1 is indifferent, k > 1 favours mixed bundles.
note: Box 2 says p != q (two parameters, as in K&G m and n) is needed for diminishing marginal utility. The main text instead attributes diminishing marginal utility to other unsatisfiable drives. Internal inconsistency in J&S; the text also says agents minimise the maximum distance (L-infinity), which matches Eq 2 only as k tends to infinity.

statement: Juechems & Summerfield Eq 3: R_{t+1} = delta_t - delta_{t+1}, which is K&G's drive reduction; with A_theta = 0 and k = 1, R = X x U
work: Juechems & Summerfield 2019, doi 10.1016/j.tics.2019.07.012
note: Corrected form: J&S invoke no theorem and do not use the K&G SDR/SDD equivalence. Their sentence 'mathematically identical to reward' is about one dimension, where the drop in distance equals the volume of liquid given (citing K&G 2014); they add it breaks down as theta tends to theta*.

statement: Expected free energy (Smith, Friston & Whyte 2022, Eq 13): G_pi = D_KL[ q(o|pi) || p(o|C) ] + E_{q(s|pi)}[ H[p(o|s)] ], risk plus ambiguity
work: Smith, Friston & Whyte 2022, doi 10.1016/j.jmp.2021.102632
note: No variable labelled reward: preferences are encoded within a prior distribution. Validation confirmed Eq 13 and that the EFE sum has no temporal discount.

statement: Derived: substituting p(o|C) proportional to exp(-D(o)) into the risk term gives, per time step, expected drive minus outcome entropy plus ambiguity, plus a constant; the policy score sums these over the horizon undiscounted
work: Derived in 047 from Smith, Friston & Whyte 2022, doi 10.1016/j.jmp.2021.102632 and Keramati & Gutkin 2014, doi 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: KL[q||p(o|C)] = -H[q] + E_q[D(o)] + ln Z.

statement: Derived: for gamma < 1, K&G's theorem makes ranking by discounted potential-difference reward the reverse of ranking by discounted state cost D, which equals (up to an affine map) active inference's discounted risk objective; the two differ by the entropy and ambiguity terms and the discounting
work: Derived in 047 from Keramati & Gutkin 2014, doi 10.7554/eLife.04811 and Smith, Friston & Whyte 2022, doi 10.1016/j.jmp.2021.102632

statement: Free energy F is an upper bound on surprise: F >= -ln p(s-tilde | m); organisms act to keep sensory states within expected (preferred) bounds
work: Friston 2010, doi 10.1038/nrn2787
note: From abstract and standard account only; not read at source. Metadata confirmed in validation, content not.

statement: Homeostatic trajectory p = {K_0, K_1, ...} from H_0; P(H_0) is the set of such trajectories that, started at H_0, end at H*

statement: Reward is defined as drop in drive: r_t = D(H_t) - D(H_{t+1}), with H_{t+1} = H_t + K_t
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, doi 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: What the theorem actually fixes is this choice r = delta D, not the algebra after it (file §2, 'What the theorem actually is').

statement: Operand and operator for the algebra (the file's own translation): operand is an agent's state vector with a setpoint as fixed attribute; operator is an additive outcome vector K; drive is a norm of the deficit; reward is the drop in that norm; all interaction between drives sits in the exponent m

statement: Motivation dynamics (Eq. 7): m_i' = v~_i m_U - m_i ( 1/v~_i - v~_i m_U + sigma_i (1 - m_i - m_U) ), with v~_i = v*_i v_i, v*_i > 0 a gain, sigma_i > 0 the stop-signal strength
work: Seeley et al. 2012, Science 335, 108-111, DOI 10.1126/science.1210361; analysed in Pais et al. 2013, PLoS ONE, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0073216; Reverdy & Koditschek arXiv:1703.01662v2

statement: v_i' = lambda_i ( phi_i(x) - v_i ) (Eq. 8): urgency rises with distance from goal and relaxes toward it with timescale 1/lambda

statement: Two-task symmetric instance (Eq. 9, N=2, goals (1,0) and (-1,0)): x' = -m_1(x - x*_1) - m_2(x - x*_2); m_1' = (v* v_1) m_U - m_1 (1/(v* v_1) - (v* v_1) m_U + sigma m_2); m_2' symmetric; v_i' = lambda(phi_i - v_i); the system has S_2 symmetry when the two values are equal

statement: Theorem 2: as epsilon_lambda = 1/lambda -> 0, the reduced system (18) has a deadlock equilibrium; for sigma > 6 the dynamics undergo a supercritical Hopf bifurcation giving stable periodic solutions at (deadlock equilibrium, epsilon_v,0), where epsilon_v,0 is the root in [0, 1/2] of 4(2 - sigma) eps^2 - 4(2 - sigma) eps + (6 - sigma) = 0; for sigma = 8, epsilon_v,0 = (3 - sqrt 6)/6, about 0.09175
work: Reverdy & Koditschek, arXiv:1703.01662v2 (no DOI in file); journal successor Reverdy, Vasilopoulos & Koditschek, IEEE T-RO 37(4) 1239-1251, DOI 10.1109/TRO.2020.3043720 (not read)
size_dependence: Bifurcation occurs as epsilon_v falls through epsilon_v,0, i.e. as the gain v* rises.
note: CORRECTED form, per validation log: earlier version had lambda -> 0 and (2 - sigma)^2 eps^2, both extraction artefacts. At sigma = 8 the corrected equation is -24 eps^2 + 24 eps - 2 = 0; the earlier form gives about 0.061, not 0.09175. Proof uses the standard Hopf theorem (Lemma 6 simple pure-imaginary pair; Lemma 7 d Re(lambda)/d eps < 0; Lemma 8 first Lyapunov coefficient negative).

statement: Conjecture 20 (stated by the authors): the periodic orbit of the reduced planar problem is hyperbolic, with Floquet multipliers 1 and rho_2 < 1
work: Reverdy & Koditschek, arXiv:1703.01662v2 (no DOI in file)
size_dependence: Stated only for sigma = 8; authors say numerics suggest it holds for generic sigma > 6.

statement: Theorem 3 (conditional on Conjecture 20): for sigma > 6 there exists a stable limit cycle of (11) for sufficiently small but finite epsilon_lambda and epsilon_v; equivalently, at fixed lambda, for sufficiently large but finite v*
work: Reverdy & Koditschek, arXiv:1703.01662v2 (no DOI in file)

statement: Pais et al. Eq. 1 (deterministic part): dy_A = ( y_U gamma_A - y_A (alpha_A - y_U rho_A + y_B sigma_B) ) dt + noise, symmetric for y_B, with y_U = 1 - y_A - y_B

note: Uses the circle's structure, which the pooled-matrix MDS supports (see Schwartz & Cieciuch line, with the validation-log correction).

statement: Default composition is additive across needs, with prepotency as an optional gate whose weight is an editable setting.
note: Based on Tay & Diener's separability finding (abstract only), read as support for a parallel-drive algebra rather than a hierarchy.

statement: Families of drives are merged into one operand with sub-parameters where measurement does not separate members: [belonging, care, kin], [status, power, achievement], [threat: fear, self-protection, disease], [seeking, curiosity, autonomy], [mating]; the merge is a modelling judgement, not a claim about true primitives.
work: none; derived from the 050 concordance table and pair-level measurement (Pedersen 2014; Billet 2023)
note: Pattern 1 of 050 §3: no primitive scores M at the drive level in the strict sense; the M ratings sit on SDT needs and Schwartz values, the least drive-like lists.

statement: Scoring rule for the concordance: M = recovered by a measurement procedure that did not presuppose it, in a sample other than the proposer's; P = partial (reliability, outcome validity or home-lab structure only); - = no measurement evidence found.
work: none (method of 050)
note: Replaces a count of theories ('recurs across theories', file 15) with a test. Under this rule SDT and Schwartz samples get M only for samples, not labs, because the proposers co-author the studies.

statement: Chen et al. 2015: need satisfaction predicts well-being and need frustration predicts ill-being, equivalently across Belgium, China, USA and Peru (study 1 N = 685 in Belgium and China; study 2 N = 1,051 in four countries); the adapted scale shows measurement equivalence across groups.
source: 050 §2.3; validation log entry for Chen et al.
work: Chen, B., Vansteenkiste, M., Beyers, W., et al. (2015). Motivation and Emotion 39(2), 216-236, doi 10.1007/s11031-014-9450-1
size_dependence: Study sizes given per study (N = 685; N = 1,051); no effect sizes recorded in 050.
note: Abstract only. Tests outcomes, which is circular for SDT (a need is what thwarted, harms well-being). Corrected in the validation log: 'partly independent' withdrawn, since Deci and Ryan are co-authors. Fit indices not checked in full text.

statement: ANPS six-factor CFA in a clinical sample (N = 546 personality-disorder patients): poor to mediocre fit (chi-square 7828.18, df 3387, RMSEA 0.049, CFI 0.759, TLI 0.752, WRMR 2.112); subscale internal consistency 0.74 to 0.87.
work: Pedersen, G., Selsbakk, J. M., Wilberg, T., & Karterud, S. (2014). PLoS ONE 9(10), e109394, doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0109394
size_dependence: Clinical sample, 77% female, mean age 32; the shorter ANPS-S and BANPS fit better (BANPS CFI .933, TLI .924, RMSEA .053; ANPS-S CFI .863, TLI .851, RMSEA .063).
note: One study, one clinical sample; no out-of-sample prediction. Author attribution corrected in validation log from 'Pedersen, W. S.' to Pedersen, G. et al. CFA and Table 8 numbers confirmed in article XML.

statement: ANPS inter-scale Pearson correlations (Table 3), one clinical sample: FEAR-SADNESS .59 and PLAY-SEEK .50 (abstract: too highly correlated); PLAY-CARE .39, CARE-SADNESS .36, SEEK-CARE .24, ANGER-SADNESS .25, FEAR-ANGER .22, SEEK-ANGER .14, CARE-FEAR .16, PLAY-FEAR -.22, SEEK-FEAR -.28, SEEK-SADNESS -.07, PLAY-SADNESS -.06, CARE-ANGER -.03, PLAY-ANGER .01.
work: Pedersen et al. 2014 doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0109394
size_dependence: Single clinical sample; the file says it is not general.
note: The questionnaire route fails to separate FEAR from SADNESS and PLAY from SEEKING in these data. Does not refute the systems as brain systems. Could seed a prior correlation for the five Panksepp-derived drives (050 §4), only for this sample.

statement: Meta-analysis of 21 samples (612 effect sizes): pooled r SEEKING-Openness .47, SEEKING-Extraversion .34, PLAY-Extraversion .55, CARE-Agreeableness .40, ANGER-Agreeableness -.41, ANGER-Neuroticism .46, FEAR-Neuroticism .69, SADNESS-Neuroticism .62; Conscientiousness in the lower effect-size range for all six systems.
work: Marengo, D., Davis, K. L., Gradwohl, G. Ö., & Montag, C. (2021). Scientific Reports 11, 7453, doi 10.1038/s41598-021-84366-8
note: Correlational bridge between Panksepp-style scales and Big Five coordinates. Not an out-of-sample prediction. Full text read via Europe PMC.

statement: FSMI reliability: 11-subscale, 65-item instrument with alphas .77 to .94; prioritising information about a motive correlates with one's own score on it, mean r .25 and .26 across two measures, and .15 and .05 for mate retention.
work: Billet, M. I., McCall, H. C., & Schaller, M. (2023). Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 49(4), 495-509, doi 10.1177/01461672211069468
note: Reliability and a correlational check only. Billet et al. do not test factor structure, so no independent CFA is shown from this source. Scale n/a: the file assigns none, and the study is about information prioritised when meeting another person.

statement: FSMI dataset descriptor (42 countries, N = 15,915, two waves) reports no confirmatory factor analysis, no invariance test and no alphas; the Technical Validation section says only that the scale has established reliability and validity, citing Neel et al. 2016.
work: Pick, C. M., Ko, A., Kenrick, D. T., et al. (2022). Scientific Data 9, 499, doi 10.1038/s41597-022-01579-w
size_dependence: Country and wave counts (wave 1 N = 8,998 in 32 countries; wave 2 N = 6,917 in 29 countries; 19 in both, N = 10,907) are from the dataset abstract, not full text.
note: Structural claim not tested in the dataset paper. 'Not found' for an independent CFA is a search result, not a shown absence (050 §5).

statement: Schwartz PVQ-RR across 49 cultural groups (N = 53,472, 32 language versions): 15 of 19 values reliably measured in the vast majority of groups, two more in most; configural and metric invariance almost always; scalar invariance not expected by the authors; pooled-matrix MDS reproduces the circular order with no reversals.
size_dependence: Measured across 49 cultural groups; file gives no size dependence.
note: Corrected form (validation log): the circle is NOT reproduced in every group. The MDS is on the pooled correlation matrix, and each group's projection is Procrustes-rotated toward the theorised target, so per-group order is assessed against an imposed target. Four of 19 values not reliably measured in most groups (two of those reliable in most). Authors are the instrument's proposers.

statement: MFQ-2 developed on 25 populations (Study 1 N = 3,360; Study 2 N = 3,902; Study 3 N = 1,410), six foundations; the authors claim it fares well across contexts.
work: Atari, M., Haidt, J., Graham, J., Koleva, S., Stevens, S. T., & Dehghani, M. (2023). JPSP 125(5), 1157-1188, doi 10.1037/pspp0000470
note: Abstract only; fit statistics not quoted in 050 and not checked. Proposers' own group, so independence limited. Invariance numbers listed under Unconfirmed in 050.

statement: Iran moral foundations: six studies (N = 1,945) test Persian MFQ structural validity and a US-Iran comparison, and add an Iran-specific foundation ('Qeirat').
work: Atari, M., Graham, J., & Dehghani, M. (2020). Evolution and Human Behavior 41(5), 367-384, doi 10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2020.07.014
note: Abstract only. A 'scalar non-invariance between US and Iran' detail appears only in a search summary and is not in the abstract; unverified. Atari and Graham are MFT authors, so not independent.

statement: Five-factor MFQ failed to converge across populations: 'it is difficult to specify Moral Foundations Questionnaire items in a quantitative five-factor model that will converge nonproblematically across a wide variety of populations' (27 countries).
size_dependence: Across 27 countries; no size dependence recorded.
note: Abstract quotation, restated in the abstract's own words in the validation log. Independent critique.

statement: Dutch-translated MFQ20 in an online student sample (N = 1,496): five-factor model failed to converge (Fairness and Purity too highly correlated); three-factor retained at CFI/TLI .720/.680, RMSEA .081; Sacredness Scale five-factor fit better (CFI/TLI .940/.930, RMSEA .06).
work: De Buck, M., & Pauwels, L. (2023). Psychologica Belgica 63(1), 92-104, doi 10.5334/pb.1188
size_dependence: One convenience student sample (authors at Ghent University), translation-specific.
note: Fit numbers confirmed in full text (validation log). Independent critique.

statement: Tay & Diener 2011: need fulfilment is associated with subjective well-being across world regions in 123 countries, and these associations are largely independent of whether other needs are fulfilled.
size_dependence: 123 countries; no effect sizes recorded in 050.
note: Abstract only. Supports separability and additivity; argues against strict prepotency, per 050 §2.7. Survey used is unconfirmed (see contradiction on Gallup World Poll).

statement: Reiss & Havercamp 1998 factor study: EFA and CFA across 7 studies (N = 2,548) yield a 15-factor solution.
work: Reiss, S., & Havercamp, S. M. (1998). Psychological Assessment 10(2), 97-106, doi 10.1037/1040-3590.10.2.97
note: Corrected in validation log: the earlier 'yielding 16' description is not the 1998 result; 15 factors. Abstract only.

statement: No independent confirmatory factor analysis of the FSMI seven-factor structure, no independent replication of the Reiss 16-factor structure, and no study administering FSMI, SDT, ANPS and Schwartz lists jointly to the same people was found.
source: 050 §5 (Does not exist, or was not found)
work: none; a negative search result across the works in 050
note: Recorded as 'not found', not 'shown absent': the search budget ran out, so these were not re-tested in the validation pass. The joint-sample study is the empirical gap that would settle the minimal set.

statement: Tay & Diener 2011 survey: file 36 states the Gallup World Poll, tagged 'standard account, not verified', while 050 §2.7 says the survey could not be confirmed and calls the Gallup attribution commonly reported.
note: Side 1: file 36, Gallup World Poll, not verified. Side 2: 050 §2.7, survey unconfirmed (Gallup commonly reported). Both unverified, so not strictly contradictory. Verdict: unresolved. File 36's note should not be read as confirmation.

statement: Doğruyol, Alper & Yilmaz 2019: file 15 says the five-factor MFT structure is stable across WEIRD and non-WEIRD samples but with metric non-invariance (from search snippets); 050 gives only the title, which claims stability, and says the result was not read.
work: Doğruyol, B., Alper, S., & Yilmaz, O. (2019). Personality and Individual Differences 151, 109547, doi 10.1016/j.paid.2019.109547
note: Neither file has read the abstract. The two files do not conflict on fact, but the metric non-invariance qualifier sits oddly beside the title's stability claim. Verdict: unresolved.

statement: Reiss desire count: file 15 §6 says 16 basic desires (Reiss 2004); 050 §2.2 says the 1998 factor study reports 15 factors and that the 16-factor claim was corrected; file 19 mentions up to 23 Reiss needs.
source: 050 Cross-checks, Contradictions 4; 050 §2.2, validation log; file 19 (NPC table)
note: Verdict in 050: no contradiction between the two papers' own figures, since 2004 added a desire (16 in 2004, 15 in 1998). The 23 in file 19 is unresolved and must not be used. The validation log counts the 16-from-1998 claim as a material error, corrected to 15.

statement: Panksepp count: 050 §1 says 7 systems, 6 in the ANPS (LUST omitted); file 15 says seven systems with no ANPS count.
work: Davis & Montag 2019 doi 10.3389/fnins.2018.01025; Panksepp 1998
note: Verdict in 050: consistent, but file 15 does not support the 6-in-ANPS detail, which rests on 050 alone (Pedersen 2014 is the source for the ANPS scale itself).

statement: Fear of death, called terror or anxiety, is the one drive TMT supplies; it is the death-fear input the operand would carry.
work: Pyszczynski, Solomon & Greenberg 2015, Adv. Exp. Soc. Psychol. 52, 1-70, DOI 10.1016/bs.aesp.2015.03.001
note: Chapter not read; stated from its abstract via a search summary. File says no source gives dynamics for this input.

statement: Two anxiety buffers: (1) faith in the absolute validity of a cultural worldview (W), and (2) self-esteem earned by living up to that worldview's standards of value.
work: Pyszczynski, Solomon & Greenberg 2015, Adv. Exp. Soc. Psychol. 52, 1-70, DOI 10.1016/bs.aesp.2015.03.001
size_dependence: Buffer strength (self-esteem) is listed as a secondary moderator (§8).
note: Same chapter, abstract only. Buffer pair is the operand structure proposed in §8 (W_i and a buffer pair).

statement: Fear as an input to affiliation: fear (anticipated threat) raises affiliation, independent of the mortality-salience route.
work: Schachter 1959, The Psychology of Affiliation, Stanford UP (no DOI in file); Gump & Kulik 1997, DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.72.2.305; Taylor et al. 2000, DOI 10.1037/0033-295X.107.3.411
size_dependence: Schachter studies are small-sample; sign moderated by similarity, sex and utility (see contradiction on sign).
note: None of the three works was read in this file; Schachter is 'recalled' per 42 and unconfirmed per 49. Treated as the affiliation route, not TMT.

statement: Uncertainty (uncertainty about an afterlife) is a drive-like state that can take the place of death-fear as the input to identification.
work: Hohman & Hogg 2011, Eur. J. Soc. Psychol. 41(6), 751-760, DOI 10.1002/ejsp.818
size_dependence: Effect present only among people uncertain about an afterlife.
note: Abstract read, not the paper. File says this reframes the operator input from fear to uncertainty; competing account of MS-style results, itself priming-based.

statement: Fear as an appraisal-tendency input to risk judgement (the emotion-to-risk operator, distinct from TMT).
note: Standard account / search summary; Crossref gave no abstract. File says this belongs to a different operator, emotion -> risk judgement.

statement: Mortality-salience hypothesis (verbal): reminding people of death increases defence of worldview and self-esteem.
work: Greenberg, Pyszczynski & Solomon 1986, DOI 10.1007/978-1-4613-9564-5_10 (not read); Pyszczynski, Solomon & Greenberg 2015, DOI 10.1016/bs.aesp.2015.03.001 (not read)
note: File states 'Operators / equations. None.' This is a verbal hypothesis, recorded as the law the algebra would encode. Standard account, not checked against the chapters. Under the ledger rule nothing sa feeds an equation.

statement: Anxiety-buffer hypothesis (verbal): strengthening a buffer reduces anxiety or defensiveness after a reminder.
work: Greenberg, Pyszczynski & Solomon 1986, DOI 10.1007/978-1-4613-9564-5_10 (not read); Pyszczynski, Solomon & Greenberg 2015, DOI 10.1016/bs.aesp.2015.03.001 (not read)
note: Verbal hypothesis, no functional form. Standard account, not read at source.

statement: DTA hypothesis (verbal): threatening a buffer raises the accessibility of death-related thoughts.
work: Greenberg, Pyszczynski & Solomon 1986, DOI 10.1007/978-1-4613-9564-5_10 (not read); Steinman & Updegraff 2015, DOI 10.1177/0146167215607843 (related meta-analysis, not read)
size_dependence: Delay between prime and outcome is the moderator linked to DTA (Steinman & Updegraff).
note: Verbal hypothesis, standard account. File records no multi-lab test of DTA; the search that would check this was not run (validation log).

statement: fear -> affiliation is a signed positive coupling: positive on average, moderated by situational similarity, sex and utility, not an unconditional gain.
work: Schachter 1959 (no DOI in file); Gump & Kulik 1997, DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.72.2.305; Taylor et al. 2000, DOI 10.1037/0033-295X.107.3.411; Rofe & Lewin 1988 (no DOI in file, cited via 049)
size_dependence: Sign and size depend on similarity, sex and affiliation utility (Rofe & Lewin, abstract only).
note: Built on sources not read, so under the ledger rule it cannot feed an equation until read. Validation of Rofe & Lewin's male effect size is unresolved.

statement: Appraisal-tendency law (Lerner & Keltner): fearful people give pessimistic risk estimates and make risk-averse choices; angry people give optimistic estimates and risk-seeking choices.
note: Standard account / search summary. Partly contradicted by Lu et al. for risk preference (see empirical line for Lu et al.).

statement: Operator defend(person, MS): W_i -> W_i + delta, with delta an unspecified positive function of the reminder and of buffer strength.
work: Greenberg, Pyszczynski & Solomon 1986, DOI 10.1007/978-1-4613-9564-5_10 (not read)
size_dependence: Buffer strength (secondary moderator).
note: The file's own proposed form. Sources give only a sign and a moderator list, no functional form.

statement: Operand person: a worldview-commitment scalar W_i, a buffer pair (worldview faith, self-esteem), and a fear level F_i.
work: Pyszczynski, Solomon & Greenberg 2015, DOI 10.1016/bs.aesp.2015.03.001 (not read)
note: File: TMT adds the buffer structure and a death-fear input; no source gives dynamics for any of these.

statement: Operator affiliate: F_i -> belonging_i, positive, form unknown, supported via Schachter, attachment and tend-and-befriend, independent of TMT.
work: Schachter 1959 (no DOI in file); Taylor et al. 2000, DOI 10.1037/0033-295X.107.3.411
note: Operator the algebra could adopt; supporting works not read in this file.

statement: Operator compensate (substitution): distinct threats (death, uncertainty, social rejection) feeding one defence variable, substitutable for each other.
work: Heine, Proulx & Vohs 2006, DOI 10.1207/s15327957pspr1002_1 (cited via 42, not read); Proulx & Inzlicht 2012, DOI 10.1080/1047840x.2012.702372 (not read)
note: Priming evidence only, untested at scale. File says keep out of the base layer. Only substitution test read is Treger et al. Study 5, which did not support an effect on the essay measure.

statement: Death-fear -> worldview-defence kept, if at all, as a soft parameter: prior centred near zero (section 5) or prior mean near 0.1 (section 8), upper bound about d = 0.2, flagged contested.
note: Two prior centres given in the file (near zero vs near 0.1); the file does not reconcile them. File: death-fear -> worldview-defence should not be an axiom.

statement: Moderators to carry as parameters if a defence operator is wanted: delay between prime and outcome, culture (US largest), and buffer strength (self-esteem, secondary).
work: Burke, Martens & Faucher 2010, DOI 10.1177/1088868309352321; Steinman & Updegraff 2015, DOI 10.1177/0146167215607843 (not read)
size_dependence: Delay is the strongest theoretical moderator; ML4 gave no significant benefit for Author Advised longer delays. Culture figures for Asian samples second-hand (Yen & Cheng via Treger).
note: Culture evidence is second-hand (Burke abstract; Yen & Cheng via Treger).

statement: Many Labs 4 (2022 revision): mortality-salience prime vs TV prime, essay-author rating (pro minus anti-US). Random-effects g all sites: Set 1 g = 0.07 [-0.03, 0.17], p = .187; Set 2 g = 0.09 [-0.03, 0.21]; Set 3 g = 0.09 [-0.04, 0.22]; heterogeneity not above chance; Author Advised sites only g = 0.08, 0.17, 0.19, none significant; five high-TMT-knowledge sites g = 0.02 [-0.18, 0.23]. Analysed 17 labs, N = 1,550 after exclusions (recruited 21 labs, 2,281).
work: Klein et al. 2022, Collabra: Psychology 8(1), 35271, DOI 10.1525/collabra.35271
size_dependence: Power 95% to detect d = 0.18 (Set 1), 0.21 (Set 2), 0.22 (Set 3). Original studies of about 12 per cell.
note: Read from the 2022 OSF preprint revision, not the 2019 text. Collabra PDF not fetched; abstract via Crossref. Tests only the prime-to-essay-rating link, under one delay structure, in US students; did not measure fear, affiliation or DTA. Outcome is individual ratings, outside the three scales. Validation: the 'g 0.07 to 0.13' summary range is not traced (see contradiction).

statement: Many Labs 4 (2019 preprint, superseded): g = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.06, 0.12], on 2,220 analysed participants (Exclusion Set 1, all 21 labs).
source: 051 §2 (Sample, and a discrepancy in 17); Validation log
work: Klein et al. 2022, Collabra: Psychology 8(1), 35271, DOI 10.1525/collabra.35271
size_dependence: Recruited 2,281; 2,220 is the 2019 analysed count; the 2022 revision applied preregistered exclusions to reach 1,550.
note: Validation correction: 17's '21 labs, 2,220 participants' is the superseded 2019 analysis; recruited total is 21 labs / 2,281. Read from the 2019 preprint.

statement: Original effect: Greenberg et al. 1994 reported d = 1.34 (t(53) = 4.87) for mortality salience vs TV salience on essay-author ratings, with 59 US introductory psychology students in five conditions (about 12 per cell).
work: Greenberg, Pyszczynski, Solomon, Simon & Breus 1994, JPSP 67(4), 627-637, DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.67.4.627
size_dependence: About 12 per cell; file calls d = 1.34 an inflated early estimate of that profile.
note: Tagged [read, via ML4] in the file; the original paper's text was read through the ML4 report. Validation log confirms authors, d and sample via ML4 text.

statement: Chatard, Hirschberger & Pyszczynski 2020 critique: at 40 or more per cell, Hedges' g = 0.10 (SE 0.06, 13 studies); below 40 per cell, g = -0.06 (SE 0.10, 8 studies); Mann-Whitney U = 24.0, p = .046; restricted to 40-per-cell Author Advised labs the effect is significant ('the data actually do replicate').
work: Chatard, Hirschberger & Pyszczynski 2020, OSF preprint, DOI 10.31234/osf.io/ejubn
size_dependence: Per-cell size: 13 studies at or above 40 per cell vs 8 below; ML4 included 8 of 21 studies below the 40-per-cell guideline.
note: Preprint, not peer-reviewed as far as the file found. Read in full. Validation confirmed all figures. File also notes Chatard's objection that the anti-US essay measure may not tap worldview post-election.

statement: Bayesian multiverse (Haaf et al. 2020 preprint): 29 of 33 model-averaged Bayes factors give evidence against an overall mortality-salience effect (1.42-to-1 to 44.69-to-1); the other four give weak evidence for an effect (1.11-to-1 to 1.61-to-1), all from the two smallest datasets with optimistic priors. Overall d between 0.03 and 0.18.
work: Haaf, Hoogeveen, Berkhout, Gronau & Wagenmakers 2020, OSF preprint v1 (14 April 2020), DOI 10.31234/osf.io/cb9er; published as Hoogeveen et al. 2023, AMPPS 6(3), DOI 10.1177/25152459231182318
size_dependence: 18 exclusion constellations (11 unique after overlap); three priors (default Cauchy, Oosterwijk t centred 0.35, Vohs normal centred 0.3, all truncated positive).
note: Read the 2020 preprint, not the 2023 published version. The published numbers differ (see contradiction). Full-sample null Bayes factors (default / Oosterwijk / Vohs): 12.60 / 44.69 / 16.64; 7.95 / 16.84 / 7.20; 4.18 / 4.01 / 2.49 for Klein's three analyses.

statement: Chatard-style subset (7 Author Advised studies at or above 40 per cell): null Bayes factors default / Oosterwijk / Vohs of 3.82 / 1.42 / 1.45 (N = 700 / 386 / 229 subsets, Set 1 / 2 / 3). Corrected form: under Set 1 (N = 700) optimistic priors give 2.75 to 5.84 in favour of the null; under Sets 2 and 3 Bayes factors are 0.62 to 1.45, uninformative.
work: Haaf et al. 2020 preprint, DOI 10.31234/osf.io/cb9er; Hoogeveen et al. 2023, DOI 10.1177/25152459231182318
size_dependence: Subset keeps about 10 per cent of the initial data; authors call the results essentially inconclusive.
note: Validation corrected the file's earlier wording ('0.6 to 1.5', 'uninformative' throughout). The subset cannot discriminate; it does not show an effect.

statement: Burke, Martens & Faucher 2010 meta-analysis: 277 experiments from 164 articles, mean effect r = .35 (file converts to d of about 0.75) across worldview- and self-esteem-related outcomes; larger for American samples (r = .37 per Treger), college students, longer delay, and people-related attitudes. Uncorrected for publication bias.
work: Burke, Martens & Faucher 2010, Pers. Soc. Psychol. Rev. 14(2), 155-195, DOI 10.1177/1088868309352321
size_dependence: Moderators: American samples, college students, longer delay, people-related attitudes.
note: From the abstract. Validation confirmed 164 articles, 277 experiments, r = .35, moderators; the d conversion checked. File's own correction: 17's 'supported the effect' should quantify these and say uncorrected for bias.

statement: Schindler et al. 2023 meta-analysis of the MS x social-norm interaction: g = 0.34, 95% CI [0.26, 0.41] over 64 effect sizes; bias-adjusted methods give smaller estimates, in several cases no longer significant, corrected g from about -0.36 to 0.15.
work: Schindler, Hilgard, Fritsche, Burke & Pfattheicher 2023, Pers. Soc. Psychol. Rev. 27(2), 195-225, DOI 10.1177/10888683221107267
size_dependence: Moderated by salient social norms.
note: Interaction, not the main effect; main effect not checked. Burke, a 2010 co-author, is also on this paper. Validation confirmed the range in the Crossref abstract.

statement: Treger, Benau & Timko 2023, five failed replications: anti-US essay g = 0.01 [-0.30, 0.31] (Study 1), g = -0.10 [-0.48, 0.29] (Study 2); mini meta-analysis on the essay measure z = 0.33, p = .738, tau-squared = .0112, I-squared = 56.5% (N pooled 1,255 across measures; 651 for the essay). Study 5 with MS, uncertainty and social-pain primes (cells about 21 to 26) found no effect on the essay measure.
work: Treger, Benau & Timko 2023, PLOS ONE 18(5), e0285267, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0285267
size_dependence: Cells of about 21 to 26 in Study 5 essay analyses; N pooled 1,255 across measures.
note: Read in full per validation log; §4 tags it [read, partial] because the mini meta-analysis table was only partly extracted. Five samples (MTurk, student, in-person).

statement: Treger, Benau & Timko 2023 mediator tests: MS vs control self-reported fear g = -0.26 [-0.64, 0.13] (wrong sign for a fear route); belongingness g = 0.06 [-0.20, 0.31], p = .68, after which belongingness was dropped as a mediator. The mortality prime did not change measured fear or belongingness.
work: Treger, Benau & Timko 2023, PLOS ONE 18(5), e0285267, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0285267
note: Scale assigned to the belongingness result (affiliation is closest to membership). The fear result sits outside the three scales. File calls this the only direct test of the TMT route to affiliation it found.

statement: Arendsen et al. 2025 meta-analysis of MS-driven consumer responses: 70 studies / 125 effect sizes (112 experiments in the review), g = 0.21 [0.14, 0.28]; Q(124) = 462.58, p < .001; 32% of variance between studies. Subcategories: 'I want more' g = 0.13 [0.01, 0.24]; pro-social g = 0.22 [0.13, 0.31]; 'protect my culture' g = 0.29 [0.19, 0.40]. Review found 47% of 114 outcomes with no main effect.
work: Arendsen, Brugman, van Koningsbruggen & Fransen 2025, Int. J. Consumer Studies 49(3), e70056, DOI 10.1111/ijcs.70056
size_dependence: Heterogeneity large; 32% of variance between studies.
note: Outcomes are consumer responses (brand, spending, donating), not worldview defence, so it does not rescue ML4's outcome. Authors ran no publication-bias checks and advise caution. Validation: abstract gives a category range of 0.13 to 0.30, so 'protect my culture' is 0.29 or 0.30 (unreconciled). CIs, Q and 47% not rechecked (Wiley 403).

statement: Chen, Benjamin, Lai & Heine 2022 p-curve of 860 published MS studies: 'there are nonzero effects in this literature'; estimated average power 26%, so direct replications are unlikely to succeed; power higher with multiple delays, for main effects over interactions, and for more recent studies.
work: Chen, Benjamin, Lai & Heine 2022, PsyArXiv, DOI 10.31234/osf.io/kuhy6 (Research Square version DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-1254756/v1, 2023, five authors incl. Y. Guo)
size_dependence: Power higher with multiple delays and for recent studies.

work: Kurzban, Duckworth, Kable & Myers 2013, Behavioral and Brain Sciences 36(6), 661-679, doi 10.1017/S0140525X12003196
note: About the first third of the target article read via PMC. Boredom is mentioned only in passing; the boredom formalisation is attributed to Kurzban by Westgate and Geana, not found formal in the target article as read.

statement: Sensation seeking is a directed search for novel, varied, complex and intense sensations, and boredom is not directed
work: Wolff, Radtke & Martarelli 2024, in Routledge International Handbook of Boredom, pp. 5-29, doi 10.4324/9781003271536-3
note: Sensation seeking as cited via Wolff. The habituation link is not checked at source.

statement: Boredom's effects on ingroup favouring and outgroup harshness are mediated by need for meaningful behaviour
work: Van Tilburg & Igou 2011, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 37(12), 1679-1691, doi 10.1177/0146167211418530
note: Abstract read; the file records no statistics. The need for meaningful behaviour is treated as a mediator, so it is drive-like rather than a measured state.

statement: Boredom is the aversive experience of wanting, but being unable, to engage in satisfying activity
work: Eastwood, Frischen, Fenske & Smilek 2012, Perspectives on Psychological Science 7(5), 482-495, doi 10.1177/1745691612456044
note: Second-hand quotation (Bench & Lench 2013 p. 482; Danckert et al. 2018). Full text not read. Attention failure is the component Wolff et al. contest (see contradictions).

statement: Boredom is the state in which the subject cannot successfully engage attention with the internal or external information needed for satisfying activity, is focused on that failure, and attributes the cause to the environment
work: Eastwood, Frischen, Fenske & Smilek 2012, Perspectives on Psychological Science 7(5), 482-495, doi 10.1177/1745691612456044
note: Three-part expansion of the definition, from the abstract page and standard account, not from the full text. Do not feed equations from this line.

statement: boredom is an affective indicator of unsuccessful attentional engagement in valued goal-congruent activity
work: Westgate & Wilson 2018, Psychological Review 125(5), 689-713, doi 10.1037/rev0000097
note: Verbatim in the journal abstract (validation log). Model text read from Westgate's 2018 dissertation, doi 10.18130/V37659F3F, which the file says reports the published model. Journal article itself not read.

statement: Attention succeeds iff task demand D equals available resources R; failure is D < R (understimulation) or D > R (overstimulation); meaning M is congruence of the activity with currently activated valued goals
work: Westgate & Wilson 2018, Psychological Review 125(5), 689-713, doi 10.1037/rev0000097
note: Dissertation read. The meaning component is the least operationalised: valued goals are whatever is currently salient.

statement: Attention-meaning mapping: a 4 x 2 table of (attention state x meaning state) to a boredom profile and a predicted response, with outputs either regulation of the fit (increase demand or resources) or a switch of activity (seek interesting or enjoyable)
work: Westgate & Wilson 2018, Psychological Review 125(5), 689-713, doi 10.1037/rev0000097
note: Table 2 of the dissertation, cell labels transcribed by the file. The file states there is no equation in the model, only this table.

statement: A boredom state is one in which an organism's functions are not adequately utilised: adequate utilisation is the activity lying inside the intersection of preferences, capabilities and perceived energy
work: Wolff, Radtke & Martarelli 2024, in Routledge International Handbook of Boredom, pp. 5-29, doi 10.4324/9781003271536-3
note: Schopenhauer-derived. The intersection is a Venn diagram, not an equation.

statement: Boredom occurs when positive and negative reward prediction errors are minimised, i.e. near-zero reward prediction error over an individual-specific time window; reward prediction error is the difference between predicted and actual reward utility for a state
work: Wolff, Radtke & Martarelli 2024, in Routledge International Handbook of Boredom, pp. 5-29, doi 10.4324/9781003271536-3
note: The authors state the definition is untested as such. Arousal is not part of the definition.

statement: Task utility Q_VOI = Q + VOI, the defined reward Q plus the value of information VOI
work: Agrawal, Mattar, Cohen & Daw 2022, Psychological Review 129(3), 564-585, doi 10.1037/rev0000309
note: Read from the preprint (eqs 9-13 block; the Q_VOI numbering is not given in the file). Equation forms were embedded as images and not re-read in validation.

statement: Boredom indexes the opportunity cost of foregoing exploration by continued engagement in the current task
work: Agrawal, Mattar, Cohen & Daw 2022, Psychological Review 129(3), 564-585, doi 10.1037/rev0000309
note: Validation corrected the opening words: the preprint sentence begins 'it indexes', with boredom as the antecedent. The file records the definition as the VOI of exploration in the external world.

statement: Boredom level B(person, activity) = Q_VOI(best alternative) - Q_VOI(current task); Disengage fires when B > 0
work: Agrawal, Mattar, Cohen & Daw 2022, Psychological Review 129(3), 564-585, doi 10.1037/rev0000309
note: The file's own operand/operator translation of read Agrawal definitions, not a source claim. The file notes it makes boredom a derived quantity of the information state, with horizon and uncertainty as the two dials.

statement: Boredom is a linear-additive combination of two independent deficits: B = f(attention misfit, meaning misfit), with coefficients of about +0.34 and -0.35 and no interaction
work: Westgate & Wilson 2018, Psychological Review 125(5), 689-713, doi 10.1037/rev0000097
note: The file's operand translation, supported by the internal meta-analysis (see empirical lines). Not stated as a law by Westgate. The file presents it as the only evidence-backed combination law it found.

statement: Trait boredom proneness is a chronic failure to respond successfully to the self-regulatory signal of state boredom; it is a property of the response, not of the signal
work: Danckert, Mugon, Struk & Eastwood 2018, in The Function of Emotions, pp. 93-119, doi 10.1007/978-3-319-77619-4_6
note: The file's operand reading is a low response-competence parameter, separating signal from effector. Trait structure: the two-factor BPS disappears when items are reworded.

statement: Boredom is a discrete emotion whose function is to motivate pursuit of new goals when the previous goal is no longer beneficial, distinct from apathy, with no commitment to the valence of the new goal
work: Bench & Lench 2013, Behavioral Sciences 3(3), 459-472, doi 10.3390/bs3030459
note: Read via PMC summary (second-hand quotations). The paper is a review with limited evidence and reports no effect sizes of its own.

statement: Boredom motivates seeking of difference: an activity differing from the current one, which the file renders as the operator Seek(difference)
note: Abstract read (file tag read via Europe PMC). The operator notation is the file's translation, not the source's.

statement: Boredom occurs when the cost of continuing the current task outweighs its benefit, particularly in comparison with currently available alternative tasks
work: Kurzban, Duckworth, Kable & Myers 2013, Behavioral and Brain Sciences 36(6), 661-679, doi 10.1017/S0140525X12003196
note: This is Westgate's gloss, read, attributed to Kurzban. The file found it not formal in the target article as read.

statement: Boredom susceptibility is a subscale of the Sensation Seeking Scale (Zuckerman), so any boredom-sensation seeking correlation is partly built into the instrument
work: Wolff, Radtke & Martarelli 2024, in Routledge International Handbook of Boredom, pp. 5-29, doi 10.4324/9781003271536-3
note: Zuckerman 1978 original not read (the file lists it under unconfirmed). Zuckerman's under-arousal claim for sensation seekers likewise not opened.

statement: Boredom proneness (BPS) indexes failure-to-launch boredom (anxious, avoidant); boredom susceptibility (ZBS) indexes seeking boredom (reward-driven, disinhibited)
work: Mercer-Lynn, Flora, Fahlman & Eastwood 2011, Assessment 20(5), 585-596, doi 10.1177/1073191111408229
note: The BPS/ZBS labels are the file's interpretation of the correlates, not the source's wording. Abstract read, with the Ns of its three studies.

statement: Boredom and curiosity about an unexplored option are both value of information of that option, so they are not exclusive
work: Eder, Maas, Schubmann, Krishna & Erle 2022, Scientific Reports, doi 10.1038/s41598-022-14775-w
note: The file's reading under the VOI model, not a source claim. Eder et al. attribute the shocks to curiosity. Abstract only.

statement: Boredom is a derived signal: positive when the marginal local information gain of staying in a patch is below the global one, so it is the relative value of switching
work: Geana 2015, PhD dissertation, Princeton University, chapter 4 (no DOI); Geana, Wilson, Daw & Cohen 2016, CogSci proceedings (not confirmed)
note: The file's operand translation of Geana's normative model. The 2016 CogSci proceedings existence is not confirmed (validation).

statement: VOI(s, a_k) = Gain(s, a_k) x Need(s, a_k)
work: Agrawal, Mattar, Cohen & Daw 2022, Psychological Review 129(3), 564-585, doi 10.1037/rev0000309
note: Read from preprint. Gain is the function of uncertainty and Need of horizon, so horizon and uncertainty are the two dials. The authors describe this as a partly myopic approximation to VOI (footnote 5).

statement: Gain(s, a_k) = E[ sum over a in A of (pi_new(a|s) - pi_old(a|s_k)) q(s, a) ], expectation over the prior of the obtained reward r
work: Agrawal, Mattar, Cohen & Daw 2022, Psychological Review 129(3), 564-585, doi 10.1037/rev0000309
note: Expected improvement in policy value from learning r. Read from preprint; published numbering may differ.

statement: Need(s, a_k) = sum over i = 1 to infinity of gamma^i delta(s_{t+i}, s_k) = gamma x sum over s' of P(s, a_k, s') M(s', s), with M the successor representation
work: Agrawal, Mattar, Cohen & Daw 2022, Psychological Review 129(3), 564-585, doi 10.1037/rev0000309; successor representation after Dayan 1993 (per the file)
note: Expected discounted number of future visits to the state. Read from preprint.

statement: r_{t,i} = rho - PE_t, with PE_t = Pr_t - N(mu_i, sigma_i), where rho is the maximum reward
work: Geana 2015, PhD dissertation, Princeton University, chapter 4 (no DOI)
note: Patch i has hidden mean mu_i and SD sigma_i. Dissertation-stage; not found as a journal article.

statement: Running mean update with learning rate 1/n: mu_{i,t} = mu_{i,t-1} + (1/n) PE_t, so a new datum's informativeness falls like 1/n
work: Geana 2015, PhD dissertation, Princeton University, chapter 4 (no DOI)
note: Variance update (eq. 5) is said to be analogous but its form is not transcribed by the file.

statement: Relative value of one more sample in the current patch versus switching (eq. 6), a function of n, N, sigma^2 and S^2, solved by dynamic programming
work: Geana 2015, PhD dissertation, Princeton University, chapter 4 (no DOI)
note: The typeset form was garbled in extraction and is NOT transcribed. The equation cannot feed the set until its form is read at source.

statement: U(a1, a2) = beta x (U(a1, a1) + U(a2, a2)); RU(a2) = U(a2, a2) / U(a1, a1); dividing is favoured when beta + beta x RU(a2) > 1
work: Kurzban, Duckworth, Kable & Myers 2013, Behavioral and Brain Sciences 36(6), 661-679, doi 10.1017/S0140525X12003196
note: Reconstructed from a garbled fetch (subscripts reconstructed). Not checked against the published article; validation did not re-check it. Check before building on it.

statement: Correlational: more intense boredom is related to lower arousal, r = -.13, 95% CI [-.22, -.05], from 75 effect sizes
work: Stempfer, Stoll, Fries, Pekrun & Goetz 2025, Communications Psychology 3, article 182, doi 10.1038/s44271-025-00358-8
note: Meta-analysis of 214 effect sizes, 72 samples, N = 6,570, pre-registered. Abstract and introduction read. Individual-level, so no target scale applies.

statement: Experimental: boredom had lower arousal than control conditions, d = -0.40, 95% CI [-0.59, -0.22], from 122 effect sizes, with significant heterogeneity
work: Stempfer, Stoll, Fries, Pekrun & Goetz 2025, Communications Psychology 3, article 182, doi 10.1038/s44271-025-00358-8
note: Relation not significant against a neutral control (waiting, doing nothing), when boredom items include mixed or high arousal, or when arousal is HRV. The file's verdict: do not make arousal a state variable.

statement: Internal meta-analysis of 14 studies (N = 1,364) regressing boredom on difficulty-concentrating (attention) and meaningfulness: attention b = .34 [.28, .40]; meaning b = -.35 [-.41, -.28]; interaction b = .004 [-.03, .04], p = .79
work: Westgate 2018 dissertation, University of Virginia, 'Why Boredom is Interesting', doi 10.18130/V37659F3F
note: Self-report, 9-point items, undergraduate and mTurk samples. Most of the 14 studies are unpublished pilot data by one lab, so shared-method bias is possible. Dissertation numbers not re-checked in validation.

statement: Study 2: boredom has a curvilinear relation to difficulty after controlling for frustration, quadratic b = .14 (.05), t(123) = 2.95, p = .004, d = .53; frustration linear in difficulty, b = .72 (.09), d = 1.39; boredom and frustration r = .12
work: Westgate 2018 dissertation, University of Virginia, doi 10.18130/V37659F3F
note: Correlational, one study, no independent replication found. The file says the result contradicts pure understimulation accounts, which predict a linear relation. Journal-paper numbers not checked.

statement: Study 1 (N = 226): manipulating attention and meaning each produced boredom; the attention manipulation predicted Inattention, and the meaning manipulation predicted Disengagement, dysphoric and agitated affect and slowed time perception
work: Westgate 2018 dissertation, University of Virginia, doi 10.18130/V37659F3F
note: The file reads meaning-failure boredom as the high-arousal kind. Self-report and manipulation-based; not replicated.

statement: Boredom rises with time on a fixed task, within and across games, with no interaction with informativeness condition; boredom depends on how much a trial can teach
work: Geana 2015, PhD dissertation, Princeton University, chapter 4 (no DOI)
note: Number-prediction task, three informativeness conditions. Geana attributes the time effect to novelty loss, fatigue or increased perceived opportunity cost. Sample size not stated in the file.

statement: Participants told they would next watch a YouTube video rated the same bandit task as more boring than those told they would count words in an article; boredom correlated with exploration of the ambiguous arm only at horizon 6, F(1,33) = 6.01, p = .02 (horizon 1: F(1,33) = 1.88, p = .17)
work: Geana 2015, PhD dissertation, Princeton University, chapter 4 (no DOI)
note: Sample about 35 (from F df). Single result at p = .02, self-report boredom. The file's key support for the opportunity-cost reading over pure habituation, and the one small study that discriminates from Wolff's account.

statement: Across three studies, boredom with a neutral task predicted choosing novel negative experiences; boredom with positive stimuli chose a more negative novel experience, and boredom with negative stimuli chose a more positive one; the key claim is difference from the boring experience, not negativity per se
note: Abstract only; sample sizes not read. The file tags it read via Europe PMC abstract. Ledger schema counts abstracts as sa.

statement: The 2013 evidence base for boredom's function is old and thin: 12 experimental boredom studies against 510 articles on other emotions (a cited count), with no effect sizes reported in the review itself
work: Bench & Lench 2013, Behavioral Sciences 3(3), 459-472, doi 10.3390/bs3030459
note: Via PMC summary, second-hand. Cites London & Monello clock manipulation, London 1972 skin conductance, and Larsen & Zarate 1991.

statement: Under a rock-paper-scissors contingency, always-winning participants reported the most boredom, always-losing participants showed initial arousal that dissipated, and those told the opponent was exploitable reported less boredom than those told it was random
work: Struk, Scholer & Danckert 2021, Frontiers in Psychology 12, 687623, doi 10.3389/fpsyg.2021.687623 (cited in Danckert et al. 2018 as Struk et al. 2015)
note: Reported via the Danckert 2018 chapter; the study itself was not read. The chapter gives no statistics.

statement: In a video boredom induction compared with sadness: heart rate up, skin conductance level down, cortisol up; Jang et al. 2015 partially replicated the decreased skin conductance
work: Merrifield & Danckert 2014, Experimental Brain Research 232, 481-491, doi 10.1007/s00221-013-3755-2
note: Reported via the Danckert 2018 chapter; the study itself was not read.

statement: Higher willingness to pay for music after boredom, associated with insula activity
work: Dal Mas & Wittmann 2017, Cortex 92, 57-69, doi 10.1016/j.cortex.2017.03.008
note: Reported via the Danckert 2018 chapter; study not read. Neural claim: insula anticorrelated with DMN when bored but not at rest.

statement: A boredom induction raised self-reported fatigue more than an effort manipulation, which the Agrawal VOI model does not predict
work: Milyavskaya, Inzlicht, Johnson & Larson 2019, Neuropsychologia 123, 159-168, doi 10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2018.03.033
note: Reported as cited in the Agrawal preprint; study not read. The file records this as a discrepancy with the model.

statement: Forward-model learning benchmark: agents with a boredom ('devaluation') term outperformed other curiosity or exploratory variants
work: Yu, Chang & Kanai 2019, Frontiers in Neurorobotics 12, 88, doi 10.3389/fnbot.2018.00088
note: Engineering result, not human data. Published 22 Jan 2019, volume 12 (validation corrected the year). Abstract read.

statement: Subjects avoid the more monotonous of two stimulus sequences; the avoidance correlates with self-reported boredom, replicates across lab and online samples, is specific to boredom rather than curiosity, and the entropy of the experienced sequence predicts choice
work: Seiler, Dan, Tüscher, Loewenstein & Rumpel 2022, Scientific Reports 12, 3162, doi 10.1038/s41598-022-06861-w
note: Abstract read. Validation added the missing reference. Individual choice; the file marks this as the only human choice study of entropy.

statement: Agent-based model of interacting bored agents choosing colour variants: boredom parameter is essential for perpetuating fashion dynamics, and highly bored agents lead population trends when acting coherently or when highly popular
work: Seiler & Rumpel 2023, Scientific Reports 13, 20480, doi 10.1038/s41598-023-47749-7
size_dependence: Population-level result. The file records no group-size dependence.
note: The only formal social boredom model found; it corrects the earlier claim that no social operand exists. Abstract read, equations not read.

statement: Participants typically did not enjoy 6 to 15 minutes alone thinking, and many chose to shock themselves
work: Wilson, Reinhard, Westgate, Gilbert, Ellerbeck, Hahn, Brown & Shaked 2014, Science 345(6192), 75-77, doi 10.1126/science.1250830
note: Abstract read, 11 studies. The 'two-thirds of men, about a quarter of women' figure is from a search summary and is NOT confirmed at source.

statement: Two parallel experiments (N = 30 in total, within-subject): one hour of a repeated clip versus a neutral documentary increased chocolate eating and self-administered shocks
work: Havermans, Vancleef, Kalamatianos & Nederkoorn 2015, Appetite 85, 52-57, doi 10.1016/j.appet.2014.11.007
note: Abstract only. Validation corrected the entry to two experiments.

statement: Boredom produced more and stronger self-inflicted shocks than neutral or sad films (N = 69), more so with a history of non-suicidal self-injury; sadness had no effect
work: Nederkoorn, Vancleef, Wilkenhoner, Claes & Havermans 2016, Psychiatry Research 237, 127-132, doi 10.1016/j.psychres.2016.01.063
note: Abstract only. Validation matched N = 69.

statement: Four experiments, N = 254: a large proportion shocked themselves, strong shocks were chosen even when no-shock or mild-shock options existed, and the authors conclude the shocks were attractive because participants were curious about them
work: Eder, Maas, Schubmann, Krishna & Erle 2022, Scientific Reports, doi 10.1038/s41598-022-14775-w
note: Abstract only. The curiosity explanation is the authors' own. A search snippet mentions a critique finding 57% did not shock themselves, not verified here.

statement: Twelve-site, eleven-country replication (N = 2,557) of the thinking-versus-doing enjoyment result; the enjoyment contrast replicated, the shock result was not tested
work: Buttrick et al. 2019, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 117, e71-e83, doi 10.1037/pspp0000198
note: Abstract read; the file's tag was upgraded in validation. The '21 replication reports' search claim was not traced.

statement: Across five studies, boredom raised liking of an ingroup name, harsher jail sentences for an outgroup offender, and ingroup evaluations; the effect was mediated by need for meaningful behaviour
work: Van Tilburg & Igou 2011, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 37(12), 1679-1691, doi 10.1177/0146167211418530
note: Abstract read; no statistics or sample sizes read. Validation confirmed the ingroup and outgroup findings.

statement: Six studies: boredom raises nostalgia, via a search for meaning
work: Van Tilburg, Igou & Sedikides 2013, Emotion 13(3), 450-461, doi 10.1037/a0030442
note: Abstract read; no statistics read.

statement: Trait boredom correlates with neuroticism, experiential avoidance, attentional and non-planning impulsivity, anxiety, depression and emotional eating (BPS); trait boredom susceptibility correlates with motor impulsivity, reward sensitivity, gambling and alcohol use, and lower neuroticism and punishment sensitivity (ZBS)

note: Studies 1-3 with N = 837, 233 and 137. Abstract read; validation confirmed the Ns and correlates. Crossref year is 2011 online, 2013 in print.

statement: Across studies, trait boredom and trait curiosity correlate in a range of roughly -0.3 to +0.5 (Eren & Coskun 2016 negative; Hunter et al. 2016 and Sung et al. 2020 positive)
