note: Via the review; the cited correlations were not checked at source. The file reads the wide range as a finding: the two traits are not opposites.

statement: Curiosity peaks at intermediate uncertainty
work: Kang et al. 2009 (cited in Seiler & Dan 2024, doi 10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1514348)
note: Via review, not checked at source. File 17 makes the same claim.

statement: Boredom-driven aggression-based entertainment is more likely with low self-control, impulsiveness and sensation seeking
work: Artak & Pfattheicher chapter, in Bieleke, Wolff & Martarelli (eds), The Routledge International Handbook of Boredom
note: Chapter summary only; the volume notes AI-assisted summaries curated by the authors. Not a measured result.

statement: Martin & Potts 2011 ERP study, used as post hoc support for the near-zero reward prediction error definition
work: Martin & Potts 2011 (cited in Wolff, Radtke & Martarelli 2024, doi 10.4324/9781003271536-3)
note: The authors admit it was not designed to test the proposition. Weak indirect support only.

statement: Simulated (not fitted) predictions of the VOI model: a repetitive task grows the VOI of the alternative until it is worth choosing over the status quo; easy and impossible tasks both have low VOI, giving a U-shape; longer horizons raise exploration
work: Agrawal, Mattar, Cohen & Daw 2022, Psychological Review 129(3), 564-585, doi 10.1037/rev0000309

statement: Predicted, untested: in Blain et al.'s multi-hour N-back study a hard task should produce fatigue (impulsive choice rises) and an easy task boredom (pupillometry or subsequent bandit exploration)
work: Agrawal, Mattar, Cohen & Daw 2022, Psychological Review 129(3), 564-585, doi 10.1037/rev0000309
note: A prediction the authors did not test. Blain et al. not read.

statement: Arousal and boredom: boredom is a low-arousal state (Berlyne-type accounts; Wundt curve; Russell circumplex; Scitovsky; WASABI derives boredom from PAD low arousal) versus boredom is only weakly and instrument-dependently low-arousal, so arousal is not a state variable of boredom
source: 054 §8 and 'Contradictions and tensions'; other side in 017 A1, 015, 019, 036 (files, not read here)
work: Stempfer et al. 2025, Communications Psychology 3, article 182, doi 10.1038/s44271-025-00358-8 (054 side); Berlyne Wundt curve per file 017 (not read here)
note: 054 side: r = -.13 correlational, d = -0.40 experimental, null against neutral controls and with high-arousal items; do not make arousal a state variable. Other side: those files describe boredom as low arousal in their own models, tagged as standard-account or design descriptions. Verdict per 054: resolved on evidence, with a wording caveat. Record as 'arousal is a weak, instrument-dependent correlate'. Berlyne-type accounts are weakly supported, not refuted. Files 017 and 019 need a pointer when next edited.

statement: Definition of boredom's attentional component: attention failure is what boredom is (Eastwood et al. 2012) versus disengagement is not the bug of boredom but one of its core features (Wolff et al. 2024)
work: Eastwood, Frischen, Fenske & Smilek 2012, Perspectives on Psychological Science 7(5), 482-495, doi 10.1177/1745691612456044; Wolff, Radtke & Martarelli 2024, doi 10.4324/9781003271536-3
note: Eastwood side via second-hand quotation and abstract; Wolff side read (revised 2022 preprint, Box 1). No verdict recorded in 054. Status: open.

statement: Mechanism of boredom: forward-looking value of announced alternatives (Agrawal VOI, Geana Exp 4.3) versus backward-looking near-zero recent reward prediction error (Wolff), predicting different outcomes when an attractive alternative is announced but unavailable
work: Agrawal, Mattar, Cohen & Daw 2022, Psychological Review 129(3), 564-585, doi 10.1037/rev0000309; Wolff, Radtke & Martarelli 2024, doi 10.4324/9781003271536-3

statement: Trait structure: the 'no subtypes' position on boredom (Danckert et al.) versus two boredom types (Westgate & Wilson MAC model: attentional and meaningless)
work: Danckert, Mugon, Struk & Eastwood 2018, doi 10.1007/978-3-319-77619-4_6; Westgate & Wilson 2018, doi 10.1037/rev0000097
note: Both sides read. The file records the conflict as stated; no verdict. Status: open.

statement: Negative seeking under boredom: boredom pushes toward negative difference and pain (Bench & Lench 2019; Havermans 2015; Nederkoorn 2016) versus curiosity about the shock explains the self-shocks (Eder et al. 2022)
work: Bench & Lench 2019, Emotion 19(2), 242-254, doi 10.1037/emo0000433; Havermans et al. 2015, Appetite 85, 52-57, doi 10.1016/j.appet.2014.11.007; Nederkoorn et al. 2016, Psychiatry Research 237, 127-132; Eder et al. 2022, Scientific Reports, doi 10.1038/s41598-022-14775-w

Verdict in 054: not exclusive in the VOI model, since both are value of information of an unexplored option, so the accounts differ in labelling more than in prediction. Status: open, pending a deep-read of Eder et al. and the critique it cites. Wilson 2014 shock proportions also unconfirmed.

statement: Difficulty and boredom: a curvilinear U-shape after controlling for frustration (Westgate & Wilson Study 2) versus a purely understimulation (linear) account of boredom

note: 054 says the curvilinear result contradicts pure understimulation accounts, which predict a linear relation. One study, dissertation numbers, journal article not read. Status: open, needs independent replication.

statement: Trait boredom and trait curiosity: the two are independent or coalesce (Seiler & Dan) versus a wide range of correlations from negative (Eren & Coskun 2016) to positive (Hunter et al. 2016; Sung et al. 2020)
work: Seiler & Dan 2024, Frontiers in Psychology 15, 1514348, doi 10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1514348; cited trait correlations not checked at source
note: Not a contradiction of the same claim, but the cited correlation signs disagree. 054 reads the range as a finding that the two are not opposites. Status: open, pending source checks of the three cited studies.

statement: Status desire is a fundamental human motive (status hypothesis)

note: Review; full text unread, claim from abstract and press summary. The file says 'fundamental' depends on the criteria chosen (see contradiction on Panksepp). Cluster Q is a guess from content; the research map was not read.

statement: Status = the respect, admiration and voluntary deference individuals are afforded by others (others-held, relative, not an internal deficit)
work: Anderson, Hildreth & Howland 2015, 10.1037/a0038781
note: Validated (checkmark) against the PubMed abstract. Abstract-level only, so provenance stays sa.

statement: Status granted by others predicts wellbeing and health; low status linked to depression, anxiety and cardiovascular disease
work: Anderson, Hildreth & Howland 2015, 10.1037/a0038781
note: Health links are largely correlational (file's verdict). Source is the press summary (PsyPost) and abstract; not verified against full text. Individual-level outcome, so no ledger scale fits; n/a used.

statement: Status = the extent to which an individual or group is respected or admired by others; power = asymmetric control over valued resources in social relations
note: Corrected form. 055 §4 tagged these as secondary and called 'asymmetric' a later gloss. File 49 §6 read the paper's PDF and quotes both verbatim, so the corrected form is the paper's own wording. Provenance is read via file 49, not via 055.

statement: Status and power form a self-reinforcing hierarchy: status creates expectations and opportunities that favour those who already hold it, and power shapes thought and action to keep or gain power (verbal positive-feedback account)
note: Verbal only: no equations, no effect sizes. 'Positive feedback' is the standard reading, not a quote. Full text unread; later papers cite it for hierarchies persisting whatever their origin in skill or luck (secondary). Mechanisms, including power priming, rest on social-priming literature with replication problems (not checked which survived).

statement: Status need is anti-homeostatic: no set point, non-satiating at the individual level
work: none (open question in 055)
note: Open. Not shown by any of the four seeds. Relative ordinal rank cannot be satiated at group level, but that is a bound by structure, not a set point. Di Tella et al. 2010 leans toward non-satiation for the individual need, on one panel with an unchecked status measure.

statement: Superior vs inferior player (stable hierarchy, n = 24): right inferior parietal Z = 6.76; ventral striatum Z = 3.99; left DLPFC Z = 4.48; P < 0.005 FDR; no region responded more to the inferior player
note: Exp 1, ages 22-43, 12 male, $1 for fast responses, ranks fixed, opponents simulated, rank from incidental skill. Full author manuscript read at PMC and numbers checked in validation. Individual-level neural measure, so no ledger scale fits.

statement: Unstable hierarchy (Exp 2, n = 24, ranks updated every four rounds), superior vs inferior: right DLPFC Z = 5.46; thalamus Z = 5.34; right amygdala Z = 4.34; posterior cingulate Z = 4.25; medial PFC Z = 3.78
note: Thalamus, amygdala and posterior cingulate activity correlated with positive affect when top-ranked (r = 0.510, 0.481, 0.478; n = 24). The file reads extra amygdala and mPFC response as instability raising the arousal attached to rank; that reading is the file's, not Zink's claim. Some clusters at uncorrected P < 0.001.

statement: Losing to a lower-ranked player (negative hierarchical value) engages ventral striatum, anterior insula and midbrain/thalamus; striatum and insula activity correlated with positive affect when top-ranked (r = 0.528, 0.444)
note: Unstable-hierarchy condition. Individual-level neural measure. n = 24 per experiment; correlations on n = 24.

statement: Beating a higher-ranked player engages pre-SMA (Z = 5.14), medial PFC and premotor cortex; premotor activity correlated negatively with trait dominance (r = -0.453, P = 0.04)
note: Individual-level neural measure. Outcomes without hierarchical value produced no activations.

statement: Hierarchical consequences of performance are neurally dissociable from, and of comparable salience to, monetary reward; hierarchical value contributed to ventral striatal activity of comparable magnitude to the primary monetary reward
note: Quoted by the fetch from the main text, tagged [read, quoted by the fetch]. But 055 Unconfirmed lists the GLM comparison as in Supplemental Results, which was not read, so the provenance rests on the fetch's quote. Standing: three samples of 24, simulated opponents, no replication located (not searched). Shows rank is reward-like in the lab, not that status is a runaway drive. Response was to the sight of a superior; saturation with repeated exposure not tested.

statement: Visual-cortex activations to superior/inferior players may track star count rather than hierarchy
work: unidentified later review (secondary search summary)
note: Caveat on Zink 2008, from a search summary of a later review; not read. Bears on the occipital/parietal results.

statement: Dominant and prestigious individuals both attain influence in group tasks; the dominant ones are less liked
note: From the abstract (validated: full author list and venue added). Full text unread.

statement: Prestige = freely conferred deference; dominance = force or the threat of force
note: From the abstract. Full text not read. Prestige is conferred by followers and so revocable; this follows from the definition and is the file's inference, not a quoted claim.

statement: Two status operands with different update rules: prest_i is a function of other agents' choices (an aggregate of followers' selections); dom_i is a function of costs imposed
note: The file's translation of the abstract's distinction, not a claim of the source. Only the qualitative bound is stated; no quantification.

statement: Prestige-seeking is a learner's drive: access to a skilled model, paid for with deference (goods, services, attention)
note: The file's account of the abstract's information-goods theory. Full text unread.

statement: Prestige-biased learning: 3- and 4-year-olds more than twice as likely to learn from a model that bystanders attended to for 10 seconds; stronger for artifact use than for food preferences

statement: Rank is a permutation of the group, so a group-wide rise leaves the mean rank unchanged (sum of ranks fixed)

note: The file's structural inference from Boyce's ordinal-rank finding, not a law Boyce states. Described as a bound on the aggregate, not an individual set point.

statement: Rank as ordinal operand with a group-level conservation law (sum of ranks fixed), making status zero-sum at group level whatever each individual wants
work: Boyce, Brown & Moore 2010, 10.1177/0956797610362671 (by implication)
note: Suggested, not established (file's wording). The data in hand cannot choose between this and the need-scalar reading.

statement: Need scalar s_i attached to rank, a felt-need operand whose dynamics are an open parameter: homeostatic (set point, adaptation after rank change) or monotone

statement: Rank-prediction-error operand (sign only, no gain) and rank uncertainty var(rank) as a separate operand from rank; utility term u(rank change) of order comparable to a monetary reward

statement: Big Man model variables: x in {0,1} cooperation; q frequency; n group size; c leader cost; b total benefit split as b/n; C = c - b/n net cost; p probability a follower copies the leader (prestige effect); s probability learned traits stick across generations; R phenotypic assortment (leader-follower plus p^2 follower-follower part); alpha bleed-over of a cooperation gene

statement: Cooperation spreads culturally only when R exceeds a threshold set by C relative to benefit (C = c - b/n)
work: Henrich, Chudek & Boyd 2015, 10.1098/rstb.2015.0013
note: Prose restatement only: the threshold's exact form is in image equations that were not seen. Do not build an equation from this line without opening the PMC figures.

statement: Cooperation will not evolve culturally unless p > 0
work: Henrich, Chudek & Boyd 2015, 10.1098/rstb.2015.0013
note: Prose statement. Equation images not seen.

statement: For large n, R reduces to p^2 (and R = s p^2 with s in the general case); p = 0.5 gives R of about 0.25; p a bit above 0.7 gives R of about 0.5
work: Henrich, Chudek & Boyd 2015, 10.1098/rstb.2015.0013

note: File states both forms in prose; the p^2-only form is not restated with s. Numbers are the file's own readings of p^2 and s p^2. Prose restatement of image equations.

statement: For p below about 0.20, cooperation is viable only in groups of about five or fewer
work: Henrich, Chudek & Boyd 2015, 10.1098/rstb.2015.0013
size_dependence: Viable only for n of about five or fewer when p is below about 0.20.

work: Henrich, Chudek & Boyd 2015, 10.1098/rstb.2015.0013

note: Prose statement. p is exogenous and not made a function of population size.

statement: Natural selection does not favour reducing the prestige effect
work: Henrich, Chudek & Boyd 2015, 10.1098/rstb.2015.0013
note: Stated result quoted in prose (validation: quote confirmed).

statement: No adaptation of happiness to status over four years (German panel, 7,812 people, 1984-2000); the five-year status effect equals an income rise of 285% of a standard deviation; right-leaning respondents appear to adapt to status but not income, left-leaning the reverse

statement: In five studies (N = 6,426), people with, or assigned, higher status were more motivated to hold status
source: 055 Cross-checks contradiction 2 (follow-up not applied to the body)

statement: The four Anderson et al. 2015 criteria are worded differently across 055 §1, 042 §1.1 and 015 §10
work: Anderson, Hildreth & Howland 2015, 10.1037/a0038781
note: 055 §1: wellbeing and health, goal-directed action, not reducible to belonging, universality. 042 §1.1: universality, functionality, automaticity, independence. 015 §10: universal, early developing, dissociable, distinct consequences. statement: Does possessing status strengthen the status motive? 055 says no seed tests satiation and cites only Di Tella 2010; 022 B2 cites Anderson, Hildreth & Sharps 2020 and says status behaves like an appetite that grows with consumption
work: Anderson, Hildreth & Sharps 2020, 10.1177/0146167220937544; Di Tella, Haisken-De New & MacCulloch 2010, 10.1016/j.jebo.2010.09.016
note: VERDICT: both partly right, unresolved as to magnitude. 055 omitted the 2020 paper and should add it (it points the same way as Di Tella: non-satiation). 022's 'grows with consumption' overreaches, because the evidence is a between-person and assignment contrast, not a within-person growth rate. statement: Magee & Galinsky's definition of power and status: 055 §4 tagged the 'asymmetric control' wording as a later gloss and the definitions as secondary, while file 49 §6 quotes both verbatim from the paper

statement: Belonging: one of four fundamental needs (belonging, self-esteem, control, meaningful existence) that ostracism threatens

statement: Self-esteem: a fundamental need, a relational need with belonging, threatened by ostracism

note: W07 p. 431: 'relational needs (belonging and self-esteem)'.

statement: Control (efficacy): a fundamental need which, with meaningful existence, when most thwarted drives controlling, provocative and even antisocial fortification

statement: Social pain: the social attachment system may have 'piggybacked onto' the physical pain system, sharing the affective pain signal (dACC and anterior insula)

statement: Tend-and-befriend (Taylor et al. 2000): an alternative response to exclusion to fight, flight or freeze, sitting beside the fear-to-affiliation question

statement: Ostracism: being ignored and excluded; used alongside 'social exclusion' and 'rejection' as Williams's vocabulary
work: Williams, K. D. (2007). Ostracism. Annual Review of Psychology 58, 425-452. DOI 10.1146/annurev.psych.58.110405.085641

statement: Reflexive stage: the immediate painful response to any form of ostracism, unmitigated by situational or individual difference factors

note: W07 p. 431, item (a) of the sequence.

statement: Need vector (B, S, C, M): the four needs (belonging, self-esteem, control, meaningful existence) that the file calls the operand of the control loop

statement: Operator exclude(a, b): lowers the need vector of b

statement: Williams's verbal sequence: (a) reflexive painful response to any ostracism; (b) threats to belonging, self-esteem, control and meaningful existence with rising sadness and anger; (c) reflective fortification where relational needs most thwarted gives prosocial fortification and efficacy or existence needs most thwarted gives controlling, provocative or antisocial responses; repeated or long episodes diminish fortification, producing helplessness, alienation and despair

statement: Composite need satisfaction moderation: immediate delta d = -0.18 [-0.47, -0.11] (k = 15); delayed delta d = -0.93 [-1.67, -0.19] (k = 3)

statement: Homogeneous subset of Cyberball studies (k = 19): d = -2.05 [-2.44, -1.65]
work: Hartgerink, van Beest, Wicherts & Williams (2015). PLoS ONE 10(5), e0127002. DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0127002

statement: Power: 2,186 participants (G*Power, power .8) would be needed to detect the moderation interaction at both time points; typical factorial study has mean n about 110 and power about .08 for the last-measure interaction

statement: Typical effect size of ostracism on self-reported distress (moods and need threat) is high, between 1.0 and 2.0

statement: Recalled social-pain episodes, especially ostracism, score on the McGill pain inventory comparable to meta-analytic chronic back pain and childbirth

note: Williams & Fitness 2004 is secondary to the review, so provenance sa. Recall data, not an induced exclusion.

statement: No moderation of ostracism distress by trait self-esteem, individualism-collectivism, introversion-extraversion, gender, loneliness, need for belonging or social anxiety; distress not lower when the ostracisers are told to be a script or a computer (Zadro et al. 2004); no moderation by despised outgroup membership (Gonsalkorale & Williams 2006), cost of throw, or ball versus bomb
work: Williams, K. D. (2007). Ostracism. Annual Review of Psychology 58, 425-452. DOI 10.1146/annurev.psych.58.110405.085641

note: Williams's own 2007 argument for resistance to moderation. The file records it as a claim that Hartgerink's first-measure moderation partly contradicts.

statement: A Cyberball-like game with the human features removed and no visualisation instruction produced no distress (Law & Williams 2006)
work: Williams, K. D. (2007). Ostracism. Annual Review of Psychology 58, 425-452. DOI 10.1146/annurev.psych.58.110405.085641
note: Counter-evidence Williams reports against the simple need-threat account, as cited in W07.

statement: Trait self-esteem did not moderate reactions to rejection (Leary et al. 1998, as reported by Williams 2007)
work: Williams, K. D. (2007). Ostracism. Annual Review of Psychology 58, 425-452. DOI 10.1146/annurev.psych.58.110405.085641; Leary et al. (1998), as cited, no citation details in the file
note: Read only as reported in W07. Relevant because the sociometer treats trait self-esteem as the resting readout; this is the file's 'split' quantitative test.

statement: Leary et al. (1995), five studies: state self-esteem changes parallel assumed acceptance or rejection implications; exclusion lowers self-esteem when the reason is personal but not when random (no self-presentation mediation); trait self-esteem correlates highly with how generally included one feels
note: [secondary] from search summaries. Scenario and self-report evidence, mostly. Sample sizes not obtained.

statement: Gerber & Wheeler (2009), 88 studies: rejection lowers mood (d = -0.50) and self-esteem (d = -0.70); no decrease in arousal and no flattened affect ('needs account', not 'numbness account')

statement: Gerber & Wheeler (2009): frustrated belonging d = 0.69 and frustrated control d = 1.16
work: Gerber, J. & Wheeler, L. (2009). Perspectives on Psychological Science 4, 468-488. DOI 10.1111/j.1745-6924.2009.01158.x
note: Abstract figures, validated against the Crossref abstract. Sign convention as in the abstract.

statement: Gerber & Wheeler (2009): measures contrasting belonging and control (d = -1.17) produce antisocial responding; measures that do not allow control to be restored cause prosocial responding (d = 1.21)
work: Gerber, J. & Wheeler, L. (2009). Perspectives on Psychological Science 4, 468-488. DOI 10.1111/j.1745-6924.2009.01158.x
size_dependence: Moderators are measurement-type categories, not composition or group size.
note: Corrected form (validation): the prosocial condition is 'do not allow for control to be restored', not 'can be restored' (049 had reversed it). Gerber's moderators are measurement types, not within-person tests of the rule.

statement: Blackhart et al. (2009), 192 studies: rejection causes 'a significant shift toward a more negative emotional state' but 'typically an emotionally neutral state marked by low levels of both positive and negative affect'
work: Blackhart, Nelson, Knowles & Baumeister (2009). Personality and Social Psychology Review 13, 269-309. DOI 10.1177/1088868309346065
note: Abstract quotations match (validation). No CIs in the abstract.

statement: Blackhart et al. (2009): self-esteem among rejected persons is no different from neutral controls; acceptance raised self-esteem moderately
work: Blackhart, Nelson, Knowles & Baumeister (2009). Personality and Social Psychology Review 13, 269-309. DOI 10.1177/1088868309346065
note: Challenges the sociometer's central prediction (see contradictions).

statement: Twenge et al. (2001), aggression: excluded participants gave a more negative job evaluation to an insulter (Exps 1-2) and blasted a target with more aversive noise whether the target had insulted them (Exp 4) or was a neutral stranger (Exp 5); not more aggressive toward someone who praised them (Exp 3)
work: Twenge, Baumeister, Tice & Stucke (2001). If you can't join them, beat them: effects of social exclusion on aggressive behavior. JPSP 81(6), 1058-1069. DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.81.6.1058
note: Abstract read (EPMC); sample sizes not obtained. Single lab, five experiments; no registered replication found.

statement: Twenge et al. (2001): the exclusion responses were specific to social exclusion (as opposed to other misfortunes) and were not mediated by emotion
work: Twenge, Baumeister, Tice & Stucke (2001). If you can't join them, beat them: effects of social exclusion on aggressive behavior. JPSP 81(6), 1058-1069. DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.81.6.1058
note: Abstract statement. Exclusion was induced by telling people they would be alone later in life, or that others had rejected them.

statement: Eisenberger et al. (2003), ESE versus inclusion, dorsal ACC at (x = -8, y = 20, z = 40): t = 3.36, r = 0.71, P < 0.005
work: Eisenberger, Lieberman & Williams (2003). Does rejection hurt? An fMRI study of social exclusion. Science 302(5643), 290-292. DOI 10.1126/science.1089134
note: Sample size N = 13 is from a search summary, not the report text (unconfirmed; validation could not retrieve the PDF). Single ESE block in fixed order. Peak-voxel values. Uncorrected P = 0.005 with cluster size 10.

statement: Eisenberger et al. (2003): distress correlated with ACC activity in the ESE contrast at (x = -6, y = 8, z = 45) r = 0.88, P < 0.005, and at (x = -4, y = 31, z = 41) r = 0.75, P < 0.005
work: Eisenberger, Lieberman & Williams (2003). Science 302(5643), 290-292. DOI 10.1126/science.1089134
note: Peak-voxel correlations chosen for the contrast. The file's 'observations, mine' flags inflation (standard account, voodoo-correlation critique) and small N. Not stable at N = 13 per the file.

statement: Eisenberger et al. (2003): anterior insula (x = 42, y = 16, z = 1) t = 4.07, r = 0.78, not associated with distress; right ventral PFC (x = 42, y = 27, z = -11) t = 4.26, r = 0.79 and (x = 37, y = 50, z = 1) t = 4.96, r = 0.83; RVPFC versus distress r = -0.68; RVPFC versus ACC r = -0.81
work: Eisenberger, Lieberman & Williams (2003). Science 302(5643), 290-292. DOI 10.1126/science.1089134
note: Statistics as read; no CIs. Validation did not re-read these values.

statement: Eisenberger et al. (2003): ACC mediates RVPFC to distress, Sobel Z = 3.16, P < 0.005; residual direct path beta = -0.17, P > 0.5
work: Eisenberger, Lieberman & Williams (2003). Science 302(5643), 290-292. DOI 10.1126/science.1089134
note: Regulation claim in the paper's own terms, read. Mediation statistics not re-read at validation.

statement: Eisenberger et al. (2003), ISE versus inclusion, ACC at (x = -6, y = 21, z = 41): t = 4.34, r = 0.78; no RVPFC activation even at P = .05; ACC registered exclusion but did not generate a self-regulatory response
work: Eisenberger, Lieberman & Williams (2003). Science 302(5643), 290-292. DOI 10.1126/science.1089134
note: Authors' interpretation: explicit awareness may be needed for attribution and regulation.

statement: Eisenberger et al. (2003), behavioural: participants felt ignored and excluded during ESE (t = 5.33, P < 0.05)
work: Eisenberger, Lieberman & Williams (2003). Science 302(5643), 290-292. DOI 10.1126/science.1089134
note: Self-report manipulation check.

statement: Eisenberger (2012) samples: OPRM1 study n = 125 genotyped, n = 30 scanned; endotoxin study n = 39; test statistics only, no effect sizes reported
work: Eisenberger (2012). The neural bases of social pain. Psychosomatic Medicine 74(2), 126-135. DOI 10.1097/psy.0b013e3182464dd1
note: Validation re-checked the sample figures against the text. The paper's argument predicts that pain sensitivity correlates across domains and that factors altering one alter the other (baseline heat, OPRM1, endotoxin, social support, acetaminophen). Only the first 100,000 of 110,859 characters were read.

statement: Rotge et al. (2015), meta-analysis of 46 articles and 940 subjects, mostly Cyberball: significant activation-likelihood in both ventral and dorsal ACC for social pain and self-reported distress; distress involves more specifically subgenual and pregenual ACC
work: Rotge, Lemogne, Hinfray, Huguet, Grynszpan, Tartour, George & Fossati (2015). SCAN 10(1), 19-27. DOI 10.1093/scan/nsu110
size_dependence: Children show greater subgenual than adult activation; a ventro-dorsal gradient is related to exclusion-phase length.
note: Abstract (read at validation); full paper not read. Cyberball engages anterior midcingulate to a lesser extent than other tasks.

statement: Kross et al. (2011): strong-rejection manipulation (viewing an ex-partner photo after an unwanted break-up) activated secondary somatosensory cortex and dorsal posterior insula; diagnostic of physical pain with positive predictive value up to 88% across 500+ studies
work: Kross, Berman, Mischel, Smith & Wager (2011). PNAS 108, 6270-6275. DOI 10.1073/pnas.1102693108
note: Abstract read. Sample sizes not obtained. The overlap is in sensory regions for strong rejection only.

statement: Wager et al. (2013), four studies, 114 participants: the pain signature discriminates heat from warmth at 93-94%; social versus physical pain at 85% sensitivity (CI 76-94) and 73% specificity (CI 61-84); 95% in a forced-choice test of which condition was more painful
work: Wager, Atlas, Lindquist, Roy, Woo & Kross (2013). An fMRI-based neurologic signature of physical pain. NEJM 368(15), 1388-1397. DOI 10.1056/nejmoa1204471
note: Abstract read; validation confirmed the 85%/73% figures and CIs against the abstract. Stimulus induction for social pain not described in the file.

statement: Woo et al. (2014), 60 participants: classifiers reach 92% (physical pain) and 80% (social rejection) out of sample, each at chance on the other; representations uncorrelated even within dACC; distinct connectivity (N = 91 resting-state); 'rather than co-opting pain circuitry, rejection involves distinct affective representations in humans'
work: Woo, Koban, Kross, Lindquist, Banich, Ruzic, Andrews-Hanna & Wager (2014). Separate neural representations for physical pain and social rejection. Nature Communications 5, 5380. DOI 10.1038/ncomms6380
note: Abstract read. The file's cross-check says Woo uses ex-partner photos rather than Cyberball.

statement: Lieberman & Eisenberger (2015), Neurosynth reverse inference across over 10,000 fMRI studies: the best psychological description of dACC function is related to pain processing, not executive, conflict or salience processing
work: Lieberman & Eisenberger (2015). PNAS 112, 15250-15255. DOI 10.1073/pnas.1515083112
note: Abstract read. Reverse inference from a meta-database, not an ostracism outcome, so scale n/a. Disputed by Yarkoni (see contradictions).

statement: Yarkoni's rebuttal (blog): z-scores are not probabilities; the 'pain' base rate in Neurosynth is about 3.5%, 'memory' about 16%, 'motor' about 18%; empirical-prior pain posteriors peak about 15-20% (posterior insula) and most dACC voxels are 10% or less; 'motor' posterior is higher than 'pain' throughout dACC; 'fear' has no voxels above 5%
work: Yarkoni, T. (Dec 2015). Blog post, talyarkoni.org. No DOI; not peer-reviewed
note: [secondary, read via fetch]. The file has not seen Lieberman & Eisenberger's reply in full.

statement: DeWall et al. (2010): acetaminophen reduced self-reported social pain over three weeks (Exp 1) and dACC and anterior insula responses to rejection (Exp 2)
work: DeWall et al. (2010). Psychological Science 21(7), 931-937. DOI 10.1177/0956797610374741
note: Abstract summary read. Sample sizes not retrieved; no preregistered replication found. Ethics n/a because the file does not describe consent terms for drug administration.

statement: Fairbairn et al. (2022), three studies, N = 438: alcohol administration did not reduce the ostracism effect on mood or need satisfaction in intoxicated versus sober participants
work: Fairbairn, Creswell, Hales, Williams & Wilkins (2022). Mixing misery and gin. Pers Soc Psychol Bull 48(8), 1269-1283. DOI 10.1177/01461672211038450
note: Corrected bibliographic details at validation (DOI, volume, pages). Abstract read. Supports 'difficult to diminish', the claim Hartgerink questions.

statement: Williams's signature moderation claim (reflexive measures moderated less than reflective measures) versus Hartgerink's data: first measures were moderated at least as much as last measures (first delta d = -0.46; last delta d = -0.20, not significant at .05)
work: Williams, K. D. (2007). Ostracism. Annual Review of Psychology 58, 425-452. DOI 10.1146/annurev.psych.58.110405.085641; Hartgerink, van Beest, Wicherts & Williams (2015). PLoS ONE 10(5), e0127002. DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0127002
note: Verdict as the file gives it: the proposition lacks support overall. Authors' alternative: many 'first' measures were not truly reflexive, and no fixed window defines either. That alternative is untested here; the composite need result (k = 3) shows the predicted pattern.

statement: 'Both first and last measures are susceptible to moderation' (Hartgerink abstract, quoted in 042 and 017) versus the last-measure point estimates, which are not significant at .05 in the main models
work: Hartgerink, van Beest, Wicherts & Williams (2015). PLoS ONE 10(5), e0127002. DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0127002

statement: Hartgerink last-measure figures: intercept d = -0.76 (time-predictor model) versus summary average -0.73; last-measure moderation -0.20 (time-predictor model) versus -0.19 (Table 3)
work: Hartgerink, van Beest, Wicherts & Williams (2015). PLoS ONE 10(5), e0127002. DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0127002
note: Verdict: resolved as two different models, not an internal inconsistency. 056 is right; 049 wrongly called the paper inconsistent. Both reported figures are kept.

statement: Hartgerink's headline first-measure effect given as 'd > |1.4|' in the abstract versus d = -1.36 with CI upper bound -1.54 in the Results
work: Hartgerink, van Beest, Wicherts & Williams (2015). PLoS ONE 10(5), e0127002. DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0127002
note: Verdict: rounding in the abstract versus the Results. Use d = -1.36 from the Results.

statement: Late stage label: 'resignation' (Williams 2009, per 042 and 017) versus 'acceptance' (Williams 2007, read)
work: Williams, K. D. (2009). Ostracism: a temporal need-threat model. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology 41, 275-314. DOI 10.1016/S0065-2601(08)00406-1; Williams, K. D. (2007). Ostracism. Annual Review of Psychology 58, 425-452. DOI 10.1146/annurev.psych.58.110405.085641
note: Verdict: unresolved. W09 was not read in any file, so 'resignation' is confirmed only through secondary descriptions. Treated as a labelling difference, not a conflict in claims. Page range 275-314 versus 279-314 also unresolved.

statement: Self-esteem after rejection: Gerber & Wheeler d = -0.70 (88 studies) versus Blackhart et al. 'no different from neutral controls' (192 studies)
work: Gerber, J. & Wheeler, L. (2009). Perspectives on Psychological Science 4, 468-488. DOI 10.1111/j.1745-6924.2009.01158.x; Blackhart, Nelson, Knowles & Baumeister (2009). Personality and Social Psychology Review 13, 269-309. DOI 10.1177/1088868309346065
note: Verdict: unresolved. Hypothesis, not a finding: Blackhart's larger set probably includes life-alone and similar paradigms, but neither inclusion criteria was read. Neither abstract gives CIs.

statement: Blackhart et al. (2009): rejection does not lower state self-esteem relative to a neutral control, a challenge to the sociometer's central prediction
work: Blackhart, Nelson, Knowles & Baumeister (2009). Personality and Social Psychology Review 13, 269-309. DOI 10.1177/1088868309346065; Leary, Tambor, Terdal & Downs (1995). JPSP 68(3), 518-530. DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.68.3.518
note: Verdict: unresolved in the file. Leary 1995 was not read, so the sociometer side is secondary only.

statement: Life-alone studies (Baumeister/Twenge) find no mood effect of exclusion, while Williams's need-threat account reads Cyberball as threatening mood and need together; Twenge finds aggression without mood change
work: Williams, K. D. (2007). Ostracism. Annual Review of Psychology 58, 425-452. DOI 10.1146/annurev.psych.58.110405.085641; Twenge, Baumeister, Tice & Stucke (2001). JPSP 81(6), 1058-1069. DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.81.6.1058
note: Verdict as the file gives it: these are two mechanisms, not one. Williams reads the life-alone null as helplessness-induced 'cognitive deconstruction'. The Twenge side is abstract-only (sa).

statement: The four need measures 'usually show high levels of intercorrelation' and there are 'few compelling reasons to separate' them (W07), while the model's fork requires them to separate in the response
work: Williams, K. D. (2007). Ostracism. Annual Review of Psychology 58, 425-452. DOI 10.1146/annurev.psych.58.110405.085641
note: Verdict: unresolved in the sources. Argues for a low-dimensional or single factor at the measurement level.

statement: dACC activity is a social-pain signal shared with physical pain (Eisenberger et al. 2003) versus separate neural representations: Woo et al. (2014) classifiers at chance on each other's condition, and Wager et al. (2013) separating the two at 73% specificity
work: Eisenberger, Lieberman & Williams (2003). Science 302(5643), 290-292. DOI 10.1126/science.1089134; Woo, Koban, Kross, Lindquist, Banich, Ruzic, Andrews-Hanna & Wager (2014). Nature Communications 5, 5380. DOI 10.1038/ncomms6380; Wager, Atlas, Lindquist, Roy, Woo & Kross (2013). NEJM 368(15), 1388-1397. DOI 10.1056/nejmoa1204471
note: Verdict as the file gives it: unresolved; the file's weight of evidence is against identical substrate. The control-loop claim does not need shared neural substrate, so this does not bear on the algebra.

statement: Dorsal-ACC-specific social-pain account (Eisenberger 2003; Somerville et al. 2006, known only through Eisenberger's editorial) versus Rotge et al. (2015): significant activation in both ventral and dorsal ACC, and the effect is not dACC-specific
work: Rotge, Lemogne, Hinfray, Huguet, Grynszpan, Tartour, George & Fossati (2015). SCAN 10(1), 19-27. DOI 10.1093/scan/nsu110; Eisenberger, Lieberman & Williams (2003). Science 302(5643), 290-292. DOI 10.1126/science.1089134
note: Verdict: unresolved. Eisenberger's SCAN editorial (read) calls the debate a 'pendulum' over decades, citing Kawamoto 2012 and Cooper 2014 (dACC still responsive) versus Masten 2009 and Bolling 2011 (vACC).

statement: Lieberman & Eisenberger (2015) reverse inference that dACC function is pain processing versus Yarkoni's rebuttal that the posterior probabilities are low and the 'motor' posterior exceeds 'pain' throughout dACC
work: Lieberman & Eisenberger (2015). PNAS 112, 15250-15255. DOI 10.1073/pnas.1515083112; Yarkoni, T. (Dec 2015). Blog post, talyarkoni.org. No DOI
note: Verdict: unresolved. Yarkoni's critique is a blog, not peer-reviewed, and Lieberman & Eisenberger's full reply was not obtained.

statement: Fairbairn et al. (2022): alcohol did not diminish the ostracism response, which sits oddly with a simple borrowed-pain-signal story that anaesthetics blunt, and with DeWall et al. (2010): acetaminophen reduced it
work: Fairbairn, Creswell, Hales, Williams & Wilkins (2022). PSPB 48(8), 1269-1283. DOI 10.1177/01461672211038450; DeWall et al. (2010). Psychological Science 21(7), 931-937. DOI 10.1177/0956797610374741
note: The file says 'sits oddly', not a verdict. Unresolved. DeWall sample sizes not retrieved.

statement: Gerber & Wheeler d = 1.21 prosocial condition given as 'can be restored' in 049 section 2 versus 'do not allow for control to be restored' in 056 section 3
work: Gerber, J. & Wheeler, L. (2009). Perspectives on Psychological Science 4, 468-488. DOI 10.1111/j.1745-6924.2009.01158.x
note: Verdict: resolved, 056 is right and 049's original wording was reversed. Checked against the Crossref abstract.

statement: Zadro's 45-minute recovery for high social anxiety attributed to 'Zadro et al.' in 049 versus Hartgerink's wording in 056, with Zadro (2004) interviews cited separately from W07
work: Hartgerink, van Beest, Wicherts & Williams (2015). PLoS ONE 10(5), e0127002. DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0127002; Williams, K. D. (2007). Ostracism. Annual Review of Psychology 58, 425-452. DOI 10.1146/annurev.psych.58.110405.085641
size_dependence: Recovery time for socially anxious participants: about 45 minutes (second-hand).
note: Verdict: no conflict. These are different Zadro works and should not be merged. The 45-minute figure is second-hand via Hartgerink.

statement: Guilt aversion: a player feels guilt in proportion to how far he believes he lets another player down relative to what that player expects, so utility depends on a second-order belief
work: Battigalli & Dufwenberg 2007, AER 97(2) 170-176, doi:10.1257/aer.97.2.170
size_dependence: Sensitivity theta varies across players; file says the effect is small and conditional, not a general law
note: Model section read in file 21, not in 057. File's verdict: real but conditional, heterogeneous and modest-sized causal driver.

statement: Promise-keeping per se: a preference to keep promises that is not reducible to changed payoff expectations (Vanberg's commitment-based explanation, CBE)
work: Vanberg 2008, Econometrica 76(6) 1467-1480, doi:10.3982/ECTA7673
size_dependence: Cell-dependent in the one replication (Di Bartolomeo et al. 2019)
note: Vanberg's claim is 'people have a preference for promise keeping per se'. Contested: see contradiction on CBE. File says the dispute is over what triggers guilt, not whether guilt exists.

statement: Positive surprise: guilt-averse players may also like to exceed others' expectations
work: Khalmetski, Ockenfels & Werner 2015, JET 159 163-208, doi:10.1016/j.jet.2015.05.008
note: Abstract-level only. Extends guilt aversion to positive surprise.

statement: Altruism term (delta_D / r) times (12 - pi_R(a)) to the power r, added to Ederer-Stremitzer's utility when estimating
work: Ederer & Stremitzer 2017, GEB 106 161-178, doi:10.1016/j.geb.2017.09.012
note: delta_D and theta_D identified per subject from first-order conditions at sigma = 0 and sigma = 1. Estimation device, not derived from theory. Symbol placement from reconstructed text.

statement: Second-order belief: i's belief about j's belief about i's action or about j's payoff
work: Battigalli & Dufwenberg 2007, AER 97(2) 170-176, doi:10.1257/aer.97.2.170
note: Operand of the guilt operator. Elicited in experiments as an average guess, not paired per player (Charness & Dufwenberg 2006).

statement: Guilt sensitivity theta_i >= 0: per-player parameter scaling the guilt term; Charness & Dufwenberg's gamma_B is the same role; Ederer-Stremitzer's gamma_D is theta in this file
size_dependence: Zero-inflated across dictators (see empirical result)
note: The theta symbol is this file's renaming; the paper's symbol is gamma_D. Charness & Dufwenberg assume sensitivity is independent of tau_B.

statement: Conditional guilt aversion: guilt is switched on only by a promise, with indicator sigma in {0,1} multiplying the guilt term
work: Ederer & Stremitzer 2017, GEB 106 161-178, doi:10.1016/j.geb.2017.09.012
size_dependence: Effect appears only under a promise in Ederer-Stremitzer; the 2019 own-promise null and no-promise effects in other studies count against the gate
note: Ederer-Stremitzer say their design was not suited to directly test conditional guilt aversion, and their gate is estimated, not independently tested.

statement: Simple guilt (Battigalli-Dufwenberg) versus guilt from blame: the two forms the vocabulary distinguishes; Ederer-Stremitzer use simple guilt
work: Battigalli & Dufwenberg 2007, AER 97(2) 170-176, doi:10.1257/aer.97.2.170
note: File gives no formula for guilt from blame.

statement: Expectations-based explanation (EBE): a promise changes behaviour through second-order expectations; commitment-based explanation (CBE): through a promise-keeping preference
work: Di Bartolomeo, Dufwenberg, Papa & Passarelli 2019, GEB 113 137-146, doi:10.1016/j.geb.2018.07.009
note: Authors say the two explanations are not mutually exclusive.

statement: False consensus: a trustworthy player believes others expect trustworthiness, so a belief-behaviour correlation can arise without guilt; it violates the independence of guilt sensitivity from the belief
work: Charness & Dufwenberg 2006, Econometrica 74(6) 1579-1601, doi:10.1111/j.1468-0262.2006.00719.x
note: Vanberg and Ellingsen et al. argue the correlation is explained equally well by false consensus; Charness & Dufwenberg concede this.

statement: Claim gate g(claim): 1 under a promise, and a small or zero value otherwise, multiplying the guilt term (file's proposed operator)
work: Ederer & Stremitzer 2017, GEB 106 161-178, doi:10.1016/j.geb.2017.09.012
size_dependence: Gate shape not tested; ES estimate effectively g(no promise) = 0
note: File's own proposal, not a source's formula. Keep g as a free parameter per file §4.

statement: Obligation(i -> j): a belief-independent term attached to a made promise, additive with Guilt (CBE)
work: Vanberg 2008, Econometrica 76(6) 1467-1480, doi:10.3982/ECTA7673
note: File's own proposal. Nobody has estimated its size separately from Guilt.

statement: Let-down(i -> j) = max(0, E_i[E_j[m_j]] - m_j(a_i))^k; base form max(0, E_j[m_j] - m_j)
work: Battigalli & Dufwenberg 2007, AER 97(2) 170-176, doi:10.1257/aer.97.2.170; Ederer & Stremitzer 2017, GEB 106 161-178, doi:10.1016/j.geb.2017.09.012
size_dependence: Hinge: zero above the level where shortfall is zero
note: ES form is read; base form read in Battigalli-Dufwenberg via file 21.

statement: Charness-Dufwenberg prediction: B's guilt is gamma_B * 10 * tau_B when B chooses Don't Roll; B rolls iff 14 - gamma_B * 10 * tau_B < 10, so higher tau_B raises the likelihood of Roll
work: Charness & Dufwenberg 2006, Econometrica 74(6) 1579-1601, doi:10.1111/j.1468-0262.2006.00719.x
note: Stated at p. 1583. Assumes guilt sensitivity independent of tau_B.

statement: U_D(a) = pi_D(a) - sigma * (theta_D / k) * (max{E[pi_R | mu_D(rho)] - pi_R(a), 0})^k = 14 - 4a - sigma * (theta_D / k) * 12^k * (max{mu_D(rho) - a, 0})^k, with pi_D(a) = 14 - 4a and pi_R(a) = 12a
work: Ederer & Stremitzer 2017, GEB 106 161-178, doi:10.1016/j.geb.2017.09.012
size_dependence: k = 1 nests Charness-Dufwenberg with corners; k > 1 gives interior solutions; data fit used r = k = 2
note: Reconstructed: Greek symbols lost in extraction; placement of sigma inferred from text. Check against the journal PDF before using theta or k placements in any algebra equation.

statement: Guilt(i -> j) = theta_i * g(claim_ij) * Let-down(i -> j) / k, the file's composition of the ES conditional structure
work: Ederer & Stremitzer 2017, GEB 106 161-178, doi:10.1016/j.geb.2017.09.012
note: File's own composition, not a source equation. Per file, nothing sa feeds an equation; this line should be upgraded or kept as a proposal.

statement: Derived prediction from the hinge: for a guilt-averse player, giving is non-decreasing in E_i[E_j[m_j]] and flat above the level at which the shortfall is zero, so correlation tests pooling the whole range dilute the effect
work: Battigalli & Dufwenberg 2007, AER 97(2) 170-176, doi:10.1257/aer.97.2.170
size_dependence: Flat above zero-shortfall level
note: Follows from the definitions, not a theorem. File says the empirical regularities are not theorems and that the sign-varying result of Khalmetski-Ockenfels-Werner is consistent with it.

statement: Existence of sequential equilibrium in the formal guilt-aversion game (the only formal result in the belief-based guilt literature the file records)
work: Battigalli & Dufwenberg 2007, AER 97(2) 170-176, doi:10.1257/aer.97.2.170; Battigalli & Dufwenberg 2009, JET 144(1) 1-35, doi:10.1016/j.jet.2008.01.004
note: Attributed to file 21, not read in 057. Existence says nothing about whether human guilt follows the functional form (file's cross-check of 21 line 207).

statement: Charness & Dufwenberg 2006: B's average guess of A's guess, Roll versus Don't Roll: 54.2 vs 39.6 (no messages, (5,5)); 73.2 vs 45.1 (B messages); 69.6 vs 50.0 (A messages); 69.4 vs 41.7 ((7,7), no messages); 66.9 vs 36.9 ((7,7), B messages); Z 1.99 to 3.52, one-tailed
work: Charness & Dufwenberg 2006, Econometrica 74(6) 1579-1601, doi:10.1111/j.1468-0262.2006.00719.x
size_dependence: Five treatments, 15 sessions, UCSB, 24-36 per session
note: Correlational: beliefs elicited after choices, averages over all A's not the paired A. File does not claim causation. Roll 67% vs 44% and In 74% vs 56% from the same paper.

statement: Charness & Dufwenberg 2006 promises: Roll 79% (38/48) after a promise vs 33% (14/43) without; A's guesses 64.4 vs 50.5 (p < 0.05 pooled), B's guesses 63.1 vs 54.7; promise raises A's guess about 27.5%
work: Charness & Dufwenberg 2006, Econometrica 74(6) 1579-1601, doi:10.1111/j.1468-0262.2006.00719.x
note: Paper itself says 'the effects are modest'. Promise is endogenous (chosen), not an exogenous shift.

statement: Vanberg 2008 partner-switch random dictator: Roll 69% (no switch) vs 54% (switched), Z 2.20, p 0.03; second-order belief 0.76 vs 0.71 (p 0.14); promised and not switched 73% (227/309) vs promised and switched with partner holding a promise 54% (129/238); the latter's second-order beliefs rose with partner promise (p 0.03) while Roll did not (p 0.60); logit coefficient on second-order belief positive and significant in every specification
work: Vanberg 2008, Econometrica 76(6) 1467-1480, doi:10.3982/ECTA7673
size_dependence: 192 subjects, 6 sessions, 8 rounds; 384 decisions per cell
note: Logit coefficient printed as 352 in extraction; file presumes 0.352 (decimal lost). Vanberg attributes the belief coefficient to guilt or false consensus. Not an exogenous belief shift for non-switched promisors.

statement: Ellingsen et al. disclosed-belief test: correlation between disclosed belief and donation is near zero, Pearson -0.075 (dictator, p 0.497), 0.085 (trust back-transfer, p 0.434), -0.071 (hidden-action, p 0.646); mean belief 41.6% among Rollers vs 45.7% among Don't Rollers (p 0.657)
work: Ellingsen, Johannesson, Tjøtta & Torsvik 2010, GEB 68(1) 95-107, doi:10.1016/j.geb.2009.04.021
size_dependence: Scandinavian students; file flags population specificity as a caveat
note: Read from the December 2007 working paper (WP 14/07), not the 2010 version. Robustness exclusion analyses range -0.026 to 0.122. 455 total across three experiments (171 + 196 + 88, including three monitors). File's corrected description of exclusions: dropping four all-givers and six high-belief cases gives 0.099 / 0.051.

statement: Reuben, Sapienza & Zingales 2009 lost-wallet game: low expectation (under $10) lowered return from $53.75 to $40.63 (Wilcoxon p 0.030; 54% reduced, 33% unchanged, 13% increased); high expectation (over $70) raised it from $52.14 to $58.29 (p 0.125, not significant); Tobit: low-expectation sender return $31.77 lower (43%)
work: Reuben, Sapienza & Zingales 2009, Economics Letters 104(2) 89-91, doi:10.1016/j.econlet.2009.04.007
size_dependence: Asymmetric: low expectation lowers giving, high does not significantly raise it
note: 52 Northwestern MBA students, within-subject; senders paid for expectation accuracy to discourage strategic reporting. Fits a hinge max(0, E - actual); also compatible with a social-norm reading.

statement: Ederer & Stremitzer 2017: mean contribution $5.76 (reliable device) vs $5.28 (unreliable), Wilcoxon p < 0.01, small in magnitude, driven by promisors; second-order beliefs 0.64 vs 0.53 (p < 0.01) yet first-order 0.28 vs 0.24 (p 0.15, n.s.); behaviour moved only under a promise
work: Ederer & Stremitzer 2017, GEB 106 161-178, doi:10.1016/j.geb.2017.09.012
size_dependence: Beliefs moved in all message conditions (no message 0.59/0.48, empty talk 0.59/0.43, promise 0.72/0.64) but behaviour only under promise; opt-out after promise 7.3% vs 21.6% after no message
note: 1,120 decisions. Among promisors whose choice differed across devices (not all promisors), 40% chose Don't Perform under unreliable vs 5% under reliable. Read as Cowles DP 1931R. Best single causal belief-channel evidence per file, but effect small.

statement: Ederer & Stremitzer 2017 estimated guilt sensitivity (r = k = 2): just under 50% of dictators have theta_D = 0, about 25% sit at a corner with theta_D >= 20, about 25% lie between; zero-inflated and bimodal
work: Ederer & Stremitzer 2017, GEB 106 161-178, doi:10.1016/j.geb.2017.09.012
size_dependence: Identified for the 104 dictators observed both with and without a promise
note: In-sample identification, not out-of-sample. Student sample. Gate estimated, not independently tested.

statement: Di Bartolomeo et al. 2019 manipulation and EBE test: promisors' second-order belief 0.80 (switch probability 25%) vs 0.66 (75%), Z 2.20, p 0.027; without promise 0.38 vs 0.40; non-switched promisors Roll 51% (high belief) vs 58% (low belief), Z 0.93, p 0.345, no support for EBE in own-promise cell
work: Di Bartolomeo, Dufwenberg, Papa & Passarelli 2019, GEB 113 137-146, doi:10.1016/j.geb.2018.07.009
size_dependence: Rome, December 2015; 192 subjects, 768 dictator decisions, 575 promises
note: Shifter works only under a promise. Authors' fn. 4 notes Vanberg's design cannot test the expectation channel for the non-switched promisor.

statement: Di Bartolomeo et al. 2019 CBE test: non-switched vs switched dictators both holding a promise: 58% vs 28% at 75% switching (Z 2.20, p 0.027, supports Vanberg); 51% vs 47% at 25% switching (Z 0.52, p 0.600, no support); CBE supported in one cell of two
work: Di Bartolomeo, Dufwenberg, Papa & Passarelli 2019, GEB 113 137-146, doi:10.1016/j.geb.2018.07.009
size_dependence: Replication cell-dependent: holds at 75% switching, not at 25%
note: Authors' own summary: 42% reneged in the cell with most promise-keeping (58%).

statement: Di Bartolomeo et al. 2019 guilt-aversion test among switched dictators: switched promisors facing a promise-holding recipient 47% (high belief) vs 28% (low), Z 1.99, p 0.046; switched non-promisors 29% vs 27%; at 25% switching, promise-holding recipient 47% vs 24% (p 0.046); at 75%, 28% vs 27%
work: Di Bartolomeo, Dufwenberg, Papa & Passarelli 2019, GEB 113 137-146, doi:10.1016/j.geb.2018.07.009
size_dependence: Supported in two of four cells, both with a promise-holding recipient
note: Table 5 summary: EBE no, CBE yes in one cell of two, GA yes in two cells of four.

statement: Di Bartolomeo, Dufwenberg & Papa 2023 (December 2021 working paper): unilateral B-to-A message in Charness-Dufwenberg's trust game, 226 undergraduates, 1,130 pairs, 527 promises: In 76% after a promise vs 49% without, Z 2.52, p 0.012; no support for CBE; results opposite of Vanberg's, supporting EBE
work: Di Bartolomeo, Dufwenberg & Papa 2023, JESA 9(1) 77-89, doi:10.1007/s40881-023-00128-4
size_dependence: Unilateral promise versus Vanberg's back-and-forth chat; authors' reconciliation
note: Read in Sapienza working paper No. 215, not the journal text (publisher bot wall); journal numbers could differ. Validation upgraded this from fetch summary to read.

statement: Khalmetski 2016 sender-receiver lying game: lying is significantly less frequent when receivers are expected to have higher payoff expectations, but only when the lying incentive is at a moderate level
size_dependence: Present only at moderate lying incentive
note: File tags read, but text read is abstract and conclusion of the Bath accepted manuscript. Use the manuscript wording 'high expectations can be rationalized from the sender's informational perspective', not the 'legitimate expectations' gloss, which is not in the paper.

statement: Khalmetski, Ockenfels & Werner 2015 dictator games: strong causal effect of recipients' expectations on dictators' transfers; correlation between transfers and expectations can be both positive and negative, obscuring the effect in the aggregate
work: Khalmetski, Ockenfels & Werner 2015, JET 159 163-208, doi:10.1016/j.jet.2015.05.008
size_dependence: Sign varies across subjects, so pooled correlation is uninformative
note: Abstract-level only; quotes checked against the accepted manuscript abstract. How expectations were varied not read.

statement: Bellemare, Sebald & Suetens 2018: about 60% of decision makers have stake-dependent guilt sensitivity; for that group, average sensitivities are significantly above zero at all stakes but decrease as stakes rise
work: Bellemare, Sebald & Suetens 2018, Experimental Economics 21(2) 316-336, doi:10.1007/s10683-017-9543-2
size_dependence: Sensitivity falls as stakes rise
note: Abstract-level only. 'Above zero at all stakes' applies to the 60% group only (validation narrowed it).

statement: Bellemare, Sebald & Suetens 2019: economic guilt sensitivity, identified while controlling for false consensus, has Spearman correlations above 0.2 in absolute value with TOSCA-3 in binary trust and dictator games, significant in both; no correlation with TOSCA-3's shame, externalization or detachment
work: Bellemare, Sebald & Suetens 2019, Journal of Economic Psychology 73 52-59, doi:10.1016/j.joep.2019.05.002
size_dependence: Individual-level measure
note: Read as the Copenhagen preprint (abstract and introduction only). Bracht & Regner 2013 came first as a bridge; the earlier claim that this was the only bridge is removed. Relevant to file 41's guilt row.

statement: Ismayilov & Potters 2016: promises appeared to raise trustworthiness, but a control treatment banning promises showed no drop in cooperation; conclude self-selection, cooperative trustees are the ones who promise
work: Ismayilov & Potters 2016, Experimental Economics 19(2) 382-393, doi:10.1007/s10683-015-9444-1
note: Abstract only. Year and venue resolved in validation.

statement: Schwartz, Spires & Young 2019: manipulated promise delivery and found no support for the internal consistency rationale; only delivered promises are relevant
work: Schwartz, Spires & Young 2019, Experimental Economics 22 530-551, doi:10.1007/s10683-018-9567-2
size_dependence: Only delivered promises matter
note: Abstract only. Not a same-game replication of a belief-shift result. Added in validation.

statement: Charness & Dufwenberg 2006 belief-behaviour correlation (Roll 67% vs 44%, belief gap significant in all treatments) as evidence for guilt aversion, versus the same correlation as explained by false consensus
work: Charness & Dufwenberg 2006, Econometrica 74(6) 1579-1601, doi:10.1111/j.1468-0262.2006.00719.x; Vanberg 2008, Econometrica 76(6) 1467-1480, doi:10.3982/ECTA7673
note: Side A: CD read the correlation as guilt aversion; they concede false consensus can explain it. Side B: Vanberg and Ellingsen et al. say false consensus explains it equally well. Verdict in file: correlation with elicited beliefs is not good evidence in either direction; causal evidence exists only where beliefs were shifted from outside. Status: open.

statement: Ellingsen et al. disclosed-belief null (no relationship between belief and giving in three experiments) versus Reuben et al. 2009 and the exogenous-shift studies (Ederer-Stremitzer, Khalmetski, Khalmetski-Ockenfels-Werner) that find effects
work: Ellingsen, Johannesson, Tjøtta & Torsvik 2010, GEB 68(1) 95-107, doi:10.1016/j.geb.2009.04.021; Reuben, Sapienza & Zingales 2009, Economics Letters 104(2) 89-91, doi:10.1016/j.econlet.2009.04.007
note: Side A: disclosed belief has near-zero correlation with giving, and the null is strong. Side B: exogenous shifts find small positive or sign-varying effects, and Reuben finds a one-sided effect. Verdict in file: not necessarily in conflict; different designs, and the ES effect exists only under a promise, which Ellingsen's games lack. File 21 calls the null contested; 057 says it is more than contested. Status: open.

statement: Vanberg 2008 promise-per-se effect (Roll 73% vs 54%, p 0.03) versus Di Bartolomeo et al. 2019 (replicated in one of two cells) versus Di Bartolomeo, Dufwenberg & Papa 2023 (opposite pattern, supports EBE)
work: Vanberg 2008, Econometrica 76(6) 1467-1480, doi:10.3982/ECTA7673; Di Bartolomeo, Dufwenberg, Papa & Passarelli 2019, GEB 113 137-146, doi:10.1016/j.geb.2018.07.009; Di Bartolomeo, Dufwenberg & Papa 2023, JESA 9(1) 77-89, doi:10.1007/s40881-023-00128-4
size_dependence: Cell-dependent: 2019 replicates at 75% switching (58 vs 28) but not 25% (51 vs 47)
note: Verdict in file: unresolved; no study cleanly measured both effects' magnitudes. Authors' reconciliation: Vanberg's back-and-forth chat tested informal agreements, not unilateral promises. Status: open.

statement: Ederer-Stremitzer promise gate (belief shifts without a promise did not move behaviour) versus Di Bartolomeo et al. 2019 own-promise null (51% vs 58%) and the no-promise effects in Reuben, Khalmetski and Khalmetski-Ockenfels-Werner
work: Ederer & Stremitzer 2017, GEB 106 161-178, doi:10.1016/j.geb.2017.09.012; Di Bartolomeo, Dufwenberg, Papa & Passarelli 2019, GEB 113 137-146, doi:10.1016/j.geb.2018.07.009; Reuben, Sapienza & Zingales 2009, Economics Letters 104(2) 89-91, doi:10.1016/j.econlet.2009.04.007
note: Verdict in file: the promise gate reconciles most apparent contradictions but not all; the 2019 own-promise null and the no-promise effects both count against it. Gate treated as an interpretation. Status: open.

statement: File 21 lists Charness & Dufwenberg 2011 'Participation' as supporting guilt aversion (guilt from blame), while file 057 classes it as a reciprocity or status model that does not test the second-order-belief channel
note: Neither file read the paper; the AER abstract could not be checked. Verdict in file: unresolved. Do not use either characterisation until the abstract is read.

statement: File 057 states neither file mentions Vanberg 2008, while file 21 lists Vanberg as the main rival to guilt aversion in its further reading
work: Vanberg 2008, Econometrica 76(6) 1467-1480, doi:10.3982/ECTA7673
note: Verdict in file: 057 is partly wrong; file 21 names Vanberg with no content and no confirmed DOI. Suggested wording: File 21 lists Vanberg only as unread further reading. Not edited elsewhere.

statement: File 21 line 207 presents guilt and anger as two drives with a belief-based mechanism and theorems, while file 057 says the theorems do not show human guilt follows the functional form
work: Battigalli & Dufwenberg 2007, AER 97(2) 170-176, doi:10.1257/aer.97.2.170
note: Verdict in file: 21 overstates what is proved; 21's own later validation weakened its claims, so the two are compatible.

statement: File 41 implies the dispositional-guilt prosociality figure (r = .13, k = 63) bears on the economic guilt parameter, while file 057 finds the economic sensitivity correlates with TOSCA-3 (Spearman above 0.2 in absolute value)
work: Bellemare, Sebald & Suetens 2019, Journal of Economic Psychology 73 52-59, doi:10.1016/j.joep.2019.05.002
note: Verdict in file: the bridge runs in the opposite direction from what 41 implies; the r = .13 figure and the economic parameter may be measuring related traits. Unresolved.

statement: File 21 cites a 2017 GEB Bellemare, Sebald & Suetens paper (doi 10.1016/j.geb.2016.11.002) as an exogenous belief-shift study, not read, while file 057 cites the 2018 and 2019 Bellemare papers
work: Bellemare, Sebald & Suetens 2019, Journal of Economic Psychology 73 52-59, doi:10.1016/j.joep.2019.05.002
note: Verdict in file: not a conflict; different papers by the same authors. 057 does not cover the 2017 paper, so its exogenous-shift list is incomplete on this point.

statement: drive: restoration or defence of status/reputation (masculine reputation), the drive the insult operator acts on
work: Cohen, Nisbett, Bowdle & Schwarz 1996, JPSP 70(5) 945-960, doi 10.1037/0022-3514.70.5.945
note: Named as the drive in the file's Drives/operands line, from abstract/summary; primary text not read. Group parameter is region of upbringing.

statement: dominance/status as the driver: violence typically arises when someone wants dominance, even without a substantive grievance
work: Gould 2003, Collision of Wills, doi 10.7208/chicago/9780226305516.001.0001
note: Abstract/summary level; book not read.

statement: reputation and self-protection under weak state protection (herding origin)
note: Cohen & Nisbett 1994 abstract (Crossref) says Southern white males endorse violence conditionally, for self-protection, defence of honour and socialising children. Book not read.

statement: retaliation for social-identity threat (the authors' interpretation of school violence in honour states)
work: Brown, Osterman & Barnes 2009, Psychological Science 20(11) 1400-1405, doi 10.1111/j.1467-9280.2009.02456.x
note: Interpretation by the authors, from the Crossref abstract; drive-like rather than a formal drive.

statement: sanction and solidarity display: vengeance as a purposeful sanction against collective aggression and a display of the aggrieved family's cohesion
work: Gould 2000, Revenge as sanction and solidarity display, ASR 65(5) 682-704, doi 10.1177/000312240006500504
note: Framing from the abstract, which the file records as read via Crossref; Gould calls vendettas highly strategic yet altruistic.

statement: retaliation threshold theta: a person parameter that the algebra would introduce as a free parameter; the response-curve crossing point, observable only as a step between two groups
note: No source states a retaliation threshold as a number or an equation; it is a construct inferred from the pattern. The algebra introduces the parameter rather than importing it. 25 (B2) has the same threshold parameter per the Cross-checks section.

statement: retaliation threshold is a function theta(person, culture, situation), not a universal scalar; the same trait maps onto behaviour differently under honour, face and dignity logics
note: The file's own reading of the abstract (the only seed warning against a scalar threshold). 058 Cross-checks say 25 (B2 Evidence) agrees: the typology cuts against reading culture as one scalar.

statement: insult(a,b) is a state-changing operator on b's reputation operand
note: The file's translation into algebra notation, not the source's own notation. The paper gives only the verbal cycle. Cross-checks say 25 uses insult(a,b) and retaliate(b,a).

statement: insult(a,b) raises b's response where rank(a,b) is ambiguous and lowers it where rank is settled
work: Gould 2003, Collision of Wills, doi 10.7208/chicago/9780226305516.001.0001
note: [my inference] by 058, a reading of Gould's thesis rather than a stated result; the book was not read.

statement: rank ambiguity: disputes arise when the ordering of a pair is unsettled, and people fight to settle it; conflict is more likely between social equals or friends than between people whose rank is settled
work: Gould 2003, Collision of Wills, doi 10.7208/chicago/9780226305516.001.0001
note: Abstract/summary level. Cross-checks say 39 (section 13) also takes Gould's comparative static: conflict peaks where rank is ambiguous, between near-equals.

statement: honour as a real stake: an insult is felt as dishonour even absent concrete harm
work: Gould 2003, Collision of Wills, doi 10.7208/chicago/9780226305516.001.0001
note: The file marks this as publisher/blurb level.

statement: contest(a,b) settles an ambiguous rank; avenge(g1,g2) is conditioned on collaborative aggression (verbal operators)
note: Verbal operators from the file's reading. No formal model found. Cross-checks say 39 uses Avenge/Settle (Boehm), a different naming.

statement: side_with(c,a), mediate(c; a,b), ignore: third-party operators, where a third-party function maps a dyadic dispute and an observer configuration to escalation or settlement
work: Cooney 1998, Warriors and Peacemakers, doi 10.18574/nyu/9780814723678.001.0001
note: Verbal operators; the file calls this the part of the literature closest to an algebraic object. Cross-checks say 39 and 058 both frame a third party or settlement operator as the thing that breaks the cycle.

statement: lambda: insult rate, insults per person per unit time
work: none (candidate formalisation)
note: [my inference], not from any source. Unvalidated; offered only because the direction asked how insult rates feed violence.

statement: insult-aggression cycle (verbal): an insult diminishes the man's reputation and he responds with aggression or dominance to restore it
note: Verbal only; no formal statement or derivation, from abstract/summary.

statement: prediction: region by insult interaction on threat appraisal, physiology and aggression
note: Verbal prediction, no formal derivation. Its tests are the Cohen 1996 empirical-result lines in this ledger batch.

statement: herding hypothesis (verbal law): mobile wealth lost overnight plus weak state protection yields a reputation of toughness and a low private threshold for responding to insult; Scots-Irish settlers carried it to the South and to western areas
note: Shape from abstract/summary. The herding origin is a historical inference (058 Empirical standing). Cross-checks say 25 also treats the origin story as a historical inference.

statement: institutions in honour-culture regions treat honour-related violence more leniently
note: Verbal prediction; field evidence is in the Cohen & Nisbett 1997 empirical-result line.

statement: individual men's norm-endorsement predicts response to insult
note: Verbal prediction. Partial support only from IJzerman et al. 2007, a different country, N = 42, unconfirmed.

statement: P(conflict) is higher in symmetric dyads than in asymmetric ones
work: Gould 2003, Collision of Wills, doi 10.7208/chicago/9780226305516.001.0001
size_dependence: interaction frequency between equals (contact or exposure); not known whether Gould conditions on it
note: Stated as a testable empirical regularity, not a deduction. Base-rate problem unresolved: interactions between equals are more frequent.

statement: revenge probability depends on the group character of the original act (collaboration, violence against non-disputants), not on the injury alone
note: Testable regularity, not a deduction. Rests on a single Corsican court-records case.

statement: violence is explained by who surrounds the killer and victim (family, friends, neighbours, onlookers, police, judges), not by their own characteristics
work: Cooney 1998, Warriors and Peacemakers, doi 10.18574/nyu/9780814723678.001.0001
note: Summary level, from the book's description; the file says the book was not read.

statement: branching escalation: r = F(s; theta, c) is the response probability, k is the mean follow-on provocations per retaliation, m = r * k; chains die out for m < 1 and can sustain feuds for m >= 1
work: none (candidate formalisation)
note: [my inference], not from any source; unvalidated. No data in the sources constrains k, and there is no source test of an m threshold. The file says nobody should mistake it for a literature result.

statement: violent story endings, region by insult interaction: F(1,78) = 7.65, p < .005; means 2.30 (Southern insult), 1.40 (Southern control), 1.73 (Northern insult), 2.05 (Northern control)
size_dependence: region of upbringing (Southern or Northern) is the group parameter
note: Figures from Schimmack's 2019 audit (secondary), re-checked against it. Study 2, a different scenario, found no significant effects (all F < 1). Lab only; no out-of-sample test.

statement: chicken game, +3,-1,-1,-1 focused contrast (insulted Southerners against the other three cells): t(142) = 3.45, p < .001; distances about 3 ft for insulted Southerners, 9 ft for uninsulted Southerners, 5 ft for Northerners
size_dependence: region of upbringing
note: The only result the audit calls clearly significant. A focused contrast, not an omnibus interaction. Lab only.

statement: self-reported anger, Southerners 3.05 vs Northerners 2.34: F(41) = 1.61, p between .10 and .15, not significant
size_dependence: region of upbringing
note: Audit says Experiments 2 and 3 gave weak and inconsistent anger results, so none of the three studies significantly supports the anger claim. Conflicts with the 25 snippet that says Southern men 'were more upset' (see contradictions).

statement: hormones, planned contrasts only: cortisol t(165) = 2.14, p < .03; testosterone t(165) = 2.19, p < .03; testosterone change +12% insulted Southerners, +4% control Southerners, +6% insulted Northerners, +4% control Northerners
size_dependence: region of upbringing
note: Cortisol percentages (+79%, +42%, +33%) are unconfirmed: absent from the audit, untraceable, inconsistent across summaries. Effects appear only in planned contrasts, not omnibus tests.

statement: no replication, registered report or meta-analysis of the 1996 insult experiments found
note: An absence claim from the original author's two searches; the validation pass could not re-test it because the search budget was spent. The audit states the experiments have never been replicated, to its author's knowledge.

statement: insulted men who endorsed honour norms reported more anger and less joy, fear and resignation than insulted low-honour men (Dutch train-station field experiment, N = 42)
work: IJzerman, van Dijk & Gallucci 2007, Emotion 7(4) 869-875, doi 10.1037/1528-3542.7.4.869
size_dependence: individual honour-norm endorsement, not region
note: N = 42 and the results come from a search summary, unconfirmed against the paper. Individual differences in another country; not a replication of the regional effect. Scale chosen as nearest category: individual norm conformity.

statement: argument-related homicide among white males is more common in the South and in western regions initially settled by southerners; the gap is not fully explained by poverty and not present for felony homicide
size_dependence: regional composition; ecological-fallacy caveat at population level; confounds named as economics, guns, climate, migration
note: Observational and correlational. The file calls the regional homicide pattern the sturdiest claim in the seeds. Nisbett 1993 abstract was elided by the publisher; the pattern is from summaries and the 1997 university summary.

statement: Southern white males endorse violence conditionally, for self-protection, defence of honour and socialising children, not unconditionally; the authors tie this to Southern gun ownership and homicide types
size_dependence: regional composition

statement: employers and newspapers respond more sympathetically to honour-related killing in the South and West: Southern and western firms gave more understanding and warmth to an applicant who had killed in an honour conflict, with controls showing the sympathy was specific to honour violence; newspapers wrote more sympathetic, justifying stories about a stabbing after a family insult
size_dependence: region
note: Covert field letters and planted news facts. Sample sizes and tests not seen. Study details are abstract-level.

statement: county-level FBI Supplementary Homicide Reports 1983-1998, argument-related White male offenders: positive interaction of 1850 Presbyterian-church share with 1850 cattle and pigs per capita; negative effect of 1850 crop production
work: Baller, Zevenbergen & Messner 2009, JRCD 46(3) 275-300, doi 10.1177/0022427809335164

note: The authors call the result highly consistent with the herding thesis. Correlational, county-level, abstract-level only.

statement: controlling for demographics, high-school students in honour states were more likely to report bringing a weapon to school in the past month; honour states had more than twice as many school shootings per capita over 20 years
work: Brown, Osterman & Barnes 2009, Psychological Science 20(11) 1400-1405, doi 10.1111/j.1467-9280.2009.02456.x
size_dependence: state-level; 'honour state' is the authors' classification

statement: vengeance was rare, typically occurring when the original incident involved collaboration or violence against non-disputants; it rarely extended beyond the nuclear family, and when it did, distant kin were the actors; targets were chosen on specific acts of solidarity, and revenge was calibrated to show the aggrieved family's cohesion equalled the offender group's
size_dependence: kin reach: nuclear family, distant kin only occasionally
note: Corsican court records, a single case. Gould calls vendettas highly strategic yet altruistic. Against the picture of honour as an automatic low-threshold reflex (see contradictions).

statement: homicide flourishes when authority is very strong or very weak, when third-party ties are strong, and when group boundaries are sharply defined; violence is non-monotonic in authority (U-shape)
size_dependence: third-party tie strength, boundary sharpness and authority strength
note: Social control of homicide in over 30 societies, plus interviews with several dozen prisoners, from library and CV descriptions. The file cannot tell whether the U-shape is statistical or typological. No quantitative test confirmed. Phillips & Cooney 2005 abstract not obtained.

statement: the same individual type who is most helpful, honest and likely to act with integrity in one cultural logic (honour, face or dignity) is least likely to do so in another (two experiments)
size_dependence: cultural logic (honour, face, dignity)
note: Abstract read. Traits, sample sizes and effect sizes not obtained. The definitions of the three logics come from summaries, not the abstract. Cited for measurement follow-up by Yao et al. 2017, listed by search only.

statement: relative to Whites in northern states, White populations in southern and western states have higher intimate-partner violence, more school shootings and lower mental-health help-seeking

Cite 058's wording (anger n.s.; cortisol and testosterone only in planned contrasts).

note: Both sides: 39 (rank ambiguity, Corsican records) vs 058 (Gould 2000 conditional revenge). Verdict per the file: compatible, since they are different Gould works (2003 book vs ASR 2000 paper) on the same data. No file is wrong. 39 does not mention the conditionality, so cite both together.

statement: Uninfluenced set point P* = a/(1 - r): the level a speaker would hold if the partner's score were zero (1995 'set point', 1999 'steady state')
work: Cook, Tyson, White, Rushe, Gottman & Murray 1995, Journal of Family Psychology 9(2):110-130, doi 10.1037/0893-3200.9.2.110; Gottman, Swanson & Murray 1999, Journal of Family Psychology 13(1):3-19, doi 10.1037/0893-3200.13.1.3
