note: The file says no drive is modelled anywhere in the papers; the drive reading (homeostatic set point, nearest to Keramati-Gutkin D = |H* - H| in file 47) is the file's own §8 mapping, not a source claim. The 1999 paper says the set point mixes enduring individual and prior-relationship (spillover) components.

statement: Emotional inertia r: the lag-one autoregression coefficient of a speaker's own series (relaxation rate 1 - r toward the set point)
work: Cook et al. 1995, Journal of Family Psychology 9(2):110-130, doi 10.1037/0893-3200.9.2.110; Gottman, Swanson & Murray 1999, Journal of Family Psychology 13(1):3-19, doi 10.1037/0893-3200.13.1.3
size_dependence: Estimated per speaker per couple; 1999 husband inertia about 0.3 to 0.4 in the newlywed sample
note: Cook links inertia to arousal as a hypothesis only. The file's identification of inertia with drive recovery speed is its own §8 mapping (medium strength).

statement: Negativity threshold K_- and positivity threshold K_+: the partner-score levels at which an S-shaped influence function starts to have an effect
work: Gottman, Swanson & Murray 1999, Journal of Family Psychology 13(1):3-19, doi 10.1037/0893-3200.13.1.3; Gottman, Levenson, Swanson, Swanson, Tyson & Yoshimoto 2003, Journal of Homosexuality 45(1):65-91, doi 10.1300/J082v45n01_04
size_dependence: Fitted from an ogive on 150 six-second blocks per spouse; the file calls this the weak link (averaged over few observations at the extremes)
note: A threshold on the partner's input, not on the agent's own drive. The 1999 paper states that a 'more negative' negativity threshold means a husband must become more hostile before the wife responds. Its mapping to a dead-zone or fear-trigger is the file's §8 candidate, not sourced.

statement: Repair term E_R R(K): an upward jump in the series when partner negativity crosses the threshold K, with effectiveness E; described by the authors as a communication strength
work: Gottman, Levenson, Swanson, Swanson, Tyson & Yoshimoto 2003, Journal of Homosexuality 45(1):65-91, doi 10.1300/J082v45n01_04

note: The exact trigger function R is not given in the paper; it defers to the 2002 book, not read. The regulatory-controller reading (Powers-style) is the file's §8 candidate, and the file notes repair is an additive jump, not a feedback law.

statement: Damping term E_D D(K): a mirror of repair that reduces the positive effect of positive affect after a positivity threshold K is crossed; described by the authors as a communication deficit
work: Gottman, Levenson, Swanson, Swanson, Tyson & Yoshimoto 2003, Journal of Homosexuality 45(1):65-91, doi 10.1300/J082v45n01_04

note: The paper says the sign of the damping measure is expected to be negative and that its magnitude matters. The file's §8 'brake on over-positivity' reading is its own (weak mapping); the authors say they 'do not yet fully understand' it.

statement: Marital negativity detector: the 1999 label for a low-magnitude (smaller absolute value) negativity threshold, i.e. a spouse who responds to milder negativity
work: Gottman, Swanson & Murray 1999, Journal of Family Psychology 13(1):3-19, doi 10.1037/0893-3200.13.1.3
size_dependence: Stable husbands mean -5.36 vs divorced -7.71 (125 couples)
note: Label, not a separate measured quantity. The file reads it as the same finding as 'good couples react early' in another vocabulary.

statement: 1999 in-sample: uninfluenced steady state separates stable from divorced couples: wife 0.51 vs -2.26, F(1,123) = 14.86 p < .001; husband 0.72 vs -1.89, F(1,123) = 18.40 p < .001 (108 stable vs 17 divorced)

statement: 1999 in-sample: no out-of-sample test of the Gottman-Swanson-Murray divorce-prediction parameters was found in the papers read

note: The file states this as 'not found in the papers read', not as a search-tested negative (the web-search budget ran out before this claim could be checked).

statement: 1999 in-sample: husband negativity threshold -7.71 (divorced) vs -5.36 (stable), F(1,123) = 8.25 p < .01; wife negativity threshold -6.06 vs -6.23, F = 0.03 (n.s.)

statement: 2003 model with repair and damping: N_{t+1} = r1 N_t + a + I_{P->N}(P_t) + E_PR R(K_P) + E_PD D(K_P); P_{t+1} = r2 P_t + b + I_{N->P}(N_t) + E_NR R(K_N) + E_ND D(K_N)

statement: Estimation: influence functions are zero at zero partner score; by least squares fit W_{t+1} = r1 W_t + a on the subset H = 0 and H_{t+1} = r2 H_t + b on the subset W = 0; residuals I_HW = W_{t+1} - r1 W_t - a and I_WH = H_{t+1} - r2 H_t - b are then fitted by an ogive with six parameters per influence function (A to F)
work: Gottman, Swanson & Murray 1999, Journal of Family Psychology 13(1):3-19, doi 10.1037/0893-3200.13.1.3; Cook et al. 1995, doi 10.1037/0893-3200.9.2.110

note: The ogive formula is not printed in the 1999 paper (named parameters only) and is deferred to the book. Cook's footnote 7 calls the zero-influence assumption 'arbitrary' and suggests nonzero influences could be estimated; asymmetry 'would be theoretically interesting'.

statement: Bilinear (two-slope) influence function: two straight lines through the origin, one slope for positive partner scores and one for negative; differences in slopes are the operational definition of power in the relationship
work: Gottman, Levenson, Swanson, Swanson, Tyson & Yoshimoto 2003, Journal of Homosexuality 45(1):65-91, doi 10.1300/J082v45n01_04; Cook et al. 1995, doi 10.1037/0893-3200.9.2.110

statement: Sigmoid (ogive) influence function: zero inside a band around zero, a bounded constant beyond a positivity threshold and a bounded negative constant beyond a negativity threshold
work: Gottman, Swanson & Murray 1999, Journal of Family Psychology 13(1):3-19, doi 10.1037/0893-3200.13.1.3

statement: Experiment versus simulation: no effect of data origin (Group 1 F(1,12) = 0.206, p = 0.658; Group 2 F(1,12) = 0.619, p = 0.447); topology effect present in both; Complete and Star above Ring and Path (Bonferroni p < 0.01)

statement: Drive-like state: the agent's state is the pair (x, x'), with x the displacement from equilibrium and x' its rate; the oscillator is second order, so drive level and its velocity are both state.
work: Hu, Boker, Neale & Klump (2014), doi 10.1037/a0032476
note: The displacement-from-equilibrium definition is read (Hu Eq. 1). The reading of (x, x') as the algebra's operand is the file's own untagged translation (§7), so sa.

statement: Fear mapping: a partner's fear level acts as the displacement-coupling operator S (company pulls my setpoint toward theirs); the partner's rate of change of arousal acts as the velocity-coupling operator F.
work: none; interpretive reading by the file's author
note: The file says explicitly this is an interpretive reading, not something the sources fit to fear data. No intervention is proposed.

statement: Candidate control parameter for a drive analogue of HKB: possibly the tempo of the drive cycle (how fast the drive cycles through arousal and reduction).
work: none; analogy to Kelso (2008) frequency control parameter
note: Named by the file as needing a choice; no source tested drive tempo as a control parameter.

statement: Single damped linear oscillator: x'' = eta*x + zeta*x' + e, with x the displacement from equilibrium, eta the regression coefficient of x on x'', zeta that of x' on x''.
work: Hu, Boker, Neale & Klump (2014), doi 10.1037/a0032476
note: Read at source (PMC7480173, validated 2026-10-29). Single-agent form; the regression reading of eta and zeta is as Hu et al. state it.

statement: Oscillation requires eta < 0 and eta + zeta^2/4 < 0 (Hu et al.'s wording).
work: Hu, Boker, Neale & Klump (2014), doi 10.1037/a0032476
note: Validated against PMC7480173.

statement: Period of the single oscillator: lambda = 2*pi / sqrt(-(eta + zeta^2/4)) (Hu Eq. 2).
work: Hu, Boker, Neale & Klump (2014), doi 10.1037/a0032476
note: Validated against PMC7480173.

statement: Unidirectional coupling of x onto y (Hu Eq. 4): x'' = eta_x*x + zeta_x*x' + e_x; y'' = eta_y*y + zeta_y*y' + gamma_x*x + gamma_xdot*x' + e_y.
work: Hu, Boker, Neale & Klump (2014), doi 10.1037/a0032476
size_dependence: Dyad only; the file treats no more than two oscillators in this family.
note: Validated against PMC7480173. Coupling is between two variables of one person in Hu's data, but the same form is applied to a dyad in the Boker model.

statement: Bidirectional case: two single oscillators plus coupling terms in both directions, described as the intrinsic regulation of each variable and the extrinsic drive from the other.
work: Hu, Boker, Neale & Klump (2014), doi 10.1037/a0032476
note: Text read; their Figure 3 image was not read.

statement: rties dyadic model: per dyad and partner type, the second derivative is regressed on own state, own first derivative, partner state and partner first derivative, with no intercept, giving 8 parameters.
work: Butler & Kuelz, rties R package vignette coupled_oscillator_V05 (github.com/cran/rties); no DOI in file
size_dependence: Per dyad and per partner type.
note: Raw Rmd read in validation; quoted labels and the 8-parameter count confirmed.

statement: Symmetric bidirectional dyad (x'' = eta*x + zeta*x' + gamma*y + g*y'; y'' = eta*y + zeta*y' + gamma*x + g*x'): sum and difference modes decouple, u = x+y with u'' = (eta+gamma)u + (zeta+g)u', and v = x-y with v'' = (eta-gamma)v + (zeta-g)v'.
work: derived in 061; not published by the cited sources
size_dependence: Symmetric linear two-member case only.
note: [derived], the file's own algebra from read equations. Validation log: re-derived and correct. Per rule, provenance sa because not tagged [read].

statement: Stability of the symmetric linear dyad: both modes are stable iff zeta + |g| < 0 and eta + |gamma| < 0 (from zeta+g<0, zeta-g<0, eta+gamma<0, eta-gamma<0).
work: derived in 061; no source states it (061 §8)
size_dependence: Two-member symmetric linear case only; n of three or more not covered.
note: [derived]. Validation log: re-derived and correct. The file calls this the one small theorem available and says it is its own, not the literature's.

statement: Velocity-coupling sign effect in the symmetric dyad: the in-phase mode has damping coefficient zeta+g and the anti-phase mode zeta-g, so g>0 makes the in-phase mode the less damped (first to amplify) and g<0 does the same for the anti-phase mode.
work: derived in 061
size_dependence: Symmetric linear two-member case.
note: [derived]. The file says this is consistent with the Hu et al. sign results (g>0 synchronising, g<0 desynchronising).

statement: Displacement coupling in the symmetric dyad shifts mode frequencies to eta +/- gamma, producing beating, and can destabilise: if eta + |gamma| >= 0, one mode has no restoring force.
work: derived in 061
size_dependence: Symmetric linear two-member case.
note: [derived]. Softened in validation: displacement coupling does not change mode damping in the symmetric case (the earlier 'does not change energy balance' was dropped).

statement: Steady-state transfer function for y driven by x = cos(w t): H = (gamma_x + i*w*gamma_xdot) / (-w^2 - eta_y - i*w*zeta_y). At resonance (w^2 = -eta_y) with zeta_y<0, velocity coupling gives net 0 degrees (in phase), displacement coupling gives net -90 degrees (y lags x a quarter cycle).
work: derived in 061, checked against Hu et al. (2014) sign results
size_dependence: Agreement with Hu's offsets holds at resonance only; away from resonance the offsets differ.
note: [derived]. Validation log: steady-state transfer function and resonance phases re-derived and correct.

statement: HKB coupled-oscillator system: x1'' + x1'(alpha*x1^2 + beta*x1'^2 - gamma) + omega^2*x1 = I12, with I12 = (a + b*(x1 - x2)^2)*(x1' - x2'), and the symmetric equation for x2 with I21.
work: Avitabile, Slowinski, Bardy & Tsaneva-Atanasova (2016), doi 10.1007/s00422-016-0691-9; Slowinski, Al-Ramadhani & Tsaneva-Atanasova (2020), doi 10.1137/19M1279381
note: The self term is a hybrid Van der Pol (alpha) and Rayleigh (beta) limit-cycle oscillator, not the linear oscillator of §1. HKB's coupling is state-dependent in gain; the Boker term is constant gain at the same place (acceleration).

statement: Delayed HKB coupling: (x_i'(t) - x_j'(t - tau_j))*(a + b*(x_i(t) - x_j(t - tau_j))^2).
work: Slowinski, Al-Ramadhani & Tsaneva-Atanasova (2020), doi 10.1137/19M1279381 (credits HKB 1985 and Varlet et al. 2012)
size_dependence: Depends on delay tau.
note: Read in PMC6986925 during validation. Credit corrected: the delayed form F is Varlet et al. (2012), not Banerjee & Jirsa.

statement: HKB sign result, at fixed intrinsic parameters: in the first quadrant (a, b both positive) anti-phase is the only stable state; in the third quadrant (both negative) in-phase is stable and anti-phase unstable; phase-locked intermediate relative phases are stable in the fourth quadrant and unstable in the second.
work: Avitabile, Slowinski, Bardy & Tsaneva-Atanasova (2016), doi 10.1007/s00422-016-0691-9
size_dependence: Depends on the fixed intrinsic parameters of the source.
note: Validation correction: the first quadrant is anti-phase only, not converse bistability; phase-locked states are stable only in the fourth quadrant.

statement: Reduced relative-phase equation: phi' = -a*sin(phi) - 2b*sin(2phi), with potential V(phi) = -a*cos(phi) - b*cos(2phi); rescaled to phi' = -sin(phi) - 2k*sin(2phi) with k = b/a.
work: Kelso (2008), Scholarpedia 3(10):1612 (no DOI in file)
size_dependence: k corresponds to the cycle-to-cycle period, so k falls as movement frequency rises (frequency is the control parameter).
note: Read at source in validation. The a and b of the reduced equation are not the coupling coefficients of I12.

statement: Both in-phase (phi = 0) and anti-phase (phi = pi) are stable for k > 0.25; at the critical k_c = 0.25 anti-phase loses stability and the system switches to in-phase, with hysteresis.
work: Kelso (2008), Scholarpedia 3(10):1612 (no DOI in file)
size_dependence: Threshold k_c = 0.25 is a property of the reduced equation.
note: Hysteresis confirmed in validation.

statement: Mapping from coupling to reduced parameters: for coupling (x1' - x2')*(alpha + beta*(x1 - x2)^2) and oscillation amplitude r, a_red = -(alpha + 2*beta*r^2) and b_red = beta*r^2/2; the classical bistable regime (a_red, b_red > 0) needs beta > 0 and alpha < -2*beta*r^2.
work: Kelso (2008), Scholarpedia 3(10):1612 (no DOI in file)
size_dependence: Depends on amplitude r.
note: Added in validation (previously an Unconfirmed item). The sign flip on a is explicit.

statement: A constant-gain linear velocity coupling alone (the Boker-style term) does not produce the HKB transition: HKB 1985 considered and rejected linear couplings of position and its first-order derivative as inadequate.
work: Kelso (2008), Scholarpedia 3(10):1612 (no DOI in file), citing Haken, Kelso & Bunz (1985), doi 10.1007/BF00336922
note: A model-comparison result (what HKB's model predicts), not a data test. HKB 1985 itself was not read; the claim is as Kelso reports it.

statement: Slowinski et al. (2020) model comparison against published finger-movement findings: the phenomenological coupling F gives only a qualitative account of the loss of anti-phase stability as frequency rises; the neurologically motivated coupling G (with cross-talk r, nonlinearity delta, strength eps and delays tau) gives a quantitative account of both the amplitude drop and the loss of anti-phase stability.
work: Slowinski, Al-Ramadhani & Tsaneva-Atanasova (2020), doi 10.1137/19M1279381; G credited to Banerjee & Jirsa (2007), doi 10.1007/s00422-006-0114-4
size_dependence: Depends on delta, r, eps and tau.
note: Model comparison against published findings, not new experiments. Banerjee & Jirsa fixed delta = 1; Slowinski et al. free it. Read in PMC6986925 during validation.

statement: With tau = 0.08 s the model shows sizeable parameter ranges where bistable in-phase/anti-phase at low omega gives way to in-phase only as omega rises.
work: Slowinski, Al-Ramadhani & Tsaneva-Atanasova (2020), doi 10.1137/19M1279381
size_dependence: Depends on tau = 0.08 s and on omega.
note: Model result; validation confirmed parameter values and tau = 0.08 s.

statement: Delay increases the size of parameter regions of bistability (in-phase and anti-phase coexisting).
work: Slowinski, Tsaneva-Atanasova & Krauskopf (2016), Eur. Phys. J. Spec. Top. 225:2591-2600, doi 10.1140/epjst/e2015-50327-6
size_dependence: Depends on delay.
note: The 2016 paper was not read; the claim is taken from the 2020 paper's restatement, which was read. Validation credit corrected to Slowinski, Tsaneva-Atanasova & Krauskopf (2016).

statement: Negative a and b in HKB's coupling mean dissipative coupling on the velocity difference that damps any difference between the two oscillators; mapped to the Section 4 notation, the partner-velocity coefficient is g = -a, so negative a is g > 0.
work: derived in 061 from Avitabile et al. (2016), doi 10.1007/s00422-016-0691-9
note: The quadrant results are read; the dissipative gloss and g = -a are the file's own [derived] reading. Consistent with, not identical to, the Boker-style term (HKB's gain is state-dependent and its self term is a limit cycle).

statement: Hu et al. simulation of phase effects: gamma_xdot > 0 gives phase synchronisation of y to x (0 degree offset); gamma_xdot < 0 gives phase desynchronisation (180 degree offset); gamma_x > 0 drags y back (270 degree offset); gamma_x < 0 pushes y forward (90 degree offset). Both nonzero: an offset set by the signs and relative sizes.
work: Hu, Boker, Neale & Klump (2014), doi 10.1037/a0032476
size_dependence: Offset depends on relative sizes of gamma_x and gamma_xdot when both are nonzero; magnitude sets how fast y is (de)synchronised.
note: Simulation, not data. Validated against PMC7480173. The derived transfer function agrees at resonance only.

statement: Identifiability in simulation: when eta_x = eta_y the estimation breaks down. Accurate estimation held only for gamma_xdot in roughly -0.1 to 0.1 and gamma_x in roughly -0.02 to 0.02 at eta about -0.05, with gamma_x systematically over-estimated.
work: Hu, Boker, Neale & Klump (2014), doi 10.1037/a0032476
size_dependence: Breaks down when partners' intrinsic frequencies are equal; ranges specific to the simulated condition (eta about -0.05).
note: Ranges and over-estimation validated against PMC7480173. Practical meaning (the file's reading, sa): partner coupling is estimable only when partners' tempos differ and coupling is smaller than self-regulation.

statement: Hu et al. twin data (Klump et al. 2012 study: 198 female twins, 45 days of ratings and salivary hormones; 181 with ovulatory cycles analysed): AIC 2271.8 with all four coupling terms, 2268.4 with velocity coupling only, 2281.6 uncoupled. The velocity-only model fits best.
work: Hu, Boker, Neale & Klump (2014), doi 10.1037/a0032476
note: In-sample AIC on one person's variables (estradiol, emotional eating, negative affect), not a dyad. Validation corrected the sample: the earlier '63 women' was wrong.

statement: Hu et al. coupling estimates: estradiol velocity into eating 0.049 (SE 0.016, p < .05); eating velocity into estradiol -0.062 (SE 0.022, p < .05). Authors' interpretation: estradiol synchronizes eating and eating desynchronizes estradiol.
work: Hu, Boker, Neale & Klump (2014), doi 10.1037/a0032476

statement: Between-person shuffle test (one person's hormones paired with another, non-twin, person's eating): coupling estimates peaked at zero, with an interval excluding the observed effect.
work: Hu, Boker, Neale & Klump (2014), doi 10.1037/a0032476
note: Control for the twin result. Description tightened in validation.

statement: rties example data: the coupled model explains on average R^2 = 0.72 versus 0.69 for the uncoupled model, a gain of about 2%; the vignette says coupling is not critical for describing the dynamics but may predict system variables better.

note: An illustration on the package's example data, not a finding (the file's own reading). Validated in the raw Rmd.

statement: Partner-velocity parameters in the rties dyadic model are highly sensitive to the derivative-estimation settings tau and embed.
work: Butler & Kuelz, rties vignette coupled_oscillator_V05 (github.com/cran/rties)
size_dependence: Depends on derivative-estimation settings tau and embed.
note: Vignette wording confirmed in validation.

work: Helm, Sbarra & Ferrer (2012), Emotion 12(4):748-762, doi 10.1037/a0025036
note: Abstract level only; no sample size or effect sizes read; no open full text.

statement: HKB behavioural result for finger and limb movement: switch from anti-phase to in-phase coordination as movement frequency rises, with hysteresis.

Hu et al. read partner displacement as shifting frequency/phase and partner velocity as shifting damping.

note: Labels quoted from the raw rties Rmd. Negative own-derivative = damping (convergence to homeostatic levels); positive = amplification; zero = constant amplitude.

statement: Co-regulation: partners' mutual influence has a homeostatic effect, resulting in both partners returning to a stable set-point following some disruption.
work: Butler & Kuelz, rties vignette coupled_oscillator_V05 (github.com/cran/rties), citing Butler & Randall (2013) and Reed, Barnard & Butler (2015)

statement: Co-dysregulation: partners' mutual influence results in increasingly volatile fluctuations away from a set-point.
work: Butler & Kuelz, rties vignette coupled_oscillator_V05 (github.com/cran/rties), citing Butler & Randall (2013) and Reed, Barnard & Butler (2015)

statement: Sign convention of the damped oscillator: Hu's eta = -k and zeta = -c map the textbook form x'' + c*x' + k*x = 0 (c, k > 0) onto eta < 0 for regulation and zeta < 0 for damping; eta > 0 means no regulation.

statement: V_i = D^i(x_0) + (γ−1)·S_i − (tail term vanishing for bounded D^i as the horizon grows), holding pointwise on each trajectory for any dynamics and joint policy
work: 062 own derivation, no source

statement: argmax_{π_i} V_i(π_i, π_{−i}) = argmin_{π_i} S_i(π_i, π_{−i}) for every π_{−i}
work: 062 own derivation, no source

statement: The Nash equilibrium sets of the reward game and of the drive game are identical; with a random x_0 whose law does not depend on policies, the same holds in expectation
work: 062 own derivation, no source

statement: If reward at step t uses weight w_t, r_t = D(x_t; w_t) − D(x_{t+1}; w_t), the sum differs from the telescoped drive sum by Σ_{t≥1} γ^{t−1}(w_t − w_{t−1})·D_{p,t}
work: 062 own derivation, no source

work: 062 own derivation, no source

work: 062 own derivation, no source

statement: D^i(x) = Σ_j W_ij·D_j(x_j); r^i_t = β_i·Σ_j W_ij·ρ^j_t, with ρ^j_t = D_j(x_{j,t}) − D_j(x_{j,t+1}); linear in W
work: 062 own derivation, no source
note: [derived] The worked model uses the separable own drive D_i = Σ_k x_{i,k}^2 (n=2, m=1).

statement: Symmetric equilibrium effort e(w) = a·b·v / (k² + N·b²·v), with v = 1 + (N−1)·w and total effort g = N·e, from e_i(k² + b²v_i) = b·v_i·(a − b·Σ_{j≠i} e_j)
work: 062 own derivation, no source
size_dependence: Depends on N through v and N·b²·v; stated for the symmetric case only
note: [derived] Selfish w = 0: e_0 = ab/(k² + Nb²). Team w = 1: e_1 = abN/(k² + N²b²), the team optimum (unique minimiser).

statement: Free-riding ratio (selfish total effort over team total effort): g_0/g_1 = (k² + N²b²) / (N·(k² + N·b²))
work: 062 own derivation, no source
size_dependence: Tends to 1/N as k²/b² → ∞; equals 1 as k → 0; strictly below 1 for N ≥ 2 and k > 0
note: [derived] Numeric check: the file labels these TOTAL efforts g_0, g_0.5, g_1 (not ratios). N=2, a=b=k=1: 0.667, 0.750, 0.800; N=5, same: 0.833, 0.9375, 0.9615. N=2, b=1, k=3, w=0: ratio 0.591. Shortfall vs team total: 6% at w=0.5, 17% at w=0.

statement: Sharing game (one unit R held by agent 1, deficits d_1, d_2): c* = (d_1 − w·d_2 + w·R)/(1 + w); passed amount R − c* = (R − d_1 + w·d_2)/(1 + w), positive iff w·d_2 > d_1 − R
work: 062 own derivation, no source
size_dependence: Threshold depends on the partner's deficit d_2; with equal deficits the critical weight is w = 1 − R/d, below which no sharing is optimal
note: [derived] Corrected in validation: the earlier wording 'whatever the partner's deficit' was false. The paper tested only w = 0.5 (read); the threshold is not in the paper.

statement: Gradient-play Jacobian J = 2k²·I + 2b²·v·1ᵀ has eigenvalues 2k² (multiplicity N−1) and 2k² + 2b²·Σ_i v_i; all positive for nonnegative couplings, so gradient play is locally and, for this linear system, globally asymptotically stable at the Nash equilibrium
work: 062 own derivation, no source
note: [derived] Numeric N=2, w=(0,1), k=0.5: eigenvalues 0.5 and 6.5. Stability is named by dynamics; not assumed for deep-RL PPO with LSTM (§5.3).

statement: Exact potential iff ∂²U_i/∂e_i∂e_j = ∂²U_j/∂e_j∂e_i, i.e. v_i = v_j; equal coupling weights give a potential game whose minimiser is the equilibrium
work: Monderer & Shapley 1996, doi:10.1006/game.1996.0044
note: [from abstract/standard account]. Corrected: 'maximiser' changed to 'minimiser' because the U_i are costs. 23 §9 says 'maximiser' for payoffs (same statement, opposite sign convention). Applying it to a continuous game is a scope issue: see contradiction 4.

statement: With weights r_i = 1/v_i, diag(1/v)·J = 2k²·diag(1/v) + 2b²·11ᵀ has a positive definite symmetric part for every positive v; the unweighted symmetric part can go negative
size_dependence: Unequal weights make the unweighted symmetric part indefinite for small k
note: [standard account; Rosen not opened] Corrected: the earlier 'uniqueness only for equal weights or large k' was wrong. Numeric N=2, w=(0,1), b=1: unweighted smallest symmetric eigenvalue 0.338 at k=0.5 and −0.082 at k=0.2; weighted with v=(1,2), k=0.2: 0.060.

statement: Jacobi best-response iteration converges iff (N−2)·b²·v < k², with v = 1 + (N−1)·w; spectral radius (N−1)·s with s = b²v/(k² + b²v)
work: 062 own derivation, no source
size_dependence: N = 2 always converges for nonnegative coupling; for N > 2 it fails once group size or coupling is large; coupling lowers the threshold

statement: Damped update e ← (1−α)e + α·BR(e) converges iff α < 2/(1 + (N−1)·s) in the symmetric case
work: 062 own derivation, no source
size_dependence: Bound depends on N through (N−1)·s
note: [derived] Corrected in validation from 'learning rate small relative to 1/(1 + b²v/k²)', which is not sufficient in general (e.g. s = 0.5, N = 10). Sequential updating also restores convergence.

statement: For w < −1/(N−1) (so v < 0) the constrained solution is e = 0; for −1/(N−1) < w < 0 the interior formula holds and effort falls continuously below the selfish level
work: 062 own derivation, no source
note: [derived] Example N=2, w=−0.5, a=b=k=1: e = 0.25 per agent against 0.333 at w = 0.

statement: Σ_i V_i = Σ_j c_j·(agent j's own-reward return), with column sum c_j = Σ_i W_ij; for symmetric equal weights c_j = 1 + (N−1)·w
work: 062 own derivation, no source

work: none (project assumption, Aldred's target)

statement: General model: x(t+1) = A(t, x(t)) x(t), with a_ij >= 0 and sum_j a_ij = 1 (self-weight included)
work: Hegselmann & Krause 2002, JASSS 5(3), 2 (no DOI)
note: Unifying object for the classical, Friedkin-Johnsen, time-variant and bounded-confidence variants.

statement: Classical (French-DeGroot): x(t+1) = A x(t), with A fixed and stochastic
work: Hegselmann & Krause 2002, JASSS 5(3), 2 (no DOI)
note: DeGroot is the unanchored case, G = 0 in H&K notation, lambda_i = 1 in P&T notation.

statement: Friedkin-Johnsen: x(t+1) = G x(0) + (I - G) A x(t), G = diag(g_i), 0 <= g_i <= 1
work: Hegselmann & Krause 2002, JASSS 5(3), 2 (no DOI); Friedkin & Johnsen 1990, doi:10.1080/0022250X.1990.9990069 (not read)
note: P&T form x(k+1) = Lambda W x(k) + (I - Lambda) u (P&T 2017 eq. 20) is the same model with u = x(0) as the special case.

statement: Bounded confidence: I(i,x) = { j : |x_i - x_j| <= eps_i }, and x_i(t+1) = |I(i,x(t))|^(-1) sum_{j in I(i,x(t))} x_j(t)
work: Hegselmann & Krause 2002, JASSS 5(3), 2 (no DOI)
note: Weight a_ij(x) = 1/|I| on I and 0 off it; state-dependent, so not linear.

statement: Theorem 1 (H&K Appendix): for every x(0) there is c with x_i(t) -> c for all i; holds if any two agents share some k with a_ik > 0 and a_jk > 0 (DeGroot 1974); holds iff some power A^(t0) has a strictly positive column (Berger 1981)
work: Hegselmann & Krause 2002, JASSS 5(3), 2 (no DOI); DeGroot 1974, doi:10.1080/01621459.1974.10480137 (not read)
note: DeGroot 1974 read only as restated in H&K and P&T.

statement: Theorem 2 (H&K Appendix): with A in Gantmacher normal form, lim x(t) exists for every x(0) iff every diagonal block A_i is primitive, equivalently 1 is the only root of A of modulus 1; consensus iff g = 1 and A_1 primitive; only essential agents' initial opinions matter
work: Hegselmann & Krause 2002, JASSS 5(3), 2 (no DOI)
note: Read at source in the H&K appendix.

statement: Theorem 12 (P&T 2017): x(k+1) = W x(k) is convergent iff all closed strong components of G[W] are aperiodic; it reaches consensus iff G[W] is quasi-strongly connected and the only closed strong component is aperiodic
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002
note: Cited by P&T to refs [10, 86].

statement: Corollary 13 (P&T 2017): if all self-weights w_ii > 0, the model is convergent, and reaches consensus iff G[W] is quasi-strongly connected
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002
note: P&T say the second part was proved in Harary 1959 and included without proof in [53]; see the Harary contradiction below.

statement: Under full regularity, x(k) -> (p_inf^T x(0)) 1, with p_inf the left eigenvector of W (P&T eq. 8)
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002
note: p_inf,i is French's measure of social power, the weight of x_i(0) in the final group opinion.

statement: Contraction: min_i x_i(k) is non-decreasing and max_i x_i(k) is non-increasing, so the profile stays in the convex hull of the initial profile; the system is Lyapunov stable but not asymptotically stable (eigenvalue 1)
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002
note: Gives bounded drive levels for free when drives start inside a range.

statement: Corollary 14 (P&T 2017): with s >= 1 totally stubborn source agents reaching all others, the model converges and the limit is determined by the stubborn agents' opinions; with exactly one, consensus on its opinion; with two or more, consensus among them is impossible
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002
size_dependence: Depends on the number of totally stubborn sources (one gives consensus, two or more do not).
note: The limit is fixed by whoever holds the sources, so it steers others without their consent.

statement: Theorem 3 (H&K Appendix, credited to Friedkin & Johnsen 1990): with M = (I - G)A and G != 0, A irreducible, x(inf) = (I - M)^(-1) G x(0) for every x(0); consensus iff x_i(0) = c for all i with g_i > 0
work: Hegselmann & Krause 2002, JASSS 5(3), 2 (no DOI); Friedkin & Johnsen 1990, doi:10.1080/0022250X.1990.9990069 (not read)
note: Statement read as restated in H&K; the 1990 paper itself was not read. H&K gloss: consensus only for very special initial profiles when degrees are positive.

statement: Theorem 21 (P&T 2017): on the P-dependent block, Lambda^11 W^11 is Schur stable (spectral radius < 1); the full model is convergent iff r = n or the P-independent block W^22 is regular; the limit is x(inf) = V [u^1; x^2(inf)] with V stochastic
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002
note: P&T say this is formulated in refs [19, 125] without rigorous proof; the final opinion of each agent is a convex combination of prejudices and P-independent final opinions.

statement: Corollaries 22-23 (P&T 2017): the model is asymptotically stable iff every agent is P-dependent, then V = (I - Lambda W)^(-1)(I - Lambda); it holds if Lambda < I, or Lambda != I and W irreducible; convergence iff A = Lambda W is regular
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002
note: Cor 22 is the file's source for the convergence margin; 74's lambda_i < 1 statement is a special case of it.

statement: Continuous-time forms: Abelson dx/dt = -L[A] x; Taylor with anchor dx/dt = -(L[A] + Gamma) x + Gamma u, Gamma = diag(gamma_i) >= 0
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002
note: Agent i is prejudiced if gamma_i > 0; stubborn if u_i = x_i(0) and a_ij = 0. Neither file reads Taylor 1968.

statement: Theorem 18 and Corollary 19 (P&T 2017, continuous time): -(L11 + Gamma11) is Hurwitz on the P-dependent block, with x^1(inf) = M [u^1; x^2(inf)], M stochastic; -(L[A] + Gamma) is Hurwitz iff every agent is P-dependent
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002
note: Continuous analogue of Theorem 21 and Corollary 22.

statement: Theorem 20 (P&T 2017, containment): for the vector Taylor model with k static leaders in R^d, the following are equivalent: Hurwitz stability; every agent is directly or indirectly influenced by a leader; every agent's final position lies in the convex hull of the leaders for every choice of leaders and initial conditions
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002 (citing their ref [115])
note: Proof by projection: for any v, v^T x_i follows the scalar model. This is why the linear theorems extend to vectors. Hypothesis list not checked against ref [115].

statement: Scalar bounded confidence (symmetric uniform eps): order of opinions is preserved; a split with |x_i - x_j| > eps persists forever; if consensus is approached the initial profile is an eps-profile; for n = 2, 3, 4 consensus iff eps-profile; false for n = 5; true for an equidistant eps-profile at n = 5; false for n = 6
work: Hegselmann & Krause 2002, JASSS 5(3), 2 (no DOI)
size_dependence: Consensus depends on n (n = 2, 3, 4 versus 5 and 6).
note: Properties credited to Krause 2000 in H&K section 3D; H&K state consensus in finite time if there is any.

statement: Theorem 5 and Theorem 6 (H&K Appendix): consensus in finite time under a confidence-chain condition over windows; for every initial profile there are a finite t* and a partition into maximal subgroups, each in exact consensus for t >= t*
work: Hegselmann & Krause 2002, JASSS 5(3), 2 (no DOI)
note: Theorem 6 first proved by Dittmer 2000/2001. Fragmentation into finitely many clusters is a theorem; cluster count and location are simulated.

statement: Theorem 13 (P&T 2018): vector bounded confidence with trust set I_i(x) = { j : ||x_j - x_i|| <= d } reaches a fixed point in finitely many steps for any norm; best known bound 2n^4 steps for m >= 2 (Euclidean); lower bound Omega(n^2)
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2018, Part II, Annual Reviews in Control 45, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2018.03.005
size_dependence: Step bound 2n^4 grows with the number of agents n.
note: Components can merge as well as split in m >= 2 (R^3 tetrahedron example reaches consensus in 3 steps); the file's 'mystery' remarks are in §4.2.

statement: Lemma 14 (P&T 2018): with weights phi(||x_j - x_i||) on phi in {0} U [a, b] and phi(0) > 0, convergence holds without finite-time termination
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2018, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2018.03.005
note: Heterophily kernels were reported to facilitate consensus, cited to ref [143] by P&T.

statement: Theorem 17 (P&T 2018, truth-seeking bounded confidence): the opinions of all truth seekers (lambda_i < 1) converge to T; the remaining agents either converge to T or freeze at a value with |x_i - T| >= d
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2018, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2018.03.005 (citing [82, 98] and the scalar case [153, 154])
note: Convergence is asymptotic, not finite-time. Open: consensus at T in the presence of non-seekers. P&T's lambda notation is swapped here (see contradiction).

statement: Theorem 18 (P&T 2018, Chazelle & Wang 2017 inertial HK): x_i(t+1) = (1 - lambda_i) x_i(t) + (lambda_i/|I_i|) sum_{j in I_i} x_j; if every lambda_i is in {0, 1} the opinions converge
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2018, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2018.03.005; Chazelle & Wang 2017, doi:10.1109/TAC.2016.2644266
note: Unlike Theorem 17, stubborn agents need not share one opinion. P&T do not state convergence for general lambda_i in (0,1) with heterogeneous anchors.

statement: Theorem 19 (P&T 2018): asymmetric scalar intervals [x_i - d + eta_i, x_i + d] with eta = max eta_i < d terminate in finite time
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2018, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2018.03.005 (citing [133, 146])
note: Heterogeneous left and right endpoints in general are described by P&T as 'still waiting for thorough analysis'.

statement: Result from P&T 2018 (citing Chazelle): general directed state-dependent influence graphs can be chaotic or even Turing-complete, though not robustly
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2018, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2018.03.005 (citing Chazelle)
note: Stated as a warning on directed state-dependent graphs, not a formula; the Chazelle source was not read.

statement: Parsegov et al. 2017 eq. 17 (multi-issue FJ): x_i(k+1) = lambda_ii C sum_j w_ij x_j(k) + (1 - lambda_ii) u_i, with C in R^(m x m) the matrix of multi-issue dependence structure; stacked form x(k+1) = [(Lambda W) (x) C] x(k) + [(I_n - Lambda) (x) I_m] u
work: Parsegov, Proskurnikov, Tempo & Friedkin 2017, IEEE Trans. Autom. Control 62(5), doi:10.1109/TAC.2016.2613905
note: C is applied after averaging the neighbours and not to the prejudice term; C is the same for all agents and independent of the network. C = I_m gives ordinary FJ. Founding source of the C-coupled model (see contradiction).

statement: Theorem 2 (Parsegov et al. 2017, stability): the model is stable iff rho(Lambda W) rho(C) < 1; the limit is x'_C = (I_mn - Lambda W (x) C)^(-1) [(I_n - Lambda) (x) I_m] u (eq. 23)
work: Parsegov, Proskurnikov, Tempo & Friedkin 2017, doi:10.1109/TAC.2016.2613905
note: If rho(C) = 1, stability equals plain FJ stability (no oblivious agents). Proof via the Kronecker spectrum lemma. Proofs in the appendix were skimmed, not verified line by line.

statement: Remark 2 (Parsegov et al. 2017): stability holds whenever the FJ model is stable and C is row-stochastic or ||C||_inf <= 1, and also whenever rho(C) < rho(Lambda W)^(-1); these conditions are sufficient, not necessary
work: Parsegov, Proskurnikov, Tempo & Friedkin 2017, doi:10.1109/TAC.2016.2613905
note: Consequence noted by the file: stubbornness buys room for self-amplifying drive coupling (rho(C) > 1). Untested whether human drive coupling has this form. The file proposes a cheap simulation check of this remark.

statement: Theorem 3 (Parsegov et al. 2017, convergence): with n' < n non-oblivious agents, the model converges iff C is regular and either C_inf = 0 or W^22 is regular; the limit has a block formula (eq. 24)
work: Parsegov, Proskurnikov, Tempo & Friedkin 2017, doi:10.1109/TAC.2016.2613905
note: Block formula not transcribed in the file.

statement: Remark 1 (Parsegov et al. 2017, invariance): if C is row-stochastic, box constraints [a, b] on every component are preserved; [0,1]^m needs C substochastic; [-1,1]^m needs ||C||_inf <= 1; any convex set D with C D contained in D is invariant
work: Parsegov, Proskurnikov, Tempo & Friedkin 2017, doi:10.1109/TAC.2016.2613905
note: Bounded drive levels follow from this when C is stochastic or substochastic.

statement: Remark 3 (Parsegov et al. 2017): a general initial-state map x_i(0) = D u_i leaves the stability and convergence conditions unchanged and changes only the formula for the limit
work: Parsegov, Proskurnikov, Tempo & Friedkin 2017, doi:10.1109/TAC.2016.2613905
note: Relevant to the algebra's choice of initial state versus anchor.

statement: Kronecker composition law: rho(Lambda W (x) C) = rho(Lambda W) rho(C), so the social and intra-personal stability margins multiply
work: Parsegov, Proskurnikov, Tempo & Friedkin 2017, doi:10.1109/TAC.2016.2613905 (via the Kronecker spectrum lemma, Lemma 4)
note: The file calls this the nearest thing in the family to a theorem about composing two kinds of operator, and the result most worth carrying into the algebra.

statement: Per-drive decoupling: if x^d(k+1) = Lambda_d W_d x^d(k) + (I - Lambda_d) u^d for each drive d, the system is m decoupled scalar FJ systems, and the column-wise theorems apply
work: Parsegov, Proskurnikov, Tempo & Friedkin 2017, doi:10.1109/TAC.2016.2613905; Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002
note: The file's derivation from read theorems. Using different W_d per drive keeps decoupling but gives m influence graphs rather than one.

statement: Equilibrium factorisation: the equilibrium drive is V U with V = (I - Lambda W)^(-1)(I - Lambda), a fixed operator depending only on (Lambda, W), so equilibrium is linear in the baselines U
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002 (Corollary 22)
note: The file's operator-on-operands reading, V as operator and U as operand.

statement: Control via P-dependence: steering an individual to the convex hull of the sources needs only that it be reachable from a source
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002 (Corollary 19, Theorem 20)
note: The target is the hull of the sources, not an arbitrary point. The file links this to notes/2026-10-29-drives-as-the-core.md.

statement: Virtual controller (McClelland): two control loops holding one shared variable at different references act as one controller whose gain is the sum of the competitors' gains and whose reference lies between theirs
work: McClelland 2004, The collective control of perceptions: constructing order from conflict, Int. J. Human-Computer Studies 60, doi:10.1016/j.ijhcs.2003.08.003 (not read)
note: Search and secondary only (Taylor's PCT page, a 1993 talk); the equation form was not verified. This is the only control-loop item, not averaging; it cannot feed an equation.

statement: FJ-family model is experimentally validated for small and medium-size groups (reviewers' claim quoted by P&T 2017 section 6, citing refs [19, 93, 125-127])
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002
size_dependence: Validated for small and medium groups only, per the claim.
note: Validations are by Friedkin and co-workers; independence open (D210). No effect sizes or out-of-sample test are recorded in the file.

statement: Parsegov et al. 2017 Example 2: a four-person group's influence matrix W, reconstructed from real data by the method of Friedkin & Johnsen 1999, is used to test the model
work: Parsegov, Proskurnikov, Tempo & Friedkin 2017, doi:10.1109/TAC.2016.2613905 (its ref [15] = Friedkin & Johnsen 1999, Advances in Group Processes 16, 1-29)
size_dependence: Four persons only.
note: Same network as H&K's example, so it is Friedkin and Johnsen's own data, not an independent test. The 2016 Science paper is a different work, now ruled out as the ref [15] (see validation log).

statement: Worked example: initial opinions (25, 25, 75, 85) go to (60, 60, 75, 75) under FJ on the four-agent network
work: Hegselmann & Krause 2002, JASSS 5(3), 2 (no DOI), citing Friedkin & Johnsen 1999 p. 6
size_dependence: Four agents.
note: A prediction on Friedkin and Johnsen's own data, not out of sample; no error reported in the file.

statement: Abelson's diversity puzzle: the DeGroot consensus prediction is at odds with bimodal opinion outcomes; Abelson 1964 quoted as asking 'what on earth one must assume in order to generate the bimodal outcome'
work: Hegselmann & Krause 2002, JASSS 5(3), 2 (no DOI), quoting Abelson 1964
note: The file states this as a puzzle, not a fit to data.

statement: Truth-seeker simulation: for some d, consensus is reached with few stubborn individuals and destroyed as their number increases (non-monotone in the number of stubborn agents)
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2018, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2018.03.005, quoting ref [82] (Hegselmann & Krause 2015, doi:10.3934/nhm.2015.10.477)
size_dependence: Non-monotone in the number of stubborn agents.
note: Simulation finding only, not an out-of-sample prediction.

statement: Cluster count and location for scalar and vector bounded confidence (and anchored variants): simulated, not proved; scalar phase diagrams over eps, asymmetric intervals and cluster count as a function of n and eps are simulation
work: Hegselmann & Krause 2002, JASSS 5(3), 2 (no DOI); Proskurnikov & Tempo 2018, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2018.03.005
size_dependence: Number of clusters depends on n and eps (simulated).
note: H&K say rigorous analytical results are difficult to obtain in the nonlinear case.

statement: Small additive noise destroys clusters in the HK model and leads to quasi-consensus; non-local random interactions restore disagreement; numerical HK is sensitive to floating-point inaccuracy
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2018, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2018.03.005 (citing ref [163] and ref [82])
note: Method behind these findings is not stated in the file; it is a reason the discontinuous trust set is fragile.

statement: Experimental support for DeGroot-type updating exists
work: none cited in the file (points to file 05 and direction D210)
note: Unsourced in this file; left to file 05 and D210 and not verified here.

statement: Parsegov et al. 2017 identification Example 6 uses hypothetical final opinions, and the paper's numerical examples are illustrative; no application of the C-coupled model to measured data was found
work: Parsegov, Proskurnikov, Tempo & Friedkin 2017, doi:10.1109/TAC.2016.2613905
note: Negative finding: no fit to measured multi-issue data, and for drives no dataset with both W and a multi-drive state was observed.

statement: Operand: a pair (agent, drive vector x_i in R^m_{>=0}) with an anchor u_i in R^m and a susceptibility lambda_i in [0,1] (or its complement, stubbornness)
work: Parsegov, Proskurnikov, Tempo & Friedkin 2017, doi:10.1109/TAC.2016.2613905; Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002
note: This file's proposal for the algebra, not a definition from a source.

statement: Operators: the influence operator W (row-stochastic, asymmetry allowed, acting by row-averaging); the anchor operator x -> (I - Lambda) u + Lambda x; the intra-person coupling C (m x m), acting after averaging; a state-dependent W(x) for bounded confidence
work: Parsegov, Proskurnikov, Tempo & Friedkin 2017, doi:10.1109/TAC.2016.2613905; Hegselmann & Krause 2002, JASSS 5(3), 2 (no DOI)
note: Only the first three have theorems; the state-dependent W(x) has none for the anchored, asymmetric case.

statement: Primitive quadruple for the algebra: anchor, susceptibility, influence matrix, coupling matrix (u, Lambda, W, C), with the affine one-step map and the Kronecker law as the adopted composition rules
work: Parsegov, Proskurnikov, Tempo & Friedkin 2017, doi:10.1109/TAC.2016.2613905
note: Recommendation of this file. It also recommends not adopting bounded confidence as a drive operator until a vector-valued, anchored, asymmetric version has a proof or data demand it.

statement: Trust set I_i(x) = { j : ||x_j - x_i|| <= d } for a chosen norm, with the update equal to the average over I_i
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2018, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2018.03.005 (eq. 18)
note: With a Euclidean or sup norm a large gap on one coordinate switches off influence on all of them; per-coordinate trust sets give m decoupled scalar HK systems, and no source gives a theorem for a hybrid.

statement: Susceptibility classes (Parsegov et al. Definition 2 and P&T terminology): stubborn means lambda_i < 1; totally stubborn means lambda_i = 0; oblivious means neither stubborn nor influenced by a stubborn agent; P&T's anchored or prejudiced means gamma_i > 0 in the Taylor form
work: Parsegov, Proskurnikov, Tempo & Friedkin 2017, doi:10.1109/TAC.2016.2613905 (Definition 2); Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002 (footnote 17)
note: Terminology collision: 'stubborn' in P&T 2017 and the DeGroot-with-zealots literature means the totally stubborn case. Corrected in validation: the words are Parsegov et al.'s, not P&T's.

statement: P-dependent agent: lambda_i < 1, or reachable by a walk from a prejudiced agent; P-independent agents are the rest
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002 (Theorem 21, Corollaries 22-23)
note: The condition on which the stability and convergence theorems rest.

statement: Coupling matrix C: same for all agents, independent of the network, acting after averaging; c_pq is the contribution of the q-th issue of the averaged opinion to the p-th issue of the updated opinion
work: Parsegov, Proskurnikov, Tempo & Friedkin 2017, doi:10.1109/TAC.2016.2613905 (MiDS, eqs 17 and 22)
note: Limitation stated by the file: C is linear, constant and acts on the social average, so a person-specific, state-dependent coupling is not covered by Theorems 2-3.

statement: Social power p_inf,i: the weight of agent i's initial opinion x_i(0) in the final group opinion (French's measure), given by the left eigenvector of W
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002 (eq. 8)
note: Non-uniform social power is what the asymmetry of a stochastic W gives.

statement: Lewin's resultant force, identified with the linear-averaging form: the force on person i's state = sum_j w_ij (x_j - x_i) (Abelson form), plus gamma_i (u_i - x_i) for the anchor (Taylor form)
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002 (Abelson and Taylor forms); Lewin 1936/1951 (not read)
note: The file's own identification from the form of the equations, not an author's claim. Do not write 'Lewin proved' or 'Lewin's model is FJ'. Lewin's own work is not read.

statement: Trust-set kernel phi(||x_j - x_i||): weights that depend smoothly on distance instead of the threshold trust set
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2018, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2018.03.005 (Lemma 14)
note: Preserves convergence but not finite-time termination; the threshold is what makes HK simulations sensitive.

statement: Which paper introduced the C-coupled multi-issue model: file 05 gives the Kronecker form as Friedkin et al. 2016 (Science); file 063 credits Parsegov et al. 2017 as founding
work: Parsegov, Proskurnikov, Tempo & Friedkin 2017, doi:10.1109/TAC.2016.2613905; Friedkin, Proskurnikov, Tempo & Parsegov 2016, doi:10.1126/science.aag2624 (Science 354, 321-326)
note: Side A: 05 §4 gives the Kronecker form under the 2016 Science paper. Side B: 063 says arXiv v1 (19 May 2015) predates Science, so the stability and convergence theory is Parsegov et al.'s. Verdict: 063 is right on priority and theorems; 05's attribution should read Parsegov 2017 applied in Friedkin 2016. Open only on whether the Science equation matches eq. 22 (unchecked).

statement: Harary 1959 and the second part of P&T Corollary 13: P&T say the proof is Harary's and that it was included without proof in [53]; file 05 records a Wagner-versus-P&T disagreement
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002 (footnote 8); Harary 1959, A criterion for unanimity in French's theory of social power (no Crossref record; not read)
note: Side A (P&T footnote 8): refs [53, 76] address only the French model, but the proof uses only the diagonal entries' positivity. Side B: file 05's Wagner disagreement, whose content this file does not state. Verdict: unresolved; settlement belongs to direction D211. Harary's own text not read.

statement: Friedkin 1999 cited as two different works: file 24 §10 and file 67 §2 cite Friedkin 1999 (choice shift, ASR 64(6)); file 063 cites Friedkin & Johnsen 1999 (Advances in Group Processes 16, 1-29)
work: Friedkin 1999, Choice shift and group polarization, American Sociological Review 64(6), 856-875 (not read here); Friedkin & Johnsen 1999, Social influence networks and opinion change, Advances in Group Processes 16, 1-29 (not read)
note: Verdict: no contradiction. They are distinct papers by different author lists; readers should not merge the two 1999 references. Both are unread.

statement: Susceptibility range: file 74 §2 restricts lambda_i to [0, 1) and asserts stability; file 063 allows lambda_i = 1, bringing in P-dependence
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2017, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2017.03.002 (Corollary 22)
note: Verdict: no contradiction. 74's statement is a special case of Corollary 22; 74 should not be read as covering unanchored agents, and its DeGroot remark (lambda_i = 1) steps outside its range. File 74 was not read here.

statement: P&T 2018 Theorem 17 notation: P&T's text calls the non-seekers lambda_i = 0, but their own eq. (32) makes a non-seeker lambda_i = 1
work: Proskurnikov & Tempo 2018, doi:10.1016/j.arcontrol.2018.03.005 (eq. 32)
note: Verdict (validation): read 'non-truth-seekers' wherever P&T write lambda_i = 0 in that passage; the draft had copied the slip and a caution is now in the file.

statement: McClelland 2004 title: files 05, 07 and 18 use 'Collective control of perception'; files 063, 16 and 66 use the Crossref form 'The collective control of perceptions: constructing order from conflict'
work: McClelland 2004, Int. J. Human-Computer Studies 60, 65-99, doi:10.1016/j.ijhcs.2003.08.003 (Crossref metadata; not read)
note: Verdict: the Crossref form is right; 18 §16 and 07 carry the shortened form.

statement: Within file 063: §5.5 says it cannot verify H&K 2002's sentence attributing FJ-type susceptibility estimation to French 1956 and treats it as unreliable, but the validation log says the sentence matches the PDF
work: Hegselmann & Krause 2002, JASSS 5(3), 2 (no DOI)
note: Verdict: resolved in validation at source; the sentence is in H&K 2002 as quoted. The attribution is still odd, since FJ is dated 1990, so the claim that French used FJ-type models is not verified.

statement: Positive and negative affect as two separate, non-opposed channels (positive word share, negative word share); their use is scarcely correlated, r = -0.04, t(620,587) = -38.01
work: Kramer, Guillory, Hancock 2014, PNAS 111(24), DOI 10.1073/pnas.1320040111
note: File says this is affect only, 'no drive in the algebra's sense'. Listed because it is the only two-channel affect structure the file records.

statement: Happiness as a persisting individual state that spreads along ties (four-item happiness scale, Framingham offspring cohort, 1983-2003)
work: Fowler, Christakis 2008, BMJ 337 a2338, DOI 10.1136/bmj.a2338
size_dependence: Effect decays with time and with network distance
note: Observational; file says identification is unestablished (see 064 §5 and §4).

statement: Learned fear of unseen (masked) faces, acquired by Pavlovian conditioning, by observing a confederate's expression, or by verbal instruction
work: Olsson, Phelps 2004, Psychological Science 15(12), 822-828, DOI 10.1111/j.0956-7976.2004.00762.x
note: Read at abstract only in validation; no effect size. File names it the only fear-specific source on the list.

statement: Moral outrage, which observers overperceive in the posts of others, inflating beliefs about intergroup hostility
work: Brady et al. 2023, Nature Human Behaviour 7(6), 917-927, DOI 10.1038/s41562-023-01582-0
note: Read at abstract only. File's operand implication: the receiver acts on a perceived, not true, sender state.

statement: Out-group animosity, whose expression drives engagement more than in-group or affect-only language (group-membership tag of a message)
work: Rathje, Van Bavel, van der Linden 2021, PNAS 118(26), DOI 10.1073/pnas.2024292118
note: Read at abstract only. File flags this as an operand-level distinction (in-group vs out-group source) absent from Kramer and Coviello.

statement: Conformity or social-influence bias: a conformity operator that the file calls a different drive from emotional mimicry
work: Muchnik, Aral, Taylor 2013, Science 341(6146), DOI 10.1126/science.1240466; Lorenz, Rauhut, Schweitzer, Helbing 2011, PNAS 108(22), DOI 10.1073/pnas.1008636108
note: Both read at abstract only. The 'drive' label is the file's own framing ('a different drive from emotional mimicry'), not a source's.

statement: Kramer estimator: weighted linear regression of a person's percentage of positive (or negative) words on an experimental-condition dummy, weighted by the likelihood that the person had an emotional post omitted from their feed on a given viewing; posting volume checked by Poisson regression
work: Kramer, Guillory, Hancock 2014, PNAS 111(24), DOI 10.1073/pnas.1320040111
note: Estimator as the file transcribes it from the paper.

statement: Approximate effect size d ~ 2t / sqrt(df) (the file's reconstruction, used to test the printed d values)
work: Computed in 064 from Kramer, Guillory, Hancock 2014, DOI 10.1073/pnas.1320040111
note: The file's own arithmetic, not a source's formula. Approximate for a weighted regression. It reproduces three of four printed d values; the fourth (0.001) does not reproduce, which the validation log confirmed.

statement: Coviello two-stage model: stage 1 predicts friends' emotion from friends' rainfall with time and city fixed effects; stage 2 regresses emotion on predicted friends' emotion, moderated by a binary tie a_ijt and divided by the receiver's degree d_jt, with time and city fixed effects; the coefficient is gamma
work: Coviello, Sohn, Kramer, Marlow, Franceschetti, Christakis, Fowler 2014, PLoS ONE 9(3), e90315, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0090315
size_dependence: Gamma is divided by receiver degree, so per-friend influence falls as friend count rises
note: Read in full from PLOS XML in the validation pass; formulas were images in the earlier summary fetch, so the wording is the file's paraphrase of them.

statement: Fowler and Christakis model: H_ego(t) = f(age, sex, education, H_ego(t-1), H_alter(t), H_alter(t-1)), fitted by generalised estimating equations with independent working correlation, reported as risk ratios; the contagion term is the coefficient on H_alter(t)
work: Fowler, Christakis 2008, BMJ 337 a2338, DOI 10.1136/bmj.a2338
note: The symbolic form is the file's own notation ('my notation'); the specification is the paper's.

statement: Ferrara and Yang stimulus-response: bucket valence V(b) = 2p/(n+p) - 1 on a -1 to +1 scale; response valence is linear in stimulus valence with R^2 = 0.975
work: Ferrara, Yang 2015, PLoS ONE 10(11), e0142390, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0142390
note: Corrected in validation: the scale is bucket valence on -1 to +1, not the -4 to 4 polarity. No slope or intercept is printed.

statement: Shalizi and Thomas theorem: latent homophily, contagion and covariate effects are generically confounded in observational network data, so direct contagion effects cannot be nonparametrically identified from such data without strong parametric assumptions or substantive knowledge ruling out latent homophily
work: Shalizi, Thomas 2011, Sociological Methods & Research 40(2), 211-239, DOI 10.1177/0049124111404820
note: File calls this 'a theorem, not a quibble'. Read in arXiv 1004.4704v3 in the validation pass.

statement: Corollary (Shalizi and Thomas section 2.2): asymmetries in regression coefficients that match asymmetries in network ties do not establish direct contagion
work: Shalizi, Thomas 2011, Sociological Methods & Research 40(2), 211-239, DOI 10.1177/0049124111404820
note: This is the device Fowler and Christakis's direction-of-tie test relies on.

statement: Simple imitation models can produce substantial correlations between an individual's enduring traits and their choices
work: Shalizi, Thomas 2011, Sociological Methods & Research 40(2), 211-239, DOI 10.1177/0049124111404820
note: A model result from the paper, stated in words rather than as an equation.

statement: Suggested operator: de_j = gamma * sum_i w_ij (e_i - e_j), for receiver j's expressed state e_j from sender set S with exposure weights w_ij, with gamma small enough that the system's spectral radius is below one for realistic feed sizes
work: Not from a source; the file's own proposal
size_dependence: Spectral-radius condition depends on feed size; Coviello's ratio above 1 per post is read as a sum over a large audience, not a per-edge gain
note: File marks this '[mine, not from a source]'. Calibrate gamma only from randomised or instrumented designs; treat the rest as upper-bound priors.

statement: Emotional contagion as operationalised by Kramer et al.: exposure to verbal affective expressions leads to similar verbal expressions (with 'cross-emotional' and 'withdrawal' effects)
work: Kramer, Guillory, Hancock 2014, PNAS 111(24), DOI 10.1073/pnas.1320040111
note: Expression-level definition only; it says nothing about change in a receiver's state.

statement: A post is positive or negative if it contains at least one positive or negative word in LIWC2007
work: Kramer, Guillory, Hancock 2014, PNAS 111(24), DOI 10.1073/pnas.1320040111
size_dependence: Share of positive words is 3.6% and negative 1.6% of all words in the experiment
note: Measurement definition; the file treats LIWC attenuation as an unknown factor, not a reason to doubt the sign.

statement: Primitive emotional contagion: the tendency to automatically mimic and synchronize facial expressions, vocalizations, postures, and movements with those of another person and, consequently, to converge emotionally
work: Hatfield, Bensman, Thornton, Rapson 2014, Interpersona 8(2), 159-179, DOI 10.5964/ijpr.v8i2.162 (quoting Hatfield, Cacioppo, Rapson 1994)
note: Corrected in validation: the quote says 'facial expressions' and is attributed to the 1994 book, which the file did not read. Earlier wording said 'facial expression' from the 1993 article.

statement: Three-stage mechanism of primitive emotional contagion: Mimicry, then Feedback, then Contagion; plus a fourth proposition that people rely on cognitive assessments as well as feedback from caught emotions when divining another's emotions
work: Hatfield, Bensman, Thornton, Rapson 2014, Interpersona 8(2), 159-179, DOI 10.5964/ijpr.v8i2.162
note: Framework only, with no equations. The 1993 article (DOI 10.1111/1467-8721.ep10770953) was not read.

statement: gamma (Coviello) quantifies the total effect of a user on all her friends
work: Coviello, Sohn, Kramer, Marlow, Franceschetti, Christakis, Fowler 2014, PLoS ONE 9(3), e90315, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0090315
size_dependence: Total over a friend set, so not a per-edge gain
note: Corrected in validation: this is the authors' own definition (proof in their Text S1, not read). The file had first called it its own inference.

statement: Fowler and Christakis's three explanations for an association between alter and ego happiness: induction, homophily, confounding; separated by lagged ego happiness (controls endowment), lagged alter happiness (controls homophily) and direction of friendship ties (tests unobserved shared exposure)
work: Fowler, Christakis 2008, BMJ 337 a2338, DOI 10.1136/bmj.a2338
note: File's view: the separation depends on the model being right, which Shalizi and Thomas show is untestable from data.

statement: Severity of a test of influence (Mayo's notion): bound the asymmetry attainable without influence, so that a large enough observed asymmetry would count as a severe test of influence
work: Shalizi, Thomas 2011, Sociological Methods & Research 40(2), 211-239, DOI 10.1177/0049124111404820
note: Proposal only. The paper states no bound, so the file records no number for it.

statement: Randomised platform experiment (N = 689,003; one week; positive posts reduced): own positive words -0.10 pp (t(310,044) = -5.63, d = 0.02); negative words +0.04 pp (t = 2.71, printed d = 0.001); negative posts reduced: negative words -0.07 pp (t(310,541) = -5.51, d = 0.02); positive words +0.06 pp (t = 2.19, printed d = 0.008)
work: Kramer, Guillory, Hancock 2014, PNAS 111(24), DOI 10.1073/pnas.1320040111
size_dependence: Each person's feed is cut 10% to 90% by User ID; effects are per-person word share after one week; the authors cite scale ('hundreds of thousands of emotion expressions per day') as their defence
note: Predicts word choice in status updates after reduced exposure, not mood. Only the same-valence d = 0.02 is the defensible headline; the printed 0.001 does not reproduce from its own t (implied about 0.0097). Scale assigned by me (individual expression), the file does not give one.

statement: Poisson and post hoc tests on Kramer's design: omitting emotional content reduced words produced (z = -4.78 when positivity reduced, z = -7.219 when negativity reduced, both P < 0.001; 96.7% and 99.7% as many words); same-valence effect sizes do not differ (Fisher z = -0.36, P = 0.72); cross-emotional effect shows no negativity bias (z = -0.09, P = 0.93)
work: Kramer, Guillory, Hancock 2014, PNAS 111(24), DOI 10.1073/pnas.1320040111
note: Post hoc tests. Scale assigned by me as for the main Kramer result.

statement: Rainy day in a city lowers positive posts by 1.19% [0.78, 1.60] and raises negative posts by 1.16% [0.78, 1.55]
work: Coviello, Sohn, Kramer, Marlow, Franceschetti, Christakis, Fowler 2014, PLoS ONE 9(3), e90315, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0090315
size_dependence: City-day aggregates over the 100 most populous US cities, 1,180 days
note: Rainy days elsewhere have just as strong an effect, per the file's restricted model. Scale assigned by me (city-level aggregates), the file does not give one.

statement: One additional positive post causes 1.75 [1.51, 1.99] more positive posts among friends; one additional negative post causes 1.29 [1.19, 1.38] more negative posts among friends
work: Coviello, Sohn, Kramer, Marlow, Franceschetti, Christakis, Fowler 2014, PLoS ONE 9(3), e90315, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0090315
size_dependence: Totals over a user's friend set, to be divided by audience size before use as a per-edge gain
note: Positive vs negative contagion differ at p = 0.001. The method cannot estimate contagion within subpopulations, per the authors. Scale assigned by me.

statement: Cross-effects: one positive post reduces friends' negative posts by 1.80 [1.27, 2.33]; one negative post reduces friends' positive posts by 1.26 [0.81, 1.70]; the cross-effects differ at p = 0.12
work: Coviello, Sohn, Kramer, Marlow, Franceschetti, Christakis, Fowler 2014, PLoS ONE 9(3), e90315, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0090315
size_dependence: Totals over friend set
note: Upward-bias routes flagged by the file: rain changes topics (weather words), and rain may change posting volume, breaking the exclusion restriction.

statement: Ratio of indirect to direct effect about 1.5 to 1 for emotional contagion, against about 2 to 1 for giving in a public-goods experiment and about 4 to 1 for voting mobilisation (the latter two as cited by the authors)
work: Coviello, Sohn, Kramer, Marlow, Franceschetti, Christakis, Fowler 2014, PLoS ONE 9(3), e90315, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0090315
note: Benchmark figures are the authors' citations, not checked by the file.

statement: Within a friend set, a friend within a mile who becomes happy raises the probability of being happy by 25% (95% CI 1% to 57%); coresident spouse 8% (0.2% to 16%); sibling within a mile 14% (1% to 28%); next-door neighbour 34% (7% to 70%); no effect between coworkers; effect decays with time and distance and extends to three degrees of separation
work: Fowler, Christakis 2008, BMJ 337 a2338, DOI 10.1136/bmj.a2338
size_dependence: Decays with time and network distance; coworkers show none while neighbours show a large effect
note: Tagged [read: abstract] in the file, though the validation log says all six effect sizes and CIs were confirmed in Europe PMC full text. Observational and confounded (Shalizi and Thomas; Lyons 2011).

statement: Over-exposure to negative content before a negative post is 4.34% above a null baseline and to positive content before a positive post is 4.50% above; no difference for neutral posts (Mann-Whitney p < 10^-6 for both)
work: Ferrara, Yang 2015, PLoS ONE 10(11), e0142390, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0142390
size_dependence: Null model reshuffles stimuli (baseline 34.44% positive, 48.27% neutral, 17.29% negative)
note: 3,800 random English-tweeting users plus followees. Observational, so confounded by homophily. Numbers are percent over-exposure relative to a null, not a transmission coefficient.

statement: Susceptibility: low-susceptibility users are 1.6 times more likely to adopt positive than negative content; high-susceptibility users 3.96 times
work: Ferrara, Yang 2015, PLoS ONE 10(11), e0142390, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0142390
size_dependence: Depends on individual susceptibility
note: Observational. Scale assigned by me.

statement: Stimulus-response is linear in stimulus valence with R^2 = 0.975; stimulus -1 gives response about -0.8 and stimulus +1 gives about +0.6
work: Ferrara, Yang 2015, PLoS ONE 10(11), e0142390, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0142390
note: End points as the text gives them; no slope or intercept printed. Corrected in validation to the bucket-valence scale.

statement: Across 563,312 messages on three issues, each additional moral-emotional word raised diffusion by 20%, and the effect was stronger within ideological groups than between them
size_dependence: Stronger within ideological groups than between
note: Read at abstract only. Diffusion (retweet) of message content, not contagion of a receiver's state; observational, so confounded. Burton 2021 is a placebo test against it.

statement: Observers overperceive authors' moral outrage in online networks; preregistered experiments show this inflates beliefs about intergroup hostility
work: Brady et al. 2023, Nature Human Behaviour 7(6), 917-927, DOI 10.1038/s41562-023-01582-0
note: Read at abstract only. Experiments are with consenting participants (file does not say otherwise). Scale assigned by me (beliefs about group hostility).

statement: Out-of-sample prediction, model comparison and specification-curve analyses show the moral contagion model performs no better than an implausible XYZ contagion model; purely correlational large-sample evidence with standard significance testing is unsafe
work: Burton, Cruz, Hahn 2021, Nature Human Behaviour 5(12), 1629-1635, DOI 10.1038/s41562-021-01133-5
note: Read at abstract only; corpora and XYZ definition unread. Bears on the dictionary approach in general, not only Brady.

statement: Across 2,730,215 posts, posts about the political out-group were shared about twice as often; each out-group term raised the odds of a share by 67%; out-group language predicted shares about 4.8 times as strongly as negative-affect language and 6.7 times as strongly as moral-emotional language; out-group language predicts angry reactions
work: Rathje, Van Bavel, van der Linden 2021, PNAS 118(26), e2024292118, DOI 10.1073/pnas.2024292118
note: Read at abstract only. Engagement with content, not receiver state.

statement: Randomised prior ratings on a social news aggregator: a positive prior rating raised the likelihood of a positive rating by 32% and final ratings by 25% on average; negative prior ratings inspired correction (asymmetric herding)
work: Muchnik, Aral, Taylor 2013, Science 341(6146), 647-651, DOI 10.1126/science.1240466
note: Read at abstract only. Randomised, so identified; the closest identified analogue in this set to a conformity operator. Scale assigned by me (ratings).

statement: Lab experiment (N = 144, five consecutive estimation periods, with no, average or full information about others) shows three effects: social influence reduces diversity without gain in collective accuracy; range reduction moves the truth to the edge of the estimates; confidence rises after convergence without accuracy gain
work: Lorenz, Rauhut, Schweitzer, Helbing 2011, PNAS 108(22), 9020-9025, DOI 10.1073/pnas.1008636108
size_dependence: Lab group of 144 participants
note: Read at abstract only; numeric effect sizes unread. Identified small-N lab result on convergence of judgement. Consent assumed for lab participants; file does not state it.

statement: Registered replication report of the facial feedback hypothesis (Strack, Martin, Stepper 1988), 17 direct replications: funniness-rating difference 0.03 units (95% CI -0.11 to 0.16) against 0.82 in the original
work: Wagenmakers et al. 2016, Perspectives on Psychological Science 11(6), 917-928, DOI 10.1177/1745691616674458
note: Read at abstract only. Lab participants assumed to consent (file does not say). Scale assigned by me (individual rated emotion).

statement: Facial feedback meta-analysis (286 effect sizes from 138 studies): the overall effect is significant but small and heterogeneous; larger for affective judgements of a stimulus than for emotional experience; publication bias detected for judgements but not for experience
work: Coles, Larsen, Lench 2019, Psychological Bulletin 145(6), 610-651, DOI 10.1037/bul0000194
note: Read at abstract only. The d = 0.20 figure is unconfirmed for the 2019 paper (seen only for an earlier thesis version). Consent assumed; file does not say.

statement: Preregistered adversarial multi-lab test (n = 3,878 in 19 countries): facial mimicry and voluntary facial action tasks could both amplify and initiate happiness; evidence less conclusive for the unobtrusive pen-in-mouth task
work: Coles et al. 2022 (Many Smiles Collaboration), Nature Human Behaviour 6(12), 1731-1742, DOI 10.1038/s41562-022-01458-9
note: Read at abstract only; effect size not retrieved. Mimicry is the closest of the three tasks to Hatfield's stage 1 to stage 2 route.

statement: Lab experiment with a trained confederate acting one of four moods: groups with positive contagion reported better cooperation
work: Barsade 2002, Administrative Science Quarterly 47(4), 644-675, DOI 10.1307/3094912 (as the file gives it: DOI 10.2307/3094912)
size_dependence: Small lab groups
note: Not re-read; no abstract retrieved in validation, description rests on file 027. Sender is an actor (confederate), and replication status unknown.

statement: Skin-conductance fear learning to unmasked stimuli is similar across Pavlovian, observational and instructed routes; with masked CS+, the Pavlovian and observational groups show learning and the instructed group does not
work: Olsson, Phelps 2004, Psychological Science 15(12), 822-828, DOI 10.1111/j.0956-7976.2004.00762.x
note: Read at abstract only; no effect size. Observationally transmitted fear behaves like directly conditioned fear and unlike told fear. Consent assumed (shock-paired lab study); file does not state it.

statement: Validation of LIWC versions on cancer-survivor writing: good sensitivity for LIWC2001, 2007 and 2015 against human coders; LIWC2007 and 2015 are significantly more likely to overidentify emotional content; LIWC2001 has better precision for overall and negative emotion
work: McDonnell, Owen, Bantum 2020, JMIR Formative Research 4(10), e18246, DOI 10.2196/18246
note: Read at abstract only. A measurement validation on a different corpus (cancer survivors' writing, not status updates), so the file's 'scale' field does not really apply; membership assigned by default. No reliability estimate for Facebook status updates exists in the file.

statement: Kramer et al. headline effect: 'as small as d = 0.001' (064) vs '[from abstract]' tag in 018 §2 for the same phrase
work: Kramer, Guillory, Hancock 2014, PNAS 111(24), DOI 10.1073/pnas.1320040111
note: Side A (064): the phrase is in the Discussion, not the abstract; printed d = 0.001 is the smallest of four effects and does not reproduce from its own t = 2.71 (implied about 0.0097), so 0.001 is probably a typo for 0.01. Side B (018): the tag is '[from abstract]'; its quotation of the paper's wording is right. VERDICT: 064 right on the tag and the arithmetic; the 0.001 typo is an unconfirmed inference without the authors' data.

statement: Kramer's d = 0.001 headline: 064 says it belongs to one of four effects with same-valence effects d = 0.02, vs 027 summary saying 'd = 0.001 in the one experiment' and 'the one large experiment is d = 0.001'
work: Kramer, Guillory, Hancock 2014, PNAS 111(24), DOI 10.1073/pnas.1320040111
note: Side A (064): the paper reports two experiments and four effects; the headline same-valence effect is d = 0.02. Side B (027): line 137 states it correctly; lines 220 and 242 over-generalise. VERDICT: 064 right.

statement: Facial feedback: 064 says the evidence is small and heterogeneous, and the original pen-in-mouth result failed a 17-lab replication (0.03 units vs 0.82) vs 018 §1 'mimicry and facial feedback are supported in the review's account [from abstract]'
work: Hatfield, Bensman, Thornton, Rapson 2014, Interpersona 8(2), 159-179, DOI 10.5964/ijpr.v8i2.162; Wagenmakers et al. 2016, DOI 10.1177/1745691616674458
note: Side A (064): adds the replication record from Wagenmakers 2016 and Coles 2019 abstracts. Side B (018): reports what the 2014 review claims. VERDICT: difference of emphasis, not fact; 064's fuller statement is safer. 018 should read 'claimed by the review', not 'established'.

statement: Observational layer cannot supply a gain: 064 headline 3 says only randomisation or an instrument identifies contagion, and omits any weaker valid test; 09 §F3 cites VanderWeele, Ogburn, Tchetgen Tchetgen 2012 as a valid test of the null of no contagion by lagging the alter's state one extra period
work: VanderWeele, Ogburn, Tchetgen Tchetgen 2012, DOI 10.1515/2151-7509.1050 (as cited in 09)
note: Not a contradiction of the gain claim: a valid null test is not an identified gain, so 064's headline 3 stands. 064 should cite VanderWeele et al. as the qualification on Shalizi and Thomas. UNRESOLVED on power: 09 says Shalizi replied the test's power is unknown.

statement: LIWC measurement critique of Panger 2016: 018 §2 describes a dictionary built for longer texts that misreads negation and sarcasm in short status updates [from abstract] vs 064, which did not retrieve Panger's text and treats it as search coverage only
work: Panger 2016, Information, Communication & Society 19(8), 1108-1126, DOI 10.1080/1369118X.2015.1093525
note: UNRESOLVED: neither file retrieved Panger's abstract or text (publisher 403). McDonnell 2020 gives partial support for LIWC over-identifying emotion in cancer-survivor writing, not for the negation or sarcasm claim. The Grohol and blog negation claims are plausible but unverified (064 §2).

statement: Group-level emotion: a group-specific, identification-dependent emotion profile that differs from the same person's individual profile, is shared within the group, and contributes to regulating attitudes and behaviour (Smith et al.'s four criteria)
size_dependence: Samples are US university students (Study 1 N=110, Study 2 N=445) rating chronic, self-reported emotions for a few categories; file says the claims are about trait-like profiles, not transient states in interacting groups
note: Cluster letter E is guessed from content; the file names no cluster. The authors say the criteria need not each hold universally (p. 432). File 065 §7: criterion 1 supported for a narrow construct, 2 as association, 3 as shared profile only, 4 weak-moderate. No dynamical law in this line.

statement: General group emotion (no event specified): emotion about belonging to a group, which Kuppens and Yzerbyt 2014 argue is primarily or even exclusively a reaction to individual concerns about the nature of one's belonging
size_dependence: Four studies: N=32 and 113 (UCL students), 132 (Cardiff students), 120 (Belgian francophones online, not stated as students)
