note: Contested by the Smith line; see contradiction line on what the measure captures.

statement: Group-based emotion (event-driven): emotion as a reaction to a specified group event, such as an unfair event, which tracks group-based appraisals of immediate group concerns
size_dependence: Studies 3 (N=132) and 4 (N=120) only
note: File says whether event-based and belonging emotions share variance beyond identification was not read (065 §10).

statement: Collective effervescence: Durkheim's intense shared emotional activation and unison during gatherings, with Collins's multi-faceted synchrony account; measured in the meta-analysis as perceived emotional synchrony (PES, k=28) and related self-report scales
work: Pizarro et al. 2022, doi 10.3389/fpsyg.2022.974683
size_dependence: Demonstrations are a subset (15 of 54 event-type entries as listed by the authors); heterogeneity I2 mostly 90%+
note: Perceived synchrony is a self-report, not a computed dispersion (per file 18, as cited in 065 cross-checks). Gives no direct test of the Durkheim feedback loop.

statement: Collective emotional climate: perceived 'positive climate' and 'negative climate' ratings of a group's emotional atmosphere, a construct separate from collective effervescence
work: Pizarro et al. 2022, doi 10.3389/fpsyg.2022.974683
size_dependence: k=4 (positive) and k=5 (negative) studies
note: File 065 notes 'collective emotions' in Pizarro means perceived emotional climate, a different aggregation from the Smith group mean; the perceived-versus-actual distinction is passed to D242.

statement: Intergroup emotions: anger and fear (and anger and contempt in Study 3) elicited by group-based appraisals when group identity is salient; intergroup anger is distinct from intergroup fear, and the tendency to act against the outgroup is distinct from moving away from it
size_dependence: No sample sizes or effect sizes read
note: Abstract only (PubMed 11045741). Anger mediates the effect of perceived ingroup strength on offensive action tendency (see empirical line).

statement: Shared anger as a basis for new self-categories: fit between own and ingroup anger shapes self-categorisation and willingness for collective action, and greater when the shared emotion is anger; follow-up finds self-categorisation with angry targets only when own anger is high
work: Livingstone et al. 2011, doi 10.1037/a0023223; follow-up Livingstone et al. 2016, doi 10.1080/02699931.2015.1023702
size_dependence: 2011: minimal and natural groups; 2016: N=89 with feedback on eight co-present others
note: Both abstract only. The only item in the original read that runs emotion -> group membership, the reverse of the IET arrow. The draft's claim that the 2016 abstract calls the 2011 study the only prior test was removed in validation.

statement: Agent valence and arousal modelled as stochastic (Brownian-agent) states coupled to a shared communication field, from which collective emotions (bimodal valence) can emerge once or repeatedly
work: Schweitzer & Garcia 2010, doi 10.1140/epjb/e2010-00292-1
size_dependence: Per file 18 (cross-check, not 065), emergence once versus recurring depends on a saturating versus superlinear feedback switch
note: Abstract only. A model, not fitted to Smith-type data. File 066 flags a sign slip in the preprint's equation (17), which does not touch this claim.

statement: Smith multilevel model: Level 1: grpem_ij = B0j + B1j*indem_ij + B2j*grpavg_i + r_ij; Level 2: B0j = gamma00 + mu0j; B1j = gamma10 + gamma11*ident_j + mu1j; B2j = gamma20 + gamma21*ident_j + mu2j
size_dependence: Estimated on N about 40-420 per group; the authors' split-sample check (footnote 6) gave virtually identical results; excluding self from grpavg changes little at N about 100-400
note: Specification after Singer 1998, usable as a measurement model. grpavg_i is a mean of the same respondents' reports. Seger et al. 2009 fn 1: expected correlation between all-N and (N-1) mean vectors above .99. No out-of-sample test.

statement: Convergence: gamma20 > 0 after controlling individual emotion; identification moderates convergence: gamma21 > 0
note: Convergence here is a shared profile, not an influence process: contagion, conformity and common appraisal are not separated (authors, p. 443). File 065 §2.3 problem 2.

statement: File's own restatement of the fitted operator F_G (from Tables 3 and 7): g_j approx. B1*a_j + B2*ebar(G), with B2 about .5-.9 and B1 about .1-.5, and the weight on the group mean rising with identification (gamma21 about +.1 to +.3; negative for Republicans in Study 2 on the individual term)
size_dependence: Fitted separately by group and study (Tables 3 and 7)
note: This is the file's own restatement, not an equation the authors give. Its DeGroot/Friedkin-Johnsen analogy (sample mean as anchor) is the file's, fitted to cross-sectional profiles, not time series. Within-sample fit only; no out-of-sample prediction (file 07 caution).

statement: Worked prediction (p. 442): a Democrat at average identification with individual irritation 3 and group-mean irritation 5 is predicted to report 4.54 as a Democrat, moving more than 75% of the way toward the group mean; one scale point above average identification gives 5.08
size_dependence: Depends on identification level, one scale point above average
note: Illustrative in-sample arithmetic from the authors' fitted model, not a validated out-of-sample prediction.

statement: Brownian-agent dynamics for valence and arousal coupled to a shared communication field, with conditions derived for bimodal valence (collective emotions) to emerge once or repeatedly
work: Schweitzer & Garcia 2010, doi 10.1140/epjb/e2010-00292-1
size_dependence: Per file 18 (cross-check): saturating versus superlinear feedback decides once versus recurring
note: No equation text was read; abstract only. Ledger rule: nothing sa feeds an equation, so this must not be used as an equation source until the preprint is read. Cross-check file 066 flags a sign slip in the preprint's equation (17).

statement: Individual and group-framed emotion profiles correlate .52 (IU), .25 (Democrats), .33 (Republicans) in Study 1 and .24-.33 in Study 2, accounting for 6%-25% of group-emotion variance; Level x Emotion interactions significant in all three groups in both studies (Study 1 between-subjects F(11,82)=2.35*, F(11,26)=2.31*, F(11,30)=2.64*; Study 2 F(12,4368)=12.35***, F(12,2316)=20.78***, F(12,1824)=13.41***)
size_dependence: Study 1 analysed N 94-101 (IU), 38-40 (Democrats), 42 (Republicans); Study 2 Americans 349-405, Democrats 195-229, Republicans 154-173
note: Pages corrected in validation: r = .52/.25/.33 at p. 435, Study 2 at p. 438. Distinctness means the mean profile across emotions differs by framing; it does not rule out reduction to individual emotion plus a category cue. In-sample only.

statement: After controlling individual emotion, the group-average profile coefficient gamma20 is .55*** (IU, N=101), .71*** (Democrats, N=40), .67*** (Republicans, N=42) in Study 1, and .76*** (Americans, N=349), .81*** (Democrats, N=220), .89*** (Republicans, N=160) in Study 2
size_dependence: Coefficients may partly reflect generic agreement on which emotions are high for any target (item difficulty, common stereotype); no non-group baseline in Studies 1-2 beyond Emotions x Group interactions
note: Shared profile is robust; convergence as a process is untested. Individual-emotion coefficients .07-.45 (Table 3) and .14-.23 (Americans, Democrats) in the same models. Split-sample check (footnote 6) virtually identical. Within-sample, no out-of-sample test.

statement: Identification moderates convergence (gamma21 on the group-average term): significant in Study 2 for Americans (.22***), Democrats (.23***) and Republicans (.11***), and in Study 1 for Republicans only (.33***); Study 1 Democrats .14 (p<.10) and IU .07 n.s.; identification by individual-emotion interaction is opposite in sign across groups and called 'extremely weak and conditional' by the authors
size_dependence: Moderation present in all three groups in Study 2, in one of three in Study 1
note: In-sample. File 065 §2.3 gives the authors' worked example separately.

statement: Study 2 identification correlates positively with positive group emotions (mean .52, 18 of 18 positive) and negatively with negative group emotions (mean -.15, 18 of 18), except anger at the outgroup (mean .33); group-emotion correlations with identification exceed individual-emotion ones in 33 of 36 (Study 1) and 39 of 39 (Study 2) cases
size_dependence: Study 1 mean positive .49 (18/18) and negative -.17 (16/18)
note: Direction of causation unspecified. Authors say Study 2 'was unable to discriminate' disidentification from reappraisal for negative emotion. Criterion 2 is a correlation of unspecified direction.

statement: Group emotions predict action intentions better than individual emotions: 24 of 48 effects of group emotions on behavioural intentions significant (50%) versus 8 of 48 tests of individual emotions (17%); individual-emotion effects never replicated across groups, while group anger and positive group emotions did; e.g. Americans U.S. anger to confront .49***, U.S. positive to confront .58***, individual anger to confront .32** (unstandardised)
size_dependence: Study 1 (IU) and Study 2 (Americans, Democrats, Republicans)
note: Intentions, not behaviour (willingness to tell a critic he is wrong, sign a petition). Same-session self-report, common-method variance; some avoidance scales reliability .41-.57 (fn 8); a programming error lost part of Study 2 outcomes (fn 7). No causal test. Group anger at the outgroup increased outgroup avoidance, explained post hoc. Weak-moderate per 065 §7.

statement: Category-primed emotion (no group framing) converges to the group-primed mean (coefficient .82-.83 in Experiment 1, N=98 within-subjects); identification strengthened convergence in 3 of 4 cases in Experiment 1 (not for the IU group-primed-mean model, .06 n.s.)
work: Seger, Smith & Mackie 2009, doi 10.1016/j.jesp.2008.12.004
size_dependence: Experiment 2 (N=82, between-subjects) measured emotion once and tested convergence to explicit group emotion only
note: Corrected in validation: '3 of 4' is for Experiment 1 only. Experiment 2: explicit group emotion predicts group-primed emotion at roughly the same level as individual emotions; identification by explicit-emotion interaction marginal for the US (.07, p<.06) and n.s. for IU (.06). The manipulation is category salience (priming), not any group state.

statement: General group emotions correlate r=.70 (Study 1, N=32) and r=.77 (Study 2, N=113) with explicit belonging emotions; general group emotions are not related to appraisals of immediate group concerns, whereas group-based emotions are (Studies 3, N=132, and 4, N=120)
size_dependence: Samples: UCL students (Studies 1-2), Cardiff students (Study 3), Belgian francophones recruited via a UCL Facebook group (Study 4)
note: Authors' own studies, small samples. Validation confirmed r = .70/.77 and corrected the Study 4 sample attribution.

statement: Negative general group emotion relates negatively to identification (Study 3, B=-.32, p<.01, reproducing Smith et al.); in Study 3 negative group-based emotion is unrelated to identification (B=.06, p=.60); it is positively related only in Study 4 (B=.91, p=.006 when measured first; B=.33, p=.31 when measured second)
size_dependence: Study 4 general-group-emotion simple effects order-dependent (B=-.47, p=.14 first; B=+.53, p=.11 after group-based emotions), neither individually significant
note: Corrected form: the draft claimed group-based negative emotions correlate positively with identification; that was wrong for Study 3 and only partly true for Study 4 (validation log).

statement: Pooled random-effects correlations of collective effervescence (50 studies in 41 articles, N=182,738): fusion of identity (verbal) r=.694 (k=5, N=1,031, I2 6.9); self-transcendent emotions r=.577 (k=17); individual positive emotions r=.547 (k=22); ingroup identification r=.456 (k=14); individual arousal r=.443 (k=14, N=48,316)
work: Pizarro et al. 2022, doi 10.3389/fpsyg.2022.974683
size_dependence: Heterogeneity I2 mostly 90%+ (92.7-99.2 for most criteria); design moderator: associations stronger cross-sectionally for negative emotion and identity, stronger longitudinally for positive emotion
note: Corrected in validation: the k=28 scale is the Perceived Emotional Synchrony scale. Arousal publication-bias tests non-significant (rank correlation p=.914, regression p=.702, fail-safe N 22,003). Cross-sectional self-reports collected at or after the event; method variance and retrospective sense-making inflate correlations.

statement: Collective effervescence correlates near zero with individual negative emotions (r=.047, k=14, N=2,028) and collective negative climate (r=.017, k=5, N=1,357), and moderately with collective positive climate (r=.248, k=4), ingroup commitment long-term (r=.372, k=7, N=123,962) and wellbeing (r=.316, k=17, N=6,188)
work: Pizarro et al. 2022, doi 10.3389/fpsyg.2022.974683
size_dependence: Heterogeneity I2 77.8-99.2 across these criteria
note: The one negative collective outcome is at zero: CE is not evidence about group fear or anger. Ingroup commitment is the membership-relevant criterion (stay), recorded here within the group line.

statement: In demonstrations only, collective effervescence correlates with group identity r=.52, collective efficacy .37, negative emotions .14, self-transcendent emotions .58 and morality-related beliefs .43
work: Pizarro et al. 2022, doi 10.3389/fpsyg.2022.974683
size_dependence: Demonstrations subset (15 entries in the authors' event-type list)
note: Subset result, same self-report design as the pooled estimates.

statement: Design moderator: effects are stronger in cross-sectional studies for negative emotions and ingroup identity and stronger in longitudinal studies for positive emotions; the authors read 'similar or stronger' longitudinal effects as support for collective effervescence as a cause
work: Pizarro et al. 2022, doi 10.3389/fpsyg.2022.974683
size_dependence: Pre/post versus cross-sectional designs
note: The moderator compares designs; it does not test the return arc of the Durkheim loop (solidarity to more ritual) per 065 §5.

statement: When ingroup identity is salient, perceived ingroup strength raises anger toward the outgroup, and anger mediates the effect of perceived ingroup strength on offensive action tendency; anger and fear are distinct, and the action tendency is distinct from moving away
size_dependence: Three studies; anger and fear (Studies 1-2), anger and contempt (Study 3); ingroup support measured or manipulated
note: Abstract only (PubMed 11045741). No sample sizes or effect sizes read.

statement: Willingness for collective action is greater when the shared emotion is anger, in responses to a group-relevant event where other ingroup and outgroup members' reactions were manipulated (anger versus happiness; anger versus indifference); fit between own and ingroup reactions influenced self-categorisation
work: Livingstone et al. 2011, doi 10.1037/a0023223
size_dependence: Study 1 minimal groups, Study 2 natural groups
note: Abstract only (PubMed 21728416).

statement: Participants self-categorised more with angry than sad targets, only when their own anger was high (N=89, feedback about eight co-present others' attitudes and emotions)
note: Abstract only (PubMed 25817820). Shared anger shapes a new self-category.

statement: A trained confederate expressing affect in small laboratory groups produced contagion to members and effects on cooperation and conflict
size_dependence: Small groups; per file 27 (cross-check, not 065), a 2x2 design of four enacted moods
note: Not read; [standard account] in 065. Recorded in validation as a counterexample to the claim that no member-to-member influence has been manipulated; the claim is narrowed to the Smith line.

statement: People's emotional responses to political situations shift toward others' weaker or stronger emotions depending on the situation's motive, in the lab and on Twitter
work: Goldenberg, Garcia, Halperin, Zaki, Kong, Golarai & Gross 2020, doi 10.1037/xge0000625
size_dependence: Lab and Twitter samples; sizes not read
note: Abstract only (PubMed 31192635). Counterexample to 'no member-to-member influence test' in the Smith line.

statement: Group discussion of an unfair event produced group-based emotions comparable to explicit identity salience
work: Yzerbyt, Kuppens & Mathieu 2016, doi 10.1080/02699931.2015.1045454
size_dependence: Not read
note: Abstract only (PubMed 26193426).

statement: Group-level emotion as operationalised by Smith et al.: the reported general emotion 'as a member of' a named group, rated 1-7 for a list of emotions, with no event specified; the group average is the mean of members' own ratings
size_dependence: Group-average term is grpavg_i, mean over members of that group
note: Kuppens and Yzerbyt argue this measures belonging emotion, not reactions to group concerns (see contradiction). Study 1 used 12 emotions, Study 2 used 13 (anger split into ingroup and outgroup).

statement: Distinctness: group-level emotion is distinct from individual emotion when the mean profile across emotions differs between individual and group framing (the Smith operationalisation, not reducibility to individual emotion plus a category cue)
note: File 065 §2.1 says what 'distinct' means here, not what the authors claim beyond it.

statement: Group state assumed as the mean of member states: ebar(G), the group emotion profile, is the mean over members' reported emotions; this is assumed by the algebra, not tested in the source papers
size_dependence: Pizarro's CE and climate measures are different aggregations again
note: The file's flagged unit problem; a candidate definition the algebra might adopt, with the assumption stated. Passed to D242 (actual versus perceived group state).

statement: Operands for the algebra: a group G carries a profile vector e(G) in R^k over k emotion categories, plus an identification weight w_j in [0,1] for each member j (the 4-item identification scale rescaled); a person j carries an individual vector a_j and a group-framed vector g_j(G)
size_dependence: k = 12-13 items in the Smith studies
note: File's operand proposal, not a source's definition. Nothing in the evidence says the person-level object is not simply a_j plus a category-cued shift.

statement: Salience switch: identity salience s in {0,1} (or [0,1]) selects whether group appraisals count; IET asserts this as a gate and Seger et al. 2009 manipulate it by priming
note: File's operator proposal, drawn from the IET premise (Smith 1993, quoted at p. 432) and the Seger 2009 priming design. The gate is stated in prose, not as an equation.

statement: IET premise (Smith 1993, as quoted by Smith et al. 2007): when group membership is salient, the group functions as part of the self, and situations appraised as self-relevant trigger emotions just as they always do
source: 065 §2 (quoted at p. 432 of Smith et al. 2007)
note: Read only as quoted in Smith et al. 2007 (read). The Smith 1993 chapter itself was not read (065 §10).

statement: Collective emotion as an emergent macro-level affective phenomenon mapped on three dimensions: quality (which emotion), magnitude (level), time course (trajectory)
work: Goldenberg, Garcia, Halperin & Gross 2020, doi 10.1177/0963721420901574
note: Abstract only, confirmed verbatim at Crossref (065 validation). Body unread; whether it gives a formal model is unknown. The three dimensions are the file's state-vector axes.

statement: Group-based emotion can be regulated at situation selection, situation modification, attention, appraisal and response stages (Gross's process model applied to intergroup emotion)
work: Goldenberg, Halperin, van Zomeren & Gross 2016, doi 10.1177/1088868315581263
note: Not re-read in 065; described from file 18. Criterion 4 in the Smith sense (emotion regulates behaviour) is distinct from this (people regulate their group emotion).

statement: Appraisal-to-action map: appraisal of an event against the group's concerns gives a discrete emotion which gives an action tendency (anger to approach or attack; fear to avoid)
note: File's labelled reading of the abstract, not an equation: no magnitudes, dynamics or decay. The only quantitative object in the Smith line is the regression.

statement: Collective 'what counts as collective' (von Scheve 2017, sense 1, group-membership emotions): felt because of membership or affiliation, with social identity and categorisation integral; can be felt by a single person (collective guilt as example)
note: Read in full from the FU Berlin preprint, a 1,259-word encyclopedia entry. File 18 §3 gives a coarser three-type version (cross-check); not a contradiction.

statement: Collective 'what counts as collective' (von Scheve 2017, sense 2, joint-intention or plural-subject emotions): collective or we-intentions, a normative commitment to feel in a certain way; non-aggregate and mental-state-centred (Gilbert 2002; Salmela 2012)
note: Gilbert and Salmela are cited within the entry and were not read.

statement: Collective 'what counts as collective' (von Scheve 2017, sense 3, aggregate or synchrony emotions): several individuals feeling within a time frame, usually toward the same event, with physical co-presence, mimicry, contagion and behavioural synchrony (Hatfield, Carpenter & Rapson 2014)
note: Hatfield et al. cited within the entry and not read. Maps onto collective effervescence (Pizarro 2022).

statement: Collective 'what counts as collective' (von Scheve 2017, sense 4, structure or culture-produced similarity): shared ecology, stratification, shared values, feeling rules and display norms, and emotional climates (Bar-Tal, Halperin & de Rivera 2007)
note: Bar-Tal et al. cited within the entry and not read. Von Scheve's closing assessment: a substantial gap between theoretical concepts and available measures.

statement: Whether the general group-emotion measure captures group-level emotion (Smith et al. 2007) or belonging emotion that reflects individual concerns (Kuppens and Yzerbyt 2014)
note: Side A (Smith et al. 2007): general group emotion is a group-level variable, distinct from individual emotion (criterion 1). Side B (Kuppens and Yzerbyt 2014, General Discussion p. 1586): general group emotions are emotions about group belonging, primarily or even exclusively a reaction to individual concerns. Verdict: unresolved, status open. File 065 §7 supports criterion 1 only for a narrow construct and §3 says the Smith result is about self-evaluative belonging if Kuppens and Yzerbyt are right.

statement: Within the file: §9 says the Smith line has no test of member-to-member emotional influence and no manipulation of a group's emotional state, while adjacent work (Barsade 2002; Goldenberg et al. 2020 JEP:G; Yzerbyt, Kuppens & Mathieu 2016) reports such manipulations or influence
work: Barsade 2002, doi 10.2307/3094912; Goldenberg et al. 2020, doi 10.1037/xge0000625; Yzerbyt, Kuppens & Mathieu 2016, doi 10.1080/02699931.2015.1045454
note: Side A (065 §9 as first drafted): nothing exists. Side B: counterexamples, Barsade 2002 [standard account, not read], Goldenberg 2020 and Yzerbyt 2016 [abstract]. File's verdict: claim narrowed in validation to the Smith/IET line; the 'no dynamics, no influence test' conclusion is true only of that line. Status open: the counterexamples are not read at full text.

statement: Granovetter threshold x in [0,1]: the proportion of the group an individual must see join before joining; the point where perceived benefits of acting exceed perceived costs
size_dependence: Outcome depends on the whole threshold distribution F, not its mean; the paper's examples use N=100
note: File states no named drive; the paper treats aggregation of preferences and not their origin. Threshold is a single scalar per actor.

statement: Threshold as the crossing of an approach tendency and an avoidance tendency, expressed in the variable fraction already acting (approach tendency pushed above avoidance tendency by observing others)
work: Granovetter 1978, fn. 2 (Wheeler); Miller 1944 crossing d* (cited in 16)
size_dependence: Depends on the fraction acting, so it is defined on group size through the proportion variable
note: Granovetter fn. 2 read. The Miller 1944 link is the file's own mapping and Miller was not checked in the validation pass. Listed in the file as a suggested algebra bridge, not decided.

statement: Watts vulnerability threshold phi: a node adopts state 1 if at least a fraction phi of its k neighbours are in state 1; vulnerable with one seed neighbour iff phi <= 1/k
size_dependence: Vulnerability depends on degree k, so the cascade condition depends on the degree distribution
note: Threshold drawn from f(phi) on [0,1]; degrees from p_k with mean z.

statement: Kuran utility components for a declared public position: intrinsic utility (maximal at true preference), expressive utility (value of declaring one's own view), reputational utility (maximal at the declaration that gets the most favourable response from society)
work: Rasmusen 1998, JEBO 33, 309-311, doi 10.1016/S0167-2681(98)90013-0; Kuran 1995 book (no DOI in file; JSTOR 10.2307/j.ctvt1sgqt)
size_dependence: n/a
note: Secondary only: Rasmusen's account of the 1995 book, not the primary text. Expressive utility peaking at the same point as intrinsic is Rasmusen's report of Kuran. Rasmusen's critique: expressive utility is problematic and reputational utility underspecified.

statement: Brummitt et al.'s description of the 1989 Kuran model: two utility components, reputational utility and integrity utility
work: Brummitt, Barnett and D'Souza 2015, J R Soc Interface 12(112) 20150712, doi 10.1098/rsif.2015.0712
size_dependence: n/a
note: Corrected form: the three-utility scheme (intrinsic, expressive, reputational) is the 1995 book per Rasmusen; the 1989 model has reputational and integrity utility per Brummitt et al. Both sources secondary to Kuran.

statement: Smaldino optimal-distinctiveness balance: each agent has a target frequency d* of its social identity in the visible population and moves to the SID whose frequency d_g is nearest d*
work: Smaldino et al. 2012, JASSS 15(4) 7, doi 10.18564/jasss.2030
size_dependence: Number of groups k*(d*) depends on d* and on whether information is local (spatial) or well mixed
note: Reading as a belonging-versus-distinctiveness two-drive balance is the file's own mapping, not Smaldino's wording; the model sections were read.

statement: Schweitzer-Garcia Brownian agent state: valence v and arousal a per agent, with expression when a >= tau_i and relaxation rates gamma_v, gamma_a
work: Schweitzer and Garcia 2010, EPJB 77(4) 533-545, doi 10.1140/epjb/e2010-00292-1
size_dependence: Simulations use N=1,000 agents; aggregate field is a leaky integral of expressions
note: Read from arXiv 1006.5305 preprint; published version may differ in the flagged signs.

statement: ASCRIBE emotional intensity q in [0,1] per person per emotion, updated by weighted-mean absorption from neighbours q_i* and an optional amplifier
size_dependence: n/a
note: Consensus core read in Bertozzi section 1.1 (UCLA CAM 14-36). Amplifier form is standard account, not read.

statement: Epstein grievance G = H(1 - L) (hardship times illegitimacy-complement) with net risk, compared to a threshold
size_dependence: Risk rises with local cop-to-active ratio
note: Standard account (via 24), not read at source. The file's contradiction 1 records that 068 derives the threshold in the cop-to-active ratio and finds one mean-field fixed point.

statement: McClelland controlled reference r_i: two opposed controllers acting on one shared variable, with a set point and escalating output effort
work: McClelland 2004, IJHCS 60 65-99, doi 10.1016/j.ijhcs.2003.08.003
size_dependence: n/a
note: Abstract and secondary only; paper not retrievable. Aggregation rule carried over from note 18.

statement: Granovetter difference equation: r(t+1) = F[r(t)], r(t) the proportion joined by time t, F the cumulative distribution of thresholds
size_dependence: Map is in the proportion variable r; continuous in F's shape but not continuous in the mean
note: Page 1425 of the paper, checked against the text in validation.

statement: Equilibrium: r_e is the point where F first crosses the 45-degree line from above, F(r_e) = r_e
size_dependence: n/a
note: Page 1427 of the paper. The paper asserts no oscillation without removal (p. 1426) and an equilibrium will always be reached.

statement: Monotone convergence [derived]: if F is non-decreasing and r(0)=0 then r(t) is non-decreasing and converges to the least solution of F(r) = r
work: Granovetter 1978, doi 10.1086/226707 (standard monotone-sequence argument, derived in file)
size_dependence: Holds for any finite population; limit is a fixed point when F is left-continuous at it
note: Corrected form (validation): the limit is a fixed point only when F is left-continuous there. Counterexample: F(x) = x/2 + 1/4 on [0,1/2), F = 1 from 1/2 gives a limit of 1/2 that is not a fixed point.

statement: Stability criterion for a smooth F: r_e is locally stable if F'(r_e) < 1 and unstable if F'(r_e) > 1; F'(r_e) = 1 is a saddle-node (fold) bifurcation
work: Granovetter 1978, doi 10.1086/226707 (criterion not stated in paper; derived in file)
size_dependence: For the finite step-function F the derivative does not exist; robustness is the number of individuals to add or remove
note: Labelling: 05 gives this as abstract/standard account; 066 tags it derived. Granovetter aims at a stability assessment but does not supply one.

statement: Normal-threshold fold: with mean 25 and N=100, the equilibrium r_e jumps from about 5.5 to near 100 at sigma_c = 12.222 (computed)
work: Granovetter 1978, doi 10.1086/226707 (paper states approximately 12.2; computed by 066)
size_dependence: Depends on the mean threshold, sigma and N; limit as sigma grows is 50
note: Computed by iterating r -> 100 * Phi((r-25)/sigma) from r=0; the paper's 'about six' is the left-limit value just below sigma_c.

statement: Sampling: from a uniform threshold population, P(no instigator in a crowd of 100) = (1 - .01)^100 = .37; P(zero or one rioter) = .51; P(no large riot in 10 incidents each with probability .10) = (.90)^10 = .35
work: Granovetter 1978, doi 10.1086/226707
size_dependence: Depends on crowd size of 100 and the sampling distribution
note: Model calculation, not data. The paper uses it to explain Spilerman's finding illustratively.

statement: Friend-weighting example: with influence of friends twice that of strangers, an individual with threshold 50% who knows 20 people of whom 15 joined sees a ratio 63/120 = .525 > .5 and joins
work: Granovetter 1978, doi 10.1086/226707
size_dependence: Depends on tie structure and weights
note: Arithmetic checked in validation.

statement: Watts degree-vulnerability probability: rho_k = P[phi <= 1/k] = F(1/k) for k > 0 and rho_0 = 1
size_dependence: Depends on degree k and the threshold distribution F
note: Eq. 1b of the paper.

statement: Watts cascade condition: sum_k k(k-1) rho_k p_k = G_0''(1) = z; cascades iff G_0''(1) > z (percolating vulnerable cluster)
size_dependence: Depends on mean degree z and the joint degree and threshold distributions
note: Eq. 5 of the paper. Replaces the Granovetter fixed-point test on sparse graphs with a small seed (file's equivalence item 1).

statement: Watts uniform random graph reduction: with Poisson degrees and homogeneous threshold phi*, the cascade condition is z Q(K* - 1, z) = 1, K* = 1/phi*, Q the incomplete gamma function
size_dependence: Depends on z and K*; yields two solutions in z (cascade window)
note: Quoted as printed; not re-derived in the file.

statement: Watts cascade window: the cascade condition has either zero or two solutions in z; first-order transition at the upper edge, power-law cascade sizes at the lower edge, bimodal at the upper edge
size_dependence: Lower edge z = 1.05 and upper edge z = 6.14 at n = 1,000; cumulative slope 1/2 at the lower edge
note: Theorem-like result of the paper's model; checked against simulation of the same model.

statement: Watts heterogeneity: widening the threshold distribution widens the cascade window; widening the degree distribution (power-law with cut-off) narrows it; threshold and network heterogeneity are not equivalent
size_dependence: Depends on which distribution is widened
note: Paper's own statement, checked in validation.

statement: Watts average global-cascade size tracks the whole connected component S, not the vulnerable cluster; a small percolating vulnerable cluster activates the entire component (random graphs)
size_dependence: Stated only for random graphs, at least within that class
note: Paper's surprising result as quoted in the file.

statement: Schweitzer-Garcia expression rule and field: s_i(t+Dt) = sign(v_i) Theta[a_i - tau_i]; dh_+/dt = -gamma_+ h_+ + s N_+ + I_+
work: Schweitzer and Garcia 2010, EPJB 77(4) 533-545, doi 10.1140/epjb/e2010-00292-1
size_dependence: Field is an aggregate memory of N_+ and N_- expressions
note: Equations (4) and (7) of the preprint.

statement: Schweitzer-Garcia valence pitchfork: with b0 = b2 = 0, v = 0 is stable and unique when b1 h < gamma_v; collective emotion requires h > h* = gamma_v / b1
work: Schweitzer and Garcia 2010, EPJB 77(4) 533-545, doi 10.1140/epjb/e2010-00292-1
size_dependence: Critical field depends on b1 and gamma_v, not on N
note: Bifurcation condition is unaffected by the sign error below. Stated as a supercritical pitchfork in h (file's label).

statement: Schweitzer-Garcia arousal fixed point (linear case, eq. 22): a(h) = h d0 / (gamma_a - d1 h); agent i expresses iff h >= h_i* = tau_i gamma_a / (d0 + tau_i d1)
work: Schweitzer and Garcia 2010, EPJB 77(4) 533-545, doi 10.1140/epjb/e2010-00292-1
size_dependence: Depends on the per-agent threshold tau_i
note: h_i* is derived in the file; the equivalence to Granovetter's fixed point holds only if expression is persistent (reset makes f_s a rate, not a step).

statement: Schweitzer-Garcia dropout: with saturated feedback (d2 < 0) an agent whose arousal fluctuates below the unstable stationary level drops out permanently; superlinear feedback (d2 > 0) allows re-entry
work: Schweitzer and Garcia 2010, EPJB 77(4) 533-545, doi 10.1140/epjb/e2010-00292-1
size_dependence: n/a
note: Paper states fluctuations are essential: such a scenario cannot be sustained in purely deterministic dynamics.

statement: Smaldino prediction and observed law: the theory predicts k* = round[1/d*] active groups, but the well-mixed simulation gives k*(d*) = floor[1/(2 d*)] + 1
work: Smaldino et al. 2012, JASSS 15(4) 7, doi 10.18564/jasss.2030
size_dependence: Depends on d*; well-mixed case uses N=3,000 and k0=30; local spatial interaction gives distinctiveness much closer to optimal
note: Eq. (2) is an exact empirical law of the simulation, not a proof; the mechanism is verbal. For d* = 0.2 it gives 3 against the theory's 5.

statement: Smaldino update rule: an agent computes d_g = n_g/N for each SID and switches to the SID minimising |d_g - d*|
work: Smaldino et al. 2012, JASSS 15(4) 7, doi 10.18564/jasss.2030
size_dependence: Depends on N and on the visible population (local neighbourhood on a lattice)
note: Spatial version uses square neighbourhood of side 2r+1; runs use L=50, k0=9.

statement: Kuran equilibrium: the public share S of opposition solves a fixed-point equation with one or three equilibria; with three, two are stable and one unstable; slow change can cause a saddle-node bifurcation
work: Kuran 1989, Public Choice 61(1) 41-74, doi 10.1007/BF00116762 (via Brummitt et al. 2015, doi 10.1098/rsif.2015.0712)
size_dependence: Equilibrium count depends on the distribution of private preferences
note: Corrected attribution (validation): the equation (Eq. 8, Figs 3-7) is in Kuran 1989, not Kuran 1991 as first written. Kuran's own text unread; secondary only.

statement: Kuran two routes to a saddle-node: (1) shift in the distribution of private preferences toward the opposition; (2) change in reputational utility terms, shifting the threshold function
work: Kuran 1989, Public Choice 61(1) 41-74, doi 10.1007/BF00116762 (via Brummitt et al. 2015)
size_dependence: Depends on the private distribution and reputational weights
note: Filled in from Brummitt et al., citing Kuran 1989 section 4.1 pp. 51-53.

statement: ASCRIBE consensus: dq_i/dt = gamma (q_i* - q_i), where q_i* is the weighted mean of neighbours' q_j with weights w_ij
size_dependence: Unique weighted-mean fixed point on a connected graph; no critical mass
note: Eq. (1) of Bertozzi, read. The full weights depend on five quantities; the three-factor product is not in Bertozzi (see contradiction 2).

statement: ASCRIBE amplifying variant, decomposed [derived]: dq/dt = gamma[eta(beta q*(1-q) - (1-beta) q(1-q*)) + (1-eta)(q* - q)]; with beta = 1/2 the amplification cancels to consensus at half rate
work: Bosse et al. 2009 and 2015 (standard account; not read)
size_dependence: Tipping only with heterogeneous beta or eta across agents (derived, unverified)
note: Built on a standard-account form, so tagged sa. Per the ledger rule nothing sa may feed an equation: this line must not feed an equation until Bosse 2009 or 2015 is read.

statement: McClelland virtual controller: two controllers on one variable act as one with summed gain and reference r_v = (G1 r1 + G2 r2)/(G1 + G2)
work: McClelland 2004, IJHCS 60 65-99, doi 10.1016/j.ijhcs.2003.08.003 (rule via McClelland 1993 per Martin Taylor's PCT page)
size_dependence: Depends on gains G1, G2
note: Standard account carried from note 18; paper not read.

statement: Steiner task-typed combination: actual group performance = potential - process loss, combining members by additive, disjunctive (max), conjunctive (min), compensatory (mean) or discretionary rules
work: Steiner 1972 (no DOI in file; not checked in validation)
size_dependence: n/a
note: Standard account via 24, not re-read.

statement: Epstein activation rule: an agent acts if grievance minus net risk exceeds a threshold, with risk rising in the local cop-to-active ratio
size_dependence: Depends on the cop-to-active ratio
note: Standard account via 24. 066 calls it Granovetter with a state-dependent threshold shift; 068 finds it has one mean-field fixed point (see contradiction 1).

statement: Granovetter non-identifiability: the group outcome is not a function of any finite moment of F, so mean threshold cannot be a sufficient statistic
work: Granovetter 1978, doi 10.1086/226707 (derived from the two-crowd example)
size_dependence: Depends on the full distribution, not the mean
note: Derived theorem-grade constraint; the paper's two-crowd example (uniform 0..99 versus one replaced) is the evidence.

statement: Granovetter's paper contains no fit to data; its falsification conditions are: all or most thresholds at 0% or 100% (behaviour not contingent on others), and aggregate participation oscillating in a stable cost-benefit situation
size_dependence: Falsification of the model's form, not of a specific threshold distribution
note: Corrected form (validation): the earlier note said the model is unfalsifiable as stated; the paper gives explicit falsifying conditions and discusses pluralistic ignorance and non-monotone (two-crossing) individuals, pp. 1438-1439. The file judges the model weakly falsifiable in practice because F is a free function.

statement: Spilerman's finding that racial disorders scale with black population is re-explained by sampling variability in threshold crowds; this is an illustrative reinterpretation, not a test
work: Granovetter 1978, doi 10.1086/226707 (Spilerman regression not read)
size_dependence: Depends on population composition and crowd sampling
note: The file states Granovetter's paper has no fit; the published regression itself was not read.

Verdict: leans to Thron & Jackson on the printed formula, one replication; unresolved.

statement: Epstein's cop-reduction result tips society into rebellion, versus Thron & Jackson's 'no tipping points' with behaviour changing smoothly with parameters
source: 067 §1 Empirical standing (iii-b) and Theorems (e); 067 Cross-checks item 3 (068 result 7)

statement: Epstein's text calls the legitimacy drop 0.30, while the 0.9 to 0.7 example in the same paper is 0.20
work: Epstein 2002, PNAS 99 suppl. 3, 7243-7250, doi:10.1073/pnas.092080199; Epstein, Steinbruner & Parker 2001, Brookings CSED WP 20
note: Source inconsistency noted in 068 and carried into 067's Cross-checks, not in 067's body. Unresolved.

statement: Model II maximum age: Appendix A lists 200 for all models, while the Model II text says max_age = 100
work: Epstein, Steinbruner & Parker 2001, Brookings CSED WP 20 (Appendix A and Model II text)
note: Both sides: Appendix A (footnoted 'Departures noted in text') says 200; the Model II text says 100. Verdict per Validation log: 100 is the run value; Appendix A is overridden. Resolved in favour of the text.

statement: Grievance G: a felt, private, graded state in [0,1] per agent, G = H(1 - L); static in the model (agents leave jail "exactly as aggrieved"), with no anger accumulation, contagion, habituation or backlash.
work: Epstein, J. M. (2002). Modeling civil violence: an agent-based computational approach. PNAS 99 (suppl. 3), 7243-7250. doi:10.1073/pnas.092080199
note: Epstein calls G a felt grievance; the file's own justification for the product form is intuition only (Blitz example), and Thron & Jackson state it is untested.

statement: Fear, as a felt risk-weighted estimate N = R P (net risk), with R per-agent risk aversion U(0,1) fixed for life and P the estimated arrest probability; memoryless, recomputed from the neighbourhood each activation.
source: 068 §1 (Drives/operands; Operators [read]: N = R P); §5 Does not exist (fear is memoryless)
size_dependence: P depends on the local ratio C/A of cops to actives in vision.
note: Epstein's N is stated as the alpha = 0 case of N = R P J^alpha (J the jail term), so jail length has no deterrent effect in the printed rule.

statement: G = H(1 - L): grievance is the product of perceived hardship H and perceived illegitimacy (1 - L).
note: Justified by intuition only (British legitimacy in the Blitz, L = 1, so no grievance despite extreme hardship). Thron & Jackson say it rests solely on Epstein's plausibility argument and has never been verified empirically.

statement: P = 1 - exp[-k (C/A)_v]: estimated arrest probability from the cops-to-actives ratio in vision v, with A counting the agent itself (so A >= 1), k = 2.3.
size_dependence: Depends on C/A in vision v; the local ratio, not global counts.
note: Corrected in validation: k = 2.3 is approximately ln 10 (2.3026), not exactly; k was set so that P = 0.9 when C = A = 1, and with k = 2.3 exactly P(C = A = 1) = 0.8997. Thron & Jackson write the same form as P = 1 - 0.1^(C/A) (their eq. 4).

statement: Agent rule A: an agent is active (Q to A) if G - N > T and quiescent (A to Q) if G - N <= T, re-evaluated at each activation, so the rule has no memory; T is non-negative ("could be zero") and set to 0.1 in all runs.
note: Equation images were read as images from PMC and transcribed exactly per the file; the validation log records that equation images were not re-read in validation.

statement: Cop rule C and movement rule M: cops inspect all sites within v* and arrest a random active agent; agents and cops move to a random site within vision; asynchronous random-order activation.
source: 068 §1 (Operators, Cop rule C; Movement rule M [read, image])
size_dependence: Vision v is a model parameter (1.7 or 7 in the runs).
note: Thron & Jackson's cop rule differs slightly from NetLogo's (cops arrest before moving), per 068 §4.3.

statement: Jail: arrested actives receive a term drawn from U(0, J_max) and leave jail exactly as aggrieved as they entered.
size_dependence: J_max varied across runs (15, 30, infinite).
note: Thron & Jackson note extremists are almost always in jail in their set-up, and call the resulting small effect of extremist fraction an unrealistic feature of the model.

statement: Ripeness (tension index) = (mean G)(mean fraction quiescent) / (mean R); offered as a candidate warning indicator, shown in one run only.
note: Contradiction 1 below: this file's phrasing says a buildup precedes each outburst; the working paper names a dip as the true warning indicator. The index definition agrees in both.

statement: Interpretation of the rule: G - N is the expected utility of publicly expressing one's private grievance and T the expected utility of not expressing it (preference falsification, Kuran); individual rationality is local, excluding the agent's own effect on the social order.
note: The file takes T as a global constant in this model, the cost of speaking.

statement: Operands: H perceived hardship (exogenous per agent, U(0,1)); L legitimacy (exogenous, equal across agents, varied 0 to 1); R risk aversion (per agent, U(0,1), fixed); C and A the local counts of cops and actives within vision; deception = private grievance hidden from public expression.
note: Epstein states "I make no pretense to measuring model variables such as perceived hardship or legitimacy" and that no political or social order is represented in the model.

statement: Outburst: more than 50 actives in the population (Epstein's threshold for an outburst).
size_dependence: Defined by an absolute count, so it is a fixed crowd size in a 40 x 40 grid.
note: Thron & Jackson's critical crowd size is their own, distinct concept (68 §4.3); the file does not compare the two thresholds numerically.

statement: Repression ratio rho = C/A: the local ratio of cops to actives in vision, the single scalar on which the arrest estimate depends in the algebra.
work: Derived in prior work 068 (from Epstein 2002 equations)
size_dependence: Local, so it varies with vision; the mean-field version uses a global ratio.
note: Derived here from the printed rule, not stated by Epstein.

statement: Composition in one line: a_i = [ H_i (1 - L) - R_i (1 - exp(-k C/A)) > T ]; the agent acts iff net drive exceeds T.
work: Derived in prior work 068 (from Epstein 2002 equations)
size_dependence: Depends on C/A through the exponential term.
note: Algebraic recast of the printed rule; the file gives it as a proposal for the algebra, not as a published result.

statement: Granovetter form: for g_i = H_i (1 - L), the agent is active iff C/A < theta_i with theta_i = -ln(1 - (g_i - T)/R_i) / k, valid when 0 < (g_i - T)/R_i < 1; inert (never active) if g_i - T <= 0; active for any crowd (extremist) if (g_i - T)/R_i >= 1.
work: Derived in prior work 068 (from Epstein 2002 equations); cf. Thron & Jackson arXiv:1501.05838 §4.1
size_dependence: Activation needs A/C > 1/theta_i; the threshold is a function of the crowd-to-cop ratio, not of a count.
note: Derived here. Cross-check: 067 derives the same expression and credits Thron & Jackson sec. 4.1, which got there first; the credit should be shared, the algebra agrees.

statement: Safety-in-numbers operator: phi_j -> phi_j * (1 - exp(-k C/(A+1))) / (1 - exp(-k C/A)); an active agent lowers the fear drive of others and does not change their grievance; no operator raises grievance in neighbours.
work: Derived in prior work 068 (from Epstein 2002 equations)
size_dependence: Effect depends on C/A; diminishes as A grows.
note: File says the asymmetry is a finding about the model, not about people: the only coupling between agents is through fear. Cross-checked against 067 'only fear is coupled downward' and 24 §10.

statement: Mean-field response: with H and R independent U(0,1) and g = 1 - L > T, the fraction active when arrest estimate is P is f(P) = 1 - T/g - P/(2g) if P < g - T, and f(P) = (g - T)^2 / (2 g P) if P >= g - T; the two branches are continuous at P = g - T.
work: Derived in prior work 068 (from Epstein 2002 equations); limits cross-checked against Thron & Jackson arXiv:1501.05838
size_dependence: Assumes homogeneous H and R, uniform and independent; ignores jail and spatial correlation.
note: Validation: re-derived by hand, both branches and limits f(0) = 1 - T/g and f(1) = (g - T)^2/(2g) match Thron & Jackson's (G_max - T)^2/(2 G_max) and 1 - T/G_max with G_max = 1 - L. Not checked beyond those two limits.

statement: Zero-cop critical legitimacy: with H ~ U(0,1) and no cops, anyone can be active only if g > T, i.e. L < 1 - T; for T = 0.1 this is L < 0.9.
work: Derived in prior work 068 (from Epstein 2002 equations)
note: Not the same quantity as Ormazabal et al.'s L_c = 1 - 2T; see Contradiction 7. The file says the no-police consensus phase at L = 0.90, T = 0.10 is exactly this bound.

statement: Mean-field fixed point is unique and smooth: with x the active fraction, kappa = k c/rho and P(x) = 1 - exp(-kappa/x), F(x) = f(P(x)) is increasing (positive feedback), F(0+) = (g - T)^2/(2g) > 0; for L = 0.8, T = 0.1, large-vision limit, x = 0.37, 0.12, 0.046 at kappa 0.02, 0.028, 0.036 with a floor of 0.025 at large kappa; one fixed point for L in {0.5, 0.7, 0.8}, no hysteresis.
work: Derived in prior work 068 (from Epstein 2002 equations); consistent with Thron & Jackson 'no tipping points' [read]
size_dependence: Finite-vision scan over N in {10, 30, 107} and cop counts from 0.05 to 30; the large-vision numbers are the reported ones. The jail sink and heterogeneity in local cop count are left out.
note: Derived numerically, not a published theorem. Not rerun in validation for the finite-vision scan. Says nothing about the spatial model, which is Contradiction 4.

statement: Thron & Jackson: outbursts in the model are entirely produced by lapses in cop coverage; cops are placed randomly so the count in a vision circle is Poisson, and where it is low a knot of actives forms and spreads.
work: Thron, C. & Jackson, E. (2015). Practicality of Agent-Based Modeling of Civil Violence: an Assessment. arXiv:1501.05838 [physics.soc-ph]
size_dependence: Depends on cop density and vision (Poisson count per circle).
note: Stated as an argument, not a proof, per the file. Thron & Jackson's venue is IOSSBR 2012 with 'JSSR 2013, Volume II', no DOI; treat as conference-reviewed at most.

statement: Thron & Jackson analytic argument: the model is a Markov chain, so waiting times between outbursts are approximately exponential (memoryless) beyond a time window; the model exhibits self-organised criticality, so outburst sizes should be roughly power-law.
source: 068 §4.3 (analytic claims, at the level of argument)
work: Thron, C. & Jackson, E. (2015). arXiv:1501.05838
size_dependence: Exponential only past a time window; power-law sizes argued from SOC.
note: Argument, not proof. Support offered is ACLED riot-size data for Africa and Nigeria showing heavier-than-exponential tails. Epstein's own exponential tail was reported only after truncation (Contradiction 6).

statement: Thron & Jackson reduced characterisation: all population behaviour is fixed by the activist response f(y), y = A/C, with four numbers (extremist fraction, inert fraction, critical crowd size, saturation crowd size); they replace Epstein's response with a logistic function with exponent p in their own implementation.
work: Thron, C. & Jackson, E. (2015). arXiv:1501.05838
size_dependence: Critical crowd size and saturation crowd size are the size-dependent parameters.
note: Corrected in validation: the phrase 'reduces the number of free parameters' in their abstract refers to the f(y) characterisation, not to the logistic choice; the logistic function and exponent are their own modification, not Epstein's.

statement: Thron & Jackson limits: extremist fraction (G_max - T)^2 / (2 G_max) and inert fraction 1 - T/G_max, with G_max = 1 - L.
source: 068 §4.1 (Thron & Jackson state the same two limits [read])
work: Thron, C. & Jackson, E. (2015). arXiv:1501.05838
note: Thron & Jackson do not give the full f; the file's own f reproduces these two limits.

statement: Ormazabal et al.: a dashed line of critical legitimacy L_c = 1 - 2T for a one-dimensional lattice without police, the line of equal active and passive concentrations (AP to PA phases), obtained by assuming an average agent (mean H = 0.5, so mean G = T).
work: Ormazabal, Urbina, Borotto & Astudillo (2022). Phase diagram in a one-dimensional civil disorder model. Phys. Rev. E 105, 054110. doi:10.1103/physreve.105.054110 (arXiv:2110.00835)
size_dependence: One-dimensional, Moore and random neighbourhoods; not Epstein's motion rule.
note: Corrected in validation: L_c = 1 - 2T is their equal-concentration line under the average-agent assumption, not a no-activity bound. Phases with police added: six ordered majority phases, one disordered, and the consensus phase.

statement: Zou et al. (2012): a civil-violence ABM reduces to two coarse-grained degrees of freedom, the number of jailed citizens and the number of active ones, cutting computation time by a factor of approximately 20.
source: 068 §4.5 (from abstract, re-read on APS page in validation)
work: Zou, Fonoberov, Fonoberova, Mezić & Kevrekidis (2012). Model reduction for agent-based social simulation: Coarse-graining a civil violence model. Phys. Rev. E 85, 066106. doi:10.1103/PhysRevE.85.066106
note: Reduced equations and any bifurcation analysis were not read; unconfirmed beyond the abstract.

statement: Individual deception: aggrieved agents go quiescent when cops are near and active when cops leave; the model's individual-level response to repression.
size_dependence: Depends on local cop presence.
note: Simulation outcome of the printed rule, not an empirical result. Epstein does no data fitting; the model is qualitative.

statement: Free assembly catalyses outbursts: a chance cluster of actives lowers local C/A, lowers P, and recruits the mildly aggrieved ('a single spark can cause a prairie fire'); Epstein reads this as the rationale for banning assembly and for curfews.
size_dependence: Depends on local cluster size lowering C/A.
note: Ethics marked n/a because the finding itself is a dynamic; Epstein's policy reading (banning assembly, curfews) is the steering-relevant part and is his interpretation, not a tested result.

statement: Punctuated equilibrium: long quiet spells broken by outbursts, persisting over 20,000 iterations.
size_dependence: Vision and cop density set in the runs; the spatial fluctuation mechanism is argued by Thron & Jackson.
note: Simulation outcome. The file's replication did not reproduce it with the printed exponential rule at v = 7 (see the replication line); it did with the floor rule.

statement: Waiting time between outbursts (outburst = more than 50 actives), over 100,000 iterations: mean 60, SD 55, suggesting a Weibull or perhaps lognormal; after truncating waits under 30, a negative exponential fit with R-squared 0.98, slope -0.07, intercept 3.5 (OLS on logged data); rigorous identification left to future research.
size_dependence: Model-internal; the file does not report a size dependence.
note: Fit is a simulation result, not an out-of-sample test. The file's own replication did not reproduce the mean-60 waiting time from the printed rule (see the replication line).

statement: Outburst size (total activation), mean 708, SD 230; no distribution identified.
note: Simulation outcome. Thron & Jackson argue power-law sizes from SOC and cite ACLED for heavier-than-exponential tails.

statement: Salami tactics: legitimacy cut from 0.9 to 0.2 in small steps (a percent per cycle) produced no spike; a single cut from 0.9 to 0.7 at t = 77 produced an explosion. Epstein: the rate of change (the derivative) of legitimacy is what emerges as salient.
source: 068 §1 (Results reported, item 6); Validation log (0.30 versus 0.20 source inconsistency); cross-check 067 results (d)

statement: Cop reductions produce a tipping point under incremental decline of cops, unlike incremental legitimacy decline (Epstein relates this to Tocqueville: liberalization is the most difficult of political arts).
size_dependence: Depends on cop density.
note: Contradicts Thron & Jackson's 'no tipping points' for the homogeneous model; mean-field supports Thron & Jackson, the spatial model is open (Contradiction 4).

statement: Model II (two ethnic groups; going active means killing out-group members): with L = 0.8 and no cops, genocide in 30 of 30 runs with a random victor (competitive exclusion); peacekeepers deployed early give safe havens; for cop densities 0 to 0.1 (50 runs per density, 15,000-cycle cap) mean time to genocide rises with peacekeeper density, but its SD also rises; the 'linear' fit is Epstein's plotted fit, with no slope or fit statistic in the text.
size_dependence: Mean time to genocide rises with peacekeeper density over 0 to 0.1.
note: Corrected in validation: 'rises roughly linearly' reworded to Epstein's plotted linear fit, since the text reports no fit statistic.

statement: Thron & Jackson (their own set-up: 80 x 80 grid, 4,480 agents, 152 cops, vision 7, J_max 100, 1,000 steps, 200 simulations per parameter set): outburst frequency rose about 1000-fold across excitable fraction 0.6 to 1.0.
work: Thron, C. & Jackson, E. (2015). arXiv:1501.05838
size_dependence: Excitable fraction is the varied parameter.
note: Not Epstein's set-up; a simulation result. No out-of-sample test.

statement: Thron & Jackson: a 10% fall in critical crowd size gave about 25% more outbursts and about 25% larger peaks.
work: Thron, C. & Jackson, E. (2015). arXiv:1501.05838
size_dependence: Critical crowd size is the varied parameter.
note: Simulation result under their own parameterisation.

statement: Thron & Jackson: doubling the extremist fraction slightly reduced outburst frequency (about 5%), which they attribute to extremists being almost always in jail and call 'due to unrealistic features of the model'.
work: Thron, C. & Jackson, E. (2015). arXiv:1501.05838
size_dependence: Extremist fraction is the varied parameter.
note: The authors themselves flag the result as an artefact of the model.

statement: Thron & Jackson: ACLED riot-size data for Africa and Nigeria show heavier-than-exponential tails, offered as support for the self-organised-criticality argument.
work: Thron, C. & Jackson, E. (2015). arXiv:1501.05838 (ACLED data)
note: Empirical support offered by the authors for a model-output shape; the file does not report a fit to the riot data.

statement: Thron & Jackson simulation finding: no tipping points and smooth change in behaviour with parameters.
work: Thron, C. & Jackson, E. (2015). arXiv:1501.05838
size_dependence: Parameter-dependent, smooth.
note: Simulation finding; the file's mean-field scan agrees for the homogeneous version only (Contradiction 4).

statement: Ormazabal et al.: a one-dimensional phase diagram with order-disorder phases: without police, active-majority AP, passive-majority PA, a disordered phase and an all-passive consensus phase (at L = 0.90 for T = 0.10); with police, six ordered majority phases, one disordered and the consensus phase; transitions described as continuous, read from stationary distributions.

statement: Replication of Epstein's printed rule (author's own quick re-implementation, single seeds): with v = 7, L = 0.82, J_max 30, cops 0.04, 1,500 steps, mean actives 0.8, max 16, no outbursts; with the NetLogo-style floor rule P = 1 - 0.1^floor(C/A), v = 7, 800 steps, mean actives 33, max 350, 28 outbursts, mean wait 23.7 (SD 6.1); with v = 1.7, L = 0.82, persistent mass rebellion (mean actives 259); with v = 1.7, L = 0.89, J_max 15, activity hovering at the outburst threshold (mean 64, 6 crossings, mean wait 1.5).

statement: Pais parameterisation: gamma_i = rho_i = v_i, alpha_i = 1/v_i, beta = sigma, a constant value-independent inhibition strength (N = 2)
work: Pais, Hogan, Schlegel, Franks, Leonard, Marshall 2013, PLoS ONE 8, e73216, doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0073216
note: Read in full by file 029 (per 069 §Method, cited, not re-read in 069); tagged [read] in 069.

statement: Pais's model is Reina's model at r = 1 AND constant beta; r = 1 alone is not enough, because Reina's beta = h v is not constant
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
note: Corrected form: the earlier wording treated r = 1 as sufficient; the validation log tightened it to require both conditions.

statement: Reina requires v >= 1: below it some states go negative and are not biologically meaningful
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
note: Stated in Reina App. B.

statement: Weber-law property: for N = 2 the minimum value difference separating two options scales with the mean value, Delta v ~ v-bar, with the coefficient set by r (by sigma in Pais)
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
note: From Reina Fig. 6b.

statement: structural contrast: in cross-inhibition, inhibited bees return to uncommitted, not to the rival option; this is the structural difference from direct-switching (Marshall et al. 2009)
work: Marshall, Bogacz, Dornhaus, Planque, Kovacs, Franks 2009, J R Soc Interface 6, 1065-1074, doi 10.1098/rsif.2008.0511
note: Full citation added in validation (was incomplete). Marshall 2009 is not stated as read in 069; 029 §B2 is cited.

statement: operator inventory: linear operators on one agent's state (discover u to i; lapse i to u) and bilinear pair operators (recruit i,u to i,i; block j,i to j,u); both are Markov-type transition operators on a categorical state and the ODE is their mean-field limit
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
size_dependence: Mean-field and well-mixed: no network structure.
note: 069's own reading for the algebra; the file says group-level quantities r and quorum are parameters of the interaction operators, not drives.

statement: committee mapping (proposal, none validated): x_i = share of members publicly committed to proposal i; x_u = undecided or listening members; v_i = perceived value of proposal i, with a single shared v assumed; r = h/k = social-to-independent ratio, the time spent lobbying versus fact-finding; quorum = the exogenous threshold at which the chair or rules declare a decision
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
note: Mapping proposal, unsourced and untested (file 069 §5); the file says human committees are only cited as analogy with no fitted data.

statement: dx_i/dt = gamma_i x_u - alpha_i x_i + rho_i x_i x_u - x_i sum_{j=1..N} x_j beta_ji (general form of the four transition operators, Reina Eq. 1 / A1)
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411

statement: dx_i/dtau = v x_u - x_i/v + r v x_i x_u - r v x_i sum_{j!=i} x_j, for equal qualities v (dimensionless form, R)
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
note: Reina Eq. 3 / D3 specialised; the sum was rewritten explicitly by 069.

statement: sigma* = 4 v^3 / (v^2 - 1)^2, the N = 2 Pais pitchfork threshold: below sigma* one stable symmetric attractor (deadlock), above it two attractors appear; exists only for v > 1, approximately 4/v for large v; for v <= 1 no sigma breaks the tie
work: Pais, Hogan, Schlegel, Franks, Leonard, Marshall 2013, PLoS ONE 8, e73216, doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0073216
note: Matches Reina App. B3, read. Numerics reproduced in validation: v = 2 gives sigma* = 3.56; sigma = 3.2 settles at (0.381, 0.381); sigma = 3.91 at (0.488, 0.262). The file's reading: equal high-value options are broken, equal low-value options deadlock; the required stop-signal strength falls as options get better.

statement: symmetric equilibrium condition v U - x/v + v x U - sigma x^2 = 0 with U = 1 - 2x (x_A = x_B = x)
work: Pais, Hogan, Schlegel, Franks, Leonard, Marshall 2013, PLoS ONE 8, e73216, doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0073216
note: Derived in 069 and checked numerically; not taken from a source. At v = 2, sigma = 3.2 it gives x = 0.38129 (see contradiction on the 0.41 value in 029).

statement: antisymmetric-perturbation eigenvalue lambda = rho U - alpha = vU - 1/v; lambda = 0 gives U = 1/v^2 and x = (v^2 - 1)/(2 v^2)
work: Pais, Hogan, Schlegel, Franks, Leonard, Marshall 2013, PLoS ONE 8, e73216, doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0073216
note: Derived in 069 (sigma terms cancel); checked numerically.

statement: Reina App. B (N = 3, r = 1, equal options): non-symmetric equilibria exist only for 8 v^3/(1 - 4 v^2) < beta < 0 (for v > 1/2); since beta >= 0 is required, the only real stable equilibrium is the symmetric deadlock
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
size_dependence: N = 3 and above: the binary pitchfork does not generalise; the Pais parameterisation cannot break N >= 3 ties.
note: Derived via a discriminant condition, Eq. B1.

statement: N = 2 reduces to Reina Eq. B2 (4 alpha gamma rho / (rho - alpha)^2) and B3 (the sigma* of the Pais threshold)
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
size_dependence: N = 2 only; does not generalise to N >= 3.
note: Form of B2 quoted as the file gives it.

statement: Pais parameterisation integrated at N = 3 (v = 2, 5) and N = 4 (v = 5) with beta from 0.5 to 50 always converges to the symmetric split, e.g. (0.118, 0.118, 0.118) at beta = 50, v = 2; (0.169 each) at N = 3, v = 5, beta = 50; (0.133 each) at N = 4, v = 5, beta = 50
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
size_dependence: N = 3 and N = 4 tested; symmetric split persists.
note: Derived numerical check by 069, confirmed in validation; a numerical check, not a proof.

statement: symmetric N-option Jacobian eigenvalues: a + (N-1) b (total commitment, stable) and a - b with multiplicity N-1 (between-option), where a = -v - 1/v + r v (u - N x), b = -v - 2 r v x, and lambda_between = -1/v + r v (u - (N-2) x)
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
size_dependence: Multiplicity N-1 of between-option eigenvalues.
note: Derived in 069 from (R); symmetric point x_i = x, u = 1 - N x.

statement: second bifurcation r2 (deadlock loses stability) solves A w^2 + B w - c^2 = 0 with c = 1/(2(N-1)), m = N v^2, A = c(1+m) - (2N-1) c^2, B = v^2 - c(2+m) + 2(2N-1) c^2, and r2 = 1/(w v^2) for the positive root w
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
size_dependence: Quadratic in N.
note: 069's own quadratic; it replaces Reina Eq. D4, whose printed form did not survive text extraction. Verified numerically only for the cases listed.

work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
size_dependence: Grows with N; the v-dependence fades as v grows.
note: Derived numerically in 069; reproduced in validation for N = 2, 3, 4, 6, 8.

statement: large-v limit: r2 approaches 2(N-1)(N-2) from above (e.g. 4.19, 12.16, 24.15, 84.13 at v = 5 against 4, 12, 24, 84)
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
size_dependence: r2 is quadratic in N; the dependence on quality fades as v grows.
note: Derived by fit to the table in 069; reproduced in validation.

statement: first bifurcation r1 (saddle-node, decided states appear while deadlock is still stable): v = 2 / v = 5: N=3: 2.98 / 1.75; N=4: 4.49 / 3.12; N=5: 5.92 / 4.56; approximately linear in N
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
size_dependence: Roughly linear in N.
note: Numerical, approximate to about 0.01, depends on 069's 'decided state' criterion. r1 values were not re-checked in validation. Reina's analytic form (Eq. D2/D4) not transcribed.

statement: Reina's own statement: r1 grows quasi-linearly with N, r2 grows quadratically with N; the influence of v decreases quadratically
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
size_dependence: r1 linear in N; r2 quadratic in N.
note: Quoted by 069 as Reina's text; Reina Eq. D4 closed form not transcribed.

statement: N = 3 phases in r: (I) r < r1, deadlock the only attractor; (II) r1 < r < r2, deadlock coexists with a stable decision for each option (hysteresis: noise or bias needed to leave deadlock); (III) r > r2, deadlock is a saddle, stable only along x_1 = x_2 = x_3, and a random one of the N options is chosen
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
size_dependence: Specific to N = 3.

statement: for odd N >= 5, extra unstable saddles appear between r1 and r2; they do not change the three macro-phases; no periodic attractors (Reina Fig. 2 caption)
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
size_dependence: Odd N >= 5 only.

statement: Reina's consequence: too many equal options preclude breaking the tie at a given signalling ratio; the cost of tie-breaking rises as N^2; 'this result suggests a limit on the maximum number of equal options that can be concurrently evaluated'
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
size_dependence: N^2 cost of tie-breaking.
note: No direct experimental test of the N^2 scaling or of phase II hysteresis was found in any animal (069 §4); the N^2 law is a model prediction.

statement: best-of-N ODEs (Reina Eq. 3 / A9), with kappa = v_inferior / v_best, x_A = best, x_B = pooled inferior: dx_A/dtau = v x_u - x_A/v + r v x_A [x_u - kappa x_B]; dx_B/dtau = (N-1) kappa v x_u - x_B/(kappa v) + r v x_B [kappa x_u - ((N-2)/(N-1)) kappa x_B - x_A]; x_u = 1 - x_A - x_B
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
size_dependence: Reduction aggregates the N-1 inferior sub-populations; Reina states it is qualitatively correct for arbitrarily large N.
note: Four parameters: N, v, kappa, r.

statement: best-of-N five phases A-E for N = 3 in (r, kappa): at low r a single attractor, but the best option's share may be too small to reach quorum; the low-share region grows with N and shrinks as kappa falls
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
size_dependence: Low-share region grows with N.
note: Reina's appendix text on this region is self-contradictory; see the contradiction line on Reina's kappa parenthetical.

statement: model timing check (Reina Fig. 7): k = 0.1, h = 0.3, v = 10, N = 3, kappa in {0.25, 0.5, 0.75} converges on field-experiment timescales if t is read in hours (Reina cites Seeley and Buhrman 2001 for the field times)
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
note: A model timing check against field times cited by Reina; not an out-of-sample fit.

statement: Reina's headline: the key parameter is the relative time spent discovering versus signalling; conflicting pressures: symmetric choice wants high r (r2 grows with N^2), best-of-N wants moderate r (too much signalling locks in an inferior early leader); resolvable by a time-dependent signalling strategy
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
size_dependence: Symmetric choice needs high r growing with N^2; best-of-N needs moderate r.
note: Headline statement of the model's trade-off, as the file gives it from Reina's abstract.

statement: stop signals aimed at dancers for rival nest sites are observed in honeybees (Seeley et al. 2012), grounding the cross-inhibition operator empirically
work: Seeley, Visscher, Schlegel, Hogan, Franks, Marshall 2012, Science 335, 108-111, doi 10.1126/science.1210361
note: Read from the abstract only (file 029 [read: abstract]). Cited by Reina as ref 5. The pitchfork and deadlock result is credited to this paper in 029 §B1 and 048 §2.

statement: Reina, Zakir, De Masi, Ferrante 2023: two opposed factions of inflexible minorities, or individuals switching on individual rather than social information, can hold a population in persistent indecision; compared with the voter model (equal options) and the weighted voter model (unequal options), cross-inhibition alone reaches a stable majority despite such asocial behaviour; mean-field results confirmed with 100 locally interacting robots
work: Reina, Zakir, De Masi, Ferrante 2023, Commun Phys 6, 236, doi 10.1038/s42005-023-01345-3
size_dependence: Tested with 100 locally interacting robots.

statement: committee prediction 1 (untested, conditional on the human mapping): equal-quality proposals with low lobbying (r < r1) stalemate, drifting to undecided mixtures; raising r breaks the tie, at random
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411

statement: committee prediction 2 (untested, conditional on the mapping): the r needed for a tie among N equal options grows about N^2, so a long shortlist of near-equals stalls; shortening the list is cheaper than raising lobbying
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
size_dependence: N^2 deadlock cost.

statement: committee prediction 3 (untested, conditional on the mapping): hysteresis in phase II, so an inert committee stays inert unless shocked; a small bias then tips it
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
note: Model prediction only; untested.

statement: committee prediction 4 (untested, conditional on the mapping): in best-of-N, high r speeds consensus but lets an early inferior proposal win; low r keeps the true best discoverable; time-dependent r (explore first, then lobby) is the model's own remedy
work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411

work: Reina, Marshall, Trianni, Bose 2017, Phys Rev E 95, 052411, doi 10.1103/PhysRevE.95.052411
