statement: McDougall instinct flight/fear: an instinct pairing fear with the impulse to flee
work: McDougall 1908, An Introduction to Social Psychology, Methuen (no DOI)

statement: McDougall instinct pugnacity/anger: an instinct pairing anger with the impulse to fight
work: McDougall 1908, An Introduction to Social Psychology, Methuen (no DOI)

statement: McDougall instincts repulsion/disgust, self-abasement/subjection, self-assertion/elation and parental/tender emotion, each an emotion-impulse pair
work: McDougall 1908, An Introduction to Social Psychology, Methuen (no DOI)
note: Later editions add gregariousness, acquisition and construction; the list varied between editions.

statement: McDougall sentiments: organised systems of emotional dispositions around an object, built from instincts, with the will as arbiter; no formal rules
work: McDougall 1908, An Introduction to Social Psychology, Methuen (no DOI)
note: Combination is weak and informal.

statement: Murray psychogenic needs, about 20 in number, including achievement, affiliation, aggression, autonomy, deference, dominance, exhibition, harmavoidance, nurturance, order, play, rejection, sentience, succorance and understanding
work: Murray 1938, Explorations in Personality, Oxford University Press (no DOI)
note: Factor structure of need scales is far smaller than 20; the PRF's needs correlate heavily (file, from abstract/standard account).

statement: Murray's informal relations between needs: fusion (one action serves several), subsidiation (one serves another), conflict (opposed needs) and inhibition
work: Murray 1938, Explorations in Personality, Oxford University Press (no DOI)
note: Named relations, informal; never formalised (file).

statement: Murray press: environmental forces (alpha: actual; beta: perceived) acting on needs; the need x press pair is an interaction, and thema is a need-press unit
work: Murray 1938, Explorations in Personality, Oxford University Press (no DOI)
note: The file reads press as a proto-operator by which the environment, including other people, acts on a drive.

statement: Maslow's five needs: physiological, safety, love/belonging, esteem and self-actualisation (later transcendence)
work: Maslow 1943, Psychological Review 50(4), DOI 10.1037/h0054346
note: Validation log: DOI added (Crossref).

statement: Maslow prepotency: a lower need dominates until relatively satisfied; stated by Maslow as a tendency, not a strict ordering; the pyramid drawing is not Maslow's
work: Maslow 1943, Psychological Review 50(4), DOI 10.1037/h0054346
note: Hierarchy weakly supported (file: Tay & Diener 2011).

statement: Kenrick et al. 2010 needs: immediate physiological needs, self-protection, affiliation, status/esteem, mate acquisition, mate retention, parenting (self-actualisation dropped)
work: Kenrick, Griskevicius, Neuberg & Schaller 2010, Perspectives on Psychological Science 5(3), DOI 10.1177/1745691610369469
note: Partly from search abstract (file).

statement: Kenrick et al.: the levels overlap and are dynamic; the dominant need depends on life-history stage and context, so priority is a state-dependent function of situation, not a fixed hierarchy
work: Kenrick, Griskevicius, Neuberg & Schaller 2010, Perspectives on Psychological Science 5(3), DOI 10.1177/1745691610369469
note: File reading: state-dependent weights of operands, not an operator. No algebra in source.

statement: Fundamental social motives: self-protection (from interpersonal threat), disease avoidance, affiliation, status, mate acquisition, mate retention, kin care
work: Neuberg, Kenrick & Schaller 2011, Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews 35(4), DOI 10.1016/j.neubiorev.2010.08.011; measured instrument Neel et al. 2016, JPSP 110(6), DOI 10.1037/pspp0000068
note: Neel et al. 2016 is the Fundamental Social Motives Inventory, named in the file as the source to use for an operationalised list.

statement: Each fundamental social motive is a functional system with its own cues, cognitive biases and behaviours, activated by situational cues; motives bias one another; there are no composition rules
work: Neuberg, Kenrick & Schaller 2011, Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews 35(4), DOI 10.1016/j.neubiorev.2010.08.011
note: Cue-activation of motives is the operator class the file proposes (motives as operand-state, cues as operators).

statement: McClelland's motives nAch (achievement), nAff (affiliation) and nPow (power), a reduction of Murray's list
work: McClelland 1961, The Achieving Society, Van Nostrand (no DOI); McClelland 1987, Human Motivation, Cambridge UP (no DOI)

statement: McClelland combinations are configural profiles with predictive claims (e.g. high nPow, low nAff and high activity inhibition as the leadership motive pattern), not an algebraic rule
work: McClelland 1961, The Achieving Society, Van Nostrand (no DOI)

statement: Reiss's 16 basic desires: power, independence, curiosity, acceptance, order, saving, honor, idealism, social contact, family, status, vengeance, romance, eating, physical activity and tranquility
work: Reiss 2004, Review of General Psychology 8(3), DOI 10.1037/1089-2680.8.3.179
note: Abstract read; list from the standard account (file).

statement: Reiss: the desires are largely unrelated and may have separate evolutionary histories; there is no interaction law, and individuals differ by profile (a weighting of each desire)
work: Reiss 2004, Review of General Psychology 8(3), DOI 10.1037/1089-2680.8.3.179
note: Relatedness claim comes from the author's own data; file asks for checking against other labs.

statement: Self-determination theory needs: autonomy, competence and relatedness, treated as necessary nutrients whose thwarting lowers wellbeing
work: Ryan & Deci 2000, American Psychologist 55(1), DOI 10.1037/0003-066X.55.1.68
note: Needs do not compose or trade off in the theory; the model is satisfaction vs frustration of each.

statement: SDT regulation types form a one-dimensional continuum from amotivation through external, introjected, identified and integrated regulation to intrinsic motivation; the social environment's autonomy-supportive vs controlling behaviour is the one explicit operator class
work: Ryan & Deci 2000, American Psychologist 55(1), DOI 10.1037/0003-066X.55.1.68

statement: Fiske's five core social motives, BUCET: belonging (core), understanding, controlling, enhancing self, trusting
work: Fiske 2004, Social Beings: A Core Motives Approach to Social Psychology, Wiley (no DOI); BUCET reuse: North & Fiske 2013, DOI 10.1093/oxfordhb/9780195398700.013.0004
note: Book not read; content from standard account (validation: unconfirmed content, existence not in doubt).

statement: Fiske's grouping: understanding and controlling are the two cognitive motives, enhancing self and trusting the two affective ones; belonging is the core that the others serve; no formal rules
work: Fiske 2004, Social Beings, Wiley (no DOI)
note: Corrected in validation: the cognitive/affective grouping replaces an earlier pairing of understanding and controlling. Trusting is relational, a candidate operator more than an operand (file).

statement: Belonging (need to belong): frequent, affectively positive interactions within a stable relational frame; treated as a need, it satiates once a few close bonds exist
work: Baumeister & Leary 1995, Psychological Bulletin 117(3), DOI 10.1037/0033-2909.117.3.497
note: Corrected in validation: a garbled sentence on 'not satisfied by more' was rewritten as satiation.

statement: Status (respect and admiration of others) proposed as a fundamental human motive
work: Anderson, Hildreth & Howland 2015, Psychological Bulletin 141(3), DOI 10.1037/a0038781
note: Distinguished from power and money; status is gained within groups (file).

statement: Primitive-hood criteria for status (Anderson et al.): universality, early development, dissociability from power and other motives, and distinctive downstream effects on wellbeing and behaviour
work: Anderson, Hildreth & Howland 2015, Psychological Bulletin 141(3), DOI 10.1037/a0038781
note: File: a ready-made admission test for a primitive set.

statement: Panksepp's seven primary emotional systems: SEEKING (expectancy), RAGE (anger), FEAR (anxiety), LUST, CARE (nurturing), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), PLAY (social joy); subcortical, evolutionarily conserved circuits
work: Panksepp 1998, Affective Neuroscience, Oxford UP (no DOI); overview Davis & Montag 2019, Frontiers in Neuroscience 12, DOI 10.3389/fnins.2018.01025
note: Seven systems and dominance remark read in Davis & Montag; Davis & Montag write PANIC/SADNESS. Capitals mark brain systems.

statement: Panksepp systems form a nested hierarchy (primary process, secondary learning, tertiary cortical control) and a seesaw-like balance between triggering and inhibiting a primary emotion
work: Davis & Montag 2019, Frontiers in Neuroscience 12, DOI 10.3389/fnins.2018.01025
note: Corrected in validation: the specific inhibitory pairs (FEAR suppressing PLAY; CARE vs RAGE) are NOT in Davis & Montag; FEAR-PLAY is standard in Panksepp's own work, CARE vs RAGE unconfirmed. Interactions are verbal.

statement: Social Dominance is not included as a primary emotional system: Panksepp concluded insufficient evidence, treating it as acquired
work: Davis & Montag 2019, Frontiers in Neuroscience 12, DOI 10.3389/fnins.2018.01025

statement: Ekman's basic emotions: anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness and surprise, with contempt later added
work: Ekman 1992, Cognition and Emotion 6(3-4), DOI 10.1080/02699939208411068
note: Criteria: universal facial expressions, distinctive physiology, automatic appraisal, quick onset. Ekman allows blends and emotion families but gives no composition rules (file).

statement: Core affect as a primitive state with two dimensions, valence (pleasure-displeasure) and arousal, with emotions as categorisations on top
work: Russell 1980, JPSP 39(6), DOI 10.1037/h0077714; Russell 2003, Psychological Review 110(1), DOI 10.1037/0033-295X.110.1.145
note: Geometry only; it cannot separate fear from anger (both high arousal, negative valence).

statement: Russell circumplex geometry: angle = quality, radius = intensity, opposition = antipode; composition as vector addition in the plane is a natural reading, not a law Russell states
note: Corrected in validation: the circumplex-fit critique first credited to Larsen & McGraw is misattributed; their work concerns mixed emotions (see contradictions).

statement: Schwartz's basic values: ten in the original theory (self-direction, stimulation, hedonism, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition, benevolence, universalism); nineteen in the 2012 refinement
work: Schwartz 1992, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology 25, DOI 10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60281-6; Schwartz et al. 2012, JPSP 103(4), DOI 10.1037/a0029393
note: Values are slow-changing dispositions that weight drives rather than being drives (file's algebra reading).

statement: Schwartz value structure: values form a circle; adjacent values are compatible and opposed values conflict; two bipolar axes (openness to change vs conservation; self-enhancement vs self-transcendence); trade-offs are positional
work: Schwartz et al. 2012, JPSP 103(4), DOI 10.1037/a0029393
note: Algebra reading: a circular signed compatibility graph (+ neighbours, - opposites) writable as a matrix. File: the only validated opposition structure.

statement: Moral foundations: original five care/harm, fairness/cheating, loyalty/betrayal, authority/subversion, sanctity/degradation; MFQ-2 six are care, equality, proportionality, loyalty, authority and purity
work: Graham et al. 2013, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology 47, DOI 10.1016/B978-0-12-407236-7.00002-4; Atari et al. 2023, JPSP 125(5), DOI 10.1037/pspp0000470
note: Corrected in validation: the count is version-dependent. Liberty/oppression was a candidate sixth in Graham et al. 2013 but is not among the MFQ-2 six. Fairness and loyalty are group-referent.

statement: Moral foundations pluralism: foundations are separate, politics is explained by differential weighting of them, and conflict arises when foundations disagree on a case; no composition rule
work: Graham et al. 2013, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology 47, DOI 10.1016/B978-0-12-407236-7.00002-4

statement: Berridge's wanting (incentive salience, dopamine-mediated, cue-triggered motivation) and liking (hedonic impact), with learning as a third component; they dissociate
work: Berridge & Robinson 1998, Brain Research Reviews 28(3), DOI 10.1016/S0165-0173(98)00019-8; Berridge 1996, Neurosci. Biobehav. Rev. 20(1), DOI 10.1016/0149-7634(95)00033-B
note: A decomposition within any reward, not a taxonomy of drives.

statement: Two-field drive: each drive carries a wanting field (drive to act) and a liking field (satisfaction on attaining), rather than one scalar; manipulating cues changes wanting without changing liking
work: Berridge & Robinson 1998, Brain Research Reviews 28(3), DOI 10.1016/S0165-0173(98)00019-8
note: Algebra reading in the file, not a claim of the source.

statement: Plutchik's eight primary emotions: fear, anger, joy, sadness, acceptance (later trust), disgust, anticipation (also expectancy) and surprise
work: Plutchik 1980, A general psychoevolutionary theory of emotion, in Plutchik & Kellerman (Eds.), Emotion: Theory, Research, and Experience, Vol. 1, pp. 3-33, Academic Press (no DOI)
note: Names read at source (Postulate 5). The wheel order and intensity levels (serenity/joy/ecstasy) are from the standard account.

statement: Plutchik's postulates: all other emotions are mixed or derivative states, occurring as combinations of primaries; primaries form polar opposite pairs; emotions vary in similarity and in intensity; similarity and polarity lead to a circle
work: Plutchik 1980, A general psychoevolutionary theory of emotion, in Plutchik & Kellerman (Eds.), Vol. 1, pp. 3-33, Academic Press (no DOI)
note: Postulates 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 read at source. Blend names are elicited from judges and treated as states or personality traits.

statement: Plutchik's four opposite pairs: joy-sadness, trust-disgust, fear-anger, surprise-anticipation, each with a functional reason (gain vs loss, taking in vs ejection, attack vs flight, unpredictable vs predictable)
work: Plutchik 1980, A general psychoevolutionary theory of emotion, in Plutchik & Kellerman (Eds.), Vol. 1, pp. 3-33, Academic Press (no DOI)
note: File treats the opposites as theory; 'opposites conflict' is contested by mixed-emotion work (see contradictions).

statement: Plutchik dyad rule: a dyad is a mixture of two primaries classified by wheel distance as primary (adjacent), secondary (two apart) or tertiary (three apart); opposites are conflicted. The 24 dyads give names such as love (joy+trust), curiosity (trust+surprise), pride (anger+joy), hope (anticipation+trust), despair (fear+sadness)
work: Plutchik 1980 chapter (Vol. 1, pp. 3-33) for postulates; dyad names from Wikipedia, not the 1980 chapter
note: Distance classes derived from wheel order by validation, not stated in the 1980 chapter. First names are the commonly reproduced ones; second names and the four opposite-mixture names (Bittersweetness, Ambivalence, Frozenness, Confusion) are Wikipedia-only and unconfirmed. Properties: commutative, binary, closed on names not primitives, no identity or inverse beyond opposites.

statement: 24 dyads + 4 opposite pairs = 28 = C(8,2), so the Plutchik table covers every unordered pair of the eight primaries
work: Plutchik 1980 chapter (Vol. 1, pp. 3-33) for primaries; dyad table from Wikipedia
note: Counting identity stated in the file; the table entries it counts are sa.

statement: Hull's drive D, the state variable multiplied by habit strength in the reaction potential
work: Hull 1943, Principles of Behavior, Appleton-Century (no DOI)
note: From standard account.

statement: Hull's reaction potential: E = D x H (drive times habit strength)
work: Hull 1943, Principles of Behavior, Appleton-Century (no DOI)
note: File: arithmetic on scalars, not an operator with stated laws.

statement: Atkinson's achievement tendency: T = M x P x I, with motive M, probability of success P and incentive I = 1 - P
work: Atkinson 1957, Psychological Review 64(6), DOI 10.1037/h0043445
note: Corrected in validation: multiplicative laws are added to the composition-law inventory; the earlier claim of none was false.

statement: Atkinson's model predicts maximal approach at P = 0.5 (testable consequence of T = M x P x I)
work: Atkinson 1957, Psychological Review 64(6), DOI 10.1037/h0043445
note: Prediction, not an outcome measured here; file states it as a testable consequence.

statement: Atkinson & Birch's dynamics of action: action tendencies change continuously under instigating, consummatory and inhibitory forces, with differential equations deciding which activity is expressed and when it switches
work: Atkinson & Birch 1970, The Dynamics of Action, Wiley (no DOI found)
note: File: the calculus of conflict resolution listed as missing, at least for individual action.

statement: Carver & Scheier affect as control: affect is the rate of discrepancy reduction toward a goal, a derivative rather than a level
work: Carver & Scheier 1990, Psychological Review 97(1), DOI 10.1037/0033-295X.97.1.19

statement: Kuppens et al. affect dynamics: an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model on the valence-arousal plane with person-level home base, variability and attractor strength, i.e. a fitted stochastic differential equation for core affect
work: Kuppens, Oravecz & Tuerlinckx 2010, JPSP 99(6), DOI 10.1037/a0020962
note: Standard account; not read at source.

statement: Keramati & Gutkin homeostatic drive: drive is the distance of internal state from setpoint; reward is defined as drive reduction
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, eLife 3, DOI 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: A drive defined as a function, the file's counterexample to 'no theorems about drives'.

statement: Keramati & Gutkin theorem: reward maximisation under drive-reduction reward equals homeostatic stability
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, eLife 3, DOI 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: File: a proved result about homeostatic drives (standard account, not read).

statement: Bach's PSI urges: physiological needs, affiliation, certainty and competence, with numeric deficit dynamics and urge competition
work: Bach 2009, Principles of Synthetic Intelligence (PSI), Oxford UP, DOI 10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195370676.001.0001
note: Formalises Dorner's Psi theory; close to the file's core set.

statement: OCC compound emotions as conjunctions of appraisal-based types, e.g. anger = reproach + distress, gratitude = admiration + joy, gratification = pride + joy, remorse = shame + distress
work: Ortony, Clore & Collins 1988, The Cognitive Structure of Emotions, Cambridge UP, DOI 10.1017/CBO9780511571299
note: The file's nearest thing to a typed composition grammar for affect; computational and widely implemented in agent models.

statement: Barrett's constructed emotion: discrete emotions are constructed from core affect plus concepts plus context, not stored as brain kinds
work: Barrett 2017, Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience 12(1), DOI 10.1093/scan/nsw154; Lindquist et al. 2012, Behavioral and Brain Sciences 35(3), DOI 10.1017/S0140525X11000446
note: Volume and pages of Barrett 2017 unconfirmed (Crossref gives article number only). The file says the choice of primitives is then a modelling decision.

statement: Evaluative space model: positivity and negativity as two separable activation functions, with co-activation (ambivalence) and a stated combination into a response
work: Cacioppo & Berntson 1994, Psychological Bulletin 115(3), DOI 10.1037/0033-2909.115.3.401
note: File: the formal answer to fear and desire at once. From standard account.

statement: Mixed emotions: people can feel happy and sad at the same time; opposite-valence states co-occur
work: Larsen, McGraw & Cacioppo 2001, JPSP 81(4), DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.81.4.684; Larsen & McGraw 2011, JPSP 100(6), DOI 10.1037/a0021846
note: File: falsifies treating valence as one bipolar axis (see contradictions). From abstract/standard account.

statement: Tay & Diener 2011: needs are universal across 123 countries, but fulfilment does not follow a strict order, weakening Maslow's strict hierarchy
size_dependence: Country-level (123 countries)
note: Validation: issue (2), title and DOI added (Crossref). File's standing: hierarchy weakly supported.

statement: Priming studies: a threat cue sharpens outgroup vigilance; a mating cue raises status-seeking in men; activation of one motive biases others (e.g. disease avoidance raises outgroup avoidance)
work: Neuberg, Kenrick & Schaller 2011, Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews 35(4), DOI 10.1016/j.neubiorev.2010.08.011
note: Priming-based evidence, much from experiments of the kind hit by the replication crisis; treat effect sizes with caution. No effect sizes given in the file.

statement: Explicit self-attributed motive questionnaires correlate near zero with implicit (TAT-coded) motives; implicit motive reliability is modest
work: McClelland, Koestner & Weinberger 1989, Psychological Review 96(4), DOI 10.1037/0033-295X.96.4.690
note: Validation: DOI and title added (Crossref).

statement: Group-level nAch was claimed to predict economic growth (macro scaling claim)
work: McClelland 1961, The Achieving Society, Van Nostrand (no DOI); McClelland 1987, Human Motivation, Cambridge UP (no DOI)
size_dependence: Group-level aggregate claim; file says contested
note: File: contested.

statement: Reiss's 16 desires are largely unrelated in the author's own data; the 16-factor structure has thin independent replication
work: Reiss 2004, Review of General Psychology 8(3), DOI 10.1037/1089-2680.8.3.179
note: Deserves checking against other labs (file).

statement: Ryan & Deci's need structure: three-factor need satisfaction structure broadly supported across many countries, with debate over separating autonomy from competence and over satisfaction vs frustration factors (four-culture study)
work: Chen et al. 2015, Motivation and Emotion 39(2), DOI 10.1007/s11031-014-9450-1
note: Validation: full citation and DOI added (Crossref).

statement: Schwartz 2012: the nineteen values are discriminated by CFA and MDS across 15 samples in 10 countries (N = 6,059); some value scale reliabilities are low
work: Schwartz et al. 2012, JPSP 103(4), DOI 10.1037/a0029393
note: Weakness: the circular order is fit by ordering, not derived.

statement: The ten-value circular order of Schwartz's values has been replicated in dozens of countries by multidimensional scaling
work: Schwartz 1992, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology 25, DOI 10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60281-6
size_dependence: Cross-national (dozens of countries)
note: From standard account.

statement: Plutchik's circle: similarity ratings of 40 emotion words against reference terms, plus an independent semantic-differential factor analysis, placed the words round a circle; the two angular placements correlate .90
work: Plutchik 1980, A general psychoevolutionary theory of emotion, in Plutchik & Kellerman (Eds.), Vol. 1, pp. 3-33, Academic Press (no DOI); reporting Plutchik & Conte 1978
note: Read at source in validation. This is the circle's own empirical support.

statement: Plutchik's dyad names were elicited from judges asked to imagine the result of mixing primaries; there is no test that co-occurrence of two emotions produces the named blend
work: Plutchik 1980, A general psychoevolutionary theory of emotion, in Plutchik & Kellerman (Eds.), Vol. 1, pp. 3-33, Academic Press (no DOI)
note: Corrected in validation: the claim 'mostly not empirically derived' was too strong; they are judge-derived from naming exercises. The causal claim has no support found in the file.

statement: Ekman's cross-cultural recognition of posed facial expressions was the main support for basic emotions; critics note forced-choice method inflates agreement, and physiological signatures do not separate reliably
work: Ekman 1992, Cognition and Emotion 6(3-4), DOI 10.1080/02699939208411068; Gendron et al. 2014, Emotion 14(2), DOI 10.1037/a0036052
note: Gendron et al. 2014 (Himba participants) found weaker agreement. Validation: full citation and DOI added.

statement: Lindquist et al. 2012 meta-analysis: discrete emotions such as anger, disgust, fear, happiness and sadness do not derive from consistent, specific activity in any anatomically defined area
work: Lindquist, Wager, Kober, Bliss-Moreau & Barrett 2012, Behavioral and Brain Sciences 35(3), DOI 10.1017/S0140525X11000446
note: From abstract. Rival meta-analysis below.

statement: Vytal & Hamann 2010 voxel-based meta-analysis: discrete neural correlates of basic emotions are found
work: Vytal & Hamann 2010, J. Cognitive Neuroscience 22(12), DOI 10.1162/jocn.2009.21366
note: Moved from unconfirmed to confirmed in validation. File: the question is open.

statement: Remington, Fabrigar & Visser 2000: formal tests find the affect structure broadly circumplex but not an exact equal-spacing circle
work: Remington, Fabrigar & Visser 2000, JPSP 79(2), DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.79.2.286
note: MDS of word ratings reproduces the circle across many languages (file's standing). Watson & Tellegen 1985 (DOI 10.1037/0033-2909.98.2.219) is an alternative axis choice for the same space.

statement: Moral foundations measurement: the five-factor MFQ structure is not invariant across all countries; Iurino & Saucier 2020 found it does not converge in all of 27 countries; MFQ-2 six-factor structure was validated across 25 populations by its authors
work: Iurino & Saucier 2020, Assessment 27(2), DOI 10.1177/1073191118817916; Atari et al. 2023, JPSP 125(5), DOI 10.1037/pspp0000470
note: File's verdict: weak-to-moderate structural support, cross-cultural invariance not established. Validation: a 2024 study was replaced by Atari et al. 2023.

statement: Deprivation of belonging causes harm and pathology, and motivation to form further bonds satiates once a few close bonds exist; evidence from ostracism, loneliness and social-pain research
work: Baumeister & Leary 1995, Psychological Bulletin 117(3), DOI 10.1037/0033-2909.117.3.497
note: Cross-cultural universality asserted (file).

statement: Status striving has its own downstream effects on wellbeing and behaviour, distinct from power and money, and interplays with belonging
work: Anderson, Hildreth & Howland 2015, Psychological Bulletin 141(3), DOI 10.1037/a0038781
note: From abstract/standard account.

statement: Berridge: strong animal evidence (taste-reactivity, dopamine depletion) that wanting and liking dissociate; human evidence supportive but partly indirect
work: Berridge & Robinson 1998, Brain Research Reviews 28(3), DOI 10.1016/S0165-0173(98)00019-8
note: Addiction is the file's example of wanting without liking.

statement: Panksepp's systems: brain stimulation evidence in animals; human evidence indirect (imaging, Affective Neuroscience Personality Scales)
work: Panksepp 1998, Affective Neuroscience, Oxford UP (no DOI); Davis & Montag 2019, Frontiers in Neuroscience 12, DOI 10.3389/fnins.2018.01025
note: The question of discrete circuits is open (file).

statement: Dollard et al. frustration-aggression: anger as the response to blocked drives or violated status, as the file uses it; anger is a reactive emotion in every list that names it, except Murray and Reiss, where aggression and vengeance are standing needs
work: Dollard, Doob, Miller, Mowrer & Sears 1939, Frustration and Aggression, Yale UP, DOI 10.1037/10022-000
note: Source added in validation for the anger entry; the file's use is its own proposal.

statement: Candidate core primitive set (at least three theories each): affiliation/belonging (with attachment and trust), status/dominance/power, fear/self-protection (with disgust as a threat subtype), curiosity/exploration/understanding (SEEKING), autonomy/control/competence, care/nurture/kin, anger/aggression, and mating
work: Cross-walk of the taxonomies in 15 (sections 1-18); no single source
note: Counts: affiliation 12, status 10 (9 after validation), fear 10, curiosity 8 (7 after validation), autonomy 6, anger 6, nurture 8, mating 5. Lineages not fully independent; counts are the file's coding, not a measured overlap.

statement: Weaker candidate primitives: play, order/acquisition, grief/loss
work: Cross-walk of the taxonomies in 15 (sections 1-18); no single source
note: Play 4, order/acquisition 4, grief/loss 3 in the cross-walk.

statement: Admission rule for a primitive set: candidate primitives are admitted by cross-theory recurrence (at least three theories from plausibly independent lineages), not by factor analysis alone
work: Cross-walk of the taxonomies in 15 (sections 1-18); no single source
note: The file's own rule for its core set. The file notes that no primitive set has agreed identity (lists differ 5 to 20).

statement: Discrete neural correspondence of basic emotions: Lindquist et al. 2012 find no consistent region-specific signature; Vytal & Hamann 2010 find discrete neural correlates
work: Lindquist et al. 2012, Behavioral and Brain Sciences 35(3), DOI 10.1017/S0140525X11000446; Vytal & Hamann 2010, J. Cognitive Neuroscience 22(12), DOI 10.1162/jocn.2009.21366
note: Side A: Lindquist 2012, no consistent region-specific signature. Side B: Vytal & Hamann 2010, discrete correlates. Verdict: unresolved; the file says the question is open.

statement: Discrete emotion circuits: Panksepp's subcortical discrete systems and Ekman's basic emotions vs Barrett's constructionism, which denies discrete emotion circuits
work: Panksepp 1998, Affective Neuroscience, Oxford UP (no DOI); Ekman 1992, DOI 10.1080/02699939208411068; Barrett 2017, DOI 10.1093/scan/nsw154
note: Side A: discrete basic emotions and circuits. Side B: emotions constructed from core affect, concepts and context. Verdict: unresolved; the file calls the question open and contested.

statement: Universality of basic emotion recognition: Ekman 1992 cross-cultural recognition of posed faces vs Gendron et al. 2014, weaker agreement in a remote culture
work: Ekman 1992, Cognition and Emotion 6(3-4), DOI 10.1080/02699939208411068; Gendron et al. 2014, Emotion 14(2), DOI 10.1037/a0036052
note: Side A: universal recognition supports basic emotions. Side B: Himba participants show weaker agreement; forced-choice inflates agreement. Verdict: unresolved in the file (listed as a critique).

statement: Maslow's strict prepotency hierarchy vs Kenrick et al.'s context-dependent, dynamic priority and Tay & Diener's finding that fulfilment does not follow a strict order
work: Maslow 1943, Psychological Review 50(4), DOI 10.1037/h0054346; Kenrick et al. 2010, Perspectives on Psychological Science 5(3), DOI 10.1177/1745691610369469; Tay & Diener 2011, JPSP 101(2), DOI 10.1037/a0023779
note: Side A: hierarchy by prepotency, stated as tendency. Side B: dynamic overlapping priority; no strict order in data. Verdict: unresolved; file's standing is that hierarchy is weakly supported.

statement: Opposites conflict (Plutchik's opposite pairs, Schwartz-style conflict) vs mixed emotions: opposite-valence states co-occur, which the file says falsifies treating valence as one bipolar axis (Russell)
note: Side A: opposites are conflict, bipolar valence. Side B: Larsen et al. find people feel opposite valences at once. Verdict per the file: the mixed-emotion finding falsifies single bipolar valence; the bearing on Plutchik's conflict claim is not deep-read (abstract/standard account).

statement: Moral foundations count: Graham et al. 2013 five foundations plus liberty as candidate sixth vs MFQ-2 (Atari et al. 2023) six foundations: care, equality, proportionality, loyalty, authority, purity
work: Graham et al. 2013, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology 47, DOI 10.1016/B978-0-12-407236-7.00002-4; Atari et al. 2023, JPSP 125(5), DOI 10.1037/pspp0000470
note: Verdict: resolved as version-dependent. Corrected in validation: the MFQ-2 six do not include liberty; the first version blurred the two sets.

statement: Plutchik dyad names 'mostly not empirically derived' (first version of the file) vs the 1980 chapter's judge-named mixtures
work: Plutchik 1980, A general psychoevolutionary theory of emotion, in Plutchik & Kellerman (Eds.), Vol. 1, pp. 3-33 (no DOI)
note: Verdict: corrected in validation. The names are judge-derived from naming exercises; the causal claim (co-occurrence produces the blend) remains unsupported.

statement: First version's claims that Plutchik's is the only composition table and that no theory gives dynamics or theorems about drives, vs OCC 1988, Larsen et al., Atkinson 1957, Atkinson & Birch 1970, Kuppens et al. 2010, Carver & Scheier 1990 and Keramati & Gutkin 2014
work: Ortony, Clore & Collins 1988, DOI 10.1017/CBO9780511571299; Atkinson 1957, DOI 10.1037/h0043445; Kuppens et al. 2010, DOI 10.1037/a0020962; Keramati & Gutkin 2014, DOI 10.7554/eLife.04811
note: Verdict: first version overclaimed and was false for the wider literature; corrected in validation. Taxonomies themselves still give no dynamics and no theorems.

statement: Russell circumplex-fit critique first attributed to Larsen & McGraw
note: Verdict: misattribution corrected in validation. Larsen & McGraw address mixed emotions (bipolarity of valence); the circumplex-fit critique is Remington et al. 2000. The vague '1999 JPSP challenge' was removed.

statement: Panksepp's specific inhibitory pairs (FEAR suppressing PLAY; CARE vs RAGE) as cited in the standard account vs the Davis & Montag 2019 overview read in validation, which does not contain them
work: Panksepp 1998, Affective Neuroscience, Oxford UP (no DOI); Davis & Montag 2019, Frontiers in Neuroscience 12, DOI 10.3389/fnins.2018.01025
note: Verdict: unresolved. FEAR-PLAY is standard in Panksepp's own writing and is not in the read source; CARE vs RAGE is not confirmed anywhere in the file.

statement: Hull general drive D: a non-directional energiser tied to deprivation (hours without food), a scalar attribute of an organism
work: Hull 1943, Principles of Behavior; Hull 1952, A Behavior System
note: Layered form is standard account; primaries not read (Validation log).

statement: Lorenz action-specific energy: accumulates in a reservoir, a valve opens under a releasing stimulus, and the flow produces the fixed action pattern
work: Lorenz 1950 (instinct papers); Tinbergen 1951, The Study of Instinct, Oxford
note: Diagrammatic and verbal, no equation; hydraulic model abandoned in the 1950s-60s and kept as a conceptual device.

statement: Miller approach tendency A(d) and avoidance tendency V(d), both decreasing functions of distance d from a goal, with the avoidance gradient steeper
work: Miller 1944, in Hunt (ed.), Personality and the Behavior Disorders; Miller 1959; Dollard & Miller 1950, Personality and Psychotherapy
note: Linear forms A = a - b·d and V = c - e·d are standard account; qualitative form confirmed by search/secondary only.

statement: Lewin tension t: a state of a person's inner region; need raises tension, and the valence of environmental regions rises with tension
work: Lewin 1936, Principles of Topological Psychology; Lewin 1951, Field Theory in Social Science
note: Search/secondary; Lewin's own formalism stated descriptively, no theorems.

statement: Atkinson achievement motives: Ms, motive to achieve success, and Maf, motive to avoid failure
work: Atkinson 1957, Psychological Review 64, 359-372, doi:10.1037/h0043445
note: Equations read via Revelle's lecture handout and CTA paper (Eq. 9); the 1957 paper itself not read.

statement: Atkinson-Birch elements: instigating force F, action tendency T, consummatory value c, consummatory force C, inhibitory force I, negaction tendency N, resistance value r, force of resistance R
work: Atkinson & Birch 1970, The Dynamics of Action, Wiley; Revelle 2008 working draft, Cues, Tendencies and Actions, https://www.personality-project.org/revelle/publications/cta.pdf
note: Read via Revelle's CTA paper (Eqs. 1-6, 9); the 1970 book not read.

statement: CTA state vectors: cues C from the environment, tendencies T, and actions A, with cue-to-tendency matrix s, tendency-to-action matrix e, consummation c and inhibition i
work: Revelle 2008 working draft, Cues, Tendencies and Actions, https://www.personality-project.org/revelle/publications/cta.pdf
note: Revelle's CTA reparameterisation (Revelle 1986; Eqs. 10-13).

statement: Powers reference signal r: the controlled quantity is perception against a reference, and motivation is the reference value
work: Powers 1973, Behavior: The Control of Perception, Aldine
note: Search/secondary; the 'motivation is the reference value' gloss is the file's own paraphrase.

statement: Gray's three systems: BAS (reward and approach), FFFS (aversive stimuli, fear, withdrawal, freezing), BIS (resolves approach-avoidance conflict, anxiety, risk assessment)
work: Gray & McNaughton 2000, The Neuropsychology of Anxiety, 2nd ed., Oxford
note: Search/secondary; qualitative model, no equations.

statement: Higgins regulatory focus: promotion focus (ideals, advancement, gains) and prevention focus (oughts, security, losses) as two orthogonal dispositions
note: Crossref confirmed; text not read.

statement: Keramati-Gutkin physiological state vector H_t with setpoint vector H* across several physiological dimensions
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, eLife 3:e04811, https://elifesciences.org/articles/04811
note: Read from the eLife JATS XML on 2026-10-29.

statement: Allostatic setpoint: the regulated target moves with expected need, so setpoints are a function of expected context
work: Sterling 2012, Physiology & Behavior 106(1), 5-15, doi:10.1016/j.physbeh.2011.06.004
note: Abstract-level reading only. File notes other people could change expected need (relevant to a social algebra).

statement: Active-inference preferences C, encoded as a prior p(o|C) over outcomes, which the file reads as the 'drive': what an agent expects to experience
work: Smith, Friston & Whyte 2022, J. Math. Psychol., PMC8956124; Parr, Pezzulo & Friston 2022, Active Inference, MIT Press
note: The equations using C are read; calling C 'the drive' is the file's translation, not a quoted claim.

statement: Epistemic (curiosity) term: expected information gain about hidden states, which vanishes once uncertainty is resolved, leaving pragmatic value dominant
work: Friston et al. 2015, Cognitive Neuroscience 6(4), 187-214, doi:10.1080/17588928.2015.1020053; Friston et al. 2017, Neural Computation 29, 2633-2683, doi:10.1162/neco_a_00999
note: The decomposition is read in Smith, Friston & Whyte 2022; the 2015 and 2017 papers are Crossref-confirmed only.

statement: Toates incentive motivation: behaviour depends on internal state (deprivation, hormones) and external incentive together, with positive feedback as appetite builds on approach to a cue
work: Toates 1986, Motivational Systems, Cambridge University Press
note: Publisher listing found; book content not seen.

statement: Carver-Scheier affect as a derived output: negative affect when discrepancy reduction is slower than needed, positive when faster
work: Carver & Scheier 1981, Attention and Self-Regulation, Springer; Carver & Scheier 1990, Psychological Review 97, 19-35, doi:10.1037/0033-295X.97.1.19
note: Search/secondary; the 1990 paper is Crossref-confirmed only.

statement: Vroom and Eccles motivational components: valence, expectancy, instrumentality (Vroom); attainment, intrinsic, utility and cost value (Eccles)
work: Vroom 1964, Work and Motivation; Eccles, Wigfield et al. 1983 onward
note: Standard account; existence checked, not re-checked in depth.

statement: Hull 1943: reaction potential sEr = sHr × D (habit strength times drive)
work: Hull 1943, Principles of Behavior
note: Standard account; primary not read. Not to feed an equation build until checked.

statement: Hull 1952: a response is evoked iff sHr·D·V·K − (Ir + sIr) − sOr > sLr (product of habit, drive, stimulus intensity dynamism and incentive, minus inhibition and behavioural oscillation, against threshold)
work: Hull 1952, A Behavior System
note: Layered form per standard account; the multiplier J (delay) is an option in some accounts; primary not read.

statement: Spence 1956: E = H × (D + K), with drive and incentive additive, so incentive moves behaviour even at zero drive
work: Spence 1956, Behavior Theory and Conditioning
note: Additivity confirmed by search/secondary (Wikipedia citing Hilgard 1967); H multiplier is standard account.

statement: Miller net tendency N(d) = A(d) − V(d), with linear gradients A = a − b·d and V = c − e·d and avoidance steeper (e > b)
work: Miller 1944; Miller 1959; Dollard & Miller 1950
note: Standard account for the linear form; steeper avoidance confirmed by search/secondary (Brown 1948).

statement: Miller equilibrium d* = (a − c)/(b − e) = (c − a)/(e − b), positive only if c > a; the organism approaches, stops short and oscillates about d*
work: Miller 1944; Dollard & Miller 1950
note: Corollary of the linear gradients, derived in the file from the standard-account forms.

statement: Miller comparative statics: ∂d*/∂a = −1/(e − b) and ∂d*/∂c = +1/(e − b); raising approach drive moves d* closer to the goal, where fear rises, and lowering avoidance moves it closer with fear falling
work: Miller 1944; Miller 1959; Dollard & Miller 1950
note: Corrected 2026-10-29: in this linear model the distance shifts are equal in size, so the Dollard & Miller claim concerns fear at equilibrium, not distance. See contradictions.

statement: Lewin force on a person toward a region f(P,G) = F(Va(G)/e(P,G)), with f ∝ V/d for valence V and psychological distance d; resultant force is the vector sum of forces
work: Lewin 1938, The Conceptual Representation and the Measurement of Psychological Forces, Contributions to Psychological Theory 1(4)
note: Marked [standard account, not confirmed]; Lewin 1938 not read. Do not build on it until the primary is checked.

statement: Atkinson 1957 tendencies: Ts = Ms·Ps·(1 − Ps), Taf = −Maf·Ps·(1 − Ps), and resultant Tr = Ts + Taf = (Ms − Maf)·Ps·(1 − Ps)
work: Atkinson 1957, Psychological Review 64, 359-372, doi:10.1037/h0043445
note: Corrected 2026-10-29: the resultant is in the 1957 paper, not a 1964 addition. Incentive Is = 1 − Ps, If = −Ps. Read via Revelle's handout and CTA Eq. 9.

statement: Raynor extension of achievement tendency along contingent task paths: Tr = Σ_i (Ms − Maf)·P_si·(1 − P_si) + T_ext
work: Raynor, as cited in Revelle, achievement lecture handout, https://www.personality-project.org/revelle/syllabi/301/achievement.pdf
note: Summed over the chain of tasks a step leads to, plus extrinsic tendencies; Raynor's own paper not read.

statement: Atkinson corollary: Ps(1 − Ps) peaks at Ps = 0.5, so a success-oriented person (Ms > Maf) prefers intermediate difficulty
work: Atkinson 1957, Psychological Review 64, 359-372, doi:10.1037/h0043445
note: Algebraic consequence of the read equations. Empirical peak differs (see results and contradictions).

statement: Atkinson sign-flip corollary: if Maf > Ms the sign of Tr reverses, so the person avoids intermediate tasks and prefers very easy or very hard ones
work: Atkinson 1957, Psychological Review 64, 359-372, doi:10.1037/h0043445
note: The file says the fear-of-failure sign-flip is less secure (standard account).

statement: Dynamics of Action tendency: dT_i/dt = F_i − c_i·T_i while activity i is ongoing, and dT_i/dt = F_i otherwise; asymptote T∞ = F/c once expressed
work: Atkinson & Birch 1970, The Dynamics of Action; Revelle 2008 CTA draft, Eqs. 1-6
note: Read via Revelle's restatement; the 1970 book not read.

statement: Dynamics of Action negaction: dN/dt = I − r·N, which relaxes to N∞ = I/r whether or not the action occurs
work: Atkinson & Birch 1970, The Dynamics of Action; Revelle 2008 CTA draft, Eqs. 1-6
note: Resistance costs effort even when idle.

statement: Dynamics of Action achievement case: F = Ps(1 − Ps)·N_ach and I = Ps(1 − Ps)·N_avoid-failure, which recovers Atkinson 1957 as the static limit
work: Atkinson & Birch 1970, The Dynamics of Action; Revelle 2008 CTA draft, Eq. 9
note: Known defect recorded in the file: max-selection makes activities chatter, so the original needed instigating and consummatory lags.

statement: CTA dynamics with cross-inhibition: dT/dt = s·C − c·A and dA/dt = e·T − i·A
work: Revelle 2008 CTA draft, Eqs. 10-13, https://www.personality-project.org/revelle/publications/cta.pdf
note: Selection emerges from mutual inhibition among actions; the cta docs say so explicitly.

statement: CTA uncoupled scalar steady state, re-derived in the file: A∞ = s·C/c and T∞ = i·s·C/(e·c)
work: Revelle 2008 CTA draft, Eqs. 10-13, https://www.personality-project.org/revelle/publications/cta.pdf
note: Derived by setting both derivatives to zero. Printed forms differ unless s = e = 1; the file uses the derived ones. See contradictions.

statement: Vroom/expectancy-value force: Force = Σ over outcomes of (Valence × Expectancy × Instrumentality), so a zero factor gives zero motivation within an outcome
work: Vroom 1964, Work and Motivation
note: Multiplicative within an outcome, additive across outcomes is standard account; sum form not from the book.

statement: Carver-Scheier numerical affect form: affect ∝ d(−discrepancy)/dt − expected rate of discrepancy reduction
work: Carver & Scheier 1981, Attention and Self-Regulation; Carver & Scheier 1982, Psychological Bulletin 92(1), 111-135
note: Standard account only; the sources the file saw were verbal, so this is unconfirmed.

statement: Powers control loop: perception p = input function of qi; error e = r − p; output o = G·e; environment qi = qo + disturbance; at steady state p ≈ r with error shrinking as gain G rises
work: Powers 1973, Behavior: The Control of Perception, Aldine; IAPCT PDF https://www.iapct.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/PCTunderstanding.pdf
note: Search/secondary (IAPCT PDF citing the book). Stability conditions (gain, delay) are standard account.

statement: Two-controller collective control: with o_k = G_k(r_k − q) and q = o_1 + o_2 + d, steady state q = (G_1·r_1 + G_2·r_2 + d)/(1 + G_1 + G_2), a virtual reference equal to the gain-weighted mean of the references with loop gain G_1 + G_2
work: McClelland 2004, International Journal of Human-Computer Studies 60(1), 65-99, doi:10.1016/j.ijhcs.2003.08.003
note: Derived in the file from the proportional-output model; McClelland's text not read. Per ledger rule nothing sa feeds an equation until McClelland is read or the derivation is validated.

statement: Two integrating controllers (dO_k/dt = G_k·e_k) with opposed references cannot both drive error to zero, so outputs ramp in opposite directions without bound (escalation)
work: McClelland 2004, International Journal of Human-Computer Studies 60(1), 65-99, doi:10.1016/j.ijhcs.2003.08.003
note: Derived in the file; same provenance restriction as the proportional case. Matches the escalation in McClelland's 1993 demo as described secondarily.

statement: Keramati-Gutkin drive: D(H_t) = (Σ_i |h*_i − h_i,t|^n)^(1/m), with n > m > 1
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, eLife 3:e04811, https://elifesciences.org/articles/04811
note: Corrected 2026-10-29: exponent is ^(1/m), not ^(m/n). Read from the MathML in the eLife XML. The paper's claim that m = n = 1 is Euclidean is a slip (see contradictions).

statement: Keramati-Gutkin reward: r(H_t, K_t) = D(H_t) − D(H_t + K_t), with H_{t+1} = H_t + K_t
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, eLife 3:e04811, https://elifesciences.org/articles/04811
note: Eq. 2. A sensory-estimate version replaces K_t with K̂_t.

statement: Keramati-Gutkin discounted sums: SDD = Σ_{t=0}^{w−1} γ^t D(H_{t+1}) and SDR = Σ_{t=0}^{w−1} γ^t (D(H_t) − D(H_{t+1})) (continuous forms ∫ γ^t D and ∫ γ^t r)
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, eLife 3:e04811, https://elifesciences.org/articles/04811
note: Eqs. 3-4 and S1-S2.

statement: Keramati-Gutkin Proposition (Eq. 5, S3): for γ < 1, argmin over policies of SDD equals argmax of SDR, over trajectories in P(H_0) that end at the setpoint, by telescoping SDR = D_0 + (γ − 1)·SDD
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, eLife 3:e04811, https://elifesciences.org/articles/04811
note: The setpoint-reaching condition was omitted from the survey and is added (validation log). For γ = 1, SDR = D_0 − D_final, which is path-independent, so reward-seeking no longer favours stability.

statement: Keramati-Gutkin hyper-palatability: r = D(H_t) − D(H_t + K_t) + T, with T > 0 a drive-independent bonus; in the quadratic case this equals shifting the setpoint up by T/(2K_t), predicting raised steady-state intake
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, eLife 3:e04811, https://elifesciences.org/articles/04811

statement: Expected free energy, epistemic plus pragmatic form: G_π = −E_{q(o,s|π)}[ln q(s|o,π) − ln q(s|π)] − E_{q(o|π)}[ln p(o|C)]
work: Smith, Friston & Whyte 2022, J. Math. Psychol., PMC8956124 (Eqs. 12-13, Table 2); Parr, Pezzulo & Friston 2022
note: Read via a summarising fetch of Smith et al. The first term is minus epistemic value, the second minus pragmatic value.

statement: Expected free energy, risk plus ambiguity form: G_π = D_KL[q(o|π) ‖ p(o|C)] + E_{q(s|π)}[H[p(o|s)]]
work: Smith, Friston & Whyte 2022, J. Math. Psychol., PMC8956124 (Eqs. 12-13)
note: Risk is divergence of predicted from preferred outcomes; ambiguity is expected likelihood entropy.

statement: Policy selection: prior π_0 = σ(ln E − γG) and posterior π = σ(ln E − F − γG), with σ softmax, E a habit prior, F variational free energy and γ precision
work: Smith, Friston & Whyte 2022, J. Math. Psychol., PMC8956124 (Table 2)
note: Read via summarising fetch.

statement: Prospect theory value function: v(x) = x^α for x ≥ 0 and v(x) = −λ(−x)^β for x < 0, with α = β = 0.88 and λ = 2.25
work: Kahneman & Tversky 1979, Econometrica 47(2), 263-291, doi:10.2307/1914185; Tversky & Kahneman 1992, Journal of Risk and Uncertainty 5, 297-323, doi:10.1007/BF00122574
note: Parameter values universally cited, not read at source (1992 PDF URL serves HTML). They are sample medians, not population constants.

statement: Prospect theory probability weighting with γ = 0.61 for gains and δ = 0.69 for losses, and overall value Σ w(p_i)·v(x_i)
work: Tversky & Kahneman 1992, Journal of Risk and Uncertainty 5, 297-323, doi:10.1007/BF00122574
note: Confirmed by calculator pages (search/secondary); paper not read.

statement: Prospect theory derived predictions: risk aversion in gains (α < 1), risk seeking in losses (β < 1), and loss aversion at the reference point (λ > 1)
work: Kahneman & Tversky 1979, Econometrica 47(2), 263-291, doi:10.2307/1914185
note: Cumulative form's stochastic dominance is an axiomatic result, standard account.

statement: Hull reinforcement as drive reduction: an outcome is reinforcing to the extent it reduces drive
work: Hull 1943, Principles of Behavior; Hull 1952, A Behavior System
note: Abandoned for sweet-taste reward, latent learning, brain stimulation and curiosity (standard account). Keramati and Gutkin give it a formal drive function.

statement: Drive as distance from setpoint: D(H_t) is the Lp-type distance of the physiological state from the setpoint over all dimensions, a scalar
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, eLife 3:e04811, https://elifesciences.org/articles/04811
note: Single agent only. Social rewards and novelty are explicitly outside the theory's scope per the authors.

statement: Drive as surprise: D(H_t) = −ln p(H_t), the bridge from homeostatic drive to active inference
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, eLife 3:e04811, https://elifesciences.org/articles/04811
note: Identified by the paper itself.

statement: Epistemic value as expected information gain about hidden states, equal to an expected KL divergence between posterior and prior over states; curiosity is this term
work: Smith, Friston & Whyte 2022, J. Math. Psychol., PMC8956124; Friston et al. 2015, doi:10.1080/17588928.2015.1020053
note: Curiosity and goal-seeking are two terms of one objective, not separate drives (file's reading).

statement: Pragmatic value as expected log-preference over outcomes, with preferences encoded as a prior p(o|C)
work: Smith, Friston & Whyte 2022, J. Math. Psychol., PMC8956124
note: Read.

statement: Original Dynamics of Action selection rule: the activity with the greatest resultant tendency T_r = T − N is expressed (max-selection)
work: Atkinson & Birch 1970, The Dynamics of Action; Revelle 2008 CTA draft
note: Competing alternative: CTA replaces max-selection with mutual inhibition among actions, which gives a defined resting state.

statement: Achievement incentive value of success Is = 1 − Ps, so the incentive equals the difficulty-complement of the expectancy
work: Atkinson 1957, Psychological Review 64, 359-372, doi:10.1037/h0043445
note: Read via Revelle's handout and CTA Eq. 9.

statement: Conflict types (Lewin, Miller): approach-approach, avoidance-avoidance, approach-avoidance, and double approach-avoidance, the last composed of the others
work: Miller 1944, in Hunt (ed.), Personality and the Behavior Disorders; Lewin 1936; Lewin 1951
note: Standard account, and Lewin's taxonomy predates Miller's.

statement: Motivation as the reference value in perceptual control: the test for a controlled variable is whether behaviour opposes disturbances applied to it while the variable stays near its reference
work: Powers 1973, Behavior: The Control of Perception, Aldine
note: Search/secondary for the control structure; the disturbance test is standard account for PCT.

statement: Collective control: several controllers with different references acting on one variable behave as one virtual controller whose gain is the sum of their gains
work: McClelland 2004, International Journal of Human-Computer Studies 60(1), 65-99, doi:10.1016/j.ijhcs.2003.08.003; McClelland & Fararo 2006, Palgrave, doi:10.1007/978-1-137-10809-8_2
note: Text not read; from the 1993 demo description and the derivation in the file.

statement: Affect as the rate of discrepancy reduction rather than drive itself: affect is a meta-level output of progress, not an input
work: Carver & Scheier 1990, Psychological Review 97, 19-35, doi:10.1037/0033-295X.97.1.19
note: Verbal prediction; the rate-affect link is less tested.

statement: Regulatory fit: a binary match between regulatory focus and strategy, which strengthens engagement and persuasion
note: Standard account; value of fit described as 'feeling right' with no formula.

statement: Gray's conflict rule: the BIS activates when the BAS and FFFS are engaged together (goal conflict)
work: Gray & McNaughton 2000, The Neuropsychology of Anxiety, 2nd ed., Oxford
note: Search/secondary; the file says it is Miller's conflict model re-expressed physiologically.

statement: Hull-Spence: performance scales with deprivation at fixed habit, and high drive helps simple tasks but hurts complex tasks where the dominant response is wrong
work: Hull 1943; Spence 1956, Behavior Theory and Conditioning; Spence on anxiety and paired associates (search/secondary)
note: Predictions from the programme; no effect sizes or out-of-sample figures in the file.

statement: Drive-reduction reinforcement failed on saccharin reward with no need reduced, latent learning, electrical brain stimulation, and exploratory and curiosity behaviour (Harlow, Berlyne)
work: Hull 1943, Principles of Behavior; Harlow; Berlyne (cited in file, not read)
note: Standard account, not checked in the search.

statement: Lorenz hydraulic model: no evidence of energy accumulation, and aggression does not reliably rise with time since last bout
work: Lorenz 1950 (instinct papers); Tinbergen 1951, The Study of Instinct, Oxford
note: Search/secondary; the model was reframed as a conceptual device after this.

statement: Brown 1948 rat harness: approach and avoidance tendencies scale with the drive they are based on (hunger for approach, shock for avoidance), and avoidance is steeper
work: Brown 1948, Journal of Comparative and Physiological Psychology 41, 450-465, doi:10.1037/h0055463
note: Crossref confirmed by title; the content is search/secondary, not read.

statement: Boyd, Robinson & Fetterman 2011: movement is slower in avoidance conflicts than in approach conflicts (three experiments, N = 291)
work: Boyd, Robinson & Fetterman 2011, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology 47, 1192-1197, doi:10.1016/j.jesp.2011.04.017
note: Search/secondary. The file does not state the species or population; human use of the gradients is described as analogical.

statement: Atkinson ring-toss studies (Hamilton, Heckhausen) give an inverted-U in preferred difficulty, but the preferred difficulty peaks at Ps ≈ 0.3-0.4, not at 0.5
work: Revelle, achievement lecture handout, https://www.personality-project.org/revelle/syllabi/301/achievement.pdf; Hamilton and Heckhausen studies as cited
note: Read via the handout. Feather 1961 and 1964 (persistence after failure) are the other classic tests, named without results in the file. The model was extended, not refuted (file).

statement: Fear-of-failure sign-flip (avoidance of intermediate tasks) is confirmed less securely than the success-oriented peak
work: Revelle, achievement lecture handout, https://www.personality-project.org/revelle/syllabi/301/achievement.pdf
note: File marks this as standard account, not read.

statement: Keramati-Gutkin qualitatively reproduce four behavioural patterns by simulation: dose increases reward, deprivation increases reward, irrelevant drives inhibit reward, and risk aversion
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, eLife 3:e04811, https://elifesciences.org/articles/04811
note: Simulation only; parameters are not fitted to data. A reviewer questioned falsifiability and asked for cross-dataset reproduction. Out-of-sample testing not reported.

statement: Keramati-Gutkin further claimed patterns: anticipatory responding (ethanol-hypothermia tolerance), the rise and fall of responding under oral versus intragastric water delivery, and overeating of hyperpalatable food
work: Keramati & Gutkin 2014, eLife 3:e04811, https://elifesciences.org/articles/04811
note: Listed as read claims; the file does not say each one is simulated rather than observed, beyond the general simulation statement.

statement: Revelle's CTA four-person discussion model does not reproduce Antill 1974: as group size grows, extraverts' share of talk rises and introverts' falls
work: Revelle 2008 CTA draft, section on social interactions and Figure 7, https://www.personality-project.org/revelle/publications/cta.pdf; Antill 1974
size_dependence: Antill 1974: extraverts' share of talk rises and introverts' falls as group size grows; the CTA model did not reproduce this trend.
note: The only multi-agent test of CTA found in the file, and it failed. One person's talking inhibits the others' through the cross-inhibition matrix.

statement: CTA derived predictions: time allocation across activities, order of activities, persistence and resumption after interruption (Zeigarnik-like), and tendency strength after a long stretch of one activity
work: Atkinson & Birch 1970, The Dynamics of Action; Revelle & Condon 2015, J. Research in Personality 56, 70-81, doi:10.1016/j.jrp.2014.12.006
note: Standard account; results of solved differential equations, not a theorem list. Evidence for quantitative predictions is thin (file).

statement: Revelle and Michaels 1976 used the inertial property of tendencies to reconcile Atkinson with Locke on task difficulty over repeated trials
work: Revelle & Michaels 1976 (as cited in file)
note: Sentence is untagged in the file; treated as sa, not read.

statement: Expectancy-value meta-analyses: the product form adds little over additive fits, correlations with effort are modest, and the expectancy-value interaction is often not statistically supported
work: Eccles, Wigfield et al. (expectancy-value achievement model, 1983 onward); meta-analyses not named in file
note: Standard account; no specific meta-analysis cited in the file.

statement: Carver-Scheier affect and progress: supported in some studies of affect and progress; the quantitative rate-affect link is less tested
work: Carver & Scheier 1990, Psychological Review 97, 19-35, doi:10.1037/0033-295X.97.1.19
note: Standard account.

statement: Powers PCT: excellent fits on continuous tracking tasks, with limited reach into broader psychology
work: Marken; Powers 1973, Behavior: The Control of Perception, Aldine
note: Standard account, no effect sizes in the file.

statement: McClelland 1993 'Conflictive Control' demonstration: two controllers with different references on one environmental variable escalate, yet the variable behaves as if held by one virtual controller
work: McClelland 1993 demonstration as described at mmtaylor.net/PCT (search/secondary); McClelland 2004, doi:10.1016/j.ijhcs.2003.08.003
