statement: Clogging transition in one description across grains, colloids, sheep and pedestrians (Zuriguel et al.)
work: Zuriguel et al. 2014, Sci. Rep. 4, DOI 10.1038/srep07324
note: Content from the standard account.

statement: Faster-is-slower and clogging studied experimentally in a sheep herd passing through a bottleneck (Garcimartin et al. 2015)
work: Garcimartin et al. 2015, Phys. Rev. E 91, DOI 10.1103/PhysRevE.91.022808
note: File lists this as experimental support; only the title was checked.

statement: Later human studies report that the faster-is-slower effect is condition-dependent
work: not named in the file
size_dependence: Condition-dependent in human studies
note: Stated in the file as [standard], without a citation.

statement: Tsai et al.: of two contagion models run in the ESCAPES simulator, the thermodynamics-style model (Bosse et al.) reproduced a real crowd-panic video better than the epidemiological-style model; graduated fear and proximity-based contagion were the key ingredients
work: Tsai et al. 2013, Auton. Agent Multi-Agent Syst., DOI 10.1007/s10458-013-9220-6
note: One video, so weak evidence; the file calls it uncommon in this area.

statement: Kim et al.: fear level modulates a trade-off between seeking less congested areas and herding; kinetic-theory PDEs qualitatively reproduce a distressed-ant experiment
work: Kim, O'Connell, Ott & Quaini, arXiv:2012.08108
note: Abstract only; qualitative reproduction.

statement: Audience applause alternates spontaneously between incoherent fast clapping and synchronised slow clapping, interpreted as a Kuramoto-type transition from conflict between the wish to be loud and the wish to be in step
note: Title confirmed; content from the standard account. The file calls this a measured social synchrony phenomenon.

statement: Lux-Marchesi interacting agents generate fat-tailed returns (Pareto exponent about 2.6 in the working paper) and volatility clustering, with no power-law news process and no volatility dependence in the news
work: Lux & Marchesi 1999, Nature 397, DOI 10.1038/17290
note: From the abstract and the 1998 working-paper summary. Checked against statistical properties of real return series. Not a test of individual fear or greed.

statement: Epstein et al. agent model (1800 agents, 30 runs per setting): incidence all ignorers 99.9%, all hiders 27.8%, 90% hiders with 10% fleers 64% (corner-to-corner spread in 92% of runs), 90% hiders with 10% ignorers 32%; a second wave occurs when susceptibles return early
work: Epstein, Parker, Cummings & Hammond 2008, PLoS ONE 3(12), DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0003955
size_dependence: Composition of hiders, fleers and ignorers changes incidence
note: Uncalibrated; calibration listed as future work. No out-of-sample test. Historical cases cited qualitatively only.

statement: Funk et al. awareness: spread of awareness lowers outbreak size in a well-mixed population without changing the epidemic threshold
work: Funk, Gilad, Watkins & Jansen 2009, PNAS 106, DOI 10.1073/pnas.0810762106
size_dependence: Well-mixed versus local response
note: Abstract read. Direct measurement of fear-driven behaviour change is limited in these sources.

statement: Hughes et al. MARL: advantageous inequity aversion helps in Cleanup (public goods); disadvantageous inequity aversion helps in Harvest (commons), even if only one of five agents has it, though with costly fining; delaying the intrinsic signal removes the benefit
work: Hughes et al. 2018, NeurIPS, arXiv:1803.08884
size_dependence: Works with one of five agents holding the drive, at a fining cost
note: Gridworld benchmarks, not human behaviour.

statement: Jaques et al.: the causal-influence reward improves coordination and learning curves in multi-agent deep RL
work: Jaques et al. 2019, ICML, arXiv:1810.08647
note: Abstract only. Environments: Cleanup and Harvest. Benchmarks, not human behaviour.

statement: Cimpeanu et al. (theory, no human data): in well-mixed populations only social guilt evolves, and only when the social cost is small, peaking near gamma ~ c; non-social guilt is eliminated; in structured populations clustering lets guilt-prone strategies and cooperation persist over a much wider range of costs
work: Cimpeanu, Pereira & Han 2025, J. R. Soc. Interface 22(228), DOI 10.1098/rsif.2025.0164
size_dependence: Well-mixed (exact, low mutation) versus structured (lattice N = 900, scale-free N = 1000, simulation)
note: Exact results only for the well-mixed chain at low mutation; structured results are simulation.

statement: Theorems require symmetric scalar coupling, anonymity or potentials (original Summary and Close) versus theorems exist for heterogeneous non-anonymous agents with signed, directed or linear-quadratic coupling (section 14: Altafini, Ballester, Bramoulle, graphon games)
note: Side 1 (original): theorems need symmetric scalar coupling, anonymity or potentials. Side 2: section 14 theorems for heterogeneous, non-anonymous agents. Verdict: side 1 was too strong and was corrected in validation; the structural form (linear-quadratic on a known network, mean-field or graphon limit, potential, monotonicity) stands. The gap left is typed, asymmetric, nonlinear, non-monotone drives.

statement: Kuramoto incoherence is stable below K_c and unstable above it (original) versus linearly unstable above K_c but only neutrally stable below (Strogatz & Mirollo 1991)
work: Strogatz & Mirollo 1991, J. Stat. Phys. 63, DOI 10.1007/BF01029202; Strogatz, Mirollo & Matthews 1992, PRL 68, DOI 10.1103/PhysRevLett.68.2730
note: Verdict: original overstated the stability. Corrected in validation, with Landau damping added as the mechanism for decay below K_c.

statement: Jaques influence reward is equivalent to mutual information (original) versus equal to mutual information in expectation only
work: Jaques et al. 2019, ICML, arXiv:1810.08647
note: Verdict: corrected in validation to the in-expectation form; the proof is in the paper's supplement.

statement: Yin et al. oscillator game stated as a theorem (original) versus a bifurcation analysis of the linearised mean-field PDE plus epsilon-Nash approximation, not a global theorem about the N-player game
work: Yin, Mehta, Meyn & Shanbhag 2012, IEEE TAC 57(4), DOI 10.1109/TAC.2011.2168082
note: Verdict: corrected in validation. Abstract via search only.

statement: Lux-Marchesi: unimodal-to-bimodal bifurcation of the chartist fraction attributed to the 1999 Nature paper (original) versus the classic result of Lux 1995 and Kirman-type recruitment models
note: Verdict: misattribution. Removed from the 1999 paper and replaced with its critical-state account.

statement: Faster-is-slower is experimentally supported in humans (Garcimartin et al. 2014) versus later human studies report the effect is condition-dependent
work: Garcimartin et al. 2014, Transp. Res. Procedia 2, DOI 10.1016/j.trpro.2014.09.085; later studies unnamed in file
size_dependence: Depends on condition; human manipulation is competitiveness, not the model's v^0
note: Verdict: unresolved in the file. The later-study claim is a [standard] account with no citation. The human case manipulates competitiveness rather than the model's desired speed.

statement: Helbing's p_i is called nervousness (original) versus the paper's degree of panic (Helbing et al. 2000)
work: Helbing, Farkas & Vicsek 2000, Nature 407, DOI 10.1038/35035023
note: Verdict: the paper says degree of panic; the original label was not in the paper. Corrected in validation.

statement: Lasry-Lions uniqueness stated with the monotonicity condition on F alone (original) versus with the same condition on the terminal cost G and a strictness requirement (corrected)
work: Lasry & Lions 2007, Japan. J. Math. 2, DOI 10.1007/s11537-007-0657-8
size_dependence: Monotone coupling excludes herding; attractive coupling can give multiple equilibria
note: Verdict: corrected in validation. The original omitted the G condition and strictness. Multiple equilibria as herding is an interpretation, not a theorem.

statement: Potential games: any exact potential game is isomorphic to a coordination game (original) versus a decomposition into a coordination game plus a dummy game per player
work: Monderer & Shapley 1996, Games Econ. Behav. 14, DOI 10.1006/game.1996.0044
note: Verdict: original wording corrected in validation to decomposition.

statement: Response threshold: per task j a group-level stimulus s_j (the task's need) and per individual i and task j a threshold θ_ij (disposition); an inactive individual starts task j when s_j is high relative to θ_ij
work: Bonabeau, Theraulaz, Deneubourg 1996, Proc R Soc B 263, 1565-1569, DOI 10.1098/rspb.1996.0229
note: File's own description, standard account; the 1996 model is discrete-time. Not read in full text.

statement: Commitment state of a swarm: fractions uncommitted x_U, committed to site A x_A, committed to site B x_B, with x_U = 1 − x_A − x_B; each site's quality v sets how strongly its advocates recruit
work: Pais et al. 2013, PLoS ONE 8(9) e73216, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0073216
note: Full text read in validation pass 2026-10-29. Generalisation to N options (arXiv 1611.07575) is not checked.

statement: Quorum drive: an individual's local count of nest-mates met at a candidate site, with a threshold on that count that switches it from tandem-run recruitment to transport
work: Pratt 2005, Behav Ecol 16, 488-496, DOI 10.1093/beheco/ari020
note: Rule taken from titles and the standard account of the species; no abstract retrieved.

statement: Boldness as a stable trait plus a feedback variable: how being ahead or behind changes later behaviour, so that leader and follower roles emerge from social feedback rather than being read off the trait
work: Harcourt, Ang, Sweetman, Johnstone, Manica 2009, Curr Biol 19, 248-252, DOI 10.1016/j.cub.2008.12.051
note: Read as abstract. Boldness here is leaving cover to look for food. See contradiction on Jolles 2017, which finds sociability and speed rather than boldness.

statement: Fear/startle state of each fish, with a visual field that defines which neighbours it can perceive and therefore which startle signals it responds to
work: Rosenthal, Twomey, Hartnett, Wu, Couzin 2015, PNAS 112, 4690-4695, DOI 10.1073/pnas.1420068112
note: Read as abstract. File says startle is binary or graded, which the abstract does not settle.

statement: Vigilance allocation: each group member scans with probability p, and the group detects a threat if any member scans
work: Pulliam 1973, J Theor Biol 38, 419-422, DOI 10.1016/0022-5193(73)90184-7; Ward, Herbert-Read, Sumpter, Krause 2011, PNAS 108, 2312-2315, DOI 10.1073/pnas.1007102108
size_dependence: Pulliam: a member can lower its own vigilance as group size grows while overall detection stays high. Ward: speed and accuracy both rise with group size under predation threat.
note: Pulliam's model uses scanning intervals and detection time; the form (1 − p)^n is a simplification the file flags.

statement: Private information versus socially acquired information: an individual copies others when private information is costly, and copied information is not independent, so a population can lock into a maladaptive behaviour
work: Giraldeau, Valone, Templeton 2002, Phil Trans R Soc B 357, 1559-1566, DOI 10.1098/rstb.2002.1065
note: Confirmed as title and DOI only; not read. Standard account.

statement: Preference direction of each baboon, expressed by initiating movement, which others follow when several initiators agree
work: Strandburg-Peshkin, Farine, Couzin, Crofoot 2015, Science 348, 1358-1361, DOI 10.1126/science.aaa5099
note: Read as abstract.

statement: Informed subpopulations holding opposed preferences that differ in size and strength, alongside an uninformed subpopulation with no preference; the uninformed pool is the uncommitted pool x_U of the B1 model
work: Couzin et al. 2011, Science 334, 1578-1580, DOI 10.1126/science.1210280
size_dependence: Press summary says that if uninformed numbers become very large, noise erodes the majority's control and coherence. Not checked against full text.
note: The x_U identification is the file's mapping, not the paper's.

statement: Social status as a cause of drive state: changing social position changes neuroendocrine physiology (GnRH-neuron size, steroid levels) within the hour to days, so the same individual has different drive parameters at different ranks
work: Fernald 2012, Annu Rev Neurosci 35, 133-151, DOI 10.1146/annurev-neuro-062111-150520
note: Standard account of the cichlid Astatotilapia burtoni work. Fernald 2012 not read; timescales are unchecked.

statement: Exploration as a named drive term: scouts are consistent novelty-seekers across contexts, and the discovery rate γ in the B1 model is an explicit exploration term separate from recruitment ρ
work: Liang, Nguyen, Mattila, Rodriguez-Zas, Seeley, Robinson 2012, Science 335, 1225-1228, DOI 10.1126/science.1213962
note: Corrected form. The file first said curiosity and desire were essentially absent; validation found exploration and appetite present under other names. Liang read as abstract: octopamine and glutamate raise scouting, a dopamine antagonist lowers it.

statement: Appetite regulated by return-encounter rate: harvester-ant colony foraging activity is regulated by the rate at which foragers return and meet others, analysed as a feedback controller
work: Prabhakar, Dektar, Gordon 2012, PLoS Comput Biol 8, e1002670, DOI 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1002670
note: Described from the file's own summary; not read.

statement: Two selfish drives, approach a prey and move away from wolves that are already close to the safe distance, yield cooperative-looking pack hunting in simulation
work: Muro, Escobedo, Spector, Coppinger 2011, Behav Processes 88, 192-197, DOI 10.1016/j.beproc.2011.09.006
note: Rules read from abstract. Simulation only; no field fit.

statement: Helping drive: help is favoured when the relatedness-weighted benefit to the recipient exceeds the cost (rb > c)
note: Standard account. The file says Hamilton's rule's general validity is debated and was not examined here.

statement: Pais deterministic commitment dynamics: dx_A/dt = γ_A x_U − α_A x_A + ρ_A x_A x_U − σ_B x_A x_B; dx_B/dt = γ_B x_U − α_B x_B + ρ_B x_B x_U − σ_A x_A x_B; x_U = 1 − x_A − x_B
work: Pais et al. 2013, PLoS ONE 8(9) e73216, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0073216
note: γ discovery, α abandonment, ρ recruitment, σ_i cross-inhibition by bees committed to site i. Read from full text including equation images.

statement: Value dependence and noise in the Pais model: γ_i = ρ_i = v_i and α_i = 1/v_i, with σ value-independent; multiplicative noise k·sqrt(x_U² + x_A² + x_U²x_A²)·dW_A on the value-dependent rates, none on σ
work: Pais et al. 2013, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0073216; value form following Seeley et al. 2012, DOI 10.1126/science.1210361
note: Corrected form. Earlier text did not have the value dependence or the noise term.

statement: Deadlock-breaking threshold for equal options: the symmetric attractor loses stability at a pitchfork bifurcation in σ when the options have equal value v, at σ* = 4v³ / (v² − 1)²; σ* falls as v rises
work: Pais et al. 2013, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0073216; attributed by the paper to Seeley et al. 2012, DOI 10.1126/science.1210361, where it was first calculated
note: Pitchfork confirmed in validation; earlier text flagged it as a guess. For unequal values the paper describes a saddle-node bifurcation in σ instead.

statement: Value sensitivity: the minimum value difference reliably discriminated satisfies Δv / v̄ = K (Weber-like), with K set by σ (lower σ, lower K)
work: Pais et al. 2013, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0073216
note: From the full text of the paper.

statement: Derived from Pais Eq. 1 at the symmetric equilibrium (x_A = x_B = x, U = 1 − 2x): the antisymmetric eigenvalue is λ = vU − 1/v; λ = 0 gives U = 1/v², x = (v² − 1)/(2v²) and σ* = 1/(v x²) = 4v³/(v² − 1)²
work: Pais et al. 2013, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0073216 (derivation by the validator)
note: Derived by the validator from the full-text equations, so read. The file says it checks against Pais Eq. 4.

statement: Consequences of the B1 eigenvalue: σ* exists only for v > 1, so for v ≤ 1 equal options deadlock however strong the stop signal; σ* tends to 4/v for large v
work: Pais et al. 2013, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0073216 (derivation by the validator)
note: Not stated in the survey. Forward-Euler simulation at v = 2 (σ* = 3.56): symmetric split (0.41, 0.41) at 0.9σ*, broken split (0.26, 0.49) at 1.1σ*. Simulation of the model, not an empirical test.

statement: Direct switching by recruitment with zero spontaneous abandonment approximates the statistically optimal decision procedure and is asymptotically optimal (once all scouts are committed, dynamics reduce to one-dimensional diffusion); indirect switching is not optimal; the Temnothorax model needs parameters depending on both sites' qualities
work: Marshall, Bogacz, Dornhaus, Planque, Kovacs, Franks 2009, J R Soc Interface 6, 1065-1074, DOI 10.1098/rsif.2008.0511
note: Corrected form: the optimal mechanism is direct switching, not stop-signal cross-inhibition. Analysis applies the Usher-McClelland leaky-competing-accumulator result: optimal when decay equals inhibition and both are large. Optimality is could-under-conditions, not do. Read as abstract plus summary of full text.

statement: Response-threshold function: an inactive individual starts task j with probability T_θ(s) = s^n / (s^n + θ^n), with n = 2 in Bonabeau et al. 1996, so T = 1/2 at s = θ
work: Bonabeau, Theraulaz, Deneubourg 1996, DOI 10.1098/rspb.1996.0229
note: Standard account; equation not re-read in full text by the validator.

statement: Stimulus update, discrete time: s(t+1) = s(t) + δ − α·N_act/N; mean-field limit ds/dt = δ − α·N_act/N (demand grows at δ, work by the active fraction depletes it)
work: Bonabeau, Theraulaz, Deneubourg 1996, DOI 10.1098/rspb.1996.0229
note: Standard account; validation log notes the discrete-time form.

statement: Reinforcement rule: θ_ij ← θ_ij − ξΔt while i performs task j and θ_ij ← θ_ij + φΔt while it does not, bounded within [θ_min, θ_max]; initially identical individuals differentiate into specialists
work: Theraulaz, Bonabeau, Deneubourg 1998, Proc R Soc B 265, 327-332, DOI 10.1098/rspb.1998.0299
note: Rule written out in validation. Standard account; equations not re-read in full text. Bonabeau et al. 1998, Bull Math Biol 60, 753-807, DOI 10.1006/bulm.1998.0041, is also cited for the fixed-threshold model.

statement: Threshold allocation results: low-threshold individuals take up a task first and others are recruited only as stimulus rises, so work is allocated by threshold without central assignment and stimulus is kept near homeostasis
work: Bonabeau et al. 1996, DOI 10.1098/rspb.1996.0229; reviewed in Beshers and Fewell 2001, Annu Rev Entomol 46, 413-440, DOI 10.1146/annurev.ento.46.1.413
note: Derived results, standard account. The review notes few predictions of this model have been tested head-to-head against rival models.

statement: Rule-set classification: lattice-swarm builders following local configuration-to-action tables yield coherent architectures only for a few rule sets; most rule tables yield incoherent shapes
work: Theraulaz and Bonabeau 1995, Science 269, 686-688, DOI 10.1126/science.269.5224.686
note: Simulation-based, not a proof. The file calls this the nearest thing here to a structure theorem.

statement: Pulliam's group-vigilance form: if n members each scan with probability p, the probability that no one scans falls with n, so each can lower its own vigilance as group size grows (written here as (1 − p)^n)
size_dependence: Detection falls with n, so per-member vigilance can fall as group size grows.
note: The (1 − p)^n form is a simplification; Pulliam's model uses scanning intervals and detection time.

statement: Hamilton's rule: help is favoured when rb > c
note: Exact under its assumptions; general validity debated and not examined in the file.

statement: Quorum-response function: a steep threshold function of the number already committed, across taxa (the formal statement of the quorum operator in A3)
work: Sumpter and Pratt 2009, Phil Trans R Soc B 364, 743-753, DOI 10.1098/rstb.2008.0204
note: Listed as missing work; described from the file's summary, not read.

statement: Compromise-or-choose transition: as the angle between preferred directions changes, the movement system undergoes a bifurcation, compromising at small angles and choosing one direction at large angles
work: Leonard, Shen, Nabet, Scardovi, Couzin, Levin 2012, PNAS 109, 227-232, DOI 10.1073/pnas.1118318108
note: Listed as missing work; the file says this is the mathematics behind B3 and the model side of B4. Not read.

statement: Repeated bifurcations as options are approached: the same decision geometry governs individual brains and collective groups
work: Sridhar, Li, Gorbonos, Nagy, Schell, Sorochkin, Gov, Couzin 2021, PNAS 118, e2102157118, DOI 10.1073/pnas.2102157118
note: Listed as missing work; the file calls it the strongest existing case for individual and group obeying the same law. Not read.

statement: Harvester-ant task choice depends on encounter rates with other ants' cuticular hydrocarbon signatures, supporting a stimulus-by-encounter reading of task allocation
work: Greene and Gordon 2003, Nature 423, 32, DOI 10.1038/423032a
note: Existence confirmed in validation; content not read. No out-of-sample performance or effect size recorded.

statement: Temnothorax quorum is sensed by encounter rate, not absolute population: scouts switch to transport when encounters at a site exceed a threshold
work: Pratt 2005, Behav Ecol 16, 488-496, DOI 10.1093/beheco/ari020
note: Claim rests on the title. No abstract retrieved in validation; mechanism beyond the title unchecked.

statement: Honeybee scouts send stop signals (head-butts) to waggle-dancing scouts reporting other sites, the empirical correlate of cross-inhibition σ; the authors' analytic model says cross-inhibition solves deadlock over equal sites and raises reliability of swarm decisions
work: Seeley, Visscher, Schlegel, Hogan, Franks, Marshall 2012, Science 335, 108-111, DOI 10.1126/science.1210361
note: Read as abstract. The deadlock-breaking analysis is originally Seeley's, not Pais's only (validation correction).

statement: In golden shiners, a strongly opinionated minority can dictate group choice, but uninformed individuals spontaneously inhibit this and return control to the numerical majority, for a wide range of conditions
work: Couzin et al. 2011, Science 334, 1578-1580, DOI 10.1126/science.1210280
size_dependence: Press summary only: very large uninformed numbers erode the majority's control and coherence.
note: Read as abstract, with theory and experiment. Human tests of this structure are not verified in the file.

statement: Baboons follow when several initiators agree rather than following dominant individuals; they choose one direction when the angle between conflicting directions is large and compromise when it is small
work: Strandburg-Peshkin, Farine, Couzin, Crofoot 2015, Science 348, 1358-1361, DOI 10.1126/science.aaa5099
note: Corrected form. The earlier phrasing 'any individual can initiate' is not in the abstract and was softened to dominance not predicting who is followed.

statement: Golden shiner schools (about 150 fish): fear contagion is complex and fractional, not one-contact transmission; individuals with relatively few but strongly connected neighbours are the most influential and the most susceptible; cascades are predictable at the moment of initiation
work: Rosenthal, Twomey, Hartnett, Wu, Couzin 2015, PNAS 112, 4690-4695, DOI 10.1073/pnas.1420068112
size_dependence: Network weights, directed and heterogeneous; no size dependence stated.
note: Read as abstract. Potential control (moving a fish changes the cascade) is the survey's extrapolation, not a result of the paper. Out-of-sample performance not stated.

statement: Fish shoals under predation threat: speed and accuracy of group decisions both rise with group size; repeated testing found no especially able individuals; the gain is attributed to self-organised division of vigilance and social information transfer
work: Ward, Herbert-Read, Sumpter, Krause 2011, PNAS 108, 2312-2315, DOI 10.1073/pnas.1007102108
size_dependence: Speed and accuracy both rise with group size.
note: Read as abstract.

statement: Stickleback pairs: a Markov chain model of joint behaviour shows leadership reinforced by positive social feedback; bolder fish show more initiative and less responsiveness, shyer fish follow more faithfully and elicit stronger leadership in bold partners
work: Harcourt, Ang, Sweetman, Johnstone, Manica 2009, Curr Biol 19, 248-252, DOI 10.1016/j.cub.2008.12.051
note: Corrected form: the file first attributed leadership in both Harcourt and Jolles to boldness, and pairs are the unit here. Read as abstract.

statement: Stickleback shoals: sociability, not boldness, is negatively linked to swim speed and predicts spatial position and leadership; sociability plus exploratory tendency explains foraging performance, emerging from a self-organising model of speed and goal-orientedness
work: Jolles, Boogert, Sridhar, Couzin, Manica 2017, Curr Biol 27, 2862-2868, DOI 10.1016/j.cub.2017.08.004
note: Corrected form. Read as abstract.

statement: Knocking out the small subset of policing individuals in a captive macaque group makes the social network smaller, less diverse and less integrated: reduced mean degree, increased clustering, reduced reach, increased assortativity
work: Flack, Girvan, de Waal, Krakauer 2006, Nature 439, 426-429, DOI 10.1038/nature04326
size_dependence: Press coverage gives 84 pigtailed macaques.
note: Knocked-out individuals were also the highest-ranking, so removal confounds rank and policing; not separated in the file, unresolved, full text not read.

statement: Harvester-ant colony foraging activity is regulated by return-encounter rate, analysed as a feedback controller (an explicit appetite-regulation equation at colony level)
work: Prabhakar, Dektar, Gordon 2012, PLoS Comput Biol 8, e1002670, DOI 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1002670
note: Described from the file's summary; not read.

statement: Scouts are consistent novelty-seekers across food and nest-site contexts; octopamine and glutamate raise scouting, and a dopamine antagonist lowers it
work: Liang, Nguyen, Mattila, Rodriguez-Zas, Seeley, Robinson 2012, Science 335, 1225-1228, DOI 10.1126/science.1213962
note: Individual-level trait; scale is membership as the nearest of the three, a judgement not made by the file. Read as abstract.

statement: Status change by social opportunity alters neuroendocrine physiology within the hour to days in cichlid males
work: Fernald 2012, Annu Rev Neurosci 35, 133-151, DOI 10.1146/annurev-neuro-062111-150520
note: Standard account, not read. Scale is membership as the nearest of the three, a judgement not made by the file. Human status-physiology literature is not verified.

statement: Operand/operator frame: individuals carry graded internal variables; interactions are rules that read other individuals' signalled states and update one's own; group-level results are theorems or bifurcations in the induced dynamics
work: Synthesis of the works in 29 (no single source)
note: The file's own headline synthesis, not a finding of any one paper. Transfer to humans is strongest for structure, weakest for parameters.

statement: Operands and operators in B1: operands are population fractions on a commitment simplex; operators are Discover, Recruit, Abandon and Inhibit, each a flow on the simplex with a rate coefficient
work: Pais et al. 2013, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0073216
note: File calls this the most algebra-ready object in the cluster. The operator decomposition is the file's, built on read Eq. 1.

statement: Operands in A1 are (individual, task) pairs carrying a threshold, with a group-level stimulus as operand; operators are Act (probabilistic, gated by threshold), Reinforce (threshold update) and Deplete (stimulus update by the active set)
work: Bonabeau et al. 1996, DOI 10.1098/rspb.1996.0229
note: File's proposed decomposition, on standard-account rules.

statement: Stigmergy: the shared environment is the state; an operator is a local rewrite rule mapping a perceived pattern to an action that changes the pattern
work: Theraulaz and Bonabeau 1995, DOI 10.1126/science.269.5224.686
note: Grasse 1959 (coinage of stigmergy) is not verified in the file.

statement: Threshold operator on a counter: an individual's count of encounters is incremented by Encounter, and Switch fires when the count crosses the quorum threshold, changing its signalling mode
work: Pratt 2005, DOI 10.1093/beheco/ari020
note: File's proposed operator, rests on the Pratt title.

statement: Fission-fusion: a group-level operand is a partition of the individuals, changed over time by Fission and Fusion operators; the file suggests a partition lattice as the formalism
work: Aureli et al. 2008, Curr Anthropol 49, 627-654, DOI 10.1086/586708
note: Standard account; author list not verified from full text in the file's own text (validation filled it from Crossref).

statement: Guarded operator: Help(i→j) is applied if and only if rb > c
note: Operator with a guard condition; the file notes the same form in A1 and A3 and in Hawk-Dove.

statement: Role operand: a policer is present or absent in the group; Intervene(conflict) restores baseline; the invariant preserved by this operator is the algebraic form of 'policing stabilises'
work: Flack et al. 2006, DOI 10.1038/nature04326
note: The role is not a drive; recorded because the file proposes it as an operand. Rests on the abstract.

statement: Operand type as coefficient: an operand's type label (such as a personality type) biases the gain on every operator it takes part in, a coefficient rather than a new operator
work: Jandt et al. 2013, Biol Rev, DOI 10.1111/brv.12042; Modlmeier et al. 2014, Anim Behav 89, 53-62, DOI 10.1016/j.anbehav.2013.12.020
note: Read from titles only; the file's proposal, no equations.

statement: Two-layer individual state: a trait (boldness, fixed) and a role (leader or follower, dynamic, updated by the Follow operator and reinforced by social feedback)
work: Harcourt et al. 2009, DOI 10.1016/j.cub.2008.12.051
note: The file's proposed structure, rests on the Harcourt abstract.

statement: Role or status modifies an individual's drive gains: the same individual at a different social position has different drive parameters
work: Fernald 2012, DOI 10.1146/annurev-neuro-062111-150520
note: Rests on the cichlid standard account, not read.

statement: Contagion over a state-dependent directed graph: the transmission graph is a function of positions and time (a visual network), so any algebra of fear indexes the graph by state
work: Rosenthal et al. 2015, DOI 10.1073/pnas.1420068112
note: The graph as operand-derived object is the file's proposal.

statement: Muro-style operators: Approach(target) and Disperse(others) are vector-field operators whose composition gives the hunting outcome
work: Muro et al. 2011, DOI 10.1016/j.beproc.2011.09.006
note: Simulation-based; the file calls the transfer mostly illustrative.

statement: Marshall 2009 versus Seeley 2012 on the optimal colony mechanism: the earlier text said cross-inhibitory competition is equivalent to a sequential-sampling decision rule; the corrected claim is that Marshall's optimal mechanism is direct switching by recruitment with zero abandonment, which is not stop-signal cross-inhibition
work: Marshall et al. 2009, DOI 10.1098/rsif.2008.0511; Seeley et al. 2012, DOI 10.1126/science.1210361
note: Both sides: earlier text (cross-inhibition equivalent to sequential sampling) versus corrected (distinct mechanisms, Seeley's inhibited bees return to uncommitted, closer to the indirect route). Verdict in the file: resolved by correction, B1 and B2 not to be cited as one result. Ledger rule keeps contradictions open until a deep read; status left open here.

statement: Harcourt 2009 versus Jolles 2017 on what drives leadership: Harcourt attributes leadership in sticklebacks to boldness (leaving cover for food); Jolles finds sociability and speed, not boldness, predict leadership in shoals
source: 29 §D1 and Validation log (Harcourt and Jolles corrections)
note: Both sides as the file has them after correction. The file's own correction concerns its earlier attribution of leadership to boldness in both papers. Verdict: unresolved in the file; it does not say whether the two papers conflict once their different measures are taken into account.

statement: Flack 2006 knockout: removing policing individuals reduces network integration, but the removed individuals were also the highest-ranking, so rank and policing are confounded
work: Flack, Girvan, de Waal, Krakauer 2006, DOI 10.1038/nature04326
note: Both sides: the paper's causal claim against the rank confound. Verdict: unresolved; how the paper separates the two was not checked in full text. Status open.

statement: Strandburg-Peshkin 2015 on whether any individual can initiate movement: the earlier text said any individual can initiate; the abstract shows dominance does not predict who is followed, and the phrase 'any individual can initiate' is not in the abstract
work: Strandburg-Peshkin, Farine, Couzin, Crofoot 2015, DOI 10.1126/science.aaa5099
note: Verdict in the file: the softened form stands (dominance does not predict who is followed). Read as abstract.

statement: Deadlock-breaking attribution: the file first credited the cross-inhibition deadlock result to Pais 2013; the corrected attribution is that the deadlock analysis is originally Seeley et al. 2012, with Pais's threshold attributed to them
source: 29 §B1 and Validation log (Seeley 2012 and Pais 2013 entries)
work: Seeley et al. 2012, DOI 10.1126/science.1210361; Pais et al. 2013, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0073216
note: Verdict in the file: originally Seeley's, per its abstract. Pais Eq. 4 is attributed to Seeley where first calculated.

statement: Curiosity and desire as drives: the earlier closing claim said they are essentially absent from animal models; the corrected claim is that they are present as exploration and appetite under other names, and only absent as named, interacting state variables with their own dynamics
work: Liang et al. 2012, DOI 10.1126/science.1213962; Prabhakar et al. 2012, DOI 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1002670
note: Verdict in the file: the 'no common state space' closing claim stands. The corrected form is the one to record.

statement: Attachment: proximity-seeking to a preferred figure under threat; the set-goal is a degree of proximity or accessibility, not a fixed place
work: Bowlby 1969, Attachment and Loss vol. 1 (book, no DOI)
note: Not read; standard account per the file. Bowlby gives verbal structure only, no equations. Rejects the psychoanalytic secondary-drive account in favour of behavioural systems.

statement: Exploration system: activated when the attachment system is quiescent; the figure's accessibility lets it run (secure base)
work: Bowlby 1969, Attachment and Loss vol. 1 (book, no DOI)
note: Not read. File says the three systems form a priority-ordered, mutually inhibiting set; the numerical trade-off is not stated anywhere.

statement: Fear/wariness system, tied to attachment: fear raises the proximity set-goal
work: Bowlby 1969, Attachment and Loss vol. 1 (book, no DOI)
note: Not read. No quantitative rule for how much a stimulus raises the set-goal (file's stated gap).

statement: Security state s in [0,1] with dependency setpoint D; activation A_s = D - s (positive = appetence, negative = aversion)
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: Read in full. Setpoints D and E are homeostats; the chapter says exploration is homeostatic too, against the widespread antihomeostatic notion.

statement: Arousal (enterprise) state a in [0,1] with enterprise setpoint E; activation A_a = E - a; fear when arousal exceeds E, appetence for arousal (exploration/curiosity) when below
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: Read in full. The reading of fear and curiosity as two signs of one error term is the authors' own wording (confirmed in validation), not the file's gloss.

statement: Autonomy claim C in [0,1], a single parameter with D = 1 - C and E = C; described as a need for feeling competent and being respected by others
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: Read in full. File's critique: C fuses White's competence with social rank, so the model is under-differentiated. Autonomy is a third system whose social feedback is positive (stability problems); only assumptions 4 and 5 are modelled.

statement: Sharing drive: a species-unique motivation to share emotions, experience and activities with other persons; satisfied only by a partner's matching state (file's relational reading)
work: Tomasello et al. 2005, Understanding and sharing intentions, Behavioral and Brain Sciences 28(5), 675-691, DOI 10.1017/s0140525x05000129
note: Tagged [read, Crossref abstract], so abstract only. The 'satisfied only by a partner's matching state' property is the file's translation, not a source claim. Ape sharing motivation is contested.

statement: Effectance: intrinsic drive to produce effects on the environment, satisfied by increase (feeling of efficacy) rather than reduction of tension; controlled variable is action-outcome contingency
work: White 1959, Motivation reconsidered: the concept of competence, Psychological Review 66(5), 297-333, DOI 10.1037/h0040934
note: Not read; standard account. Conceptually influential, no direct test. Mastery-motivation measurement in infants not covered by the file.

statement: Contact comfort as an independent drive with its own satisfier (contact), not collapsed into the nutritive drive
work: Harlow 1958, The nature of love, American Psychologist 13(12), 673-685, DOI 10.1037/h0047884; Harlow & Zimmermann 1959, Science 130(3373), 421-432, DOI 10.1126/science.130.3373.421
note: Neither read. File corrected its vocabulary: 'secure base' is Ainsworth's term, not Harlow's. The file also notes the study is a long-standing ethical case (maltreated, isolate-reared animals).

statement: Information-rate preference (curiosity): infants seek intermediate rates of information absorption, looking away from events that are too predictable or too surprising
work: Kidd, Piantadosi & Aslin 2012, The Goldilocks effect, PLoS ONE 7(5), e36399, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0036399
note: Read at article page. The 'curiosity' interpretation is the authors'. The file notes look-away can also reflect fatigue or satiation.

statement: Separation distress (PANIC/GRIEF): an unmet security setpoint emits a signal detectable by others, reduced by contact; file's translation maps this to A_s with an output channel
work: Panksepp, Nelson & Bekkedal 1997, Ann. N.Y. Acad. Sci. 807, 78-100, DOI 10.1111/j.1749-6632.1997.tb51914.x
note: Cross-reference only; not examined in the file. Opioid substrate claim is standard account. Neural detail and replication standing are in files 15 and 22.

statement: Primary sociability: a motive to engage and share emotion with a partner, present from about 2 months and not derived from other drives
work: Trevarthen 1979, Communication and cooperation in early infancy, in Bullowa (ed.), Before Speech, Cambridge UP (no DOI)
note: Not read; abstract/standard account. File says whether primary intersubjectivity implies innate mind-reading is contested.

statement: Infant engagement drive with a setpoint on contingent responsiveness rather than on proximity (file's translation of the Mutual Regulation Model)
work: Tronick 1989, Emotions and emotional communication in infants, American Psychologist 44(2), 112-119, DOI 10.1037/0003-066x.44.2.112
note: Not read. The MRM is verbal; the setpoint-on-responsiveness reading is the file's suggestion, not stated by the source.

statement: Infant state of uncertainty about a novel or ambiguous stimulus, which drives approach or avoidance and is modulated by a caregiver's displayed emotion (social referencing)
work: Klinnert et al. 1983, Emotions as behavior regulators: social referencing in infancy, in Plutchik & Kellerman (eds), Emotion vol. 2, Academic Press, DOI 10.1016/b978-0-12-558702-0.50009-1
note: Not read. The file ties the uncertainty state to Bischof's arousal a, which is the file's mapping.

statement: Psychological proximity H(x_i): monotone decaying hyperbola with H = 1 at x = 0, H = 0 for x >= x_max, slope parameter r
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: Exact algebraic form was garbled by OCR and is not recovered; only the stated properties are recorded.

statement: Potency P_i = R_i * H(x_i), the product of proximity and relevancy
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: Read in full.

statement: Incentive magnitudes |I_si| = P'_i * F_i and |I_ai| = P'_i * (1 - F_i), with P'_i = R_i * H'(x_i), H' a separate decay with slope r'; direction from subject toward object i
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: Read in full.

statement: Total incentive I_s(y) = sum over i of I_si, and I_a likewise; the zero of the incentive field is Buridan's point
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: Read in full. A stranger and a mother can cancel, giving a zero.

statement: Joint familiarity atmosphere F = (sum_i P_i F_i) / (sum_i P_i), a potency-weighted mean bounded in [0,1]
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: Read in full. One of the only two aggregation laws stated in the file.

statement: Joint potency P = 1 - prod_i (1 - P_i), quasi-additive for small P_i and saturating at P_max = 1
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: Read in full. Two potent objects do not give double security.

statement: Security s = P * F and arousal a = P * (1 - F), products of joint potency and joint familiarity
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: OCR printed 'x = P - F'; the product reading is confirmed by the prose and the Fig. 3.1 legend (see contradictions).

statement: Momentum M_s = A_s * I_s and M_a = A_a * I_a; motor output is the vector sum M_s + M_a, damped by friction and integrated twice to give position
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: Read in full. Competition and time-sharing (McFarland) are said to be very likely the right integration but are not implemented.

statement: Pool model: A_s(T) = sum_{t=0}^{T} (D - s)_t and A_a(T) = sum_{t=0}^{T} (E - a)_t, clipped to [-1,1]; security and arousal set the rate of change of activation, not activation itself
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: Read in full. The double integral is inherently unstable and produces the undamped oscillations the authors identify with Mahler et al.'s emotional refueling.

statement: Coping as random motor unrest with standard deviation u = k * (|A_s| + |A_a| - |M_s + M_a|), applied only when positive
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: Read in full. Unrest rises when the two drives pull against each other and cancel.

statement: Acclimatization: stress q(T) = sum over time since last adaptation of (A_s - A_a); if |q| > q_lim, C moves toward 1 (dC = rho(1 - C)) or toward 0 (dC = -rho C) at rho much less than 1, and q resets to zero
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: OCR garbled the inequality signs in 16a/16b (both print q < q_lim); semantics are taken from the chapter's prose. The paper sums the difference, not each term separately, so excess security can balance excess arousal.

statement: Simulation result (not proof, single subject, other agents fixed): a stranger raises clinging only above a dependency threshold; at D = 0.75 the A_s = 0 locus contracts toward the mother when a stranger is added, at D = 0.5 it does not
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
size_dependence: Conditional on dependency D: effect vanishes below the threshold (file's derived prediction of eqs. 6-9).
note: Read in full. Authors sever social feedback loops on purpose.

statement: Simulation result: infancy (C = E = 0.25, D = 0.75): mother alone gives oscillatory refueling; mother plus stranger gives retreat to mother's lap with oscillation dying out; stranger alone gives approach with residual unrest
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: Simulation only. Qualitative reproduction of the Strange Situation pattern as the file describes it.

statement: Simulation result: puberty (C = 0.5): excursions from the mother widen; a moderately familiar stranger is approached while the mother is present; C = 0.6 is enough to sit comfortably with the stranger
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: Simulation only. Avoidance of the interval between mother and stranger is also reported.

statement: Simulation result: acclimatization (C starts at 0): an irreversible rise in C emerges, traced by the authors to the choice of familiarity coefficients (stranger F = 0.4; mother's alienness 1 - F = 0.1), not to the symmetric mechanism
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: File calls this the closest thing in the survey to a theorem about how a dyad changes a drive's setpoint. Familiarisation over time is not modelled, so the asymmetry is an input choice.

statement: Gubler (1989) fitted a modified pool model to painted-quail pairs (siblings raised together vs strangers): four modifications were needed, and sibling/stranger differences were accounted for by familiarity alone
work: Gubler 1989, doctoral dissertation, Univ. Zurich (unpublished; seen only via Gubler & Bischof 1991)
size_dependence: Pairs of siblings vs strangers; file says familiarity alone accounts for the difference.
note: Read via the chapter only; unpublished, single lab. The file reports no out-of-sample test for the quail fit. Parameters were estimated from the data.

statement: Friedlander (1987) fitted the pool model per child in a long corridor with arousal raised by an unlocalisable low-frequency sound: mean fit quality 0.7 across 15 toddlers (worst 0.4, best 0.9; 1.0 = exact, 0.0 = no better than a straight line)
work: Friedlander 1987, Univ. Zurich (unpublished; seen only via Gubler & Bischof 1991)
note: Read via the chapter only. Parameters estimated up to the second sound predicted the following minutes with only two new parameters; the file gives the example of one 21-month-old and does not say the out-of-sample test was run for all 15. Validation log corrected the earlier claim that humans were not in the source. Diener 1982 reported no results.

statement: Still-face: removing contingent response lowers positive affect and gaze and raises negative affect and self-comfort within about two minutes; positive affect and gaze partly recover at reunion, negative affect does not fully recover
work: Mesman, van IJzendoorn & Bakermans-Kranenburg 2009, Developmental Review 29(2), 120-162, DOI 10.1016/j.dr.2009.02.001 (full text not read); Li et al. 2019 and others as secondary sources
size_dependence: Dyadic: infant and caregiver. File says robust on average, variable across individuals.
note: No effect size retrieved; the file will not quote one. A search summary gives more than 80 studies. The file's summary calls the still-face effect strong, while its body says the magnitude is unverified (see contradictions).

statement: Cross-cultural still-face (Li et al. 2019): 4-month-olds in the Netherlands (123) and China (63) show the classic pattern for positive affect and gaze in both countries; Chinese infants show a different negative-affect pattern with fathers; only a minority show the expected pattern across all episodes
work: Li, Woudstra, Branger, Wang, Alink & Mesman 2019, Infancy 24(6), 893-910, DOI 10.1111/infa.12313
size_dependence: Culture (Dutch vs Chinese) and caregiver (father vs mother).
note: The file does not tag this study as read; treated as sa, since the file reports it from secondary description.

statement: Sensitivity to security link: pooled r = .24 for the 21-study Strange Situation core subset (N = 1,099), out of 66 studies (N = 4,176), described as moderately strong by Cohen's criteria
work: De Wolff & van IJzendoorn 1997, Child Development 68, 571-591, DOI 10.2307/1132107
note: From the abstract via a search snippet. Modest, not strong, in the file's words.

statement: Sensitivity to security link (replication of the figure): pooled r = .25 (k = 174, N = 22,914), near-identical to De Wolff & van IJzendoorn
work: Madigan et al. 2024, Psychological Bulletin (no DOI given in the file)
note: Search snippet only; not Crossref-checked in the file.

statement: Randomised interventions raise sensitivity more than they raise security: d = 0.33 on insensitive parenting, d = 0.20 on attachment insecurity (70 studies, 88 intervention effects)
work: Bakermans-Kranenburg, van IJzendoorn & Juffer 2003, Psychological Bulletin 129, 195-215, DOI 10.1037/0033-2909.129.2.195
note: From the abstract via a search snippet. The file calls this the sensitivity transmission gap, a known unexplained residual. The file does not say whether parents consented to the interventions.

statement: Temperament weakly associated with insecurity (d = .14, CI .08-.19), modestly with resistant (d = .30), not significant for avoidant (d = .10) or disorganised (d = .11)
work: Groh et al. 2017, Child Development 88, 770-795, DOI 10.1111/cdev.12677
size_dependence: 109 samples, N = 11,440.
note: Tagged [read, Crossref abstract] in the file, so abstract only.

statement: Attachment security is moderately stable across the first 19 years of life; patterns are best accounted for by prototype dynamics (early patterns keep some influence)
work: Fraley 2002, Personality and Social Psychology Review 6, 123-151, DOI 10.1207/s15327957pspr0602_03
note: Tagged [read, Crossref abstract], so abstract only.

statement: Attachment stability: overall r = .39, a medium-sized stability across 127 papers (n = 21,072 attachments, 225 intervals from half a month to 29 years); no significant stability over intervals longer than 15 years
work: Pinquart, Feussner & Ahnert 2013, Attachment & Human Development 15(2), 189-218, DOI 10.1080/14616734.2013.746257
size_dependence: Stability higher for intervals under two years than over five; for representational rather than behavioural measures beyond infancy; for middle-class rather than at-risk samples.
note: Read from the PubMed abstract. The age-band coefficients were not seen. See contradictions on the 'very high after 6' paraphrase.

statement: Attachment classification re-assessed about 20 years on (50 of 60 infants): 72% kept the same secure/insecure class (kappa = .44); 44% (8/18) changed where mothers reported negative life events, against 22% (7/32) where none were reported
work: Waters et al. 2000, Child Development 71(3), 684-689, DOI 10.1111/1467-8624.00176
size_dependence: Negative life events reported by mothers; the file's unqualified conclusion is moderate, not high, stability.
note: Read from the PubMed abstract. File says to model security as a slowly drifting parameter, not a fixed type.

statement: Disorganised attachment: about 15% of infants in normal middle-class families; rate 'may become twice or even three times higher' in clinical or at-risk groups; stability modest (nearly 80 studies, more than 6,000 dyads)
work: van IJzendoorn, Schuengel & Bakermans-Kranenburg 1999, Development and Psychopathology 11(2), 225-250, DOI 10.1017/s0954579499002035
size_dependence: Clinical and at-risk groups versus normal middle-class families.
note: Read from the PubMed abstract. The 15% figure is confirmed from the abstract; the file's 'from memory' tag was removed.

statement: Cross-cultural Strange Situation (32 studies, nearly 2,000 classifications, 8 countries): B is the modal class everywhere and within-culture variance exceeds between-culture variance; more A in individualist and more C in collectivist samples
work: van IJzendoorn & Kroonenberg 1988, Child Development 59, 147-156, DOI 10.1111/j.1467-8624.1988.tb03202.x
size_dependence: Culture (individualist vs collectivist).
note: The conclusion is from memory; the abstract was not retrieved, so the numbers are unverified. The file treats it as a caution about cultural assumptions, not a finding with numbers. The design details come from a search summary.

statement: Attachment classification predicts later social competence, with weaker prediction for internalising problems
work: Ainsworth tradition, standard account (no specific paper given in the file)
note: Stated as a theorem in the file, with no effect size given. Treated as sa.

statement: Proximity-seeking under threat, secure-base effect on exploration, and protest on separation: among the best replicated findings in developmental psychology; the control-systems framing itself is untested
work: Bowlby 1969, Attachment and Loss vol. 1 (book, no DOI)
note: Standard account, not read. The quantitative test of the framing is Bischof's model.

statement: Contact comfort over food: infant monkeys spent most time on the cloth surrogate regardless of which gave milk; the cloth surrogate served as a base for exploring a novel object
work: Harlow 1958, American Psychologist 13(12), 673-685, DOI 10.1037/h0047884; Harlow & Zimmermann 1959, Science 130(3373), 421-432, DOI 10.1126/science.130.3373.421
note: Neither read. The file calls the contact-over-feeding result robust, with no quantitative law; 'repeated in other primates' is unsourced in the file.

statement: Goldilocks effect: 7-8-month-olds look away as a U-shaped function of surprisal (quadratic term significant in Cox regression in both experiments); the 'around 1.25 bits' peak holds for Experiment 1 only; Exp 1 n = 42 analysed (44 tested, mean age 7.9 months), Exp 2 n = 30 (mean 7.6 months)
work: Kidd, Piantadosi & Aslin 2012, PLoS ONE 7(5), e36399, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0036399
size_dependence: Model-specific: the peak is a property of the Exp 1 stimulus set and ideal-learner model, not a constant.
note: Read at article page. Effect small in Exp 1, larger in Exp 2. No independent replication found (unconfirmed). Individual-level attention, not a group outcome.

statement: Goldilocks in infant auditory attention: 7-8-month-olds selectively attend to intermediately predictable non-social auditory sequences, presented as evidence for a domain-general principle across modalities
work: Kidd, Piantadosi & Aslin 2014, Child Development 85(5), 1795-1804, DOI 10.1111/cdev.12263
note: Tagged [from PubMed abstract]. No peak value in the abstract.

statement: Social referencing: infants modulate approach to ambiguous objects using a caregiver's emotional expression; the direction is replicated many times with objects rather than cliffs
work: Klinnert et al. 1983, Emotion vol. 2, Academic Press, DOI 10.1016/b978-0-12-558702-0.50009-1
note: Stated as blunt standard account in the file. The visual-cliff version is weaker (see the Sorce figures and the contradiction on them).

statement: Visual cliff (Sorce et al. 1985, as reported by Karasik et al. 2016): 12-month-olds at a single 30 cm drop crossed in 74% of cases with a happy maternal face and in none with fear; in the fear condition 11 of 17 (65%) moved onto the brink and retreated; 40% attrition
work: Sorce, Emde, Campos & Klinnert 1985, Developmental Psychology 21(1), 195-200, DOI 10.1037/0012-1649.21.1.195 (primary not read; figures via Karasik, Tamis-LeMonda & Adolph 2016, Frontiers in Psychology 7:797, DOI 10.3389/fpsyg.2016.00797, which was read)
size_dependence: Locomotor experience and drop-off height (Karasik et al.'s own adjustable drop-off study).
note: Percentages unverified; the file does not state them as findings. The interest, anger and sadness rates (73%, 11%, 33%) could not be traced and are not stated.

statement: Toddlers, unlike apes, point to share attention rather than only to request; 18-month-olds help an adult reach an out-of-reach object without reward
work: Tomasello et al. 2005, Behavioral and Brain Sciences 28(5), 675-691, DOI 10.1017/s0140525x05000129; Warneken & Tomasello 2006, Science 311, 1301-1303, DOI 10.1126/science.1121448
note: The helping finding's later large-scale replication was not checked. The claim that apes lack the sharing motive is contested.

statement: Two homeostats coupled through a shared stimulus and a shared actuator (distance): fear and curiosity are the two signs of one error term A_a = E - a; attachment and surfeit are the two signs of A_s = D - s
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: The one-error-term reading is the authors' own wording (confirmed in validation). The coupling framing is the file's translation. Four named states from two scalars.

statement: Familiarity detector F(object) and relevancy detector R(object) are properties of the other person relative to the subject: a directed, asymmetric relation
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: The directedness is the file's translation; cross-reference to file 20. The chapter treats F and R as fixed attributes of objects.

statement: Familiarity rises with an object's redundancy, inversely to its entropy ('collativity' in Berlyne's sense), so 1 - F is an entropy-like novelty quantity
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; Berlyne 1960, Conflict, Arousal and Curiosity (not read)
note: The chapter's own statement, read in full. Berlyne 1960 is only cited, not read.

statement: Aggregation rule: several sources combine into one drive input by a potency-weighted mean of familiarity and a saturating sum of potency
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: The file says these are the only stated aggregation laws in its sources and are directly adoptable. Equations 6 and 7 are the underlying laws.

statement: Group case: every member is a Zurich agent with the other members as objects, F_i and R_i as inter-member relations
work: Gubler & Bischof 1991, A systems theory perspective, in Lamb & Keller (eds), Infant Development, Erlbaum, ISBN 0-8058-0666-0; open copy https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/2863/1/oa_2863.pdf
note: The file's suggested extension. The chapter says group interaction could be simulated but is highly complex, with no result. The file says this does not exist in its source.

statement: Joint attention as the first ternary operator: the dyad (binary relation) comes before the triad (person, person, object)
work: Trevarthen 1979, Before Speech, Cambridge UP (no DOI); Trevarthen & Hubley 1978, Action, Gesture and Symbol, Academic Press (no DOI)
note: The file's type-structure translation; the sources were not read. The file links this to group operators, which are ternary or higher.

statement: Contingency-removal operator: the still-face sets the partner's response to zero while the partner stays present, serving as the control experiment for any dyadic law
work: Tronick, Als, Adamson, Wise & Brazelton 1978, Journal of the American Academy of Child Psychiatry 17(1), 1-13, DOI 10.1016/s0002-7138(09)62273-1
note: Not read. The operator is the file's reading of the still-face paradigm.

statement: Fear-transmission operator: a signal from agent j to agent i shifts i's arousal activation A_a (or effective F, or R); no formal model has a signal channel for this
work: Klinnert et al. 1983, Emotion vol. 2, Academic Press, DOI 10.1016/b978-0-12-558702-0.50009-1
note: Stated only qualitatively; the operator must be added to the Zurich model, which severs social feedback. File links it to group contagion models in file 18.

statement: Curiosity as a U-shaped attention response to surprisal with an individual setpoint, where surprisal = -log2 P(next event | model so far); bridge candidate: measure a as surprisal rate and keep E - a as the signed drive
work: Kidd, Piantadosi & Aslin 2012, PLoS ONE 7(5), e36399, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0036399
note: Surprisal definition is read. The bridge to Bischof's E and a is the file's interpretation and is stated in no source.

statement: Attachment strategy as a coarse parameter regime of the control law (A: low D; C: high D with weak cancel; B balances), not a state of the agent
work: Ainsworth et al. 1978, Patterns of Attachment (book, no DOI); mapping to Gubler & Bischof 1991 is the file's suggestion
note: A modelling suggestion; no source states it. Bischof's acclimatization rule is the candidate reconciliation of trait and dynamic views, untested.

statement: Temptation utility v: a second linear ranking over the same options as u, representing what pulls at the moment of choice; drive is a ranking, not a magnitude of arousal
note: File: temptation is static (a ranking) and has no satiation or recovery dynamics; v identified only up to affine transformation.

statement: Commitment utility u: what the agent would choose for a later self with no temptation
note: Paired with v; u(x) = U({x}), the value of a singleton menu.

statement: Consumption capital stock S, built by past consumption c of an addictive good and depreciating at rate delta
note: Standard account from search summaries; not read.

statement: Hot mode: a cue-triggered state in which the person uses a substance regardless of his cold-mode preferences
note: Cold mode is the true-utility maximiser; the pair is a two-mode drive-like state. Not read.

statement: Desire as a function of cue: encountering a cue raises the hedonic level of the good
note: Desire depends on the cue, not directly on the stock; agent can overconsume now to condition future desire. Not read.

statement: Habit stock X_t: a weighted average of past consumption that the felt value of current consumption is measured against
note: Abel's habit may be own past consumption or others' consumption (the Joneses). Neither Pollak nor Constantinides read.

statement: Reference point as the agent's recent beliefs about outcomes; felt value of an outcome is measured against it
note: Search summaries only. Notation from a secondary restatement; the file's Unconfirmed list says so.

statement: Planner and doer: two agents inside one person, with a priced channel from the planner (long-run self) to the doer (short-run self)
note: From abstract and standard account; not read. The file treats this as an intra-person operator.

statement: Present bias: a scalar beta that rescales drives paying off immediately, against a delta-discounted future
note: Standard account; none read. Magnitude of beta is unstable across studies and domains (see empirical lines).

statement: Visceral state (arousal intensity) that reweights the objective toward immediate drives and biases forecasts of other states
work: Loewenstein 1996, OBHDP 65(3) 272-292, doi 10.1006/obhd.1996.0028; Loewenstein & O'Donoghue 2004, SSRN 539843, doi 10.2139/ssrn.539843
note: Visceral factors include hunger, thirst, sexual arousal, pain, emotion and craving. Standard account; not read.

statement: Needs with strict priority: a lower need counts only when higher needs are satisfied (Maslow's prepotency, read as lexicographic)
work: Maslow 1943, Psychological Review 50(4) 370-396, doi 10.1037/h0054346; Georgescu-Roegen 1954, QJE 68(4) 503-534, doi 10.2307/1881875
note: File: Maslow himself said satisfaction is relative and ordering not rigid; the lexicographic reading is a later gloss. Not read.

statement: Optimal arousal level: an organism has an optimum of arousal, with both too little (boredom) and too much (stress) unpleasant
work: Scitovsky 1976, The Joyless Economy, OUP (no DOI relied on)
note: Drawn from Berlyne and Hebb. Entirely from memory; no search done. Implies a drive could have an optimum rather than a zero.

statement: Status desire: the payoff of display depends on an observer's inference about the displayer's wealth
work: Bagwell & Bernheim 1996, AER 86(3) 349-373 (no Crossref DOI)
note: Abstract-level only. The file treats the observer's belief as the operand of a social drive.

statement: Willpower as a depleting resource (stock of self-control that is spent and refilled)
work: Fudenberg & Levine 2006, AER 96(5) 1449-1476, doi 10.1257/aer.96.5.1449; Hagger et al. 2016 (cited in file, no DOI given)
note: The file records that replicated willpower-as-resource support was not found, and that the dual-self cost is a modelling device. Listed here so the algebra does not adopt it by default.

statement: Representation (Theorem 1): a preference on menus satisfies Axioms 1-4 iff there exist continuous linear U, u, v with U(A) = max over x in A of [u(x)+v(x)] minus max over y in A of v(y), and U represents the preference
note: Pure representation; the file says it is a representation, not a mechanism. Cost of restraint is max v minus v(chosen).

statement: Axioms 1-4 for menu preferences: completeness and transitivity; strong continuity (upper and lower sets closed); independence (A > B and alpha in (0,1) implies alpha A + (1-alpha) C > alpha B + (1-alpha) C); set betweenness (A >= B implies A >= A u B >= B)
note: Independence is argued to hold when the agent is indifferent to when uncertainty resolves. Noor and Takeoka and Gul-Pesendorfer 2004 relax Independence (not read).

statement: Set betweenness law: A >= B implies A >= A union B >= B, so adding an option can hurt (a tempting item) and the union lies between its parts
note: A standard chooser has A ~ A union B when A >= B; GP's agent may strictly prefer A to A union B (value of commitment). A partial-order law on a union operator.

statement: Theorem 2: for the Theorem 1 representation, (i) self-control at A, (ii) the most tempting elements are not chosen, c_A(v) and c_A(u+v) disjoint, and (iii) some B strictly inside A with c_A(u+v) = c_B(u+v) and B > A are equivalent
note: Self-control at A is defined as A = B union C with B > A > C (corrected in validation to include this definition).

statement: Theorem 3: replacing Strong Continuity with Axioms 2a-c (upper semi-continuity, lower vNM continuity, lower singleton continuity) gives either the Theorem 1 form or the overwhelming-temptation form U(A) = max u(x) subject to v(x) >= v(y) for all y in A
note: Overwhelming-temptation form is the k to infinity limit of k v (lexicographic: v first, then u); the limit can fail Strong Continuity. Read, skimmed; actual form given in validation.

statement: Theorem 4: for a regular self-control preference, (u, v) is unique up to a common positive scale and separate additive constants
note: Identification of v up to affine transformation: the file lists no validated unit or scale for temptation strength.

statement: Theorems 5-7: Set Betweenness derives from an extended preference over (menu, choice) pairs; period-2 choice is max of (u+v) for self-control agents and lexicographic v-then-u otherwise
note: Read, skimmed. Theorem 5 and 7 as summarised in the file.

statement: Theorem 8: preference for commitment of agent 1 is greater than agent 2 iff u2 and v2 are each convex combinations of u1 and v1 (up to scale)
note: Corrected in validation: Theorem 8 is a comparative statement about preference for commitment, not uniqueness (that is Theorem 4).

statement: Theorem 9: agent 1 has more self-control than agent 2 iff u2+v2 and v2 are each convex combinations of u1+v1 and v1
note: Corrected in validation: statement completed. Preference for commitment and self-control are distinct; one agent can have more of both.

statement: Beta-delta utility: U_t = u_t + beta times the sum over k of delta^k u_{t+k}, with 0 < beta <= 1 and delta in (0,1]; beta = 1 gives exponential discounting
note: Phelps & Pollak originated the form for successive generations; Laibson reinterpreted it as one person's successive selves. Standard account; not checked against primary.

statement: Strotz result: unless the discount function is exponential, plans made now will not be followed later; precommitment and consistent planning are the responses
note: Pollak 1968 (consistent planning, RES 35(2) 201-208, not DOI-checked) is noted as the correction to Strotz's solution; not read.

statement: Becker-Murphy law of motion and objective: dS/dt = c - delta S, maximising the integral of e^{-rt} U(c, S, y); U_cS > 0 (adjacent complementarity)
note: Standard account; the file says exact form not confirmed from primary.

statement: Becker-Murphy dynamic propositions: strong complementarity yields more than one steady state, some unstable (a small deviation drives consumption sharply up or down); strong addictions imply cold-turkey quitting and binges; permanent price changes have larger effects than temporary ones; cross-period consumption effects are negative
note: Propositions from search summary; proofs in the paper, not read. Threshold/bifurcation result is single-agent.

statement: Cue-gated mode switch: the probability of entering hot mode is an increasing function of cue presence and past use; a cue-triggered choice is mistaken when made in hot mode and not what cold-mode preference would choose
note: Structural claim without a formula in the file; trigger operator mode = f(cue, history). Not read.

statement: Cue theory: past consumption is encoded as cues; a cue raises the hedonic level of the good; the agent solves a dynamic programme with endogenous preferences
note: Standard account; qualitative; not estimated as a structural model. Not read.

statement: Habit utility and stock: felt utility is u(c_t - h X_t) (subtractive) or u(c_t / X_t) (ratio), with X_{t+1} = (1-delta) X_t + delta c_t
note: Standard account; neither paper read. Ratio form credited to Abel 1990 in validation.

statement: Pollak habit result: with habit, the demand function is dynamic and long-run elasticities differ from short-run ones
note: Standard account; not read.

statement: Constantinides habit result: habit makes marginal utility of consumption in bad times very high, so effective risk aversion is large with modest curvature, resolving the equity premium puzzle
note: Standard account; not read.

statement: Kőszegi-Rabin reference-dependent utility: U(c | r) = m(c) + n(c | r), with m consumption utility and n gain-loss utility; gains weighted by eta and losses by eta times lambda, lambda > 1
note: From a 2026 arXiv restatement and a conference summary, both secondary. Exact notation not checked against the primary. Lottery form and personal-equilibrium existence also unconfirmed.

statement: Masatlioglu & Raymond 2016: linear choice-acclimating personal equilibrium lies in the intersection of quadratic utility and rank-dependent utility
work: Masatlioglu & Raymond 2016, AER 106(9) 2760-2782, doi 10.1257/aer.20140973
note: As cited in a search result; not read.

statement: Kreps representation: a preference over menus with monotonicity (A contains B implies A >= B) and Kreps's axiom (A ~ A union B implies A union C ~ A union B union C) gives U(A) = sum over states s of max over x in A of u(x, s), a sum over states, not a max
note: Corrected in validation: the axiom 'A >= B implies A ~ A union B' is Gul-Pesendorfer's standard-agent axiom, not Kreps's. From abstract; not read.

statement: Dekel-Lipman-Rustichini: menu preferences can be represented by a state-dependent temptation, with a distribution of v; extends the form to uncertain temptation
work: Dekel, Lipman & Rustichini 2009, RES 76(3) 937-971, doi 10.1111/j.1467-937X.2009.00560.x; Dekel, Lipman & Rustichini 2001, Econometrica 69(4) 891-934, doi 10.1111/1468-0262.00224
note: Not read. Citation details verified against Crossref; content from abstract.

statement: Fudenberg-Levine: the long-run self can take a self-control action that changes the short-run self's utility, at a cost increasing in the forgone short-run utility; the long-run problem is a dynamic programme
note: Standard account; exact functional form not checked against the paper. The base model is said to satisfy the GP axioms, which the authors argue must be relaxed for cognitive load.

statement: Loewenstein-O'Donoghue dual-system model: behaviour is a weighted mix of deliberative and affective systems, with weight shifting to the affective system when arousal is high and self-control effort is costly
work: Loewenstein & O'Donoghue 2004, SSRN 539843, doi 10.2139/ssrn.539843
note: Qualitative. Standard account; not read.

statement: Caplin-Leahy psychological expected utility: anticipatory feelings (utility from beliefs) are added to expected utility
note: Formal bridge to psychological games (file 21). From abstract/standard account; not read.

statement: Debreu 1954: the lexicographic order on R^2 is a complete, transitive preference with no real-valued representation; continuity gives sufficient conditions for one to exist
work: Debreu 1954, in Thrall, Coombs & Davis (eds), Decision Processes, Wiley 159-165; reprinted in Debreu 1983, CUP, doi 10.1017/CCOL052123736X.007
note: Credited to Debreu, not Georgescu-Roegen (corrected in validation). Standard argument stated in the file (uncountably many disjoint intervals). Citation verified; statement standard account.

statement: Lancaster: utility is defined on characteristics through a consumption technology, z = Bx, with B a matrix mapping goods to characteristics; efficient bundles lie on a characteristics frontier
note: Not read; standard account.

statement: Keeney-Raiffa decompositions: additive U(x) = sum k_i u_i(x_i) holds iff attributes are mutually preferentially independent (ordinal) and additively independent (lotteries), with sum k_i = 1; multiplicative 1 + kU = product of (1 + k k_i u_i) under utility independence
work: Keeney & Raiffa 1976, Decisions with Multiple Objectives, Wiley (reissued CUP 1993); no DOI relied on
note: Validation: additive and multiplicative forms match the standard statement; from memory per the file's Unconfirmed list. The independence conditions are testable.

statement: Pareto frontier: a weighted-sum scalarisation finds only points on the convex part of the frontier; non-convex frontier points cannot be found by any weighting
work: Pareto 1896-97, 1906 (standard account, no DOI)
note: Standard multi-objective result, as the file states it; not checked.

statement: Harris-Laibson: the sophisticated hyperbolic consumption function has discontinuities and non-monotonicity
work: Harris & Laibson 2001, Econometrica 69(4) 935-957, doi 10.1111/1468-0262.00225
note: Moved here from Laibson 1997 in validation. Not read.

statement: O'Donoghue-Rabin 1999: for immediate costs, naive agents procrastinate more than sophisticated ones and can delay indefinitely; for immediate rewards, sophisticated agents may act too soon (preproperation)
note: Propositions about timing of completing a task with a deadline, from the standard account. Partial naivete is O'Donoghue-Rabin 2001, not 1999.

statement: Commitment demand: people pay for commitment, take smaller menus and buy restricted-access devices (support in field and lab commitment studies); demand for commitment is smaller than the model predicts for naive agents
work: Ashraf, Karlan & Yin 2006 (savings commitment, Philippines; cited, not re-checked)
size_dependence: Individual-level; no group-size dependence stated.
note: Standard account; Ashraf-Karlan-Yin not verified in validation. The representation is compatible with rival stories, so menu choice does not discriminate between them.

statement: Present bias: solid lab support in money-now-versus-later choices; the magnitude of beta is unstable across studies and across domains (money, real effort, food); estimated discount rates vary widely
work: Frederick, Loewenstein & O'Donoghue 2002 (review, standard account, not read)
note: Individual-level behavioural evidence; no target scale. Blunt verdict in file: present bias exists as a pattern; beta-delta is a convenient approximation.

statement: Field evidence of naivete (gym membership, DellaVigna & Malmendier 2006): exists but contested
work: DellaVigna & Malmendier 2006 (standard account, not verified)
note: Not verified in the file's validation. Individual-level.

statement: Much money-time-preference evidence is confounded by risk and convex utility
work: Andreoni & Sprenger 2012 (standard account, not verified)
note: Left in Unconfirmed list by validation. Individual-level.

statement: Cigarette consumption responds to announced future prices (Becker, Grossman & Murphy 1994), taken as support for forward-looking consumption
