work: Becker, Grossman & Murphy 1994 (standard account); Gruber & Kőszegi 2001, QJE 116(4) 1261-1303, doi 10.1162/003355301753265570
size_dependence: Population-level aggregate consumption; not one of the three target outcomes.
note: Scale set to n/a because aggregate consumption is not among the target outcomes (membership, group, crowd); a judgement. Validation: Gruber-Kőszegi's conclusion restated as data equally consistent with time inconsistency.

statement: Becker-Murphy model is nearly unfalsifiable: any consumption path can be rationalised by suitable preferences; forward-looking behaviour shows the future enters, not that addicts plan optimally
work: Critics as summarised in file (no specific source named)
note: Critical assessment as stated in the file; no source named, so provenance sa.

statement: Many addicts report regret and wanting-without-liking, which the rational-addiction model has no place for
work: Berridge (cited in file 22, not in this file)
note: Reference to file 22 for the wanting/liking work; not read here.

statement: Cue-triggered relapse and craving: qualitatively consistent with the Bernheim-Rangel model; not tested as a structural model
work: Robinson & Berridge incentive-sensitisation work (file 22)
note: Qualitative only. The file calls the model more plausible than rational addiction and less quantified.

statement: Exposure and advertising effects: Laibson's cue theory qualitatively supports advertising, display and exposure effects on consumption; not estimated as a structural model
note: Ethics flag is a judgement: the finding concerns exposure and advertising effects that steer consumption without the person's consent. Qualitative only.

statement: Habit formation: a well-used ingredient in macro (consumption smoothness, hump-shaped responses) and asset pricing; identification against other sources of persistence is hard
work: Campbell & Cochrane 1999 (standard account, not verified); macro and asset-pricing literature (not named)
note: File: well used, not unique; often a convenience parameter.

statement: Reference dependence: endowment effect exists, but Heffetz & List 2014 and Plott & Zeiler 2005 argue it partly depends on procedure; loss-aversion magnitude varies and Gal & Rucker 2018 argue loss aversion is overstated
work: Heffetz & List 2014; Plott & Zeiler 2005; Gal & Rucker 2018 (all standard account, not verified)
note: Individual-level evidence. File: reference dependence is real; the expectations-based form is plausible but not settled.

statement: Loss aversion lambda about 2 is a headline figure with a very wide range of estimates
work: Standard account (no single source named); see Gal & Rucker 2018 in file
note: Individual-level.

statement: Expectations as reference point: evidence from taxi labour supply and marathon finish-time bunching (Allen et al. 2017); Camerer et al. 1997 cabdriver result has been challenged by later data
work: Allen et al. 2017; Camerer et al. 1997 (standard account, not verified)
note: Individual-level: taxi drivers and marathon runners. Conflicting evidence recorded; see the contradiction line for this pair.

statement: Maslow's strict ordering is not supported: a review found little evidence for the hierarchy; needs are broadly universal across 123 countries but fulfilment of different needs is largely independent of order
work: Wahba & Bridwell 1976 (review); Tay & Diener 2011, Gallup World Poll, 123 countries (standard account, not verified)
note: Scale set to crowd (society-level, across countries); a judgement. Blunt file verdict: strict hierarchy false; soft priority defensible.

statement: Lexicographic choice appears in experiments on sacred or protected values (Tetlock) and in a minority of subjects; strict lexicographic behaviour is rare for ordinary goods
work: Tetlock (cited, no source given in file)
note: Individual-level minority of subjects. Not verified.

statement: Empathy gap: hungry people choose unhealthy snacks for later (Read & Van Leeuwen 1998); people underpredict the effect of thirst after exercise (Van Boven & Loewenstein 2003); the hot-cold effect is one of the more robust findings in this cluster
work: Read & Van Leeuwen 1998; Van Boven & Loewenstein 2003; Ariely & Loewenstein 2006 (sexual arousal, lab) (all standard account, not verified)
note: Effect sizes vary (file). Lab studies with limits on generalisation.

statement: Depleting willpower resource: replication failure of ego depletion in a multi-lab study (Hagger et al. 2016), warning against assuming a depleting resource
source: 36 §11 Empirical standing; Validation log not separately
work: Hagger et al. 2016 (standard account, not verified)
note: Individual-level lab finding; not verified in validation.

statement: Conspicuous consumption: minority groups spend more on visible goods (Charles, Hurst & Roussanov 2009); the Bagwell-Bernheim luxury-brand predictions are hard to test and not quantitatively validated
work: Charles, Hurst & Roussanov 2009 (standard account, not verified); Bagwell & Bernheim 1996, AER 86(3) 349-373
note: File: a good existence result for status goods, thin on quantitative validation.

statement: Fudenberg-Levine 2006 rationalises known anomalies (mental accounts, small-stakes risk aversion, hyperbolic-looking discounting) and fits cognitive-load evidence; it is not a decisive test against quasi-hyperbolic discounting
note: Abstract claims, corrected in validation (Allais belongs to Fudenberg-Levine 2011). File: wide fit, weak discrimination.

statement: Berlyne inverted-U between arousal or novelty and liking has mixed support
work: Berlyne (see file 16/17; Wundt curve)
note: Individual-level. Not checked in this file.

statement: Independence assumptions of additive and multiplicative utility are often violated for emotional attributes; weights for competing drives are not stable across states
work: Standard decision-analysis practice (no specific source named)
note: The file says independence can be tested, so the choice of law is empirical.

statement: Smoking spreads through social networks (Christakis & Fowler), contested on identification
work: Christakis & Fowler (standard account, no DOI)
size_dependence: Network-based; no size dependence stated.
note: Scale set to group (network); a judgement. Listed in the file as applied peer-effects work, not an axiomatic result.

statement: Kreps monotonicity versus Gul-Pesendorfer set betweenness: Kreps's agent values extra options (flexibility), GP's can be hurt by them
note: Both sides: Kreps's monotonicity (A contains B implies A >= B) is violated by GP's set betweenness (A >= A union B may fail). Verdict: unresolved as a choice of axiom; a difference of models, not a fault in either. Kreps side from abstract, GP side read.

statement: Rational addiction versus cue-triggered mistaken choice: Becker-Murphy has no place for relapse after long abstention or for mistaken choice; Bernheim-Rangel explains both
note: Both sides from abstract and standard account. Verdict: unresolved in the file; Bernheim-Rangel more plausible, less quantified.

statement: Forward-looking addiction consumption: Becker-Grossman-Murphy read the response to announced prices as support for rational addiction, while Gruber & Kőszegi 2001 find the same data equally consistent with time-inconsistent (hyperbolic) preferences
work: Becker, Grossman & Murphy 1994 (standard account); Gruber & Kőszegi 2001, QJE 116(4) 1261-1303, doi 10.1162/003355301753265570
note: Verdict as restated in validation: the data are equally consistent with both; the welfare and tax implications differ. Unresolved.

statement: Fudenberg-Levine base model is consistent with the Gul-Pesendorfer axioms, yet the authors argue those axioms must be relaxed to accommodate cognitive load
note: Internal tension as the file records it; the Fudenberg-Levine side is from abstract, GP side read. Unresolved.

statement: Strict Maslow hierarchy (lexicographic needs) versus evidence that fulfilment is independent of order (Tay & Diener 2011)
work: Maslow 1943, Psychological Review 50(4) 370-396, doi 10.1037/h0054346; Tay & Diener 2011 (standard account, not verified)
note: Verdict as stated in file: strict hierarchy is false; soft priority, with weights falling as satisfaction rises, is defensible. Maslow's own text was non-rigid, so the strict reading is a gloss.

statement: Present bias as a pattern versus the beta-delta magnitude: present bias has solid lab support, but money-based evidence is confounded by risk and convex utility, and beta is unstable across domains
work: Frederick, Loewenstein & O'Donoghue 2002; Andreoni & Sprenger 2012 (standard account, not verified)
note: Verdict as stated in file: the pattern exists; the beta-delta form is a convenient approximation. Unresolved.

statement: Loss aversion: headline lambda about 2 versus the claim that loss aversion is overstated (Gal & Rucker 2018), with endowment-effect results procedure-dependent (Heffetz & List 2014; Plott & Zeiler 2005)
work: Gal & Rucker 2018; Heffetz & List 2014; Plott & Zeiler 2005 (standard account, not verified)
note: Unresolved. Reference dependence itself is real per the file; the magnitude is not settled.

statement: Expectations as reference point: taxi and marathon evidence (Allen et al. 2017) supports it, but Camerer et al. 1997 cabdriver result has been challenged by later data
work: Allen et al. 2017; Camerer et al. 1997 (standard account, not verified)
note: Unresolved in the file; the expectations-based form is plausible but not settled.

statement: Closing claim 'no social or multi-person theorems' in the file's own 'What exists versus what does not' section versus the file's section 9 (Bagwell-Bernheim) and Battaglini-Bénabou-Tirole 2005
source: 36 §What exists versus what does not; Validation log
work: Bagwell & Bernheim 1996, AER 86(3) 349-373; Battaglini, Bénabou & Tirole 2005, JET 123(2) 105-134, doi 10.1016/j.jet.2005.04.001
note: Corrected in validation: the claim was false as stated and is narrowed to 'no axiomatic multi-person theory of temptation'. Status stays open per the schema; the corrected form is the one the file supports. Battaglini et al. not read (sa); Gul-Pesendorfer side read.

statement: Menu: a set of lotteries chosen in period 1, from which one element is chosen in period 2; preferences are over menus
note: The file: a menu is a natural algebraic object; A union B is an operator on menus.

statement: Temptation ranking v, defined from U on two-element sets with U({a}) > U({a,b}) > U({b}) via mixtures; the v so defined is linear and independent of the choice of a and b (Lemma 4)
note: Identified from menu preferences alone.

statement: Self-control at A: A = B union C with B > A > C (the agent prefers a smaller menu to A and A to the tempting option)
note: Added in validation. Commitment is planning-period behaviour; self-control is consumption-period behaviour.

statement: Cost of self-control: max v minus v(chosen), which is zero when the agent picks the v-maximiser; temptation magnitude is the gap in v
note: Derived by the file from the read Theorem 1 representation; the behavioural signature of this model.

statement: Standard decision-maker: a chooser cares only about the best element of a menu, so A >= B implies A ~ A union B
note: Corrected in validation: this axiom is GP's, not Kreps's. Set betweenness weakens it.

statement: Preference for flexibility (Kreps): valuing a larger menu, so that A contains B implies A >= B
note: From abstract; not read.

statement: Quasi-hyperbolic (beta-delta) discounting and the three agent types: naive (believes future selves act on current preferences), sophisticated (predicts true future behaviour), partially naive (believed beta between true beta and 1)
note: Partial naivete is from O'Donoghue & Rabin 2001 (corrected in validation). Sophisticated versus naive is a forecast operator on the other self.

statement: Habit stock as a leaky integrator: X_{t+1} = (1-delta) X_t + delta c_t, where X is a weighted average of past consumption
note: Standard account. Felt value is consumption minus or divided by the stock, a reusable operator.

statement: Personal equilibrium (PE), preferred personal equilibrium (PPE) and choice-acclimating personal equilibrium (CPE): consistent plans given beliefs about outcomes, with the reference point given by those beliefs
note: From a secondary restatement. The file's note: the attachment effect is that expecting to own something raises the pain of not getting it.

statement: Gain-loss utility n(c | r) with loss aversion lambda > 1, so losses weigh eta times lambda and gains weigh eta
note: Notation not checked against the primary. Disappointment is a signed, asymmetrically weighted difference between received outcome and expectation.

statement: Hot mode and cold mode: the cold mode maximises true utility; the hot mode is triggered by a cue and uses the substance regardless of preferences; choice is mistaken when made in hot mode and not what cold-mode preference would choose
note: Standard account; not read.

statement: Adjacent complementarity: past consumption raises the marginal utility of current consumption, U_cS > 0
note: Standard account; the file's own definition of addiction in the model. Not read.

statement: Single-crossing property: in a signalling game, its failure is what permits Veblen effects, defined as a premium paid for a functionally equivalent good
work: Bagwell & Bernheim 1996, AER 86(3) 349-373 (no Crossref DOI)
note: Veblen effect redefined as the authors define it in validation (not upward-sloping demand). Abstract-level only.

statement: Hot-cold empathy gap: a person in a hot state underpredicts the effect of cold states, and a cold state underpredicts the effect of hot states
note: A prediction-error operator between persons in the file's translation. Standard account; not read.

statement: Comfort versus pleasure: comfort relieves a discomfort (drive reduction); pleasure is a rise in arousal toward novelty and stimulation; pleasure is transient and needs change
work: Scitovsky 1976, The Joyless Economy, OUP (no DOI relied on)
note: From memory; the file says it is similar to but not identical with wanting versus liking (file 22).

statement: Anticipatory feelings: utility derived from beliefs about future outcomes, added to expected utility
note: From abstract/standard account; not read. Formal bridge to psychological games (file 21).

statement: Lexicographic ordering: x is preferred to y iff at the first coordinate, in priority order, where they differ, x is greater
note: Credited in the file to Georgescu-Roegen for the argument; non-representability credited to Debreu 1954. Not read.

statement: Characteristics: goods are not valued directly; they provide characteristics z = Bx through a consumption technology matrix B
note: Not read; standard account.

statement: Additive and multiplicative (utility) independence: the Keeney-Raiffa decomposition conditions on attributes; each form holds under stated independence conditions
work: Keeney & Raiffa 1976, Decisions with Multiple Objectives, Wiley (reissued CUP 1993); no DOI relied on
note: From memory; validation: forms match the standard statement.

statement: Pareto frontier: the set of non-dominated points where drives conflict without a common scale; each weight vector picks one point on a supporting hyperplane
work: Pareto 1896-97, 1906 (standard account, no DOI)
note: Standard account; the file uses it for how drives combine when they lack a common scale.

statement: Hull-style drive D as a stored deficit (operand: a drive as a state with a storage function)
work: Hull (no citation in file 40; file 16 is the source it points to)
note: Named as an operand, not tagged [read] in file 40. Standing taken from file 16, not checked here.

statement: Keramati-Gutkin drive function: distance of internal state from a setpoint, with reward as drive reduction
work: Keramati-Gutkin, as reported in file 16 (no DOI in file 40)
note: File 40 reports file 16; the claim is not tagged [read] in file 40.

statement: Homeostatic distance as the storage function (common Lyapunov function candidate) for drive modes
work: none (proposal in file 40)
note: File 40 says 'plausibly'. A proposal, not a finding.

statement: Threshold switching drives: Hull's reaction threshold sLr, Lorenz-Tinbergen release thresholds, Atkinson-Birch switching
work: file 16 (Hull; Lorenz-Tinbergen; Atkinson-Birch; no DOIs in file 40)
size_dependence: Dwell-time and threshold parameters are unobservable for individuals (file 40 §7 Costs).
note: Named as switching rules, not tagged [read] in file 40.

statement: Mode as the drive currently governing action, together with the continuous states of all drives; threshold crossing triggers a jump x+ = g(x)
work: none (file 40 translation of the hybrid framework)
note: Translation, not a finding.

statement: Curiosity and fear as competing objectives whose Pareto front expresses internal conflict; personality as the weights
work: none (file 40 translation)
note: File 40 says the weights carry all the content, so the model is circular unless weights are measured.

statement: A drive as a selection function or as the utility R in an open game: fear reshapes R, curiosity adds a term
work: Ghani et al. 2018 DOI 10.1145/3209108.3209165 (for the open-game structure)
note: Translation, not a finding. File 40 notes this presupposes argmax choice, which the drive literature aims to replace.

statement: Social preference as coutility: what one person's act costs or gives the other
work: file 21 (not read here)
note: Translation pointing to file 21.

statement: Hunger, then curiosity, then affiliation as a stable cyclic sequence with no global winner (rotation among drives)
work: Rabinovich et al. 2001 DOI 10.1103/physrevlett.87.068102 (model structure)
note: Example pattern offered as a target for the model. No empirical test on drives (see empirical line on winnerless competition).

statement: Input-state-output port-Hamiltonian system: x-dot = [J(x) - R(x)] grad H(x) + G(x) u, y = G(x)^T grad H(x), with J = -J^T and R = R^T >= 0; energy balance dH/dt = -(grad H)^T R grad H + y^T u <= y^T u
work: van der Schaft & Jeltsema 2014, DOI 10.1561/2600000002
note: Tagged [standard account]. Not re-checked in validation.

statement: Interconnection of port-Hamiltonian systems through ports by a power-conserving Dirac structure yields a port-Hamiltonian system with Hamiltonian the sum of the components' Hamiltonians, so the composite is passive with storage sum H_i
work: Cervera, van der Schaft, Bano s 2007 DOI 10.1016/j.automatica.2006.08.014 (credit, not read)
note: Tagged [standard account]. File 40 credits Cervera et al., whose paper it did not read. Its Costs note: the links are power-conserving, which is not true of persuasion or contagion between people.

statement: Dissipation inequality: V(x(t1)) - V(x(t0)) <= integral of s(u(t), y(t)) dt along all trajectories; passive: s = u^T y; finite L2-gain: s = gamma^2 |u|^2 - |y|^2
note: Tagged [standard account]. Passivity is a dissipation inequality, not a conservation law (validation correction, see contradictions).

statement: Passivity index: a system with output-feedback passivity index rho < 0 satisfies V-dot <= u^T y - rho |y|^2 and can still be interconnected stably if a neighbour has a matching excess
work: Willems 1972 DOI 10.1007/bf00276493 (standard account; file 40 names no separate source for the index)
size_dependence: Depends on the neighbour's excess matching the shortage (a pairwise condition).
note: Tagged [standard account].

statement: Interconnected dissipative systems: if s1 + s2 <= 0 under the interconnection constraint, then V1 + V2 is non-increasing along the closed loop, and the equilibrium is Lyapunov stable provided V1 + V2 is positive definite
work: Moylan & Hill 1978 DOI 10.1109/tac.1978.1101721 (N-subsystem version)
size_dependence: Moylan & Hill give the N-subsystem version, with a matrix condition on quadratic supply rates.
note: Tagged [standard account]. Global and asymptotic versions need radial unboundedness and detectability, per file 40.

statement: Negative feedback interconnection of passive systems is passive (from new external inputs to outputs); parallel interconnection of passive systems is passive
work: Willems 1972 DOI 10.1007/bf00276493 (standard account; no separate source in file 40)
note: Tagged [standard account].

statement: Small-gain: a feedback loop of finite-gain stable systems with gamma1 * gamma2 < 1 is finite-gain stable
note: Tagged [standard account]. A sufficient condition only (see contradictions).

statement: N-agent ISS small-gain: the gain matrix Gamma must satisfy a 'no cycle amplifies' condition, Gamma(s) not >= s
work: Dashkovskiy, Rueffer, Wirth 2007 DOI 10.1007/s00498-007-0014-8
size_dependence: Applies to general networks of N agents, not just two systems (the two-system theorem in §5 does not cover a group).
note: Added in validation as missing work. Not read. File 40 calls it 'the group-level version this strand would actually use'.

statement: ISS: |x(t)| <= beta(|x0|, t) + gamma(||u||_inf), with beta class-KL and gamma class-K; a cascade of ISS systems is ISS; feedback of ISS systems with gains gamma1, gamma2 is ISS if gamma1(gamma2(s)) < s for all s > 0
work: Sontag 1989 DOI 10.1109/9.28018; Jiang, Teel, Praly 1994 DOI 10.1007/bf01211469
size_dependence: Cascade property applies to hierarchies (leader to followers).
note: Tagged [standard account]. Validation wrote the Jiang-Teel-Praly condition precisely. Also Jiang, Mareels, Wang 1996 DOI 10.1016/0005-1098(96)00051-9 (credit, not read).

statement: Contraction: if a metric transform Theta(x,t) makes the symmetric part of (Theta-dot + Theta J) Theta^-1 uniformly negative definite (<= -lambda < 0), with J = df/dx, then all trajectories converge exponentially to one another at rate lambda, so the system forgets its initial condition
note: Tagged [standard account]. Entrainment: a contracting system driven by a periodic input converges to a periodic orbit of the same period (listed as a theorem in file 40 without a separate source).

statement: Parallel, hierarchical (series) and feedback combinations of contracting systems are contracting under stated conditions; feedback needs a bound on the coupling relative to the contraction rates; skew-symmetric coupling is unconditional
work: Lohmiller & Slotine 1998 §3; Slotine 2003 DOI 10.1002/acs.754 (delayed/modular, not read); Russo, di Bernardo, Sontag 2013 DOI 10.1109/tac.2012.2223355 (networks, not read)
size_dependence: Russo et al. give network conditions for contracting nodes with hierarchical interconnection.
note: Tagged [standard account]. Slotine 2003 and Russo et al. 2013 are listed as not read in file 40's Unconfirmed section.

statement: A switched system can be unstable even when every mode is stable
work: Liberzon & Morse 1999 DOI 10.1109/37.793443
note: Tagged [standard account].

statement: Sufficient conditions for switched-system stability: a common Lyapunov function (arbitrary switching); dwell time, or average dwell time (slow enough switching); multiple Lyapunov functions: each mode's Lyapunov function decreases while that mode is active and its values at successive switch-on instants form a non-increasing sequence
source: 40 §7 Theorems (validation correction to the Branicky condition)
work: Branicky 1998 DOI 10.1109/9.664150; Hespanha & Morse 1999 DOI 10.1109/cdc.1999.831330 (average dwell time); Morse 1996 (dwell time, DOI not checked)
note: Tagged [standard account]. Corrected form: the earlier 'must not increase at switching instants' was imprecise (validation).

statement: Lie-algebraic condition: if all linear modes are Hurwitz and the Lie algebra generated by the mode matrices is solvable, the switched system has a common quadratic Lyapunov function and is stable under arbitrary switching (commuting matrices are the simplest case)
work: Liberzon, Hespanha, Morse 1999 DOI 10.1016/s0167-6911(99)00012-2
note: Corrected from 'commuting-ish' to the solvable-Lie-algebra condition in validation.

statement: For strongly monotone (strongly cooperative, irreducible Jacobian) systems, almost every bounded trajectory converges to the set of equilibria, and there are no stable non-constant periodic orbits; competitive systems in dimension >= 3 can have stable limit cycles
work: Hirsch 1985 DOI 10.1137/0516030; Smith 1995 DOI 10.1090/surv/041/03; Hirsch 1988 (standard account, not DOI-checked)
size_dependence: Convergence to a single equilibrium needs extra hypotheses (Smith 1995).
note: Tagged [standard account]. Validation corrected generic convergence to require strong monotonicity.

statement: Monotone negative feedback: a negative feedback loop of monotone input-output systems converges globally if an associated one-dimensional discrete map has a globally attracting fixed point; for positive feedback, equilibria and stability are read off the intersection of the characteristic curve with the diagonal, giving multistability
work: Angeli & Sontag 2003 DOI 10.1109/tac.2003.817920; Angeli & Sontag 2004 DOI 10.1016/j.sysconle.2003.08.003; Angeli, Ferrell, Sontag 2004 DOI 10.1073/pnas.0308265100
note: Tagged [standard account]. Positive-feedback multistability is credited to the 2004 papers (validation).

statement: Winnerless competition: x_i-dot = x_i (sigma_i - sum_j rho_ij x_j); with asymmetric inhibition a stable heteroclinic channel visits saddle points in sequence, each competitor winning in turn, with no final winner
work: Rabinovich et al. 2001 DOI 10.1103/physrevlett.87.068102; May & Leonard 1975 DOI 10.1137/0129022 (credit for heteroclinic cycling)
note: Tagged [standard account]. Lotka-Volterra is a neural-population idealisation (file 40).

statement: Max-plus linear system x(k+1) = A (x) x(k), with x_i(k+1) = max_j (A_ij + x_j(k)); the growth rate is the eigenvalue lambda(A), the maximum cycle mean; after a transient x(k+c) = x(k) + c*lambda, with c the cyclicity of the critical graph; composition A (x) B = max_k (A_ik + B_kj)
work: Cuninghame-Green 1962 DOI 10.1057/jors.1962.10; Cohen, Dubois, Quadrat, Viot 1985 DOI 10.1109/tac.1985.1103925; Heidergott, Olsder, van der Woude 2005 DOI 10.1515/9781400865239
note: Tagged [standard account]. Corrected form: periodic up to linear growth; literally periodic only if lambda = 0.

statement: Maslov dequantisation: tau log sum_i exp(x_i / tau) tends to max_i x_i as tau tends to 0, so max-plus is the zero-temperature limit of log-sum-exp soft-argmax selection
work: none (file 40: 'standard, not checked against a source')
note: Explicitly unchecked in validation.

statement: Weighted-sum scalarisation with positive weights yields Pareto-optimal points but reaches only the convex hull of the front; epsilon-constraint and goal programming recover non-convex parts
note: Tagged [standard account].

statement: Gradient dynamics x-dot = -grad V with V = sum V_i: V is non-increasing; there are no non-constant periodic orbits; bounded trajectories have omega-limit sets of critical points; convergence to a single point needs more (e.g. analytic V via Lojasiewicz)
work: none given in file 40 (standard account)
size_dependence: Reciprocal coupling keeps the field gradient; asymmetric influence breaks it and can produce cycles.
note: Tagged [standard account].

statement: Multiple-gradient descent converges to Pareto-stationary points, which need not be Pareto-optimal without convexity
note: Added in validation.

statement: Passive agents coupled by symmetric (bidirectional) information flow on a graph coordinate their output differences to a prescribed set, and the passivity of the individual components guarantees network stability
size_dependence: Robust to time-varying topology. One-way influence (leader, broadcaster) breaks the symmetric structure; small-gain tools are then needed.
note: Built from a seminar abstract of the same work, not the published abstract. Exact assumptions are standard account.

statement: Willems behavioural interconnection: connecting systems through shared variables gives the intersection of their behaviours on those variables; hidden variables are eliminated by projection; an empty composite means incompatible laws
note: Tagged [standard account]. Largely linear time-invariant theory.

statement: Vagner, Spivak, Lerman: the continuous-time systems G (general ODE systems) and L (linear systems) are algebras over the operad of wiring diagrams O_W, so interconnection is associative and unital at the ODE level; a well-definedness theorem that predicts no behaviour
work: Vagner, Spivak, Lerman 2015 DOI 10.70930/tac/7tz1nkbd (arXiv:1408.1598)
note: [read] abstract and introduction. Scope is continuous time only. 'Associative and unital' and 'predicts no behaviour' are file 40's gloss.

statement: Euclidean differential systems theory: tangent T f(p, v) = Df_p . v, so a system is a differential equation s-dot = f(s, i) with readout y = r(s)
work: Myers, Categorical Systems Theory, draft 3 Sept 2023 (davidjaz.com/Papers/DynamicalBook.pdf); no DOI
note: [read] Def. 3.5.2.1 in the 2023 draft. Draft is not peer reviewed; the theorem numbering was not re-checked in validation.

statement: Myers compositionality theorem: behaviours (trajectories, fixed points, periodic orbits) of a composite can be computed from behaviours of the parts and the wiring pattern; nesting wiring patterns commutes with finding behaviours; composing behaviours with charts is associative; formally a representable lax doubly indexed functor (Thm 5.3.2.1 in the draft)
work: Myers, draft 3 Sept 2023 (Ch. 5); Myers 2021 EPTCS 333 DOI 10.4204/EPTCS.333.11
size_dependence: Whether the comparison maps are isomorphisms, so that every behaviour of the group arises from compatible behaviours of members, is not settled by 'lax' and was not checked.
note: [read] preface informal statement. Theorem number not re-checked (PDF unreachable in validation). Read the draft before relying on an equality.

statement: Trajectories, steady states and periodic orbits of coupled dynamical systems compose according to the laws of matrix arithmetic
work: Myers 2021 DOI 10.4204/EPTCS.333.11 (arXiv:2005.05956); Spivak 2015 arXiv:1512.00802 (steady-state case, first shown)
note: [from abstract]. Spivak's steady-state result cited from title only. Peer-reviewed anchor added in validation.

statement: Open-game compositionality: a profile of a composite is an equilibrium in a context iff each component's profile is a best response in the context induced for it by the other components; for sequential composition the second game's context depends on the first game's play
work: Ghani, Hedges, Winschel, Zahn 2018 DOI 10.1145/3209108.3209165
note: Untagged in file 40, so sa under the rule that read needs a [read] tag. File says 'I read the claim, not the proofs'. Validation restated compositionality as best-response-in-context.

statement: Open games form a symmetric monoidal category (up to the paper's equivalence), so sequential and parallel composition are associative and unital
work: Ghani, Hedges, Winschel, Zahn 2018 DOI 10.1145/3209108.3209165
note: Untagged in file 40.

statement: Standard games (normal form, extensive form with perfect information) embed faithfully in open games: same Nash equilibria and off-equilibrium best responses
work: Ghani, Hedges, Winschel, Zahn 2018 DOI 10.1145/3209108.3209165
note: Tagged abstract [read] in file 40.

statement: Libkind et al.: Euler's method is functorial for undirected systems, so a discrete-time simulation of the composed system equals the composition of the discrete-time simulations of the parts
work: Libkind, Baas, Patterson, Fairbanks 2022 DOI 10.4204/eptcs.372.14 (arXiv:2105.12282)
note: [read] abstract for functoriality of Euler. The 'simulation equals composition' gloss is file 40's reading. Extends an earlier result for directed systems.

statement: Winner-take-all modules coupled through shared inhibition: contraction theory gives parameter ranges where each module is stable in a high-gain regime and where modules can be aggregated arbitrarily to form large stable networks; also multistable parameter ranges retaining persistent activity
work: Rutishauser, Douglas, Slotine 2011 DOI 10.1162/neco_a_00091 (arXiv:1105.3106)
size_dependence: Modules can be aggregated arbitrarily into large stable networks (per the abstract).
note: Neural-circuit model, not behavioural. Abstract only; no out-of-sample test recorded. Scale n/a because it is neural, not one of the three target scales.

statement: Contraction applied to opinion dynamics: Ofir, Ovseevich, Margaliot (k-contraction in Lurie systems, with a nonlinear opinion-model example) and Wankhede et al. (contraction for utility-maximising opinion agents)
source: 40 Validation log correction to Summary; §6 Translation
work: Ofir, Ovseevich, Margaliot 2024 DOI 10.1016/j.automatica.2023.111341; Wankhede, Mandal, Martinez, Tallapragada 2024 arXiv:2404.04912
size_dependence: Multiple equilibria handled by k-contraction (local per basin).
note: Application of the theorem to a model; file 40 records no out-of-sample test. Ofir et al. was not read in validation (Crossref-confirmed only).

statement: Arcak 2007 passivity coordination is a theory result with no empirical test; the engineering and control uses are not applied to people
size_dependence: Symmetric graph required; time-varying topology tolerated.
note: File 40 gives no explicit empirical standing for Arcak; this line records that no test is named.

statement: Game-theoretic equilibrium predictions of human behaviour are weak at the individual level; open games inherit this and add none

work: none cited in file 40 (files 21 and 12 not read here)
note: Untagged claim relayed from files 21 and 12. Not verified here.

work: Libkind et al. 2022 Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 380(2233) DOI 10.1098/rsta.2021.0309

work: van der Schaft & Jeltsema 2014 DOI 10.1561/2600000002
note: Negative search result. The form of the claim is falsifiable only if drive energy has a measurable meaning.

statement: Contraction theory: engineering and neural-circuit models only; no empirical test on human drives
note: Empirical standing as file 40 states it.

note: Negative standing as file 40 states it.

statement: Max-plus algebra: not found applied to motivation (search result, validation included)
work: none (search result)
note: Negative search result.

statement: Open-game compositionality: 'equilibria of larger games should be defined from the equilibria of the component games' (central claim) versus 'equilibria of the whole from equilibria of the parts holds only in this contextual sense'; a component's equilibria computed against a fixed, unrelated context do not suffice. Verdict: the validation corrected the claim to best-response-in-context.
work: Ghani, Hedges, Winschel, Zahn 2018 DOI 10.1145/3209108.3209165
note: Verdict: corrected (validation, 2026-10-29). Both sides from file 40. Corrected form: a profile is an equilibrium in context iff each component's profile is a best response in its induced context.

statement: Loop-gain reading: the original 'gain product > 1: no stability certificate exists, and spirals are expected' versus the corrected reading that the small-gain condition is sufficient, so a product > 1 means only that the certificate fails; divergence follows only in special cases such as linear positive feedback with loop gain above 1 at zero frequency
note: Verdict: corrected (validation). The original overstated a sufficient condition as necessary. The de-escalation statement is a form of theorem, not a measured fact.

statement: Max-plus inhibition: the original 'no subtraction, so inhibition and dissipation are not expressible' versus the corrected form that negative weights and decay (lambda < 0) are expressible; what is missing is inhibition in the sense of non-monotone dependence, since every max-plus linear map is order-preserving and additively homogeneous
note: Verdict: corrected (validation). Min-max-plus keeps monotonicity and loses the clean eigenvalue theorem in general.

statement: Passivity and conservation: the original framing that passivity assumes conserved energy versus the corrected form that passivity is a dissipation inequality with a storage function V >= 0; conservation is a property of port-Hamiltonian links only
work: Willems 1972 DOI 10.1007/bf00276493; van der Schaft & Jeltsema 2014 DOI 10.1561/2600000002
note: Verdict: corrected (validation); §4b is the settled form. §3 still says power-conserving links, which is the port-Hamiltonian case.

statement: Contraction and attractors: 'contraction allows only one attractor' versus the precision that contraction is a property of a region, so a system can be contracting on each of several disjoint invariant regions, one per attractor; this is true only for global contraction
note: Verdict: corrected (validation). Local contraction is compatible with multistability, but says nothing about basin boundaries.

statement: Max-plus periodicity: 'the system becomes periodic' versus 'periodic up to linear growth': x(k+c) = x(k) + c*lambda, so the state is literally periodic only if lambda = 0
work: Cohen, Dubois, Quadrat, Viot 1985 DOI 10.1109/tac.1985.1103925
note: Verdict: corrected (validation).

statement: Hirsch generic convergence: convergence of almost every bounded trajectory to equilibria stated for cooperative systems versus the validation correction that generic convergence needs strong monotonicity
size_dependence: Convergence to a single equilibrium needs further hypotheses (Smith 1995).
note: Verdict: corrected (validation).

statement: Open game G : (X, S) -> (Y, R) is a 4-tuple (Sigma_G, P_G, C_G, B_G): strategy profiles, play function P_G : Sigma_G x X -> Y, coplay function C_G : Sigma_G x X x R -> S, and best-response function B_G : X x (Y -> R) -> Rel(Sigma_G); X observations, Y moves, R utilities, S coutilities

work: Ghani, Hedges, Winschel, Zahn 2018 DOI 10.1145/3209108.3209165
note: Sits within the [read]-tagged Definition 3 paragraph.

statement: A system as a behaviour B subset of W^T: the set of all trajectories of the manifest variables compatible with the laws; no fixed input/output split
note: Tagged [standard account]. Crossref has no author field for this record; authorship from the article itself.

statement: Dissipative system: with supply rate s(u, y) and storage function V >= 0; passive when s = u^T y; finite-gain when s = gamma^2 |u|^2 - |y|^2
work: Willems 1972 DOI 10.1007/bf00276493; Willems 1972 Part II DOI 10.1007/bf00276494
note: Tagged [standard account].

statement: Input-to-state stability: |x(t)| <= beta(|x0|, t) + gamma(||u||_inf), beta class-KL, gamma class-K
note: Tagged [standard account].

statement: Contraction: a system is contracting with metric transform Theta(x, t) and Jacobian J = df/dx when the symmetric part of (Theta-dot + Theta J) Theta^-1 is uniformly negative definite
note: Tagged [standard account].

statement: Cooperative system: off-diagonal Jacobian entries non-negative (no variable pushes another downward); competitive: non-positive; irreducible Jacobian gives strong cooperativity
note: Tagged [standard account].

statement: Max-plus semiring (R union {-inf}, oplus = max, otimes = +); max-cycle-mean characterisation of the eigenvalue of an irreducible matrix
note: Tagged [standard account]. File 40 notes max-plus is a semiring, not a ring (no cancellation).

statement: Switched and hybrid systems: switched system x-dot = f_sigma(t)(x) with piecewise-constant sigma; hybrid system with flow set C and jump set D, x-dot = f(x) on C and x+ = g(x) on D
note: Tagged [standard account].

statement: Pareto-optimal act: no other act improves one objective without worsening another; the Pareto front is the set of such outcomes
note: Tagged [standard account].

statement: Operad of wiring diagrams O_W, whose objects are boxes and whose morphisms are wiring diagrams; a W-algebra assigns to each box type a set of systems and to each wiring diagram a composing function
work: Vagner, Spivak, Lerman 2015 DOI 10.70930/tac/7tz1nkbd
note: [read] abstract.

statement: Theory of dynamical systems: an indexed category plus a section (Systems theory, Def. 3.5.0.4)
work: Myers draft 3 Sept 2023 (Def. 3.5.0.4); no DOI
note: [read] in file 40. Draft not peer reviewed.

statement: Resource sharer (undirected composition: systems share variables, as in Willems' interconnection) versus machine (directed input-output composition)
work: Libkind et al. 2022 DOI 10.4204/eptcs.372.14
note: Vocabulary, untagged in file 40.

statement: Dirac structure: the power-conserving interconnection law of port-Hamiltonian systems, with effort and flow variables whose product is power
work: van der Schaft & Jeltsema 2014 DOI 10.1561/2600000002; Cervera, van der Schaft, Bano s 2007 DOI 10.1016/j.automatica.2006.08.014
note: Standard account. File 40 says no conjugate pair for a drive has been identified.

statement: Potential game: the multi-agent field is a gradient, the case in which the composed dynamics has a potential
work: file 23 §9 (not read here)
note: Pointer only.

statement: AlgebraicDynamics.jl: composition of dynamical systems follows the mathematics of operads and operad algebras (Julia, on Catlab.jl); the Lotka-Volterra example is confirmed
work: AlgebraicDynamics.jl GitHub README (no DOI); latest tagged release v0.2.2 (31 Oct 2023)
note: [read] README. The README did not show mechanisms or a release date; the example and release were confirmed in validation.

statement: Shame: negative evaluation of the global self ('I am bad'); action tendency is hiding, withdrawal, denial; intensity tracks audience devaluation of the act or trait (Sznycer 2016)
work: Tangney, Stuewig & Mashek 2007 doi:10.1146/annurev.psych.56.091103.070145; Sznycer et al. 2016 doi:10.1073/pnas.1514699113
note: Global-vs-specific shame/guilt split is [standard], not read.

statement: Guilt: negative evaluation of a specific behaviour ('I did something bad'); action tendency is confession, apology, reparation, empathy for victim
work: Tangney, Stuewig & Mashek 2007 doi:10.1146/annurev.psych.56.091103.070145
note: Standard account [standard]. Baumeister et al. 1994 treats guilt as relational (see definitions).

statement: Embarrassment: breach of social convention or loss of face before an audience; display (gaze aversion, smile control, face touching, head down) appeases the audience
size_dependence: Observers attribute more embarrassment to lower-status targets (Keltner 1995).
note: Formal signal game for embarrassment not written by anyone (file's statement).

statement: Pride, authentic and hubristic: pride tracks an act or trait valued by an audience with internal attribution; authentic = unstable controllable effort, hubristic = stable global ability; these correspond to prestige and dominance routes to rank
work: Tracy & Robins 2004 doi:10.1207/s15327965pli1502_01; Tracy & Robins 2007 doi:10.1037/0022-3514.92.3.506; Cheng, Tracy & Henrich 2010 doi:10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2010.02.004
note: Appraisal tree and the 2010 dominance/prestige mapping are [standard], not read. Causal direction pride-to-rank vs rank-to-pride unsettled.

statement: Envy: unpleasant emotion of inferiority, hostility and resentment from awareness of a desired attribute enjoyed by another; benign envy (attainable gap) moves the envier up, malicious envy (unattainable gap) pulls the envied down
note: Replication status of benign/malicious split unknown to the file. Benign/malicious origin paper van de Ven 2009 is [standard].

statement: Schadenfreude: pleasure at misfortune of an envied or rival target, raised by interest in the domain and by threat of in-group inferiority; the other's outcome enters the utility with negative sign
size_dependence: Rises with in-group inferiority threat and with interest in the domain (soccer fans).
note: Sign-flip reading is the file's translation, not a source claim.

statement: Jealousy: a third party threatens a valued dyadic bond; ternary operand (self, partner, rival); action tendency mate guarding, monitoring, rival derogation, aggression in extremes
note: No accepted formal model; adaptationist explanation contested (see contradictions).

statement: Gratitude: another's intentional, costly benefit to me; three functions (moral barometer, moral motive prompting prosocial acts toward benefactor and others, moral reinforcer); reciprocate downstream or pass on upstream
note: The drive definition is abstract-level [abstract]; the formal gratitude parameters are from Nowak & Roch, which is read (see equations).

statement: Trust: intention to accept vulnerability on positive expectations of another's intentions or behaviour; modelled as a belief about the probability of reciprocation, updated by experience (dynamic belief)
work: Rousseau et al. 1998 doi:10.5465/amr.1998.926617; Chang et al. 2010 doi:10.1016/j.cogpsych.2010.03.001
note: Dynamic-belief form from one lab study; fitted variants of Chang et al. not read.

statement: Trust repair: trust is built slowly and lost quickly; after a violation, apology or denial repairs trust depending on violation type; demonstrated trustworthiness outperforms promises over time
work: Kim et al. 2004 doi:10.1037/0021-9010.89.1.104; Schweitzer, Hershey & Bradlow 2006 doi:10.1016/j.obhdp.2006.05.005
note: Asymmetry is verbal; no accepted repair equation (file's statement).

statement: Revenge: retaliation that imposes a cost on the harmdoer (and deters future exploitation), operator Punish(i to j) at cost to i; a by-product of losing future gains from the target
work: McCullough, Kurzban & Tabak 2013 doi:10.1017/S0140525X11002160; Axelrod & Hamilton 1981 doi:10.1126/science.7466396
note: Computational sketch of McCullough et al. 2013 not read in full.

statement: Forgiveness: inhibits revenge and signals benevolence to restore a relationship; in evolutionary models it is a continuous generosity parameter q in [0,1]
work: McCullough, Kurzban & Tabak 2013 doi:10.1017/S0140525X11002160; Nowak & Sigmund 1992 doi:10.1038/355250a0
note: No human measurement of q as a personal trait (file's statement).

statement: Indignation / moral outrage: a third-party reaction to a norm breach against someone else; expression is modulated by audience size and expected approval; third-party punishment is its costly form
size_dependence: Audience size and approval modulate expression.
note: Crockett 2017 content is [secondary]; no abstract retrieved. Expression may detach from felt outrage (Crockett's own open point).

statement: Compassion (empathic concern): other-oriented feeling for a person in need, producing motivation whose goal is the other's welfare (Batson); a rival account says the effect is self-other overlap (Cialdini et al.)
size_dependence: Gated by group membership and cost (Zaki 2014; Hein et al. 2010).
note: Debate unresolved (see contradictions).

statement: Empathic distress: shared suffering with weak self-other separation; aversive, self-focused, produces withdrawal; contrasted with compassion (warmth, approach) from the same trigger, selected by regulation of self-other distinction and positive affect
work: Singer & Klimecki 2014 doi:10.1016/j.cub.2014.06.054; Klimecki et al. 2013 doi:10.1093/cercor/bhs142
note: Distress-vs-compassion split rests on a handful of studies from one group (file's statement).

statement: Humiliation: enforced lowering of a person's or group's standing, perceived as unjust; in the one experimental test it produced inertia that suppressed both violent action and support for compromise, and symbolic repair restored support
note: Lindner's conceptual claim (precursor to violence) conflicts with Ginges & Atran's finding (see contradictions). Lindner's book unread.

statement: Nowak-Roch setup and replicator: altruistic act costs donor c, benefits recipient b, b > c; strategy S(p,q) with mean chain length 1/(1-p); cooperativity s = q/(1-p); with direct reciprocity r, fitness difference f(x) = alpha*beta/gamma and replicator dynamics x' = x(1-x)f(x); reduces to matrix game A(Si,Sj) = s_i*u_j with u_j = (b*r_j - c)/(1-r_j)
work: Nowak & Roch 2007 doi:10.1098/rspb.2006.0125
note: Read at source and re-verified (validation log). Alpha, beta given in file; gamma only as 'as given in the paper', not reproduced.

statement: Invasion barrier against defectors: x-hat = [c/(b-c)]*[(1-r)/r]; x-hat < 1 if and only if r > c/b
work: Nowak & Roch 2007 doi:10.1098/rspb.2006.0125
note: Read at source; validation log: exact.

statement: Nowak-Roch theorems: if both r1 and r2 exceed c/b, selection favours higher cooperativity; if both are below, lower; if r1 > c/b > r2 and s1 < s2, a stable mixed equilibrium; if direct reciprocity exists, upstream reciprocity evolves too (p hitch-hikes on r)
work: Nowak & Roch 2007 doi:10.1098/rspb.2006.0125
note: Read at source and re-verified; the only drive parameter in the cluster shown with proof to be selected for.

statement: Upstream reciprocity alone: natural selection always reduces cooperativity s, and defectors S(0,0) dominate every strategy with s > 0. Spatial case (1-D array, imitation): S(0,1) beats defectors if b/c > 4; S(1,1) beats them if b/c > 10/7; threshold h(p) for 0 < p < 1
work: Nowak & Roch 2007 doi:10.1098/rspb.2006.0125
size_dependence: Spatial structure changes the threshold.
note: Read at source; validation log: h(0) = 4, h(1) = 10/7 exact. No test of the model's specific predictions (e.g. p rising with r) known to the file.

statement: Trust belief update: b_(t+1) = b_t + alpha*(o_t - b_t), with o_t = 1 if the partner reciprocated, alpha+ and alpha- asymmetric (betrayals weigh more, per usual claim); investment a monotone function of b_t
work: Chang et al. 2010 doi:10.1016/j.cogpsych.2010.03.001
note: Generic form [standard], not the paper's fitted variants. Whether asymmetric rates won is unverified.

statement: Beta-Bernoulli trust: trust = (r+1)/(r+s+2) for r reciprocations and s defections (posterior mean)
work: Josang & Ismail 2002, Bled eCommerce Conference, no DOI found
note: Existence of the Bled paper is well attested but unchecked; the Crossref DOI 10.1007/978-3-540-45229-4_18 is a different paper and must not be used.

statement: Generous tit-for-tat forgiveness probability: q = min{1 - (T-R)/(R-S), (R-P)/(T-P)}; gives q = 1/3 for (T,R,P,S) = (5,3,1,0). Win-stay-lose-shift: repeat last move if payoff R or T, switch if P or S; WSLS beats TFT under noise
work: Nowak & Sigmund 1992 doi:10.1038/355250a0; Nowak & Sigmund 1993 doi:10.1038/364056a0
note: GTFT formula tagged [secondary]: confirmed via a secondary source quoting it and by arithmetic; Nowak & Sigmund 1992 not read. WSLS is [standard].

statement: Molander (1985): tit-for-tat degrades at arbitrarily low noise, and unconditional generosity repairs it
note: Tagged [abstract].

statement: McCullough schematic (file's reading, not McCullough's equation): P(revenge) rises with E (expected future exploitation risk) and falls with V (relationship value); P(forgive) = h(V, E, apology, ...) with dh/dV > 0 and dh/dE < 0
work: McCullough, Kurzban & Tabak 2013 doi:10.1017/S0140525X11002160
note: Fehr, Gelfand & Nag 2010 supply empirical weights; cost-benefit decomposition not fitted to field data.

statement: Shame calibration (implied, not fitted): shame_i(act) is approximately g(D_audience(act)), g monotone, D = audience negative valuation; one g per emotion (negative D for shame, positive for pride)
work: Sznycer et al. 2016 doi:10.1073/pnas.1514699113
size_dependence: Audience (who sees, what they think) is the input; audience quantification unmodelled.
note: Tested as a correlation across acts, not as a fitted g; no g fitted.

statement: Pride calibration (informal): pride intensity is approximately f(forecast audience valuation of act), f monotone
work: Sznycer et al. 2017 doi:10.1073/pnas.1614389114
note: Correlation across items, not a fitted function.

statement: Outrage diffusion: log-linear count model in which diffusion rises about 20% per moral-emotional word; learning account of escalation: expression probability updated by social feedback (likes, shares), same form as the trust update
work: Brady et al. 2017 doi:10.1073/pnas.1618923114; Brady et al. 2021 doi:10.1126/sciadv.abe5641
size_dependence: Effect bounded by group membership (Brady 2017).
note: Brady 2017 abstract tagged [abstract]; learning account [standard], fitted in 2021 study not checked. Same content as file 27.

statement: Coupled dyadic affect (Gottman et al.): each partner's affect is a difference equation with an uninfluenced set point, inertia, and an influence function of the other's last affect; fitted to coded couple conversations
work: Gottman et al. 2002 doi:10.1207/s15327957pspr0604_07; Gottman et al. 2002 book doi:10.7551/mitpress/4499.001.0001
note: Standard account, equations not read. One valence variable per person, not distinct drives.

statement: Ohtsuki-Iwasa reputation norms: of 4096 candidate norms examined exhaustively, a set of leading eight are stable; higher-order norms judge an act by donor action and recipient reputation together
work: Ohtsuki & Iwasa 2004 doi:10.1016/j.jtbi.2004.06.005
note: 4096 count tagged [abstract]; leading eight and norm content [standard]. Abstract listed as not retrieved in the Unconfirmed section, though the validation log ticks it.

statement: Schadenfreude sign relation: schadenfreude is the same relation as envy with the sign of dU_i/d(outcome_j) negative, conditional on j's rival or envied status
work: Leach et al. 2003 doi:10.1037/0022-3514.84.5.932; Levine (1998) spite model, file 21
size_dependence: Depends on group membership and self-relevant comparison.
note: File's own translation, not a published equation. Structure from file 21's Levine model, not repeated here.

statement: Trust (Rousseau et al.): a psychological state comprising the intention to accept vulnerability based upon positive expectations of the intentions or behaviour of another; trustworthiness has ability, benevolence and integrity dimensions; trust propensity is a trait (Mayer et al.)
work: Rousseau et al. 1998 doi:10.5465/amr.1998.926617; Mayer, Davis & Schoorman 1995 doi:10.2307/258792
note: Standard account [standard]. Variable-and-arrow model with no formal content.

statement: Trust-game measures: trust = x/E (amount sent over endowment); trustworthiness = y/(3x) (return over tripled amount); Send(i to j, x) then Return(j to i, y) as the minimal ordered operator pair
work: Berg, Dickhaut & McCabe 1995 doi:10.1006/game.1995.1027
note: Standard account [standard].

statement: Envy (Smith & Kim): an unpleasant, often painful emotion characterized by feelings of inferiority, hostility, and resentment caused by an awareness of a desired attribute enjoyed by another person or group
note: Quoted from abstract (tagged [abstract]).

statement: Sociometer (Leary et al.): state self-esteem is a gauge of relational value (inclusion), so self-conscious affect monitors others' valuation of the self
note: Standard account [standard].

statement: Empathy (Singer & Klimecki): sharing another's feeling while retaining self-other distinction; without that distinction it is emotional contagion
work: Singer & Klimecki 2014 doi:10.1016/j.cub.2014.06.054
note: Tagged [abstract].

statement: Embarrassment's five accounts (Keltner & Buswell): loss of self-esteem, concern for others' evaluation, absence of scripts, remedial effects of the display, and the animal appeasement parallel
note: Tagged [abstract]; validation log confirms.

statement: Reputation: each agent carries a public score r_j updated by operators on observed acts; image scoring gives to a recipient whose score is at least k, and the file records the flaw that refusing bad-reputation recipients lowers the donor's own score
work: Nowak & Sigmund 1998 doi:10.1038/31225; Wedekind & Milinski 2000 doi:10.1126/science.288.5467.850
note: Standard account [standard]; mechanism for turning private shame and pride into public stakes (file's translation).

statement: Appraisal tree (Tracy & Robins): relevance to identity goals; congruence; internal attribution; stable/global vs unstable/specific; controllability; combinations yield pride, authentic or hubristic pride, shame, guilt; usable as a typed function from appraisal variables to labels
note: Decision path [standard], not read; node order and treatment of embarrassment unverified.

statement: Guilt as relational (Baumeister, Stillwell & Heatherton): strongest in communal relationships; serves to enforce mutual concern, redistribute distress, and let less powerful partners get their way
work: Baumeister, Stillwell & Heatherton 1994 doi:10.1037/0033-2909.115.2.243
size_dependence: Strongest in communal relationships.
note: Tagged [abstract].

statement: Dominance and prestige as two distinct, two-valued operator types for acquiring rank (dominance fear-based, prestige respect-based)
work: Cheng et al. 2010 doi:10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2010.02.004; Cheng et al. 2013 doi:10.1037/a0030398
note: Mapping [standard]; both routes yield influence in new groups [abstract].

statement: Envy parameter: the disadvantageous-inequity coefficient of Fehr-Schmidt inequity aversion is read as the envy parameter
work: Fehr & Schmidt model, file 21 (not repeated here)
note: Cross-reference; the claim is held in file 21.

statement: Jealousy requires a ternary operand (self, partner, rival); almost every other drive in the cluster is dyadic or audience-based
work: Descartes (file 26, not repeated here)
note: Structural claim of the file, not an empirical result.

statement: Shame tracks others' devaluation: r = .69 (US), .79 (India), .67 (Israel) across items; across countries shame tracks other countries' devaluation; sadness and anxiety did not track devaluation
work: Sznycer et al. 2016 doi:10.1073/pnas.1514699113
size_dependence: Three countries tested.
note: Item-level correlation, not a fitted function; file's summary states r = .67 to .79 within countries.

statement: Pride tracks forecast audience valuation: mean r = +.82 (local) and +.75 (foreign) across 25 acts and traits in 16 countries (n = 2,085)
work: Sznycer et al. 2017 doi:10.1073/pnas.1614389114
size_dependence: Local vs foreign audiences differ (.82 vs .75).
note: Correlation of item means; individual-level fit unknown; causal direction unsettled. Exact per validation log.

statement: Dispositional guilt correlates with prosocial orientation at mean r = .13 (k = 63); dispositional shame about r = -.05 (k = 47, p = .07); guilt effect is method-dependent (scenario vs checklist) and stronger when shame and guilt are partialled (semi-partial)
work: Tignor & Colvin 2017 doi:10.1111/jopy.12244
size_dependence: Test format and partialling change the estimate.
note: Validated against abstract. Effects small (r about .1).

statement: Embarrassment display is distinct from amusement and follows the temporal pattern of facial expressions; observers were more accurate and attributed more emotion when target was from a lower-status group, as appeasement predicts (five studies)
size_dependence: Target status changes observer accuracy.
note: Tagged [abstract]; no effect sizes in file; moderate-size social-psych studies.

statement: Observers read embarrassment as a prosocial signal: they trust embarrassed targets more and are more willing to affiliate; more embarrassable people were more generous
work: Feinberg, Willer & Keltner 2012 doi:10.1037/a0025403
note: Tagged [abstract].

statement: Benign envy, not admiration or malicious envy, motivated studying and Remote Associates Task performance; upward comparison produced benign envy and better performance only when self-improvement seemed attainable (four studies)
work: van de Ven, Zeelenberg & Pieters 2011 doi:10.1177/0146167211400421
size_dependence: Attainability of the gap switches benign to admiration.
note: Small lab experiments; replication status unknown.

statement: Schadenfreude rose with interest in the sport and with threat of in-group inferiority (soccer fans); in Study 2, schadenfreude toward a legitimately superior rival fell when an honest-expression norm was made salient, among low-interest participants only
size_dependence: In-group inferiority threat and domain interest.
note: Corrected in validation: honest-expression effect narrowed to these actual conditions.

statement: Neural: envy engaged anterior cingulate cortex; schadenfreude engaged striatum; ACC activation in the envy study predicted striatal activation in the schadenfreude study (within-subject correlation across two experiments)
work: Takahashi et al. 2009 doi:10.1126/science.1165604
note: Tagged [abstract].

statement: Striatal activity is higher when winning more than a counterpart and lower when winning less (social comparison in the decision process); ventral striatum responds to rival-team failure (Cikara et al. 2011, standard)
work: Bault et al. 2011 doi:10.1073/pnas.1100892108; Cikara, Botvinick & Fiske 2011 doi:10.1177/0956797610397667
note: Bault tagged [abstract]; Cikara [standard]. Bault pages corrected to 16044-16049 in validation.

statement: Gratitude interventions versus measurement-only control: well-being d = .31 (CI .04 to .58, k = 5), gratitude d = .20 (CI -.04 to .44, k = 4, includes zero); versus an alternative activity: gratitude d = .46 (k = 15), well-being d = .17 (k = 20), anxiety d = .11 (CI includes zero)
work: Davis et al. 2016 doi:10.1037/cou0000107
size_dependence: Weaker once the comparison activity is active.
note: Evidence for trait-level self-help, not for interpersonal reciprocity. Tagged [abstract]; pages corrected to 20-31.

statement: Induced gratitude increased costly helping of the benefactor beyond general positive affect and increased help to a stranger; the effect dissipated once people were told the true cause of the feeling
note: Upgraded to abstract in validation; the stranger result links it to upstream reciprocity. Effect depends on participants not knowing the cause.

statement: Donations were more frequent to receivers who had been generous earlier, in a setting where direct reciprocity was unlikely (small lab game)
work: Wedekind & Milinski 2000 doi:10.1126/science.288.5467.850
note: Tagged [abstract]. Whether image scoring specifically is what people use is contested.

statement: Forgiveness meta-analysis: 175 studies, 26,006 participants; correlates perceived intent r = -.49, state empathy r = .51, apology r = .42, state anger r = -.41; situational variables explain more than victim dispositions; gender r = .01, age r = .06
work: Fehr, Gelfand & Nag 2010 doi:10.1037/a0019993
size_dependence: Situational factors dominate over victim dispositions.
note: Tagged [abstract]; effect sizes added in validation. These are the empirical weights for h(V,E,apology).

statement: Trustworthiness and trust propensity explain incremental variance in risk taking and performance beyond trust itself (132 samples); trustworthiness dimensions also predict affective commitment
work: Colquitt, Scott & LePine 2007 doi:10.1037/0021-9010.92.4.909
note: Tagged [abstract].

statement: Direct leaders (supervisors) are an especially important referent for trust (k = 106)
size_dependence: Referent identity (direct leader) matters.
note: File tags [abstract] in §D1 but its Unconfirmed section lists this abstract as not retrieved; treat as sa.

statement: Trustworthiness cues (faces) and experienced trustworthiness both affected investment, independently and synergistically; reinforcement-learning models fitted; trustworthiness is a belief updated from experience
work: Chang et al. 2010 doi:10.1016/j.cogpsych.2010.03.001
note: One lab study; model fit to behaviour, not out-of-sample forecasting of new relationships.

statement: Neural trust signals: caudate anticipated partner's intention, shifting earlier across rounds (King-Casas et al. 2005); prior moral-character information reduced striatal response to reinforcement, so priors override feedback learning (Delgado et al. 2005)
work: King-Casas et al. 2005 doi:10.1126/science.1108062; Delgado, Frank & Phelps 2005 doi:10.1038/nn1575
note: Both [standard], not checked.

statement: Trust repair: apology repaired trust better for competence violations and denial for integrity violations; separately, apology where guilt was later shown and denial where innocence was shown; effects mediated by trusting beliefs (two studies)
size_dependence: Violation type changes the best repair.
note: Draft had conflated the two findings; now stated separately. Scenario and student samples.

statement: Trust rebuilds more slowly than it fell; promises alone are less effective than demonstrated trustworthy behaviour over time
work: Schweitzer, Hershey & Bradlow 2006 doi:10.1016/j.obhdp.2006.05.005
note: Content [standard], abstract not retrieved.

statement: Punishers expect revenge to feel good, and it prolongs rumination
work: Carlsmith, Wilson & Gilbert 2008 doi:10.1037/a0012165
note: Standard account [standard].

statement: In repeated games the most successful players did not use costly punishment; about half of subjects are conditional cooperators
work: Dreber et al. 2008 doi:10.1038/nature06723; Fischbacher, Gachter & Fehr 2001 doi:10.1016/S0165-1765(01)00394-9
note: Both [standard], not checked. Human subjects behave as conditional cooperators with some generosity under noise, best strategy depends on game and feedback.

statement: Costly punishment of free-riders in one-shot public goods games sustains contributions; punishment is also levied on cooperators in some societies (antisocial punishment), large at some sites and negligible at others
work: Fehr & Gachter 2002 doi:10.1038/415137a; Henrich et al. 2006 doi:10.1126/science.1127333; Herrmann, Thoni & Gachter 2008 doi:10.1126/science.1153808
size_dependence: Varies across societies.
note: Standard account [standard]. Henrich 2006 Science replaces an erroneous book-chapter DOI.

statement: Digital media enlarge outrage triggers, lower the cost of expressing it, and raise its reputational reward, so expression can detach from feeling; engagement-maximising feeds can exploit the same motive
note: Tagged [secondary]; no abstract retrieved; content broadened in validation.

statement: Each moral-emotional word raised diffusion of moralized content by about 20%; on observational Twitter data for three US issues in 2017
size_dependence: Bounded by group membership.
note: Tagged [abstract]. Correlational, platform and period specific.

statement: Expression of outrage is reinforced by likes and shares, a reinforcement-learning explanation of escalation in online networks
work: Brady et al. 2021 doi:10.1126/sciadv.abe5641
note: Standard account [standard], fitted in 2021 study not checked.

statement: Humiliation produced an inertia effect: less support for suicide attacks, reduced expressed joy at attacks when primed, lower support for peace deals humiliating Palestinians, and symbolic Israeli compromises reducing humiliation raised support (three studies, West Bank and Gaza)
note: Corrected in validation: draft had the direction reversed (humiliation as increasing violence). Humiliation damps all action, and suppresses support for conflict resolution.

statement: Opposition to compromise over sacred issues rose when material incentives were offered (backfire) and fell when the adversary made symbolic compromises on its own sacred values (Palestinian and Israeli samples)
work: Ginges et al. 2007 doi:10.1073/pnas.0701768104
note: Tagged [abstract]. Rival explanation: backfire is general to taboo trade-offs (Tetlock, standard).

statement: Soccer fans' costly helping of an in-group member was predicted by anterior insula (empathic concern); not helping an out-group member was predicted by nucleus accumbens and negative evaluation of the other
work: Hein et al. 2010 doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2010.09.003
size_dependence: In-group versus out-group membership.
note: Tagged [abstract] in §G3, but Unconfirmed lists the abstract as not retrieved; validation log ticks it.

statement: Empathy is gated by group membership: multiple lab replications of in-group bias in empathy; motivated emotion regulation reduces compassion for large numbers of victims
work: Cikara, Bruneau & Saxe 2011 doi:10.1177/0963721411408713; Cameron & Payne 2011 doi:10.1037/a0021643
size_dependence: Number of victims and in-group membership both reduce compassion.
note: Both [standard], not checked. Effect sizes not reported in file.

statement: Across 27 emotions, shame was among the shortest and guilt outlasted shame; duration rose with event importance and rumination (durations measured, not modelled)

statement: Authentic and hubristic pride have a discriminant structure replicated in factor analysis of self-report scales

statement: Dominance and prestige both yield influence in newly formed groups, as perceived and as measured behaviourally

note: Tagged [abstract].

statement: Gratitude strengthens relationships; empathy shifts with motives to avoid or approach engagement (review, no effect sizes given)
note: Algoe [standard]; Zaki tagged [abstract].

statement: Sex difference in jealousy on continuous measures: small, theory-consistent (about g = 0.26 for hypothetical scenarios, g = 0.23 for actual infidelity across seven samples; strongest when jealousy or distress was measured)

statement: Humiliation as driver of violence (Lindner) vs humiliation as inertia damping violence and compromise (Ginges & Atran)

Side 2: the one experimental test found no humiliation-to-violence link, but an inertia effect that suppresses compromise too. Verdict: unresolved; the file's translation adopts the inertia reading.

statement: Sacred-value backfire of material incentives (Ginges et al. 2007) vs general taboo trade-off explanation (Tetlock)

statement: Compassion as altruistic motive (Batson empathy-altruism) vs compassion as self-other overlap (Cialdini et al.; Maner et al.)
note: Side 1: high-empathy people help even when escape is easy. Side 2: with overlap controlled, empathy effects vanish. Verdict: unresolved, contested and not replicated away.

statement: Sex difference in jealousy from forced-choice data (Buss et al.) vs belief-driven account with no adapted module (DeSteno & Salovey)
note: Side 1: adaptationist sex difference. Side 2: double-shot belief explanation, plus critics of format. Verdict: small difference on continuous measures is supported (Sagarin 2012, secondary); adaptationist explanation is contested.

statement: Cross-cultural regularity of shame tracking devaluation (Sznycer et al. 2016) vs reported variability as well as regularity (Sznycer & Landers 2024 preprint)

note: Side 1: monotone regularity across cultures. Side 2: preprint reports variability too; not read. Verdict: unresolved.

statement: Asymmetric trust learning rates (alpha+ not equal to alpha-, betrayals weigh more) vs symmetric update as the competing hypothesis

note: File calls the asymmetry a standard claim with mixed evidence; the fitted variants of Chang et al. are unread. Verdict: unresolved.

statement: Image scoring as what people actually use (Wedekind & Milinski) vs richer standing norms (higher-order norms, Ohtsuki & Iwasa)
work: Wedekind & Milinski 2000 doi:10.1126/science.288.5467.850; Ohtsuki & Iwasa 2004 doi:10.1016/j.jtbi.2004.06.005
note: Side 1: image scoring explains the lab data. Side 2: standing norms judge donor action and recipient reputation together. Verdict: contested in the file.

statement: status / dominance: scalar dominance weight w_i, rising on winning and falling on losing; agents on a lattice fight on meeting

statement: status desire: perceived standing in others' eyes, an ordinal relative quantity, plus a felt-need scalar; not an accumulating deprivation level
work: Anderson, Hildreth & Howland 2015, Psychological Bulletin 141(3), 574-601, DOI 10.1037/a0038781
note: Whether the felt need adapts to level (hedonic treadmill) is not established. Translation in 42: operand status(i) as ordinal rank within a group. No dynamic parameters extracted.

statement: belonging: need to belong, a fundamental need for frequent, affectively pleasant interactions with a few people in a stable, caring relation; satiable, with substitution among bonds
work: Baumeister & Leary 1995, Psychological Bulletin 117, 497-529, DOI 10.1037/0033-2909.117.3.497
note: Verbal; no equation. Satiation and substitutability are the dynamic content.

statement: belonging: four need levels (belonging, self-esteem, control, meaningful existence), each with a need-satisfaction scalar, moderated by importance, threatened by ostracism

note: Three stages: reflexive, reflective, resignation. No equations stated in the source as given in 42. Stage-based dynamics are weakly supported (see contradiction).

statement: belonging: homeostatic set-point and satiation circuits in rodents, described as the only quantitative-circuit dynamics for the belonging drive
work: Matthews & Tye 2019; Liu et al. 2025; Lee, Chen & Tye 2021 (as cited in 42; no DOIs given there)
note: Animal evidence; detail lives in file 22 and is not restated in 42.

statement: care: investment budget B split among dependants by a marginal-value rule, with a giver-receiver conflict inequality
work: Smith & Fretwell 1974, American Naturalist 108, 499-506, DOI 10.1086/282929
note: Evolutionary optimisation, not psychological dynamics. No within-person satiation, decay or caregiver-depletion model exists (42 §3).

statement: play: play-level state with a deprivation counter, gated by safety; fear and hunger suppress play
work: Burgdorf & Panksepp 2006, Neurosci. Biobehav. Rev. 30, 173-187, DOI 10.1016/j.neubiorev.2005.06.001
size_dependence: Rodent evidence; human play dynamics mostly verbal (42 §4)
note: Play activation indexed by 50 kHz calls and play-seeking; the deprivation-rebound and safety gate are the only dynamics; no equation.

statement: sexual motivation: sexual response as excitation minus inhibition, each system with individual thresholds (dual control)
work: Bancroft & Janssen 2000, Neurosci. Biobehav. Rev. 24, 571-579, DOI 10.1016/s0149-7634(00)00024-5
note: The source states no equation per 42; net drive = E - I is 42's reading. Human sexual motivation has no dynamic model in 42.

statement: competence: self-efficacy as the closest competence state variable, moved informally by success (raises) and failure (lowers), weighted by four sources (mastery, vicarious experience, persuasion, physiological state)
work: Bandura 1977, Psychological Review 84(2), 191, DOI 10.1037/0033-295X.84.2.191
note: Informal update rule; no equation (42 §6).

statement: controllability: control(i) as a belief state, the probability that the agent's action affects the outcome, updated by contingency evidence
work: Maier & Seligman 2016, Psychological Review 123, 349-367, DOI 10.1037/rev0000033; Huys & Dayan 2009, Cognition 113, 314-328, DOI 10.1016/j.cognition.2009.01.008 (not read)
note: The belief-state form is 42's translation, not a source's claim. Huys & Dayan is the computational form, located but not read in 42.

statement: autonomy, competence and relatedness as needs: need satisfaction predicts wellbeing and intrinsic motivation
work: Ryan & Deci 2000, American Psychologist 55, 68-78, DOI 10.1037/0003-066x.55.1.68
note: Verbal; 'intrinsic motivation' has no stated update equation. The three-needs structure is partly criticised as a typology.

statement: fairness: two inequity parameters (disadvantageous and advantageous), each with an age-dependent threshold that varies by culture
work: Blake et al. 2015, Nature 528, 258-261, DOI 10.1038/nature15703
size_dependence: Varies by culture across seven societies
note: The file maps these to alpha and beta in Fehr-Schmidt terms (cross-ref 21); the parameterisation is 42's translation. No within-person grievance accumulation model located.

statement: need for closure: a motive for a definite answer over ambiguity, with urgency (seizing on early information) and permanence (freezing on it)
work: Kruglanski & Webster 1996, Psychological Review 103, 263-283, DOI 10.1037/0033-295x.103.2.263
note: State variable NFC is a scalar (dispositional times situational). The update rule is not stated; closure reduces the need in the file's qualitative description.

statement: uncertainty-pressure u_i, a cognitive operand that the commit operator reduces while raising rigidity; higher u raises coupling to group consensus
work: Heine, Proulx & Vohs 2006, Pers. Soc. Psychol. Review 10, 88-110, DOI 10.1207/s15327957pspr1002_1
note: Translation only; no equation beyond the qualitative.

statement: aggression as a drive-like present internal state (affect, arousal, cognition) with no stand-alone accumulating drive; triggered by frustration or threat via negative affect, limited by fear, modulated by status
work: Anderson & Bushman 2002, Annual Review of Psychology 53, 27-51, DOI 10.1146/annurev.psych.53.100901.135231
note: 42 treats aggression as a gated output, not an operand (translation). The General Aggression Model is a process diagram with no equations. Its one accumulation model failed (see contradiction).

statement: disgust: three domain-specific sensitivities (pathogen, sexual, moral), each with its own triggers and outputs; contamination as a tag
work: Tybur, Lieberman, Kurzban & DeScioli 2013, Psychological Review 120, 65-84, DOI 10.1037/a0030778
note: Functional typology; no equations. Disgust has no dynamics law (42 §10).

statement: play as an engineered stimulation drive with a homeostatic band and an optimal-intensity regime (Kismet)
work: Breazeal's Kismet (cross-ref 19; no DOI in 42)
note: Engineered, not empirical, and unvalidated, per 42.

statement: loneliness as a self-reinforcing loop: perceived isolation raises hypervigilance, a verbal positive-feedback model
work: Cacioppo & Hawkley 2009, Trends Cogn. Sci. 13, 447-454, DOI 10.1016/j.tics.2009.06.005
note: Named by 42 as a missing belonging dynamic; record confirmed, paper not read.

statement: status as two operands: dom (dominance, deference extracted by threat) and prest (prestige, deference freely conferred on a skilled model), not one
work: Henrich & Gil-White 2001, Evolution and Human Behavior 22, 165-196, DOI 10.1016/s1090-5138(00)00071-4
note: Verbal evolutionary argument. Empirical support for two routes is Cheng et al. 2013 (DOI 10.1037/a0030398), listed as a result line. Replication outside one research tradition not established.

statement: fight(i,j): returns the winner and updates both dominance weights asymmetrically (winner up, loser down)
work: Bonabeau, Theraulaz & Deneubourg 1995, Physica A 217, 373-392, DOI 10.1016/0378-4371(95)00064-e
note: Operator as 42 proposes it for the algebra, not a definition in the source.

statement: exclude(a,b): an instantaneous drop in b's four needs, with a duration argument and stage-dependent drift afterwards
work: Williams 2009, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology 41, 275-314, DOI 10.1016/S0065-2601(08)00406-1

statement: play(a,b): a role-symmetrising, outcome-balancing operator, contrasted with fight(a,b) as status-neutral
work: Pellis & Pellis 1998, Animal Play, DOI 10.1017/cbo9780511608575.007
note: Proposed operator. The outcome balance it encodes is not an established regularity (see contradiction).

statement: aspiration threshold a_t in mate search, moved up after unexpected interest and down after unexpected rejection; a match requires both partners' aspirations to be met
work: Todd & Miller 1999, in Gigerenzer, Todd & ABC Research Group, Simple Heuristics That Make Us Smart (Oxford UP; no DOI checked)
note: From secondary accounts read via search, not primary. The DOI once given belongs to Todd & Beckage 2009. The 37%-rule gloss is removed in validation.

statement: contamination: a tag on operands, a contagion operator that tags the contacting agent, and an avoidance operator; the three disgust domains as three tag types
work: Tybur, Lieberman, Kurzban & DeScioli 2013, Psychological Review 120, 65-84, DOI 10.1037/a0030778
note: Algebra proposal from 42. The three-domain split is Tybur's hypothesis.

size_dependence: Depends on the sex ratio of the population
note: Coupling is 42's proposal; the source gives the OSR-competition link (see result line).

statement: Q = 1 / (1 + exp(eta (h_k - h_i))): probability that i wins a fight with k, where h counts past victories minus past defeats
work: Stauffer 2003, Int. J. Mod. Phys. C 14, 237-239, DOI 10.1142/s0129183103004425; Schulze & Stauffer 2004, Advances in Complex Systems 7, 289-294, DOI 10.1142/s0219525904000184 (restate Bonabeau et al. 1995, DOI 10.1016/0378-4371(95)00064-e)
size_dependence: Hierarchy transition depends on density rho and on eta

statement: at every time step all h are multiplied by (1 - f), with f = 0.1 in Stauffer's runs, so memory of fights decays exponentially
note: The forgetting term is the relaxation term of the update rule. Read in the restatement; 1995 paper not read.

statement: winner-loser update: h changes by plus or minus 1 per fight (the restated model), with decay as the relaxation term
note: 42 says the survey's earlier 'fixed increment to winner and loser' gloss is replaced by this form. Read in the restatement, not the primary.

statement: with forgetting, hierarchy formation shows subcritical or supercritical bifurcations as density rho varies; the nature of the transition depends on eta; there is a dynamical tricritical point in the rho-eta plane

statement: chimpanzees (16 animals, eight conditions) responded to inequity only when a task was required, not for free rewards; effort and procedure did not change this; males were more sensitive to social expectation, females to individual expectation

statement: dominance hierarchies are not predictable from individual attributes alone; social dynamics matter

statement: meaning threats cause fluid compensation: people strengthen other meaning frameworks (other beliefs, in-group, order)

statement: aggression follows status or ego threat among those with favourable but unstable self-views

statement: Bonabeau-type phase transition: Bonabeau et al. 1995 has sub- and supercritical bifurcations with a tricritical point in rho-eta, versus Sousa & Stauffer 2000 finding the transition an artifact of non-stationarity

note: Side A (Bonabeau 1995, abstract read): the hierarchy transition with forgetting.
